# Blog posts and long-form guides


## Pirts, Suitsusaun, Savusauna: Baltic Sauna Cultures Compared

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/baltic-nordic-sauna-cultures-compared.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** Pirts, suitsusaun, savusauna, badstu — a Latvian guide compares Baltic and Nordic sauna traditions, the löyly, and how to use each one without offending the locals.

<p class="article-lede">Most people in the world, when they think of a sauna, think of one specific thing: a small wooden room with a heater in the corner, a thermometer on the wall, an automatic timer, and a sign that says fifteen minutes is the maximum recommended session. This is what saunas have become at neighbourhood gyms and chain hotels, and there is nothing wrong with it. It does what it says on the tin.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: sauna-hero -->

<figure class="sauna-hero">
  <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-sauna/baltic-sauna-interior-vasta-stone-heater-pirts.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="sauna-hero" data-caption="Inside a Baltic sauna: a stone-filled kiuas in the centre, a birch vasta (the leafy whisk Latvians call slota and Estonians viht), and the pine bench warm enough to leave marks. Same three elements across pirts, suitsusaun, savusauna and badstu — what changes between countries is everything else." aria-label="Open full-size: Inside a Baltic sauna: a stone-filled kiuas in the centre, a birch vasta (the leafy whisk Latvians call slota and Estonians viht), and the pine bench warm enough to leave marks. Same three elements across pirts, suitsusaun, savusauna and badstu — what changes between countries is everything else.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-sauna/baltic-sauna-interior-vasta-stone-heater-pirts.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-sauna/baltic-sauna-interior-vasta-stone-heater-pirts.jpg" alt="Wood-clad Baltic sauna interior with stone-filled kiuas heater and birch vasta." loading="eager" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1067" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Inside a Baltic sauna: a stone-filled kiuas in the centre, a birch vasta (the leafy whisk Latvians call slota and Estonians viht), and the pine bench warm enough to leave marks. Same three elements across pirts, suitsusaun, savusauna and badstu — what changes between countries is everything else.</figcaption>
</figure>
<!-- END: sauna-hero -->


<p>But it is not what a sauna actually is, in the part of the world where the practice was born. In the forests and lakes between Helsinki, Tallinn, Riga, and Vilnius &mdash; and in the high valleys of Norway, where the tradition almost died and is now coming back &mdash; a sauna is a building, a ritual, a social institution, sometimes a sacred space, and historically the place where you were born and the place where you were prepared for the grave. The gym box is to <em>that</em> what a microwave dinner is to a four-hour meal cooked over wood.</p>

<p>Let me try to compare them honestly.</p>

<h2 id="finnish">Finnish <em>sauna</em>: the brand name</h2>

<p>The word <em>sauna</em> is Finnish, and the Finns won the linguistic war so completely that &ldquo;sauna&rdquo; is now the global term for every variant of the practice, in dozens of languages. There is one Finnish person for every two or three <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_sauna" rel="noopener external">Finnish sauna</a>s &mdash; roughly three million saunas for a population of five and a half million. UNESCO inscribed Finnish sauna culture on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2020.</p>

<p>The Finnish style at its most traditional is the <strong><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savusauna" rel="noopener external">savusauna</a></strong> &mdash; the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoke_sauna" rel="noopener external">smoke sauna</a>. No chimney. A pile of stones over a wood fire that burns for hours, filling the room with smoke. When the wood has burned down, the smoke is vented, the soot-blackened walls retain the heat for hours, and the air inside has a particular quality &mdash; soft, deep, almost velvet &mdash; that no electric heater on Earth has ever replicated. This is what older Finns mean when they tell you a regular sauna isn&rsquo;t really a sauna.</p>

<p>The modern, more accessible Finnish sauna is hot (80&ndash;110 &deg;C) and relatively dry. You pour water on the stones to create <em>l&ouml;yly</em>, the burst of steam that is the whole point. People generally sit in silence. Nudity is the default; mixed-gender saunas are family-only or single-sex. <em>Lauantai on saunap&auml;iv&auml;</em> &mdash; Saturday is sauna day. Almost every cottage has one. Helsinki&rsquo;s Burger King has one too, which says something about how deeply this is woven in.</p>

<h2 id="estonian">Estonian <em>suitsusaun</em>: the UNESCO original</h2>

<p>In southern Estonia, in a region called V&otilde;rumaa, you find the oldest continuous smoke sauna tradition on Earth. It was inscribed on the UNESCO list in <strong>2014</strong> &mdash; six years before the Finns made their entry &mdash; and the Estonians are quietly proud of having got there first.</p>

<p>The Estonian <em>suitsusaun</em> (in the local V&otilde;ro dialect, <em>savvusann</em>, which is closer to the Finnish word) is functionally identical to the Finnish savusauna: a stone pile, wood fire, no chimney, soot-darkened walls, soft persistent heat. What the UNESCO listing actually preserves is not the building but the <em>tradition</em> &mdash; the bathing customs, the making of bath whisks (<em>viht</em>), the building and maintenance of saunas, and crucially, the smoking of meat in the same building during the off-hours.</p>

<p>This last detail tells you something important about the smoke sauna&rsquo;s place in rural life. It was a multi-purpose building. You bathed in it on Saturday evening. You cured your ham in it during the rest of the week. You gave birth in it. You washed your dead in it before burial. It was the cleanest, hottest, most sterile space on the entire farm, and so it was where the most important biological events of human life happened. UNESCO calls this &ldquo;a way of life&rdquo; rather than an architectural form, which is exactly right.</p>

<h2 id="latvian">Latvian <em>pirts</em>: the ritual</h2>

<p>This is the one I know best, because it is mine.</p>

<p>The Latvian <em>pirts</em> shares the deep Baltic-Nordic root with all of the above &mdash; wood-fired heat, water on stones, leafy whisks, cold-water plunge, often a smoke variant in the older tradition. But somewhere in the last few decades, while the Finns were industrialising the sauna and putting one in every office basement, the Latvians took the opposite route. We turned the pirts into a <strong>ritual</strong>. A four-hour ceremonial event guided by a trained master, working on one or two people at a time.</p>

<p>Here is what that actually looks like, as practised at the better venues:</p>

<p>You arrive in the late afternoon. You meet your <em>pirtnieks</em> &mdash; your pirts master &mdash; who will spend a few minutes asking you what you need. They might pour you a herbal tea and ask you to set an intention for the session. Not in a cringing, performative way. Quietly, the way a doctor might ask what hurts.</p>

<p>You then enter the warm room. The heat builds gradually &mdash; the Latvian pirts is gentler than a Finnish sauna, with a careful balance of temperature and humidity that the masters are taught to read by feel. You are wrapped, scrubbed with salt or honey, brushed with bundles of birch, oak, juniper, mugwort, or whatever the master has chosen for your particular session, depending on the season and what they have decided you need. The whisking &mdash; <em>p&#275;ršana</em> &mdash; is not a beating. It is a rhythm, almost a percussion, performed over your whole body while you lie down with your eyes closed.</p>

<p>After each round of heat, you go out and plunge into a cold pond. Then you rest. Then you go back in. This cycle repeats three or four times over the course of three to four hours. There is honey rubbed into your skin near the end. There may be singing, herbal infusions, contrast with snow in winter. The master keeps your head cool with a wet cloth or a felt sauna hat &mdash; overheating the head is what people get wrong in untrained saunas &mdash; and times your sessions so that you sweat without exhausting yourself.</p>

<p>The whole thing is genuinely deep. By the end of it you are not so much relaxed as <em>processed</em>. People sometimes cry. People often sleep better that night than they have in months.</p>

<p>To do this work properly, a <em>pirtnieks</em> trains formally for <strong>one to two and a half years</strong> at one of several pirts schools (Lielzemenes, the Pirts School at Ziedlejas, and others) &mdash; and most masters keep studying afterwards, because there are hundreds of medicinal plants to learn, dozens of whisk techniques, a proper understanding of when to apply heat and when to release it, and an entire body of folk knowledge about the seasons. The Finns may have the most saunas per person; the Latvians, plausibly, have the most pirts masters per person.</p>

<p>A few things from older tradition still surface in modern practice. The <em>pirt&#299;žas</em> is a ritual performed soon after a baby is born &mdash; historically, the pirts was where the baby was actually delivered, and is still where mother and child take their first formal bath together. At the other end of life, the deceased were traditionally washed in the pirts before burial. Folk songs call the bathhouse <em>M&#257;ras pirts</em> or <em>Laimas pirts</em> &mdash; M&#257;ra and Laima are old Latvian goddesses, and the songs say they are present in the pirts when new life begins. Latvians did not give up these beliefs when they were Christianised. They quietly kept them in the bathhouse.</p>

<p>A proper pirts ritual at a premium venue runs <strong>&euro;150 to &euro;200 per person</strong>, sometimes &euro;300 for a couple at the more luxurious resorts (Ziedlejas, Žade&#299;ta Pirts, Meža SPA). It is not cheap. But you are paying for four hours of one person&rsquo;s full attention, in a space they have heated all afternoon for you, with herbs they collected themselves and prepared by hand. By the metric of &ldquo;money spent per actual change in how you feel afterwards,&rdquo; it is one of the better deals available in Europe.</p>

<h2 id="lithuanian">Lithuanian <em>pirtis</em>: the older sibling, less ceremonial</h2>

<p>Lithuanians do have their own sauna tradition, and the word is one letter different from ours: <em>pirtis</em> instead of <em>pirts</em>. The histories are deeply intertwined &mdash; both Latvian and Lithuanian descend from a common Baltic root, and the bathing customs developed together in pre-Christian times.</p>

<p>The Lithuanian pirtis tradition leans more toward herbal medicine and quiet ritual than the Latvian theatrical four-hour ceremony. There is a distinguished Lithuanian Bath Academy that trains practitioners. The whisk is called <em>vanta</em> in Lithuanian (versus <em>slota</em> in Latvian). The plant knowledge is similarly deep. Archaeological evidence from Kernav&#279;, the medieval Lithuanian capital, has unearthed a 14th-century smoke sauna with unbarked pine logs, suggesting that the practice was widespread in Baltic tribal life centuries before the Christianisation of Lithuania in 1387.</p>

<p>If you ask a Lithuanian about pirtis, they will tell you that <em>&ldquo;you should be in the pirts as you are in church.&rdquo;</em> It is a real saying, and it tells you a lot about how the Baltic peoples have always understood this practice.</p>

<h2 id="norwegian">Norwegian <em>badstu</em>: the tradition that almost died</h2>

<p>This one has the most surprising history.</p>

<p>The Norwegian word for sauna is <strong>badstu</strong> &mdash; <em>bad</em> meaning bath, <em>stu</em> meaning a heated room (related to the English &ldquo;stove&rdquo;). The Vikings had badstuer. Norwegian farms had them through the medieval period. Then the Reformation arrived in Scandinavia, and Lutheran moralists decided that communal nude bathing was indecent, and over the following centuries Norwegian badstu culture quietly <strong>died</strong>. By the 1860s an ethnographer was claiming to have found the country&rsquo;s last practising bather, in a remote southern valley.</p>

<p>What kept the tradition alive in Norway, ironically, was not Norwegians but <strong>Finns</strong> &mdash; the Kvens in the Arctic north and the Forest Finns in the southeast, both recognised national minorities, who never stopped bathing and never explained themselves about it. For three hundred years, the badstu in Norway was a Finnish-minority practice on Norwegian soil.</p>

<p>Then around the year 2000, something remarkable happened: Norwegians started building badstuer again. A Finnish architect named Sami Rintala built a floating sauna in a fjord. Other people copied him. Now Oslo Harbour has more than a dozen floating saunas, with bookings months in advance, and Norwegian sauna culture is undergoing a full-scale revival &mdash; but with a particular Norwegian character, much more architectural, more open, more designed-by-architects than the older Finnish tradition. Less ritual, more aesthetic.</p>

<p>The Norwegian story is interesting for what it shows: when the tradition dies, the cultural rules die with it, and what comes back is freer to invent itself. Many of the global sauna trends we are seeing now &mdash; public floating saunas, design-forward installations, accessible price points &mdash; look more like Norway than like Finland.</p>

<h2 id="gym">The gym sauna: what it is and what it isn&rsquo;t</h2>

<p>Now we come to the small wooden box at your neighbourhood gym.</p>

<p>What you have there is the modern, electric, dry-air variant &mdash; running at 80&ndash;100 &deg;C, no humidity to speak of, fifteen minutes of timer, glass door, mostly silent. Nothing wrong with it. Heat does what heat does. You will sweat, your circulation will improve, your shoulders will unclench, and on a cold winter day it is a small mercy.</p>

<p>But it is genuinely a different thing from any of the traditions described above. There is no fire, no smoke, no master, no whisk, no plant knowledge, no community, no ritual, no four-hour arc. The gym sauna is <strong>heat extraction without context</strong>, the way an espresso shot in a paper cup is caffeine extraction without the Italian caf&eacute;. Both are useful. Neither is the same as the original.</p>

<p>What&rsquo;s interesting is that the rest of the world is currently rediscovering the original. In London, in Brooklyn, in Berlin, in Melbourne, public bathhouses are reopening. People are training as bath masters. Latvians and Finns are travelling abroad to teach the techniques. The gym box is being supplemented by something deeper.</p>

<h2 id="third-place">The third place</h2>

<p>There is a sociologist named <strong>Ray Oldenburg</strong> who in 1989 published a book called <em>The Great Good Place</em>, in which he argued that human beings need three different sorts of social space to function properly. Your <strong>first place</strong> is your home. Your <strong>second place</strong> is your work. Your <strong>third place</strong> is somewhere else &mdash; neutral ground where you go regularly, where the conversations are unscripted, where you might know the regulars but you owe them nothing, and where the social hierarchies of home and work do not apply.</p>

<p>The classic third places are caf&eacute;s, pubs, barber shops, market squares, the post office. Oldenburg argued that societies which lose their third places become anxious, lonely, and politically polarised, because there is nowhere left for ordinary unobligated human contact to happen.</p>

<p>Anyone who has spent time in a Baltic or Nordic country will recognise that <strong>the sauna has been a third place here for a very long time.</strong> Saturday at the village pirts. Friends gathering at a country sauna in summer for an evening that runs late. The old men in a Finnish public sauna who have been arguing about the same things for forty years. The Estonian smoke-sauna farmer who hosts strangers and locals indistinguishably. None of this happens at home. None of it happens at work. It all happens in the third place &mdash; the heated wooden room &mdash; and it has been doing so for a thousand years.</p>

<p>The pirts, particularly, takes the third-place idea further than anywhere else I can think of. Latvian families gather at the bathhouse for birthdays, for the arrival of new babies, for the months after a death, for marriages, for the first day of spring. It is the place where major life events are processed, in a way that combines the spiritual function of a church, the social function of a pub, and the medical function of a clinic. Modern psychology is just now catching up with what we have been doing for a thousand years.</p>

<h2 id="dark-water">A word on the dark water</h2>

<p>I want to talk about the part I, personally, struggled with for years.</p>

<p>When you do a proper Latvian pirts ritual, the cold-water plunge is essential. You go from the heat into water that is barely above freezing for 10 to 30 seconds, and the contrast is what makes the whole thing work &mdash; circulation, immune response, mental clarity, all of it.</p>

<p>The problem, for me, is that the cold water is usually a Latvian pond. And Latvian ponds, to be honest, look a bit alarming the first time you see one. The water is almost black. The bottom is invisible. There is something soft and muddy underfoot. The whole thing looks like the kind of pond where, in a fairy tale, something with too many teeth lives.</p>

<p>I am happy to report that <strong>the science is on our side</strong>, and I wish someone had explained this to me earlier.</p>

<p>The dark colour of Latvian pond and lake water comes from <strong>dissolved organic matter</strong> &mdash; primarily <em>humic and fulvic acids</em> &mdash; that leach out of the surrounding peat bogs and pine forests. Sphagnum moss decomposes slowly under acidic, low-oxygen conditions, and the products of that decomposition stain the water the colour of strong tea. There is nothing wrong with the water; it is simply dressed in the colour of the land it flows through.</p>

<p>Even better: those same humic acids have <strong>mild antimicrobial properties</strong> and act as a natural sunscreen for the lake, suppressing bacterial growth and protecting aquatic life from UV damage. This is why historical travellers in northern Europe used to say <em>&ldquo;if it&rsquo;s brown, drink it down.&rdquo;</em> Bog water has been keeping people alive in this part of the world for a very long time. It looks bad and is biologically excellent &mdash; basically the opposite of most ponds in most parts of the world.</p>

<p>Once I understood this I stopped flinching when I saw the surface. The water is dark for the same reason the forest smells the way it smells. You are immersing yourself in the chemistry of the bog, which is the chemistry of this whole country. There is something almost embarrassing about being a Latvian who took twenty years to make peace with the colour of the local water, but there it is.</p>

<p>The muddy bottom underfoot is, I&rsquo;ll admit, still a separate issue. You get used to it.</p>

<h2 id="which-one">So which one should you try?</h2>

<p>If you are visiting Latvia, the answer is straightforward: book a <strong>Latvian pirts ritual</strong> with a trained pirtnieks at one of the proper rural venues. Ziedlejas in the Gauja National Park, Žade&#299;ta Pirts in J&#363;rmala, Meža SPA on the Kurzeme coast. Plan for half a day. Bring an open mind. Expect to feel something genuinely unusual happen to your body and your nervous system.</p>

<p>If you are visiting Finland or Estonia, find a real <strong>smoke sauna</strong> rather than a hotel one. The smoke sauna is the ancient form, the UNESCO-listed form, and the form that produces the soft, deep heat that everything else is trying to imitate.</p>

<p>If you are in Norway, go to one of the <strong>floating saunas</strong> in Oslo or Bergen and afterwards plunge into the fjord. It is more architectural than ritualistic, but it is genuinely lovely, and the new Norwegian movement is one of the most interesting things happening in sauna culture right now.</p>

<p>And if all you have is the gym sauna at your local fitness centre &mdash; that&rsquo;s fine too. Sit in it for fifteen minutes. Breathe slowly. Drink water afterwards.</p>

<p>Just know that there is a much deeper version of this, going back a thousand years, still very much alive in the forests of this part of Europe. And if you ever find yourself in Latvia in winter, with four free hours and &euro;150 to spend on something genuinely transformative, I cannot think of a better way to spend either.</p>

<p>Come hot. Come cold. Come back hot. Come back cold. By the end you&rsquo;ll understand why we&rsquo;ve been doing this since before there was a word for it.</p>

## A Brief History of Latvia, Told by the People Who Lived It

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/brief-history-of-latvia-first-person.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** Eight hundred years of Latvian history through the voices of the people who lived each chapter &mdash; pagan, peasant, soldier, exile, citizen. From the crusader knights to the European Union.

<p class="article-lede">You can read Latvia&rsquo;s history as a list of dates and ruling powers &mdash; the Livonian Order, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Sweden, the Russian Empire, the First Republic, the Soviets, the Nazis, the Soviets again, and finally independence in 1991. It&rsquo;s a long list, and it&rsquo;s accurate. But it is not what living through any of those centuries actually felt like.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: history-flag-hero -->

<figure class="history-hero">

<p>So instead, here are eight voices. One for each chapter. None of them is a real person &mdash; but everything they describe really happened to someone like them.</p>

<h2 id="pagan">I am a pagan, and the foreign men have come</h2>

<p><em>Around the year 1200, on the banks of the Daugava river.</em></p>

<p>Our gods live in the trees. P&#275;rkons in the oak, M&#257;ra in the running water, Saule who rises behind the pines every morning and remembers our names. We bury our dead with food and a small coin so they are not hungry on the journey. We sing at midsummer, and we sing at every funeral, and the songs are older than anyone remembers.</p>

<p>The foreign men have come up the river in boats. They wear iron and they carry a thin sign of two crossed sticks they say is their god. They say our gods are demons. They have built a stone house at the mouth of the Daugava and they call it Riga. Their priest says we must come and be washed in their water or we will burn in a fire after we die.</p>

<p>My uncle says they will take our land. My grandfather says no &mdash; they are only traders, like the Swedes before them. We will see who is right.</p>

<p>We did not see who was right for a long time. The foreign men brought more iron men. They built more stone houses. By the time my grandchildren were old, we were Christian whether we liked it or not, and we did not own the land we had farmed for a thousand years.</p>

<p>But the songs are still older than anyone remembers. We never stopped singing them.</p>

<h2 id="peasant-german">I am a peasant, and the master is German</h2>

<p><em>Around 1500, in a village somewhere in Vidzeme.</em></p>

<p>The master lives in the big stone house on the hill. He is German. His grandfather was German. His grandfather&rsquo;s grandfather was German. He does not speak our language, and we do not speak his.</p>

<p>Three days a week, my husband and I work on his land. The other days we work on our own &mdash; what they let us call our own. The harvest is split: a portion for us, a portion for him, a portion for the church. In a good year there is bread. In a bad year there is not.</p>

<p>When my eldest son was born, I went to the church to baptise him. The priest is German too. He wrote my son&rsquo;s name in his book &mdash; a German name, not the name we use at home. At home we call him by his real name, the one his grandfather had.</p>

<p>We are not slaves. They will tell you we are not slaves. But my son was born here, and he will die here, and he will work this same land for that same family in the stone house on the hill, and he will not be allowed to leave without their permission. Whatever you want to call that, that is what it is.</p>

<h2 id="swedish-book">I am a peasant&rsquo;s child, and the Swedes have given me a book</h2>

<p><em>Around 1690, in northern Vidzeme, under Swedish rule.</em></p>

<p>The Swedes came thirty years before I was born. The old people say they are different from the Germans &mdash; fairer with the harvest, harder on the masters, and they do something none of the previous rulers ever did. They make us go to school.</p>

<p>Once a week, in the winter, the priest&rsquo;s helper teaches us letters. He is a young man from a village like mine, and his Latvian is the same as ours. He says the king of Sweden has decided that every peasant child in this land must learn to read, because every peasant must be able to read the Bible in their own language.</p>

<p>In their own language. That is the part I remember.</p>

<p>My grandfather could not read. My father could not read. I am eight years old and I am holding a book that is written in <em>my</em> language &mdash; Latvian &mdash; and I can read the words on the page out loud, and they make sense.</p>

<p>I do not know yet that the Swedes will lose the great war and the Russians will come. I do not know that the master in the stone house will still be German for another two hundred years. I only know that I can read, and that this thing they have given me, no future master can take away.</p>

<h2 id="soldier">I am a soldier, and the Tsar wants me</h2>

<p><em>Around 1860, somewhere on the road south.</em></p>

<p>I am twenty-three years old. The conscription officer came to our village last spring and read out the names. Mine was on the list. Twenty-five years in the Russian army. They say it has been shortened recently to fifteen, but the old men in our village remember when it was twenty-five, and they remember the men who never came back.</p>

<p>I have been walking for six weeks. I do not know exactly where I am. The officers speak Russian, and I speak Latvian, and we manage with hand signals and with the few Russian words I have learned along the way. <em>Da. Niet. Khleb.</em> Yes. No. Bread.</p>

<p>There is a Polish boy from somewhere near Vilnius in the company next to mine. We cannot really speak to each other, but we sit together at meals because we are both far from home and we both miss our mothers. His mother makes a soup with sour cream that sounds very much like the soup my mother makes. We agreed on this with our hands.</p>

<p>I will fight for the Tsar somewhere &mdash; Crimea, the Caucasus, the Turkish frontier, I do not know yet. The empire is large, and they need bodies for all of it. If I live, I will come home to a village that has buried my parents while I was gone.</p>

<h2 id="independence">I am a young woman, and Latvia is a country</h2>

<p><em>November 1918, in Riga.</em></p>

<p>I was twenty-five when the announcement came. We had been ruled by Germans, then Russians, then Germans again during the war. And now, in a theatre on Romanova iela, a group of men signed a piece of paper that said this country is ours.</p>

<p>Latvia. <em>Latvija.</em> The word felt strange in my mouth, the way a new dress feels the first time you wear it. We had been a people for a thousand years. We had never been a country before.</p>

<p>My father cried when he read the newspaper. He was sixty years old and he had spent his entire life calling himself a subject of someone &mdash; first the Tsar, then the Kaiser. Now he was a citizen. He did not know what to do with the word. He had to practise it.</p>

<p>The next twenty years were not easy. We had to build a country with our hands &mdash; schools, ministries, an army, a currency, an opera, a football league. We had to do it while the Germans across the border were turning into something terrible and the Russians next door were turning into something worse. We did our best. We almost made it.</p>

<h2 id="deportation">I am a child, and we are leaving in the night</h2>

<p><em>June 14, 1941. A village in Latgale.</em></p>

<p>The men in uniforms came at three in the morning. My mother had one hour to pack. She put bread and warm clothes and my grandmother&rsquo;s photograph into a sheet and tied the corners. My father was not there &mdash; they had taken him a week earlier and we did not know where.</p>

<p>There were trains at the station. Long ones. Wooden cars meant for cattle. They put us inside with sixty other people from villages near ours and they locked the door from the outside. There was a hole cut in the corner of the floor for what we needed. There was no light.</p>

<p>The train moved east for three weeks. When we stopped, we stopped in a place I had no name for. They told us later it was Siberia. The cold was a different kind of cold than the cold at home &mdash; drier, sharper, without forgiveness.</p>

<p>My mother survived. My grandmother did not. My father, we learned forty years later, had been shot within two months of his arrest. I came home to Latvia in 1956 with my mother. The house we had lived in had other people in it. They were not bad people. They had been told the house was empty.</p>

<p>There would be another deportation in 1949 &mdash; forty-three thousand people from Latvia, in a single week. My cousin&rsquo;s family was in that one.</p>

<p>We were the lucky ones. We came back.</p>

<h2 id="soviet">I am a citizen of the Soviet Union, and I am tired</h2>

<p><em>Around 1985, in a Riga apartment block.</em></p>

<p>I was born in Soviet Latvia and I have lived all forty-one years of my life in it. I work in a state factory. I queue for sausage. I have a small apartment in a building that looks exactly like ten thousand other buildings between here and Vladivostok. The plumbing leaks. The neighbours hear everything.</p>

<p>We sing in choirs. This is allowed, because singing is a folk tradition and the Party tolerates folk traditions. So we sing &mdash; and the songs we sing are the same songs my pagan ancestor on the Daugava sang, the same songs the peasant child with the Swedish Bible sang, the same songs my mother sang quietly to herself in Siberia. The Party does not understand what these songs are doing. They think they are folklore. They are a country, hiding in plain sight.</p>

<p>In four years, two million of us &mdash; Estonians, Latvians, Lithuanians &mdash; will join hands across all three countries in a chain six hundred kilometres long. It will be called the Baltic Way. The Soviet Union will not recover from it.</p>

<p>I do not know any of this yet. Tonight I am queuing for sausage.</p>

<h2 id="eu">I am a citizen of the European Union</h2>

<p><em>Today, in Riga.</em></p>

<p>I was born after independence. I have a Latvian passport and a European Union passport, and they are the same document. I have studied in Germany. I have worked in Spain. I came home because I wanted to. My grandparents could not have imagined any of this.</p>

<p>Latvia is a small country. Two million people, give or take. We are members of the European Union and of NATO. Our democracy is younger than I am, and like anyone in their thirties, it is sometimes wise and sometimes a mess. We argue, loudly, about our own politics &mdash; which is not nothing, when you remember that for most of our history we were not allowed to argue about politics at all.</p>

<p>We watch the news from Ukraine with a quiet that is hard to explain to people who have not been us. We know what those tanks look like. Our grandparents knew. Our great-grandparents knew. We hope, genuinely, that our children will not have to know.</p>

<p>For now, we have something none of the voices above this one ever had. We have our country, our language, our songs, our schools, our courts, our parliament, our borders, and the freedom to leave them and come back. We have made a real life out of all of this, in less than thirty-five years.</p>

<p>We hope to keep it. We hope it will be ours forever.</p>

<p>We are aware, more than most Europeans, of what <em>forever</em> really means. But we hope.</p>

<hr>

<p><em>If you visit Latvia and want to understand any of this in more depth, the <a href="https://okupacijasmuzejs.lv/en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Museum of the Occupation of Latvia</a> covers 1940 to 1991 with extraordinary care, and the <a href="https://brivdabasmuzejs.lv/en/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Latvian Ethnographic Open-Air Museum</a> shows you the houses these voices lived in. Both are an easy day from the centre of Riga.</em></p>
<!-- BEGIN: cross-sell-cta -->
<p class="article-cta"><em>This story is the spine of every walk we lead. If you want it told as you stand in front of the buildings — the Freedom Monument, the Occupation Museum, the Riflemen Square — <a href="/#contact">get in touch</a> and we'll build it into your Riga days.</em></p>
<!-- END: cross-sell-cta -->

## Castle of Light: Riga's National Library, A Visitor's Guide

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/castle-of-light-latvian-national-library.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** Riga's Gaismas pils — the Castle of Light. The Glass Mountain folktale, Gunārs Birkerts's design, the 2014 human chain, and why Latvians love it as much as visitors do.

<p class="article-lede">There are buildings you visit because the guidebook tells you to, and there are buildings you visit because, once you step inside, something shifts. The National Library of Latvia &mdash; <em>Latvijas Nacion&#257;l&#257; bibliot&#275;ka</em>, but everyone in Riga calls it <strong>Gaismas Pils</strong>, the <strong>Castle of Light</strong> &mdash; is firmly in the second category. It is one of the few modern buildings anywhere in the Baltics that locals love as fiercely as visitors do, and the reason is not really architectural. It is emotional. It is folkloric. It is a building that holds a story Latvians have been telling themselves for a thousand winters, finally given physical form.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: nl-gallery-injection -->

<p>If you come to Riga and see only the Old Town, you have seen a beautiful medieval city. If you walk across the Daugava and spend an hour inside the Castle of Light, you start to understand Latvia.</p>

<h2 id="first-look">A glass mountain on the left bank</h2>

<p>You see it long before you reach it. From the cobbled lanes of Vecr&#299;ga (Riga&rsquo;s old town), from the spire of St Peter&rsquo;s, from almost any high point in the old quarter, a steep silver-grey peak rises on the far bank of the Daugava &mdash; angular, asymmetric, a little improbable. It looks like a piece of geometry that has decided to grow out of the riverbank. Twelve floors and a pinnacle, sixty-eight metres high, walls that lean inward at sharp angles and end in a small glass crown at the top.</p>

<p>This is one of the largest cultural buildings to go up in northern Europe in the twenty-first century, and it cost the country roughly &euro;193 million to finish. But the numbers are the least interesting thing about it. What matters is what shape it took, and why.</p>

<h2 id="architect">The architect: a man who waited fifty years to come home</h2>

<p>The Castle of Light was designed by <strong>Gun&#257;rs Birkerts</strong> &mdash; known in English as Gunnar Birkerts &mdash; a Latvian-American architect whose own life is bound up with the twentieth-century history of the country he was born in.</p>

<p>Birkerts was born in Riga in <strong>January 1925</strong>. As a teenager, he watched his country lose its independence twice in the space of a few years &mdash; first to the Soviets, then to the Germans, then to the Soviets again. In the closing months of the Second World War, ahead of the advancing Red Army, his family fled west. He was barely twenty. He never lived in Latvia again.</p>

<p>He finished his architectural studies at the Technische Hochschule in Stuttgart in 1949, emigrated to the United States the same year, and built an entire career in Detroit. He worked under Eero Saarinen &mdash; one of the most important architects of the American twentieth century &mdash; and under Minoru Yamasaki, who designed the original World Trade Center. By 1962 he had opened his own practice. Over the following five decades he produced some of the most distinctive American buildings of his generation. A short list of the projects he is best remembered for outside Latvia:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The <strong>Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis</strong> (1973), with its dramatic suspended structure</li>
  <li>The <strong>Corning Museum of Glass</strong> addition in Corning, New York (1980)</li>
  <li>The <strong>University of Michigan Law Library Addition</strong> (1981) &mdash; a famously ingenious underground library, included in the American Institute of Architects&rsquo; list of 150 most notable American buildings</li>
  <li>The <strong>Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art</strong> in Kansas City (1994)</li>
  <li>The <strong>U.S. Embassy in Caracas</strong>, Venezuela (1996)</li>
  <li>St Peter&rsquo;s Lutheran Church in Columbus, Indiana</li>
</ul>

<p>He was made a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 1970 and received Latvia&rsquo;s highest civilian honour, the <strong>Order of the Three Stars</strong>, in 1995. He worked into his late eighties. He died in Massachusetts in August 2017, aged 92, having lived to see the Castle of Light open three years earlier.</p>

<p>In 1989, when Latvia was just beginning to slip out of Soviet control, the new government commissioned Birkerts to design a national library. He was already in his mid-sixties. He took the commission and &mdash; characteristically &mdash; gave the design work to Latvia for free. He once told his close friend, the Latvian architect J&#257;nis Dripe, that <em>there are times when the need for a symbol of freedom overrides the question of quiet integration into the urban context. Sometimes it is more important that the building speaks.</em></p>

<p>The Castle of Light is the building speaking.</p>

<h2 id="folktale">The longest version of the story: the Glass Mountain and the Castle of Light</h2>

<p>Birkerts could have designed Latvia a sleek, glassy, internationally legible library in the manner of the late 1990s. He did not. He went back to Latvian folklore, and he chose two of the deepest images in it.</p>

<h3>The Glass Mountain</h3>

<p>In Latvian folktales there is a recurring figure called the <strong>Stikla kalns</strong>, the Glass Mountain (sometimes translated as the Crystal Mountain). It is a mountain so steep and so smooth that nothing can climb it. At its summit, depending on the version of the tale, sits a king&rsquo;s daughter, or a princess, or a sleeping enchanted maiden, sometimes with three golden apples in her lap. She is unreachable. She is the prize of the impossible.</p>

<p>The story belongs to a folktale family that exists across northern Europe &mdash; Latvian folklorists have catalogued more than seventy-seven Latvian variants alone, and Latvian archives are said to contain over four hundred &mdash; but in the Latvian imagination it took on a particular weight. A king announces that whoever can ride to the top of the Glass Mountain and reach his daughter will marry her. Knights come from every direction. Their horses scrabble at the slope and slide back down. Princes break themselves trying. Day after day, the mountain defeats them.</p>

<p>In most Latvian versions there are three brothers. The two older brothers are clever and proud and come to nothing. The youngest is the foolish one &mdash; <em>Mu&#316;&#311;&#299;tis</em>, &ldquo;the little fool,&rdquo; a stock figure of Latvian story-telling. He is mocked by his family, dressed in ashes and rags. But he has something the others do not: he keeps faith. He holds a vigil at his father&rsquo;s grave for three nights, and on each of those nights a magical horse appears to him &mdash; a silver horse, then a golden horse, then a horse the colour of diamonds. On three successive days he tries the mountain. He climbs a third of the way, then two-thirds, and on the final day he rides to the very top, takes the princess&rsquo;s ring (or her handkerchief, or one of her three golden apples, depending on the storyteller), and disappears before anyone sees who he is. Only at the end, summoned before the king, does he produce the proof and reveal that the boy in the ashes was the one who reached the summit.</p>

<p>This story matters because of what the mountain itself means. The Glass Mountain is a metaphor &mdash; a rather precise one &mdash; for <strong>the height of human achievement</strong>. It is the thing that cannot be reached without commitment, without faith, without a willingness to be mocked by the world while you are still trying. The princess at the top is the reward of perseverance, of wisdom, of self-mastery. She is, in a sense, what knowledge looks like.</p>

<p>The most famous adaptation of this folktale is <strong>Rainis&rsquo;s play <em>Zelta zirgs</em> (<em>The Golden Horse</em>)</strong>, written in 1909 by Latvia&rsquo;s greatest poet and political thinker. In Rainis, the youngest brother is named <strong>Anti&#326;&#353;</strong>, and the princess on the Glass Mountain is asleep, frozen in a kind of enchanted darkness, waiting for someone brave enough to wake her. Rainis wrote <em>Zelta zirgs</em> during a long political exile in Switzerland, at a time when Latvia did not exist as an independent country and would not for another decade. Every Latvian schoolchild knows what the play was really about. The sleeping princess was Latvia. The mountain was history. The youngest brother was the Latvian people, told they were too small and too foolish to make a country of their own &mdash; and reaching the summit anyway.</p>

<h3>The Castle of Light</h3>

<p>The second image Birkerts drew on is older and stranger. There is an old Latvian song &mdash; <em>Gaismas pils</em>, &ldquo;Castle of Light&rdquo; &mdash; written by the nineteenth-century poet <strong>Auseklis</strong> and set to choral music that every Latvian sings. The song tells of a great castle of wisdom and learning that long ago <strong>sank into a lake</strong>, drowned in the dark waters of war and invasion, and lies at the bottom waiting. One day, the song promises, when the people have suffered enough and earned it back, the castle will rise out of the water again, gleaming, and bring light to the land.</p>

<p>For a country that spent most of its modern history occupied &mdash; by Swedes, by Russians, by Germans, by the Soviet Union &mdash; this is not a children&rsquo;s lullaby. This is the central image of a national life. The wisdom is not lost. It is submerged. It will return.</p>

<p>Birkerts took both images and welded them into one building. The sloping silver flanks are the <strong>Glass Mountain</strong>. The little glass crown at the top &mdash; the box of light at the apex you can see clearly in the photographs &mdash; is the <strong>princess&rsquo;s crown</strong>, the prize at the summit. And the whole structure, rising out of the riverbank opposite the Old Town, is the <strong>Castle of Light</strong> itself, finally lifted out of the dark waters of the twentieth century.</p>

<p>The colours inside the building deepen the symbolism: each floor is painted in the colours of the old <strong>Latvian lats</strong> banknotes &mdash; the national currency the country used until it joined the euro in 2014, and which carried portraits of writers, folklorists, and the <em>Daina</em> maiden on its notes. Tucked away on the upper floors is the <strong>Cabinet of Folksongs</strong>, a wooden chest of drawers containing the original index cards on which <strong>Krišj&#257;nis Barons</strong> systematised over a quarter of a million <strong>dainas</strong> &mdash; Latvian folk verses, four-line poems, the closest thing the country has to a sacred text. Almost everything in the building is a quiet reference to something Latvian. The mountain you climb to reach the top of the building is, deliberately, the same mountain in the story.</p>

<h2 id="human-chain">The night of the human chain</h2>

<p>The new library was structurally complete in early 2014. Latvia had just joined the euro on 1 January, and Riga had just been named <strong>European Capital of Culture</strong> for that year. The old library &mdash; actually eleven different buildings scattered across Riga, because the collection had outgrown every home it had ever had &mdash; was about to be packed into trucks and moved across the river.</p>

<p>Then somebody had a different idea.</p>

<p>On <strong>Saturday, 18 January 2014</strong>, in the dead cold of a Latvian January, around <strong>fourteen thousand people</strong> lined up in a chain that began outside the old library on Krišj&#257;&#326;a Barona iela in the Old Town, ran through the centre of Riga, crossed the <strong>Akmens tilts</strong> &mdash; the Stone Bridge over the Daugava &mdash; and ended on the steps of the new Castle of Light on the opposite bank. The chain was roughly two kilometres long. The temperature, depending on which account you read, was somewhere around minus twelve to minus fifteen degrees Celsius. There were small children in it. There were elderly people leaning on canes. People came out of their offices and stood in line. People came in from villages outside Riga and stood in line.</p>

<p>And then they passed books.</p>

<p>One pair of cold hands to the next. From the old library to the new. The first book was lifted off a shelf by a librarian, handed to the first person in the chain, and travelled &mdash; slowly, ceremonially, through fourteen thousand pairs of mittened hands &mdash; across the city, across the river, into the new building. The Latvians called it <strong>the Path of Light</strong> &mdash; <em>Gaismas ce&#316;&scaron;</em>.</p>

<p>There is a beautiful story about this moment that Latvians like to tell. It is said that the <strong>first book passed across the chain was a Bible</strong> &mdash; and not just any Bible, but symbolically the <strong>Gl&uuml;ck Bible</strong>, the seventeenth-century Latvian translation by the Lutheran pastor <strong>Ernst Gl&uuml;ck</strong>, which is one of the cornerstones of the entire Latvian written language. Gl&uuml;ck&rsquo;s translation, finished in 1694 and printed in Riga, was the first complete Bible in Latvian, and it standardised Latvian spelling and grammar for the next three centuries. To send it across first, hand to hand, was to say: <em>this is where our literature begins; everything else follows.</em></p>

<p>The chain was supposed to deliver thousands of books that day. In the end it managed only around two thousand. The reason is recorded in interviews afterwards by people who stood in the line: <strong>everyone kept stopping to look at the books.</strong> Some held them too long because they were beautiful. Some held them too long because they could not believe they were holding them. A woman recognised a book she had read as a child. An old man recognised a book that had been banned under the Soviets and could only be read with a special permit until 1988. The line kept stalling. Nobody minded.</p>

<p>The remaining four million volumes followed in trucks over the next several months. But the trucks were not the point.</p>

<p>The point was that the human chain consciously echoed an older one &mdash; <strong>the Baltic Way of 23 August 1989</strong>, when roughly two million people from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania joined hands in a single unbroken line stretching six hundred kilometres from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius, demanding independence from the Soviet Union. Within two years, all three countries were free. Twenty-five years later, almost to the month, their grandchildren stood in the snow in Riga and used their hands for books instead of borders. Same gesture. Same country. Different chapter.</p>

<p>The two thousand books that arrived by hand on 18 January 2014 are still in the library. They have been placed on a special bookcase that rises five floors through the centre of the building. It is called the <strong>People&rsquo;s Bookshelf</strong> &mdash; <em>Tautas gr&#257;matu plaukts</em> &mdash; and any Latvian, anywhere in the world, can donate a book to it, on condition that they include a personal note explaining why the book mattered to them. It now holds many thousands of volumes in over fifty languages, and the shelf is still growing. When you walk into the atrium and look up, you are looking at a book wall that has been built, one personal story at a time, by an entire country.</p>

<h2 id="visit">What it is like to actually visit</h2>

<p>Practical things now, because part of why the Castle of Light is a great recommendation for a visitor to Riga is that it is genuinely easy and genuinely free.</p>

<p><strong>Entry is free for everyone.</strong> You walk in, leave your coat at the cloakroom (free) and your bag in a locker (one euro coin, refundable), pick up a free visitor pass at reception, and you are in. If you want a proper library card &mdash; which gives you access to reading rooms and reference materials &mdash; you bring a passport or national ID card with you. But for the architecture, the exhibitions, the People&rsquo;s Bookshelf and, above all, the view, you do not need anything except yourself.</p>

<p><strong>Go for the view.</strong> The viewing levels on the <strong>eleventh and twelfth floors</strong> are, in our opinion, the single best urban panorama in Riga. You take the lift to the eleventh, walk a flight of stairs to the twelfth, and the entire Old Town is laid out in front of you across the river &mdash; the spires of St Peter&rsquo;s, the Dome Cathedral, Riga Castle, the snake of the Daugava, the five bridges, the Central Market pavilions (built from old Zeppelin hangars), the brutalist silhouette of the Latvian Academy of Sciences, the Art Nouveau districts beyond. On a clear evening just before sunset, with the river going silver and the Old Town turning gold, it is one of those views that justifies the trip on its own.</p>

<p>The windows on the upper floors have a wrap of small black dots &mdash; partly bird-strike protection, partly a design choice &mdash; which makes serious photography slightly tricky. Bring your eyes more than your phone.</p>

<p><strong>Inside, look for:</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>The <strong>People&rsquo;s Bookshelf</strong>, rising five storeys through the central atrium</li>
  <li>The permanent exhibition <strong>&ldquo;Castle of Light and Glass Mountain &mdash; The Story of the National Library of Latvia Project&rdquo;</strong> on levels 1 and 12, which is the best place to read the building&rsquo;s symbolism in detail</li>
  <li>The <strong>&ldquo;Book in Latvia&rdquo;</strong> permanent exhibition on the ground floor &mdash; five centuries of Latvian printing, including a copy of the Gl&uuml;ck Bible</li>
  <li>The <strong>Cabinet of Folksongs</strong> (the <em>Dainu skapis</em>) &mdash; Krišj&#257;nis Barons&rsquo;s actual filing cabinet, holding hundreds of thousands of folk verses on small index cards</li>
  <li>The <strong>caf&eacute;</strong> on one of the upper floors, which has the same view as the observation deck and considerably better coffee than the ground-floor caf&eacute;</li>
</ul>

<h3>Getting there</h3>

<p>The library sits on <strong>M&#363;kusalas iela 3</strong>, on the left bank of the Daugava, directly opposite the Old Town. Three good ways to reach it:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Walking</strong> is what we recommend, and it is the most rewarding. From the House of the Blackheads or the Town Hall Square, walk down to the <strong>Stone Bridge</strong> (Akmens tilts) and cross. The walk takes ten to fifteen minutes. You get the full skyline behind you, the river under you, and the Castle of Light growing larger in front of you the entire time. On a clear morning the bridge view alone is worth the trip.</li>
  <li><strong>Tram or bus</strong> &mdash; Tram 5 stops directly outside the library; several buses also pass it. From the Old Town side, any tram crossing the Stone Bridge will get you there in a few minutes.</li>
  <li><strong>Taxi or Bolt</strong> &mdash; three or four euros from anywhere in the centre, but you will have missed the best part.</li>
</ul>

<p>Note: the river you cross is the <strong>Daugava</strong>, Latvia&rsquo;s great river, the one that runs through the entire country and is sometimes called the <em>river of fate</em> in Latvian poetry. (The Gauja, often confused with it, is a different river, further north &mdash; the one that runs through Sigulda and the Gauja National Park.)</p>


<!-- BEGIN: nl-gallery-injection -->

    <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-national-library/latvian-national-library-atrium-overlook-reading-floor-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="reading-rooms" data-caption="Reading rooms and reference areas — Latvian National Library, Riga" aria-label="Open photo 6 of 7">

<!-- END: nl-gallery-injection -->
<h2 id="why">Why we send our guests here</h2>

<p>We take small groups around Riga and the Latvian countryside, and one of the questions we get asked most often is: <em>what should I see in Riga that isn&rsquo;t in every guidebook?</em> The Castle of Light is our standard answer &mdash; not because it is hidden (it is enormous; you cannot miss it from anywhere on the Old Town side) but because most visitors stay on one side of the river and never come over.</p>

<p>This is a mistake.</p>

<p>The Castle of Light is what gives Riga its scale. From the inside it is the only place where you see the whole city at once. From the outside, viewed across the Daugava at dusk with its glass crown lit up against a winter sky, it is the only modern building in the Baltics that genuinely belongs in the same conversation as the medieval ones it faces.</p>

<p>And the story it carries &mdash; a folktale, a sunken castle, a frozen princess, a younger brother written off as a fool, a Bible carried by hand across a frozen river by fourteen thousand people who understood exactly what they were doing &mdash; is the story of the country itself.</p>

<p>If you have an afternoon in Riga, give two hours of it to the Castle of Light. Walk over the bridge. Take the lift to the eleventh floor. Look back across the river at the Old Town and try to imagine what it felt like, on a January night in 2014, to be standing somewhere in the chain &mdash; cold, gloved, smiling, passing a book.</p>

<p>You will understand more about Latvia in that one hour than in any museum in the country.</p>

<p><em>Want to see the Castle of Light as part of a wider walk through Riga&rsquo;s stories &mdash; the medieval Old Town, the Art Nouveau quarter, the layers of empire and resistance that built this city? <a href="/#contact">Get in touch.</a> Our small-group walking tours are designed around exactly this kind of detail.</em></p>

## The Cat House (Kaķu nams), Riga: The Building, the Cats, and the Story

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/cat-house-riga-meistaru.html
**Published:** 2026-05-04
**Summary:** What the Cat House on Meistaru iela actually is, the merchant-and-the-Guild story behind the bronze cats on the roof, and the architectural details most travellers walk past. Honest local's guide from Daiga.

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, what the Cat House is</h2>
<p>The Cat House (in Latvian, <em>Kaķu nams</em>) is a yellow Art Nouveau apartment building at Meistaru iela 10/12, in the centre of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. It was built in 1909 by the Baltic German architect Friedrich Scheffel for a wealthy Latvian merchant. On the roof are two black bronze cats, with arched backs and lifted tails, placed on different parts of the roofline. The house gets its nickname from these cats, and from the much-told story of why they&rsquo;re there.</p>
<p>It is free to look at &mdash; you stand on the cobbles, you look up &mdash; and most Old Town walks pass it. Three minutes south of <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, two minutes north of the House of the Blackheads, and directly across the street from one of the buildings most central to the cats&rsquo; story.</p>

<h2 id="story">The story Riga tells about the cats</h2>
<p>Every Riga guide tells this one. The version I tell goes like this.</p>
<p>In the early 1900s, the merchant who built the Cat House applied to join the Great Guild of Riga (<em>Lielā Ģilde</em>), the powerful association of Riga&rsquo;s German-Baltic merchants whose hall stood directly across the street. The Guild refused him &mdash; he was Latvian, not German, and the Guild had been a German institution for some six centuries. Insulted, the merchant commissioned the bronze cats, and had them placed on the roof of his new house with their tails turned pointedly toward the windows of the Guild building opposite. A cat&rsquo;s raised tail, in the language Riga merchants would have understood, said exactly what it looks like it says.</p>
<p>The Guild took the merchant to court. The courts agreed the cats were a deliberate insult. The cats were ordered turned around. The Guild relented, the merchant was admitted, and the cats were quietly rotated to face the building &lsquo;properly&rsquo;.</p>
<p>That&rsquo;s the story. Whether all of it is strictly true is another question, which I&rsquo;ll come back to.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-cat-house/cat-house-bronze-cat-on-turret-detail-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="cat-house" data-caption="The bronze cat on the corner turret of the Cat House, Meistaru iela, Riga, Latvia.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-cat-house/cat-house-bronze-cat-on-turret-detail-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-cat-house/cat-house-bronze-cat-on-turret-detail-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The bronze cat on the corner turret of the Cat House, Meistaru iela, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The cat on the corner turret. Arched back, raised tail, fixed in bronze for over a century.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="building">The building itself</h2>
<p>The Cat House gets the headlines for the cats, which is fair. But the building under them is also worth a minute. Meistaru iela 10/12 is a strong example of <em>National Romantic</em> Art Nouveau &mdash; the Latvian variant of <em>Jugendstil</em>, the European style sweeping the city between roughly 1899 and 1914. It&rsquo;s an early piece in that style: 1909 is solidly within the National Romantic phase, and the building shares a vocabulary with the better-known facades on Alberta iela in the Quiet Centre that everyone visits for the Art Nouveau walk.</p>
<p>From the cobbles, look up. The yellow stuccoed facade has rhythmic windows and small balconies, with three-storey-high stuccoed pilasters framing the bays. The conical green-roofed corner turret is the one carrying the more famous of the two cats. Decorative brickwork above the windows is picked out in a slightly darker tone, and the smaller balconies have wrought-iron details around the rails. None of it is shouting. It is the work of an architect with a small budget and a clear plan, and it stands up well against the better-known facades on Alberta iela that everyone visits for the Art Nouveau walk.</p>
<p>The building is also lived-in &mdash; some apartments are private homes, others have been converted into offices, and the ground floor houses a restaurant and a wine bar. The cobbles in front are part of the small open space that sits in front of the Great Guild building, which means there are always people stood here looking up.</p>

<h2 id="cats">The two cats, the Guild building, and what&rsquo;s actually true</h2>
<p>Worth being honest about a few things. The Cat House story is one of those Riga set-pieces that has been polished into something neater than the documentary record probably supports. The cats are real and on the building. The merchant&rsquo;s frustration with the Great Guild was probably real. The court case is plausible, and the rotation of the cats is the kind of detail that has to come from somewhere. But the version told to tour groups assumes the merchant was Latvian; older historians have suggested he may have been German-Baltic but from the wrong family, or simply too newly rich for the Guild&rsquo;s taste. The exact dates, the exact court ruling, and even the question of how many times the cats have been physically rotated &mdash; all of that is foggier than the polished version admits.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-cat-house/cat-house-two-bronze-cats-on-roof-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="cat-house" data-caption="Both cats visible &mdash; the famous corner-turret one and its smaller sibling on the gable, Riga, Latvia.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-cat-house/cat-house-two-bronze-cats-on-roof-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-cat-house/cat-house-two-bronze-cats-on-roof-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="Both bronze cats on the roof of the Cat House, Meistaru iela, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Both cats visible at once: the famous one on the corner turret, and its smaller sibling on the gable just below.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>What is documented and certain: the building is from 1909, designed by Friedrich Scheffel; the Great Guild building (<em>Lielā Ģilde</em>) directly opposite was built between 1854 and 1860 in a romantic medieval-revival style and is itself a major Riga landmark, today the home of the Latvian National Symphony Orchestra. The Small Guild (<em>Mazā Ģilde</em>) is around the corner. The Cat House sits squarely in the middle of the historical heart of Riga&rsquo;s German merchant class, which is why the story works at all: a sculpture of a cat with a raised tail on a brand-new National Romantic building, looking down on the windows of an institution six centuries old, would have been read in 1909 exactly the way the story says.</p>
<p>So: the cats are doing what the story says they&rsquo;re doing, even if the precise legal proceedings are blurrier. That&rsquo;s usually the way with Riga stories.</p>

<!-- TODO: native Latvian speaker review of pull-quote -->
<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Viens tirgotājs, viens Lielās Ģildes lēmums un divi melni kaķi uz jumta. Visi pārējie sīkumi paliek atvērti.</em></p><cite>&mdash; A Latvian summary: &ldquo;one merchant, one Guild decision, two black cats on the roof. Every other detail stays open.&rdquo;</cite></div>

<h2 id="practical">Practical answers</h2>

<h3>Where it is</h3>
<p>Meistaru iela 10/12, in the centre of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. Three minutes south of <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, two minutes north of Town Hall Square and the <a href="house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html">House of the Blackheads</a>, directly opposite the Great Guild building. There&rsquo;s a small open square in front of the Cat House where you can stand with a clear line of sight to the cats.</p>

<h3>Hours, costs, getting in</h3>
<p>The exterior is on a public street, free, 24/7. The building is not open to the public &mdash; the apartments are private and the offices aren&rsquo;t for visitors. The ground-floor restaurant and wine bar are open to anyone; opening hours and menus change, walk past and check. There is no &lsquo;Cat House Museum&rsquo;. You stand on the cobbles, you look up, you take the photograph, you walk on. Five minutes is plenty.</p>

<h3>Best time to photograph the cats</h3>
<p>Late morning to early afternoon, when the sun is high enough to clear the surrounding rooflines and put light on the yellow facade. The corner turret faces roughly south-east, so morning gives you the best three-quarter side light on the famous cat. Step back to the centre of the small square in front of the Great Guild for a clear angle that catches both cats in the same frame. Avoid mid-summer noon &mdash; the cats are silhouetted against bright sky and lose detail.</p>

<h3>Combining with the rest of the Old Town</h3>
<p>The Cat House is a one-stop, five-minute detail, not a destination. The neighbours that pair with it: the <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">cathedral</a> three minutes north, the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a> seven minutes north-west, the <a href="house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html">House of the Blackheads</a> two minutes south. The full route through the Old Town is in the <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">Old Town pillar guide</a>.</p>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>
<p>The Cat House is one of the small set-pieces that gives the Old Town its character. It&rsquo;s not a destination, but it&rsquo;s the kind of detail that turns a city walk into something better than a checklist of cathedrals. A small, slightly petty story about a merchant&rsquo;s pride. Two cats in bronze. A building that is itself a piece of the larger Riga Art Nouveau story. Five minutes of looking up.</p>
<p>The story behind it is half-true and half-polished, the way most good city stories are. I think it&rsquo;s worth telling either way.</p>

      Is the Cat House story true?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-ch-8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Mostly. The cats are real, the building is real, the Great Guild building opposite is real, and the social tension between the new Latvian commercial class and the German-Baltic guild establishment in early-20th-century Riga is well documented. The exact court case, the precise dates, and the question of how many times the cats have actually been physically rotated have been polished by retelling. The basic situation &mdash; a merchant placing rude bronze cats on a roof aimed at a guild that had refused him &mdash; fits the period and the architecture, even if the courtroom drama owes some of its detail to oral tradition more than to archives.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-ch-9">
      Is there a fee or guided tour for the Cat House?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-ch-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>No fee. The Cat House is on a public street; the cats are visible to anyone walking past. Most Old Town walking tours stop here for two or three minutes to tell the story; if you&rsquo;d like a half-day Old Town with a licensed Latvian guide that includes the Cat House, the Cathedral, the Three Brothers, and Town Hall Square in one route, we can do that &mdash; <a href="/#contact">get in touch</a>.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-ch-10">
      What architectural style is the Cat House?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-ch-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Latvian National Romantic Art Nouveau (a regional variant of European Jugendstil), early phase. Yellow stuccoed facade, three-storey pilasters, a conical green-roofed corner turret, decorative brick detail, wrought-iron balconies. Riga has the densest concentration of Art Nouveau buildings of any European city &mdash; mostly in the Quiet Centre district just north of the Old Town walls &mdash; and the Cat House is one of the early Old Town examples.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
