## Dainu Kalns at Turaida: A Sculpture Garden Carved Under Soviet Rule

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/dainu-kalns-folk-song-hill-turaida.html
**Published:** 2026-05-02
**Summary:** How Indulis Ranka and Anna Jurkāne built the Hill of Dainas at Turaida between 1980 and 1985 — a folk-song memorial in granite that helped seed Latvia's Singing Revolution.

<p class="article-lede">There is a wooded hill above the Gauja river, just east of Sigulda, with twenty-six granite sculptures scattered through it. Some are taller than a person. Some you could sit on. They look, at first, like an unusually serious sculpture park &mdash; the kind of place a school group walks through quickly while the teacher checks her watch. They are not. The Hill of Dainas at Turaida is the closest thing modern Latvia has to a sacred grove, and it was built between 1980 and 1985, while the country was still occupied by the Soviet Union, by a sculptor with a trailer and a crane and a very long view of what folk songs are for.</p>

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, before the long version</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Dainu kalns</strong> &mdash; the Hill of Dainas &mdash; is a stone-sculpture garden inside the <strong>Turaida Museum Reserve</strong>, about 50 km north-east of Riga.</li>
<li><strong>Twenty-six sculptures and counting</strong>, all carved in granite by <strong>Indulis Ranka</strong> (1934&ndash;2017), illustrating themes from <em>dainas</em> &mdash; the four-line Latvian folk songs that Krišjānis Barons collected in the late 19th century.</li>
<li><strong>Opened on 7 July 1985</strong>, on what would have been Barons&rsquo;s 150th birthday. The Soviet authorities approved it as a folklorist commemoration. Latvians understood it as something else.</li>
<li><strong>In July 1988, the banned red-white-red Latvian flag was raised here</strong>, beside the central <em>Dziesmu tēvs</em> sculpture, during the Baltica folklore festival. Ten weeks later, Soviet Latvia relegalised the flag.</li>
<li>Allow <strong>1.5 to 2.5 hours</strong> for the Hill of Dainas and the adjoining <strong>Dziesmu dārzs</strong> (Song Garden) amphitheater. Most visitors give it twenty minutes. They miss the point.</li>
<li>The site is at its best on weekend mornings in summer, on Jāņi (23&ndash;24 June), and during the international <strong>Baltica</strong> folklore festival when Latvia hosts (next likely turn 2028).</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="what-it-is">What Dainu kalns actually is</h2>

<p>The short version is that Dainu kalns is a folk poem rendered in stone. The longer version is harder.</p>

<p>The <em>dainas</em> are a body of around <strong>1.2 million</strong> short Latvian folk songs &mdash; most of them four lines, anonymous, agrarian, pre-Christian in their world-picture. They were sung at births and deaths, at the spring sowing and the autumn slaughter, at weddings and at the long winter evenings of weaving. They were not written down. They were sung from grandmothers to granddaughters for at least a thousand years before <strong>Krišjānis Barons</strong>, a folklorist working in St Petersburg in the 1880s and 1890s, decided to collect them on index cards and publish them in six volumes called <em>Latvju Dainas</em>. The original index cards &mdash; <strong>217,996 of them</strong> &mdash; live now in a wooden cabinet at the National Library of Latvia, registered on the UNESCO Memory of the World list. We have written about that <a href="castle-of-light-latvian-national-library.html">elsewhere</a>.</p>

<p>The dainas matter, in the Latvian imagination, the way the Vedas matter in India or the Eddas in Iceland. They are the deepest layer of the language. They contain what was sacred before Christianity arrived in 1201. Pērkons, the thunder god. Māra, the earth-mother. Saule, the sun, who is feminine in Latvian and rises from the sea at dawn. Laima, the goddess of fate, sitting at the foot of the bed when a child is born. None of these survived as a serious religion. All of them survived in the songs.</p>

<p>So when, in 1980, a sculptor named Indulis Ranka and a museum director named Anna Jurkāne quietly agreed to monumentalize the dainas in granite on a hill above the Gauja river &mdash; well. That was not a sculpture project. That was a country building itself a memory in stone, where its memory could not be turned off.</p>

<h2 id="backstory">The backstory: how a national monument got built under occupation</h2>

<p>The honest answer is that nobody asked Moscow.</p>

<p>The seed of Dainu kalns is a single piece of paper. On <strong>21 October 1980</strong>, Indulis Ranka and Anna Jurkāne signed what they called a <em>goda līgums</em> &mdash; an honour agreement, a private pact between two people. Ranka would carve. Jurkāne, then director of the Sigulda Regional Studies Museum, would find the site, the volunteers, the funding. There was no commission. No state grant. The Latvian SSR Ministry of Culture did not draw up a plan. The whole thing was, in effect, a folk project about folk songs.</p>

<p>That is unusual enough on its own. What is more unusual is the timing. 1980 was a hard year in Soviet Latvia. The Andropov KGB was tightening, dissidents were being arrested, and any cultural project with a national-identity dimension was assumed to be in some sense subversive until proved otherwise. Russification policies were intensifying. The Latvian language was being elbowed out of higher education and government. By the early 1980s, ethnic Latvians were a minority in their own capital.</p>

<p>And yet the project was built, in plain sight, on a hillside that any KGB officer with a road map could find.</p>

<p>The cover was Barons. The Soviet cultural apparatus had been gradually rehabilitating Krišjānis Barons since the 1960s, treating him as a pre-revolutionary "people&rsquo;s scholar" of acceptable peasant credentials. His 150th birthday in <strong>1985</strong> was on the cultural calendar. Riga had a new Barons monument by Teodors Zaļkalns going up in Vērmane Garden the same summer. A folklore exhibition in his honour, on a hill in a museum reserve, fit inside a politically safe envelope.</p>

<p>That was the public reading. The private reading, which was understood by Latvians and apparently not by the censors, was something else. The dainas are not just folk material. They are the country&rsquo;s memory of itself before any of the foreign rulers arrived. To carve them in granite, on the same hill where the ancient Livs had buried their dead, with crowds of volunteers from across Latvia coming on weekends to dig the foundations &mdash; that was a quiet declaration. The art historian Ruta Čaupova later called it "the greatest cultural creation of the Awakening period." She was being precise. The Awakening had not started yet in 1985. Dainu kalns helped start it.</p>

<p>The first sculpture went up in 1982. <strong>Veļu akmens</strong>, the Stone of the Departed, placed at the site of an ancient Liv settlement on the eastern slope of the hill. The Veļi are the souls of the ancestors in Latvian folk belief. Putting them there first was not an accident. It was a marker. The land was being reclaimed, ritually, three years before the official opening.</p>

<p>The hill was opened on <strong>7 July 1985</strong>, with fifteen sculptures in place. The opening daina was "<em>Stāvēju, dziedāju augstajā kalnā</em>" &mdash; "I stood and sang on the high hill" &mdash; one Barons had collected himself. The crowd was, by all accounts, larger than the authorities had expected.</p>

<h2 id="the-flag">The 1988 moment, when the meaning came out into the open</h2>

<p>Three years later, on the night of 13 July 1988, something happened on this hill that ten years earlier would have got people sent to a labour camp in the Urals.</p>

<p>The international folklore festival <strong>Baltica &rsquo;88</strong> was being held that summer in Latvia. The opening concert was at Dainu kalns. Folklore groups from all three Baltic states were performing. And during the concert, in front of the central <em>Dziesmu tēvs</em> (Father of Songs) sculpture &mdash; the one with the portrait of Barons surrounded by three generations of singers &mdash; the <strong>banned red-white-red Latvian national flag was raised in public for the first time since 1940</strong>.</p>

<p>That detail is worth slowing down on. The Latvian flag had been banned for 48 years. Showing it in 1988 was still a criminal act on the morning of 13 July. By the evening it had been raised on a hill, in front of a sculpture of a folksong collector, during a folklore concert, and the KGB had not stopped it. Within ten weeks &mdash; on 29 September 1988 &mdash; the Soviet Latvian authorities formally relegalised the flag as a "culturally historical symbol." The decision did not come from Moscow. It came from a regime that had finally seen what was no longer in its hands.</p>

<p>From 1986 onwards, Latvians had been gathering at Dainu kalns most Sundays to sing dainas together. Folklore ensembles formed and rehearsed there. The European Heritage Days dossier on the site puts it plainly: "over several years, every Sunday, the people gathered, being united in Latvian folk songs, to sing out the cravings for freedom." When the <strong>Baltic Way</strong> human chain stretched from Tallinn to Vilnius on 23 August 1989, many of the singers who joined it had spent their Sundays on this hill.</p>

<p>In 1990, while the country was unwinding the Soviet Union one institution at a time, the adjacent <strong>Dziesmu dārzs</strong> &mdash; the Song Garden &mdash; opened as an outdoor amphitheater, completing the Tautasdziesmu parks (Folk Song Park) ensemble. Latvia&rsquo;s 1990 Song and Dance Festival was the first to fully restore the pre-1940 national repertoire and openly fly the flag. The country regained its independence on 21 August 1991. None of these things happened because of Dainu kalns. All of them happened with Dainu kalns inside them.</p>

<h2 id="sculptures">Reading the sculptures, room by room</h2>
<figure style="margin:2.4rem auto;max-width:760px;">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/dainu-kalns-three-figures.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/dainu-kalns-three-figures.jpg" alt="Three granite figures sculpted by Indulis Ranka at the Hill of Dainas, Turaida" loading="lazy" decoding="async" style="width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:8px;">
  </picture>
  <figcaption style="margin-top:.6rem;font-size:.92rem;color:#7a6a55;font-style:italic;text-align:center;">Three granite figures by Indulis Ranka — among the larger sculptures on the hill. The faces emerge from the boulder rather than being carved out of it.</figcaption>
</figure>


<p>The hill has more than twenty-six sculptures across three hectares of meadow and oak. Walk past quickly and they look like organic granite forms &mdash; spheres, drops, pillars, figures emerging from rock. Slow down with the dainas in mind. They read as a 26-stanza poem about who we are. (For a sculpture-by-sculpture field guide with the daina engraved on each stone and the year of placement, see the <a href="dainu-kalns-sculpture-field-guide.html">companion field guide</a>; what follows here is the thematic groupings, not the full catalogue.)</p>

<p>The arrangement is choreographed. The hill is laid out so that the paths between the sculptures roughly mirror the structure of the dainas themselves: birth, work, courtship, marriage, family, ancestors, the gods. There is a logic to the order, even if it is not signposted in English. A few groupings to look for.</p>

<h3>The pre-Christian Latvian gods</h3>

<p>The dainas keep alive a pantheon of nature-deities the church has never quite been able to scrub out. Several sculptures honour them directly.</p>

<p><strong>Veltījums Saulei &mdash; Dedication to the Sun.</strong> Saule, the sun, who is feminine in Latvian. She rises from the sea, drives a chariot across the sky, and weeps tears that turn to amber on the Baltic shore. The sculpture is rounded, almost spherical, designed to read against the sky behind it.</p>

<p><strong>Austras koks &mdash; The Tree of Auseklis.</strong> Auseklis is the morning star. The Austras koks is the daina world-tree, the cosmic axis around which day and night, life and death, are organized. This sculpture, added in 1990 as the country was changing hands, is the most concentrated cosmological piece in the garden &mdash; the whole creation in one boulder.</p>

<p><strong>Saules ceļš &mdash; Path of the Sun.</strong> A daily journey rendered as a procession of forms. The sun&rsquo;s path through the sky is the basic clock of the agrarian dainas.</p>

<h3>The folk calendar</h3>

<p><strong>Jāņu akmens &mdash; the Midsummer Stone.</strong> Jāņi, the night of 23&ndash;24 June, is the highest-stakes folk holiday in Latvia. Bonfires, oak-leaf wreaths, all-night singing in country houses. <em>Jāņu akmens</em> is the literal centerpiece of the calendar half of the hill. If you visit on Midsummer eve, this is where the local folklore groups gather.</p>

<p><strong>Neguli, saulīte, ābeļu dārzā &mdash; "Don&rsquo;t sleep, little sun, in the apple orchard."</strong> The title is a daina line. The sun is addressed as a girl-child, told not to dawdle in the orchard. The sculpture is soft, seated, half-asleep among the apples.</p>

<h3>The life cycle</h3>

<p>A large group of sculptures tracks the human life as the dainas track it &mdash; from cradle to grave, with weddings and labour and motherhood between.</p>

<p><strong>Bitenieka līgaviņa &mdash; The Beekeeper&rsquo;s Bride.</strong> A wedding-cycle daina rendered in stone. Beekeeping is one of the deepest occupational layers in Latvian folk culture, and the beekeeper&rsquo;s bride songs are some of the gentler ones in the repertoire.</p>

<p><strong>Māte un meita &mdash; Mother and Daughter.</strong> The seated figures lean into each other. Many dainas are sung from a mother to a daughter on the eve of marriage, on the day a baby is born, at the spinning wheel through a long winter. The whole genre of <em>tautasdziesmas</em> is a transmission from one woman to the next.</p>

<p><strong>Trīs māsas &mdash; Three Sisters.</strong> A daina motif that recurs across hundreds of song variants. The three sisters represent stages of life, the three layers of the cosmos, or simply three women working in a meadow &mdash; depending on which daina you have in your head.</p>

<p><strong>Mīlestības akmens &mdash; the Stone of Love.</strong> Latvian wedding parties bring their bouquets here. It is a quiet tradition, not advertised. If you come on a Saturday in May or June, you may see a bride in white walking up to a granite boulder and laying flowers on it before driving on to her reception.</p>

<h3>The Liv layer (the older country underneath)</h3>

<p>Turaida means "garden of God" in <strong>Livonian</strong>, a Finno-Ugric language related to Estonian and now effectively extinct &mdash; the last fluent native speaker died in 2013. The Livs (Līvi) lived along the lower Gauja and the Baltic coast for centuries before the Latvians as we know them coalesced as a people. Two sculptures, in particular, mark this older layer.</p>

<p><strong>Veļu akmens &mdash; Stone of the Departed.</strong> The first sculpture placed on the hill, in 1982, on the site of an actual ancient Liv settlement. The Veļi are the souls of the ancestors. Placing them on a Liv site, not a Latvian one, was a choice.</p>

<p><strong>Lībiešu putns &mdash; The Livonian Bird.</strong> Added in 1991, the year of independence. A memorial in stone for the indigenous people whose land this was first.</p>

<h3>The centerpiece</h3>

<p><strong>Dziesmu tēvs &mdash; the Father of Songs.</strong> The portrait sculpture of Krišjānis Barons, with three generations of singers carved around his head. This is the visual center of the hill and the place to slow down longest. It is also where the banned flag was raised in 1988 &mdash; a fact that no plaque shouts about, but which any Latvian over 50 will tell you if you ask.</p>

<p>If you happen to read Latvian, the on-site plaques carry the daina line each sculpture references. If you don&rsquo;t, the simplest preparation is to read a small selection of dainas in English translation before you come. Imants Krašnais&rsquo;s versions are good. The Latvian Literature Centre has free samplers online. Even a dozen dainas in your head, pre-loaded, will change the way the hill reads.</p>

<h2 id="ranka">Indulis Ranka, the man with the trailer</h2>
<figure style="margin:2.4rem auto;max-width:760px;">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/daiga-with-guest-sculpture.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/daiga-with-guest-sculpture.jpg" alt="Daiga and a guest beside the seated mother-and-child sculpture at the Hill of Dainas, Turaida" loading="lazy" decoding="async" style="width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:8px;">
  </picture>
  <figcaption style="margin-top:.6rem;font-size:.92rem;color:#7a6a55;font-style:italic;text-align:center;">With a guest at the seated mother-and-child sculpture — one of the smaller pieces on the hill, easy to walk past, worth slowing down for.</figcaption>
</figure>


<p>The sculptor of all this, Indulis Ranka, is the kind of figure that travel writing usually struggles with because he resists the grand narrative. He was a painter who became a sculptor in his thirties because the painters&rsquo; section of the Artists&rsquo; Union was overcrowded. He could not afford professional stone-cutters, so he taught himself to carve granite by hand. He bought a small truck and a portable crane. And then for the next fifty years he located, excavated, hauled, and shaped the boulders himself, often working at night during the long Latvian summer.</p>

<p>Latvian fields are full of granite. Glacial erratics, dragged south by the ice sheets and dropped at random when the climate warmed twelve thousand years ago. Most farmers regard them as a nuisance. Ranka regarded them, in his own words, as "old friends." He spent decades scouting them &mdash; this one in a meadow near Gulbene, that one in a forest in Kurzeme &mdash; and bringing them to Turaida one truckload at a time. The Hill of Dainas was built, almost literally, one stone at a time, often after midnight, by a man with a small budget and a lot of time.</p>

<p>This matters because it shapes the work. Ranka&rsquo;s sculptures do not look like neoclassical figures hewn from a quarry slab. They keep the boulder. The form emerges from the rock the way the dainas emerge from the language &mdash; slowly, organically, with the original material always visible. A face in profile, a pair of hands, a back curving into the original surface of the stone. The Ice-Age memory of the granite is part of the piece.</p>

<p>He worked with a small constellation of collaborators. Anna Jurkāne carried the project on the institutional side &mdash; finding the volunteers, fending off the bureaucracy, raising donations from across the country. Architects Jānis Rozentāls and Ilgvars Batrags planned the site. Landscape designers Aivars Irbe and Rūta Brice handled the paths and plantings. But the carving was always Ranka, alone, with chisel and stone.</p>

<p>He died on 13 April 2017, two days short of his 83rd birthday. The hill is now, in effect, a fixed text &mdash; no new sculptures will be added by him, and none have been commissioned by the museum to extend the work since. The twenty-six (or twenty-seven, depending on how you count) sculptures are the complete set.</p>

<h2 id="visit">How to actually visit it</h2>
<figure style="margin:2.4rem auto;max-width:760px;">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/daiga-at-site-map.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/daiga-at-site-map.jpg" alt="Daiga reading the official site map of the Hill of Dainas, Turaida" loading="lazy" decoding="async" style="width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:8px;">
  </picture>
  <figcaption style="margin-top:.6rem;font-size:.92rem;color:#7a6a55;font-style:italic;text-align:center;">The official site map at the entrance lists 26 sculptures laid out across the hill, with a Latvian-only key. Worth a minute of orientation before you walk in.</figcaption>
</figure>


<p>The Hill of Dainas sits on the south-eastern slope of the Turaida Museum Reserve, about a five-minute walk down from the red-brick castle and the wooden church. The entry ticket to the reserve covers it &mdash; you do not pay separately. Most visitors approach it as the last stop on a Turaida loop and give it ten or fifteen minutes between the castle and the car park. That is not enough.</p>

<p>The right minimum is <strong>1.5 to 2.5 hours</strong> for the Hill of Dainas plus the adjacent <strong>Dziesmu dārzs</strong>, separately from the castle and the Rose of Turaida grave. If you want to read every plaque, sit on the bench by the Mīlestības akmens for a while, and walk into the Song Garden amphitheater and stand on the stage where the Baltica concerts have happened, allow three hours.</p>

<p><strong>Best times of year:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>23&ndash;24 June (Jāņi).</strong> Folklore groups gather at <em>Jāņu akmens</em>. Bonfires nearby. The single most loaded night of the Latvian folk calendar. Note the museum has limited hours around the public holiday &mdash; check the schedule.</li>
<li><strong>7 July (the anniversary of the opening).</strong> Folklore concerts most years. The 40th anniversary fell in 2025.</li>
<li><strong>The Baltica festival year.</strong> The international folklore festival rotates between Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania every three years. When Latvia hosts, Turaida is consistently a venue. Latvia&rsquo;s next likely turn is 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Summer weekends generally.</strong> Folklore ensembles, brass bands, and ethnographic groups perform at the Song Garden. The hill is alive with sound rather than a static park.</li>
<li><strong>Late September and early October.</strong> Autumn color through the oak trees, low light on the granite, almost no other visitors. My personal favorite.</li>
<li><strong>Winter.</strong> The site is open year-round. Snow on the granite changes the reading entirely. Quietest of all.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>How to get there:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Self-drive.</strong> About 50 km north-east of Riga on the A2 motorway towards Sigulda. Free parking at the Turaida reserve.</li>
<li><strong>Train.</strong> Riga &rarr; Sigulda direct, about 90 minutes. From Sigulda station, bus 12 to Turaida (15 minutes), or a 4&ndash;5 km walk through the Gauja valley.</li>
<li><strong>Guided day trip.</strong> Our <a href="/excursions/sigulda-cesis-gauja-valley.html">Sigulda, C&#275;sis &amp; the Gauja Valley excursion</a> includes Turaida and gives the full backstory on the drive over. &euro;85 per adult, year-round.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Practical bits:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>The hill is a real hill. The terrain is gentle but uneven, with grassy slopes and gravel paths. Sturdy shoes if it has rained.</li>
<li>The plaques next to each sculpture are mostly in Latvian. The museum&rsquo;s printed catalogues and the Sigulda mobile app cover the English translations. Pick up a printed map at the reserve entrance.</li>
<li>There is a small café at the reserve. No food on the hill itself.</li>
<li>The Dziesmu dārzs amphitheater is downhill from the sculpture garden, a short walk. Many visitors miss it. Don&rsquo;t.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="worth">Why most visitors miss the point</h2>
<figure style="margin:2.4rem auto;max-width:760px;">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/dainu-kalns-bench-and-sculpture.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/blog-dainu-kalns/dainu-kalns-bench-and-sculpture.jpg" alt="Bench by the Stone of Love (Mīlestības akmens) at the Hill of Dainas, Turaida" loading="lazy" decoding="async" style="width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:8px;">
  </picture>
  <figcaption style="margin-top:.6rem;font-size:.92rem;color:#7a6a55;font-style:italic;text-align:center;">The bench by the Mīlestības akmens — the Stone of Love. Latvian wedding parties stop here on the day, lay the bouquet, take a photograph, drive on.</figcaption>
</figure>


<p>The standard Turaida visit goes castle, church, Rose of Turaida grave, ten minutes at the sculptures, back to the car. That is one of the more common ways travellers waste a Latvian afternoon.</p>

<p>The Hill of Dainas is not a sculpture park you walk through. It is a folk poem you read. Each stone cites a daina or a daina-cluster, and the ones you can&rsquo;t place will mean something to the local who walks past you with her grandchildren. The site holds a country&rsquo;s memory of itself in a way nothing else in modern Latvia quite manages, including the National Library and the Occupation Museum and the Freedom Monument. Those are about events and institutions. This is about songs. And in Latvia, songs are the older claim.</p>

<p>It also holds a quieter story about how empires end &mdash; not always with marches and bullets, but sometimes with a hill, a sculptor, a museum director, and a crowd that started gathering on Sundays to sing.</p>

<p>If you are coming to Latvia for the castles and the bog and the Art Nouveau, you should still come here. Bring an extra hour. Bring a few dainas in translation. Sit on the bench by the Stone of Love and look out across the valley to where the river bends. The dainas were sung on this hill long before there was a sculpture on it, and they are still being sung on it now.</p>

<p>That is not nothing. It may be the most Latvian thing you can do in an afternoon.</p>

<hr />

<p><em>Daiga Taur&#299;te is a licensed Latvian tour guide and co-founder of Barefoot Baltic. She runs small-group day excursions from Riga. She grew up here, spent two decades in London, came home in 2024. Barefoot Baltic is licensed by Latvia&rsquo;s Consumer Rights Protection Centre (PTAC), holds ATD passenger transport licence PS-01995, and is insured by BTA Baltic for civil liability.</em></p>

## Dainu Kalns Sculpture Field Guide: All 26 Stones at the Hill of Dainas, Turaida

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/dainu-kalns-sculpture-field-guide.html
**Published:** 2026-05-04
**Summary:** What every sculpture at Dainu Kalns means, the daina each one carries, and how to walk the hill in the right order. The complete English-language guide to Indulis Ranka's 26 granite sculptures at Turaida.

<p class="article-lede">If you have read the <a href="dainu-kalns-folk-song-hill-turaida.html">long version</a>, you know what Dainu Kalns is and how it got built between 1980 and 1985 while Latvia was still occupied. This is the companion piece. It is the field guide you bring with you on the hill, because the on-site plaques are mostly in Latvian and the English signage is thin. Every one of Indulis Ranka&rsquo;s twenty-six granite sculptures, the daina (or in two cases, the pair of dainas) it carries, the year it was placed, and the order in which a sensible walk takes them in.</p>

<p>The English text below is drawn from the museum&rsquo;s own published guide to Folk Song Park, with my notes from many walks of the hill added where the booklet runs short. If you want the booklet on paper, ask at the visitors centre by the underground granary at the entrance to the reserve.</p>

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, before the long version</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>26 sculptures, all by Indulis Ranka</strong>, all granite, scattered across roughly three hectares on the south-eastern slope of the Turaida Museum Reserve.</li>
<li><strong>Placed between 1982 and 2010.</strong> The earliest is <em>Veļu akmens</em>, the Stone of the Dear Departed, placed at a Liv burial site in autumn 1982. The most recent in the catalogue is the two-part <em>Krauklīša spārns &mdash; dārgumu krātuve</em>, Raven&rsquo;s Wing &mdash; Storehouse of Treasure, installed in 2004 at the Dalai Lama&rsquo;s request.</li>
<li><strong>Numbered 1 to 26 on the official map</strong>, which is also the rough walking order if you enter from the visitors centre side and finish near the Song Garden amphitheatre.</li>
<li><strong>Each sculpture carries a daina,</strong> usually engraved on it in Latvian. Many of the dainas were ones Krišjānis Barons collected himself between 1878 and 1915 and published in the six volumes of <em>Latvju Dainas</em>.</li>
<li>Allow <strong>two to three hours</strong> for a slow walk through all 26, plus the Song Garden. Most visitors give it twenty minutes and miss the point.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="how-to-use">How to use this guide on the hill</h2>

<p>The numbered map at the entrance kiosk lists the 26 sculptures in walking order. Walk it that way. The order is not random &mdash; the architects Jānis Rozentāls and Ilgvars Batrags laid out the paths so the sculptures move you through the daina cycle: birth and song first, then the gods and the calendar, then the life cycle, then the great folkloric figures, then the natural world, and out to the river at the end with water and pike.</p>

<p>For each entry below you get: the English title, the Latvian original, the daina line that is engraved on or associated with the stone (where the booklet gives one), and a note on what the sculpture is doing and when Ranka placed it. Sculptures that pair on a single base or share a write-up in the museum guide are listed together.</p>

<p>Two practical things to know on the day. First, the plaques on the hill are mostly Latvian-only. If you are reading along on a phone, the headings below are the on-site numbers, so you can match them as you go. Second, the trails between the sculptures matter as much as the sculptures themselves. There are four named trails (the Liv Trail, the Skandinieku stream path, M&#257;ra&rsquo;s trail, the Krišj&#257;nis Barons trail, and the Sun trail) running through and around the hill. They are listed at the end of this piece because they are worth knowing about, and most visitors don&rsquo;t.</p>

<h2 id="the-26">The 26 stones, in walking order</h2>

<h3>1. Dziedādama dzimu: I Was Born Singing</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Dziedādama dzimu, dziedādama augu / Pa gadskārtu maizīte.&rdquo;</em> A daina about a girl who was born singing, raised singing, and continued singing through her life&rsquo;s seasons. The first sculpture you meet on the standard route. A soft-shouldered granite stone with a small relief portrait of the hill itself carved into one face. It sets the premise: the Latvian relationship to song is not a hobby, it is a structural condition. The folk-song archive at the Latvian Institute of Literature, Folklore and Art holds something on the order of 1.34 million dainas. The work of cataloguing them is still going.</p>

<h3>2. Šī saule, viņa saule: This World and the World Beyond</h3>
<p>An eight-line daina about the relationship between Sun and Earth, engraved on the stone in spiral form. The viewer is meant to walk around the sculpture as they read. Indulis Ranka described his intention here as wanting visitors to be &ldquo;a bit more magical and ritualistic&rdquo; in their looking &mdash; not standing in front of an object but moving with it. The two-part fieldstone was sourced in Kurzeme, where the oldest layer of folk-song motifs was collected. The sculpture stands close to the former Turaida cemetery and was unveiled at the international Baltica 2000 folklore festival.</p>

<h3>3. Neguli, saulīte, ābeļu dārzā: Sleep Not, O Sun, in the Apple Orchard</h3>
<p>The daina addresses the Sun directly as a girl-child and tells her not to dawdle, not to sleep among the apples. The foundation stone of the sculpture is shaped like the heart of an apple. The Sun must rise before dawn so that the day can begin. This is one of the early sculptures on the hill, reinstalled in 1992 in its current position. It catches the morning light cleanly if you come up early.</p>

<h3>4. Austras koks: The Tree of Austra</h3>
<p>Austra&rsquo;s Tree is one of the deepest cosmological images in the Latvian dainas. The world-tree, with roots in the earth and branches in the sky, around which day and night, life and death are organised. Auseklis, the Morning Star, often sits in the canopy. The sculpture renders the tree as a tall stone trunk with rays and stars, signalling the dawn breaking on a country waking up. It was unveiled on 2 July 1990, during the 20th Latvian Song and Dance Festival &mdash; the first festival in fifty years to fully restore the pre-1940 national repertoire and openly fly the Latvian flag. Three new shoots are carved into one side, &ldquo;nothing at all which can stop the arrival of the light.&rdquo;</p>

<h3>5. Lībiešu putns: The Liv Bird</h3>
<p>One of two sculptures on the hill explicitly placed for the Livs (L&#299;vi), the Finno-Ugric people who lived along the lower Gauja and the Latvian coast for centuries before the Latvians as we know them coalesced. The bird sits ready to wake and sing. Three small symbols are carved on the natural granite at the top: a lark, a fish, a snake. The lark is the messenger; the eagle is the king of birds. The sculpture was unveiled at an international &ldquo;small nations&rdquo; festival of Liv-Estonian-Latvian-Finn-Hungarian folklore groups held at Turaida.</p>

<h3>6. Jāņu akmens: The Summer Solstice Stone</h3>
<p>The night and morning of 23&ndash;24 June &mdash; J&#257;ņi &mdash; is the highest-stakes day on the Latvian folk calendar. Bonfires, oak-leaf wreaths, all-night singing, the search for the blooming fern. The sculpture shows two young people embraced by the Sun on J&#257;ņi morning, the Sun giving them strength and fertility. Auseklis, the Morning Star, witnesses. The stone was placed in 1991 and sits on the side of M&#257;ra&rsquo;s trail. If you visit on Midsummer eve this is the centre of the gathering on the hill.</p>

<h3>7. Dziesmu tēvs: Father of Song</h3>
<p>The visual centre of the hill and the place to slow down longest. The sculpture &ldquo;symbolises the memory of the people, their wisdom about life, and the preservation and transfer from generation to generation of Latvian folk songs.&rdquo; On one face, a respected old man who protected the songs and made up new ones &mdash; &ldquo;a song for him, a song for her, for a piece of bread.&rdquo; On the other face, three generations of singers stand together. A defender stands beside them, a young man with a chest that holds the dowry of songs. The area around <em>Dziesmu tēvs</em> is the site of folklore and ethnographic concerts every summer. Visitors are invited to sing their own folk songs here. This is also the sculpture in front of which the banned red-white-red Latvian flag was raised on 13 July 1988, during the Baltica &rsquo;88 festival, for the first time since 1940.</p>

<h3>8. Bij&rsquo; manam kumeļam: My Steed Had&hellip;</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Bij&rsquo; manam kumeļam / Zvaigžņu sega mugurā.&rdquo;</em> &ldquo;My steed had a blanket of stars on its back.&rdquo; A daina that praises the horse as the farmer&rsquo;s indispensable partner. Mythological horses pull the cart of the Sun across the sky. The sons of God ride out of the sea on grey horses with golden reins. Auseklis appears on a horse given by the Sun. Laima, goddess of fortune, presents a good horse to those she favours. Even the Liv chronicle of Turaida 1191 has a Horse of Destiny in it. The sculpture was unveiled in 1996 at a gathering where the assembled crowd sang horse-dainas together.</p>

<h3>9. Bitenieka līgaviņa: The Beekeeper&rsquo;s Bride</h3>
<p>A wedding-cycle daina dedicated to the beekeeper&rsquo;s bride. The bee is one of the oldest occupational layers in Latvian folk culture, and the bee-songs are some of the gentlest. The bride carries her trousseau, woven from threads of song. Beehives are placed nearby, in the spirit of the daina. The plaque also notes that since 2012 the Latvian folk-song collection &mdash; Barons&rsquo;s Dainu Skapis (Cabinet of Folk Songs), 217,996 cards in the original count &mdash; has been registered on the UNESCO Memory of the World register, confirming its status as a globally significant cultural heritage object.</p>

<h3>10. Veļu akmens: Stone of the Dear Departed</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Celieties, vēļu māmiņa, / Es pacelšu velēniņu.&rdquo;</em> The first sculpture placed on the hill, in autumn 1982, three years before the official opening. The veļi are the souls of the dear departed, who in Latvian folk belief continue their lives in a parallel world. After death the soul is met by Veļu māte, the Mother of Souls, who brings it across. Autumn is the season when the souls rise from the earth like a bank of fog and spend a little more time with their living people. The sculpture is a Latvian fieldstone whose natural texture reads as wave and mist. The film director Ansis Epners recorded the installation. He described the stone hanging from cables, swinging like a pendulum, and settling obediently into its foundation while a fall of oak leaves came down around the cameras. &ldquo;The moment when the first stone prepared for Folk Song Hill nestled into its foundation, which had the design of mittens.&rdquo;</p>

<h3>11. Mātes un meitas (Grūtas domas): Mother and Daughter (Difficult Thought)</h3>
<p>One sculpture, two names. The daina layer underneath is the genre of mother-to-daughter songs sung at every threshold of a girl&rsquo;s life: birth, the spinning wheel, the eve of marriage, the moment a child of her own is laid in her arms. The piece reads as a mother lifting her child to the Sun and an Earth that is &ldquo;slowly trembling&rdquo; at the daughter&rsquo;s leaving. The whole genre of <em>tautasdziesmas</em> is, in one sense, this: a transmission from one woman to the next, generation after generation, with everything important hidden inside four lines.</p>

<h3>12. Trīs jaunas māsas: Three Young Sisters</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Trīs jaunas māsas / Sēd rožu dārzā.&rdquo;</em> Three young sisters in a rose garden. The sculpture honours the fact that the Latvian folk-song repertoire is, almost entirely, women&rsquo;s work. As Garlieb Merkel observed two centuries ago: the art of Latvian song is in the hands of women, because young women are the only ones who can still feel joy under a heavy burden. Singing accompanied every task &mdash; tending livestock, threshing grain, weaving the textile that itself often carried songs woven into the pattern. The orange-and-red rock the sculpture was carved from sparkles in particular ways depending on the light: rain on it, fresh snow, summer haze, frost at the turn of the year. Folklore groups gathered here most often during the Awakening years. By common agreement it is the most sonorous spot on the hill.</p>

<h3>13. Sapņotājs: Dreamer (paired with 15. Domātājs &mdash; Thinker)</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Ar varīti jūs kundziņi, / Ar padomu bāleliņi; / Ar varīti nevarēja, / Padomiņu pievarēt.&rdquo;</em> A song of resistance against the nobility who ruled the land. The two paired figures &mdash; a sleeper and a thinker &mdash; conjure thoughts at the same time. Folk songs in Latvia, the booklet notes, do not praise war, violence, or hatred. Hatred and fierceness cannot create anything. Life and freedom in one&rsquo;s own fatherland are the values, and that fatherland is defended &ldquo;with strong words and thoughts whenever that proves to be necessary. I lay my head on the moss to protect my fatherland.&rdquo;</p>

<h3>14. Spīdolas akmens: The Stone of Spīdola</h3>
<p>Sp&#299;dola is a character from <em>L&#257;čplēsis</em> (Bearslayer), Andrejs Pumpurs&rsquo;s 1888 national epic. She is the wisdom-keeper, the figure of perpetual self-renewal, often paired with the warrior Bearslayer himself. The sculpture is the one with a portrait of Krišj&#257;nis Barons carved into it, surrounded by the ornamental motifs of Sp&#299;dola&rsquo;s folkloric world. The piece argues, visually, that the creative strength of folk song (Sp&#299;dola) and the work of preservation (Barons) are the same energy in two forms. It is one of the densest single sculptures on the hill in symbolic load. Sit on the bench opposite for a few minutes if there is one free.</p>

<h3>15. Domātājs: Thinker</h3>
<p>See entry 13 (paired with Dreamer above; they share a write-up in the museum guide and stand near each other on the hill).</p>

<h3>16. Krasts: Beach (paired with the Ring of Linden Trees)</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Liepas zied, liepas zied / Baltajiem ziediņiem; / Sādām liepu mežu, / Apkārt mūzu pagalmiņu.&rdquo;</em> A daina celebrating stands of trees around the farm. The sculpture sits inside a planted ring of linden trees that changes through the seasons; both the sculpture and the trees are meant to be read together. The ancient daina motifs underneath &mdash; linden, oak, river, beach &mdash; are the most lyrical layer of the corpus. The form of the sculpture invites you to imagine river-rounded stones on the Vidzeme coast, &ldquo;a girl sunbathing on an early summer morning,&rdquo; and the line &ldquo;I ran my sister through water and stone, sprinkling her with water and cleaving her with stone.&rdquo;</p>

<h3>17. Mīlestības akmens: The Stone of Love</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Dievin, tavu likumiņu, / Laimīn, tavu lemumiņu; / Sveši ar sveša satikās, / Mīļu mūžu nodzīvoja.&rdquo;</em> God&rsquo;s law, Laima&rsquo;s decree: two strangers met and lived a sweet life. The wedding-cycle is the most photographed part of the dainas, and the sculpture is the most photographed part of the hill. Latvian wedding parties bring their bouquets here. It is a quiet tradition, not advertised. If you visit on a Saturday in May or June you will see brides in white walking up to a granite boulder with their flowers and laying them on it before driving on to the reception. Couples also leave handwritten notes here.</p>

<h3>18. Kupenas, ziedu kupenas: Snowdrifts / Drifts of Flowers</h3>
<p>One of the four sculptures (with Flying Birds, First Buds, and Little Cloud) that share a daina-of-nature write-up in the museum guide: <em>&ldquo;Ai, ievu zemīte, / Tavu jaukumiņu! / Smildziņa ziedēja, / Sudraba ziediem.&rdquo;</em> A song celebrating the beauty of Latvia. The sculpture is a wave of low rounded forms, the drift of flowers reading as snowdrift in a different season. Through the hill in summer the actual flowers in the meadow underline the sculpted ones.</p>

<h3>19. Lidojošie putni: Flying Birds</h3>
<p>Birdsong is everywhere in the dainas. The cuckoo, the lark, the nightingale &mdash; each carries its own messages, omens, season. This sculpture renders the birds in a low cluster of forms. Look at it against the sky.</p>

<h3>20. Pirmie ziedi: First Buds</h3>
<p>The miraculous opening of flower buds, in the rhythm of nature. Smaller than its neighbours and easy to walk past. The whole nature-cluster (18&ndash;21) on this part of the hill is built around the principle that the natural world&rsquo;s small openings &mdash; a bud, a cloud, a bird&rsquo;s flight &mdash; are themselves the ground that the dainas grew from.</p>

<h3>21. Mākonītis: Little Cloud</h3>
<p>Piles of clouds in the field of the sky. The sculpture is rounded, almost weightless against the granite forms around it. This is also the start of the <strong>Krišj&#257;nis Barons trail</strong> &mdash; the 300-metre path that runs from the &ldquo;Little Cloud&rdquo; sculpture down through old oak, linden, and ash trees, past the small Dainup&#299;te River, all the way to the &ldquo;Dainas&rdquo; homestead by the Gauja where Barons spent his last summer in 1922. Both the sculpture and the trail were positioned here deliberately.</p>

<h3>22. Saules taka: Path of the Sun</h3>
<p><em>&ldquo;Sauli dej&rsquo; rītmiņā, / Zelta sētā vidiņā.&rdquo;</em> A song about the Sun dancing on the horizon. A three-part sculpture standing where the Sun trail crosses the Krišj&#257;nis Barons trail. Three words are engraved on the symbolic Sun pole &mdash; &ldquo;Sleeping,&rdquo; &ldquo;Awakening,&rdquo; &ldquo;Dancing&rdquo; &mdash; tracing the Sun&rsquo;s daily arc as the dainas track it. Installed in 1994. The sculpture pairs with the trail itself: about a kilometre of forest path along the southern side of Folk Song Hill, particularly worth walking in spring when the white anemones come up.</p>

<h3>23. Dainu kalns: Folk Song Hill</h3>
<p>The sculpture that names the hill. It sits at the foot of the Krišj&#257;nis Barons trail, near the bank of the Gauja, far enough from the central cluster that many visitors don&rsquo;t reach it. They should. Walk the trail down, sit beside this stone for a few minutes, and walk back. The whole site reads differently on the way back up than on the way down.</p>

<h3>24. Peldētāja: Swimmer (paired with 25. Zaļā līdaka &mdash; O, Green Pike)</h3>
<p>Latvia has 500 km of Baltic coastline and the Gauja runs through this whole reserve. Many dainas honour water. The sculpture group of <em>Peldētāja</em> and <em>Zaļā līdaka</em> reads against the Gauja itself, which you can hear from this part of the hill in summer. The Liv legend of the green pike &mdash; the fish playing in the waters of the Gauja &mdash; is the local folkloric anchor. The Latvian daina line behind the swimmer is &ldquo;I wore white,&rdquo; meaning purity, hard work, fair life.</p>

<h3>25. Zaļā līdaka: O, Green Pike</h3>
<p>See entry 24 (paired with Swimmer; the green pike is the Liv folkloric companion to the daina swimmer).</p>

<h3>26. Krauklīša spārns: dārgumu krātuve &mdash; Raven&rsquo;s Wing &mdash; Storehouse of Treasure</h3>
<p>The closing sculpture of the catalogue, installed in 2004. Two granite parts, with a treasury vessel donated at the request of the Dalai Lama, who visited Latvia and asked that the gift be installed at Folk Song Hill. The sculpture argues that the cultural treasures of any nation must be preserved &mdash; just as the Tibetan Endless Knot carved on the stela here, and the wing of the wise raven, are signs of nation-faith and protection across cultures. Folk Song Hill, the booklet says, has been visited over the years by guests from far and wide. They learn about the Latvian dainas; they take away the same lesson that the dainas teach &mdash; that heartfelt and true relationships among peoples are possible only through harmony and mutual respect.</p>

<h2 id="trails">The four named trails (most visitors miss these)</h2>

<p>The sculptures are the headline. The trails between and around them are the whole environment. Four are named, marked on the larger reserve map, and worth a half-hour each if you have the time.</p>

<p><strong>The Liv Trail</strong> (<em>L&#299;biešu taka</em>) starts in Folk Song Hill and ends in Folk Song Garden. The route runs through what the museum identifies as Liv landscape features, with old Liv settlement traces and a Devonian-era cliff section. If you are interested in the pre-Latvian layer of this country, this is the trail to walk.</p>

<p><strong>The Skandinieku stream</strong> is a small brook that members of the folklore group Skandinieki cleaned and exposed during a 1982 working bee. The water comes from a cave inside the deepest cave in the Turaida reserve and stays at about 5&deg;C even in summer. Mosses and lichens cover the cliff floor; ferns hang from the upper edges. The brook surfaces in two places between Folk Song Hill and Folk Song Garden.</p>

<p><strong>M&#257;ra&rsquo;s trail</strong> runs from Folk Song Hill to Folk Song Garden by another route. The folk tradition behind it is that on the morning of 25 March, M&#257;ra&rsquo;s Day, people would wash themselves in rivers, brooks, and healing wells. The custom predates Christianity in Latvia.</p>

<p><strong>The Krišj&#257;nis Barons trail</strong> is the 300-metre path described under sculpture 21 (Little Cloud). It leads to the &ldquo;Dainas&rdquo; homestead in the Gauja valley where Barons spent his last summer in 1922. There is a small commemorative marker at the homestead. The trail itself follows what is almost certainly a route Barons walked in his time at Turaida.</p>

<p><strong>The Sun trail</strong> (<em>Saules taka</em>) is described under sculpture 22. About 1 km along the southern side of the hill.</p>

<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Iesim cauri Dainu kalnam, ne tikai apkārt.</em></p><cite>&mdash; What I tell visitors at the entrance kiosk: &ldquo;let&rsquo;s go through the Hill of Dainas, not just around it.&rdquo;</cite></div>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>

<p>Most visitors to Turaida get the castle, the Rose of Turaida grave, and a brisk walk through the sculpture garden in about three and a half hours, then drive back to Riga. That itinerary will give you a perfectly fine afternoon. It will also give you about a tenth of what is actually here.</p>

<p>The Hill of Dainas earns the time you give it. Twenty minutes returns one impression. Two hours returns the dainas themselves, in the right order, with the trees and the river and the four named trails as the connective tissue. Three hours, on a quiet weekday, returns something else again &mdash; the long Latvian relationship to song that Indulis Ranka was carving in granite for thirty-five years. He died in April 2017 and the catalogue is closed at twenty-six. There is not going to be a twenty-seventh.</p>

<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions about the Dainu Kalns sculptures</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-1">
      How many sculptures are there at Dainu Kalns?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-1" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>26 in the official Folk Song Park catalogue, all by Indulis Ranka, placed between 1982 and 2010. The numbered map at the entrance lists them in walking order. Some sources count 27 if they include the Liv Bird stone separately or count one of the multi-part sculptures as two.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-2">
      Are the plaques in English?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Mostly Latvian. The on-site plaques carry the daina line each sculpture references, almost always in Latvian only. The museum&rsquo;s printed Folk Song Park guide booklet has the English translations, available at the visitors centre. The Sigulda mobile app also covers some of them. The list above is the field guide most English-language visitors are looking for.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-3">
      Who carved them?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-3" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>All 26 are by Indulis Ranka (1934&ndash;2017), a Riga sculptor who taught himself granite carving in his thirties. He worked alone with a small truck and a portable crane, locating glacial-erratic boulders in fields across Latvia and bringing them to Turaida one truckload at a time. The collaborators on the larger project were the museum director Anna Jurk&#257;ne, the architects J&#257;nis Rozent&#257;ls and Ilgvars Batrags, and the landscape designers Aivars Irbe and R&#363;ta Brice.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-4">
      Which sculpture is the centrepiece?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-4" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Number 7, <em>Dziesmu tēvs</em> &mdash; the Father of Songs. It is the visual centre of the hill, with three generations of singers carved around the head of Krišj&#257;nis Barons. It is also the sculpture in front of which the banned red-white-red Latvian flag was raised on 13 July 1988, during the Baltica &rsquo;88 festival. Within ten weeks the Soviet Latvian authorities had relegalised the flag.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-5">
      Which is the oldest sculpture on the hill?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-5" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Number 10, <em>Veļu akmens</em>, the Stone of the Dear Departed. Placed in autumn 1982, three years before the official opening of Folk Song Hill, on the site of an ancient Liv settlement. The placement was a deliberate marker: the souls of the ancestors first, on Liv ground, before any of the rest of the hill was built.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-6">
      Which is the most recent sculpture?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-6" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Number 26, <em>Krauklīša spārns &mdash; dārgumu krātuve</em>, Raven&rsquo;s Wing &mdash; Storehouse of Treasure, installed in 2004 at the request of the Dalai Lama, who donated the storehouse vessel and asked that it be placed at Folk Song Hill. The Tibetan Endless Knot carved into the stela is the cross-cultural anchor of the piece.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-7">
      How long should I plan for the sculpture park?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-7" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>For all 26 sculptures plus the Song Garden amphitheatre, allow two to three hours. For one of the four named trails (Liv, Skandinieku, M&#257;ra&rsquo;s, Krišj&#257;nis Barons, or Sun) add another 30&ndash;60 minutes. The full reserve including the castle, the Rose of Turaida grave, and the wooden church wants a half-day if you mean to do justice to it.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-8">
      Where is the Krišjānis Barons portrait sculpture?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>There are actually two. The Father of Songs sculpture (number 7) carries a portrait of Barons surrounded by three generations of singers. The Stone of Sp&#299;dola (number 14) carries a smaller portrait of Barons set inside the iconography of the L&#257;čplēsis epic. Together they make the argument that Barons&rsquo;s preservation work is the same energy as the creative work in the dainas themselves. The standalone Riga monument to Barons by Teodors Zaļkalns is in V&#275;rmane Garden, not at Turaida.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-9">
      Is the daina text engraved on each sculpture?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>For most of the sculptures, yes &mdash; either carved into the stone itself or on the small plaque next to it. The two clearest examples to go and read in person are <em>This World and the World Beyond</em> (number 2), where the daina is carved spirally so you have to walk around the stone to read it, and <em>Path of the Sun</em> (number 22), where three single words from the daina are engraved on the symbolic Sun pole.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-10">
      Is there an entry fee for the Hill of Dainas?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The Hill of Dainas is inside the Turaida Museum Reserve and is covered by the standard reserve entry ticket (around &euro;7&ndash;9 for adults, less for students and children, free for under-7s). The reserve is open year-round; check the Turaida Museum Reserve website for current opening hours and the schedule of folklore events at the Song Garden.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-dk-11">
      Can I find a printed map?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-dk-11" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes. The visitors centre at the underground granary at the entrance to the reserve carries the official Folk Song Park guide booklet (the source of the English translations above) and a printed numbered map of the 26 sculptures. Pick both up. The numbers on the map match the headings in this guide.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>
</section>

  <p><strong>Companion piece:</strong> The longer history of how the Hill of Dainas came to be built between 1980 and 1985, the role of the museum director Anna Jurk&#257;ne, the 1988 flag moment, and the Singing Revolution context is in <a href="dainu-kalns-folk-song-hill-turaida.html">Dainu Kalns: A Sculpture Garden Carved Under Soviet Rule</a>. For Krišj&#257;nis Barons himself, the man whose 217,996 cards make up the source material for most of these sculptures, the standalone biography is <a href="krisjanis-barons-father-of-dainas.html">here</a>.</p>
</div>

If you would like a half-day at Turaida with a licensed Latvian guide who walks the hill the slow way, the dainas in the right order, the trails included &mdash; we run the trip year-round at &euro;85 per adult.</p>

## Day Trips from Riga: An Honest Answer (2026)

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/day-trips-from-riga.html
**Published:** 2026-04-14
**Summary:** A licensed Latvian guide's honest comparison of the three best day trips from Riga: Rundāle, Sigulda, Ķemeri — prices, times, and who each is wrong for.

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<p>There are three day trips from Riga I would send any traveller on without hesitation. All three depart from central Riga, return the same day, run in small groups of no more than eight, and are guided by a licensed Latvian guide.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Rundāle Palace, Bauska Castle, and the Ķemeri Bog boardwalk</strong> — €85 per adult, 10 hours, runs year-round. The big baroque set-piece day, south towards the Lithuanian border. Includes lunch.</li>
<li><strong>Sigulda, Cēsis, and the Gauja Valley</strong> — €85 per adult, 10 hours, runs year-round (April–October is best). The forest-and-castles day, northeast, in Latvia's oldest national park.</li>
<li><strong>Ķemeri Bog at sunrise, and Jūrmala on the way home</strong> — €45 per adult, 6 hours, <strong>May–August only</strong>. The wild-Latvia day. 4:30 AM pickup. Back by 10:30 AM.</li>
</ul>
<p>All three include hotel pickup in central Riga, an air-conditioned minibus, a licensed guide, all applicable entrance fees, and bottled water. Reserve with nothing upfront; a 20% deposit is taken 48 hours before departure. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.</p>
<p>If you only have one day, skip to the decision tree. If you want the longer version of each, keep scrolling.</p>

<h2>How to pick in 30 seconds</h2>
<p>Four questions.</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Is it May through August, with a good weather forecast?</strong> If yes, you can actually do Ķemeri at sunrise <em>and</em> Rundāle in the afternoon, because the Ķemeri trip gets you back to Riga by 10:30 AM. You'll be a zombie by 10 PM, but you'll have seen the best of Latvia in one day.</li>
<li><strong>History person or nature person?</strong> History → Rundāle. Nature → Sigulda or Ķemeri.</li>
<li><strong>Can you handle a 4:30 AM pickup?</strong> Yes → Ķemeri is in the running. No → it's between Rundāle and Sigulda.</li>
<li><strong>Have you seen a baroque palace in the last year?</strong> Yes → Sigulda. No → Rundāle. It's one of the best-restored baroque palaces in this part of Europe and you won't get another chance easily.</li>
</ol>
<p>That's the entire decision tree.</p>
<h2>Who these trips aren't for</h2>
<ul>
<li>People who want a packed itinerary with a new stop every twenty minutes.</li>
<li>People who prefer a big coach with a microphone and fifty strangers.</li>
<li>People who want luxury-spa-level comfort. My van is comfortable and new, but it's a van, not a limousine.</li>
<li>People who want to tick off sights without hearing the story behind them. I will tell you the story whether you asked or not, because Latvia without its story is just landscape, and you can get landscape anywhere.</li>
</ul>
<p>If any of that sounds like a deal-breaker, there are plenty of good coach operators in Riga and I'll happily recommend one.</p>
<hr />
<h2>Now the longer version</h2>
<p>The most common question I get in the first twenty minutes of any tour is "Where else should we go?" The second is "We've only got one day spare — what do we do with it?" I've been answering both for two and a half years now, sometimes five times a day in August, and the long version is below.</p>
<h3>Why go anywhere at all when Riga is right there</h3>
<p>A fair question. Riga is good. Three full days in Riga is the sweet spot, to my mind: one day for the Old Town, one day for the Art Nouveau district and the Central Market, one day with no plan.</p>
<p>But there's a thing that happens to every visitor around the second afternoon. You've walked the Old Town twice, you've seen the Freedom Monument and the House of the Blackheads, you've tried Black Balsam and made a face, and you start to think: is this it? Is this Latvia?</p>
<p>No. Riga is about 620 square kilometres. Latvia is about 65,000. The rest of it — the forests, the castles, the old fishing villages, the bogs, the manor houses, the cold clean beaches — starts the moment you cross the ring road, and that's where I think most travellers fall in love with the country, not in the Old Town. The Old Town is the welcome. The rest is the place.</p>
<p>That's why day trips from Riga matter disproportionately here. In Paris or Rome you'd feel a bit guilty leaving the city. In Riga you'd be missing the point if you didn't.</p>
<h3>Rundāle Palace, Bauska Castle, and the Ķemeri Bog</h3>
<p>Rundāle is the one your Instagram friends will recognise before you even open the photos. Baroque palace, built in the 1730s by Bartolomeo Rastrelli — the same Italian architect who did the Winter Palace in St Petersburg — commissioned by the Duke of Courland for reasons that mostly involved trying to out-Versailles Versailles on a much smaller budget. He nearly pulled it off. The White Hall is the room you'll remember. The rose garden in late June is the other one.</p>
<p>We spend roughly two hours at Rundāle itself — long enough for a proper guided walk through the state rooms and the gardens, short enough that nobody gets museum-legged. Then we drive fifteen minutes to Bauska Castle, a ruined medieval fortress of the Livonian Order with a tower you can climb for a view over the Mūsa river. After Bauska we head to a quiet country restaurant I've used for years for a sit-down Latvian lunch — potatoes, pickled herring, black rye bread — before driving on to a gentle hour on the boardwalk into the Great Ķemeri Bog, a 10,000-year-old raised peatland older than the pyramids. Then back to Riga for the evening.</p>
<h3>Sigulda, Cēsis, and the Gauja Valley</h3>
<p>The northeastern day. Gauja National Park is Latvia's oldest, set up in 1973, and it runs along the valley of the Gauja river — the longest river that stays inside Latvia's borders the whole way. The valley itself is the nearest thing we have to a mountain landscape: sandstone cliffs, pine forests, and three castles close enough together that you can see all of them in a day.</p>
<p>The day starts at Turaida — the red brick castle on the ridge above the river, built in 1214, restored in the 20th century, and the home of the "Rose of Turaida" legend, which I'll tell you about on the drive up. Across the valley are the ruins of Sigulda's medieval castle and, next to them, the 19th-century neo-Gothic Sigulda New Castle, which looks like something off a romantic postcard. There's a cable car across the valley that I always take people on, because the view from the middle of the ride is worth the whole trip.</p>
<p>Then we drive forty minutes east to Cēsis. This is the part of the day I think people don't expect. Cēsis is a small medieval town with a castle, a bakery I go out of my way for, and cobbled streets that have somehow survived everything the 20th century threw at them. It's the prettiest town in Latvia, in my opinion. I'm aware I'm supposed to say Riga, and I will, but if you asked me where I'd want to live in Latvia if I didn't live in Riga, it's Cēsis.</p>
<h3>The Ķemeri bog walk and Jūrmala</h3>
<p>This is the trip most people don't know to ask for, and it's probably the most Latvian thing you can do in six hours.</p>
<p>Ķemeri National Park is a 381-square-kilometre protected area about 50 km west of Riga. Most of it is boreal forest, wetland, and bog. The Great Ķemeri Bog Boardwalk is roughly 3 km of flat wooden planking across a 10,000-year-old raised bog, with a viewing tower in the middle that you can climb for the horizon photograph everyone comes for. Small black pools between cottongrass. Carnivorous sundew plants if you know where to look, and I know where to look. In the right light it's the kind of place that makes people stop talking, which is rare in a group of eight.</p>
<p>The catch — and it's a real one — is that it's only worth it at sunrise. At midday in August it's hot and full and you'll wonder what the fuss is about. At sunrise in May, June, or July, with mist lifting off the bog and the boardwalk empty, it's the best free attraction in Latvia. Which is why my tour starts at 4:30 in the morning.</p>
<p>After the bog we drive 25 minutes to Jūrmala — Latvia's beach town, a long ribbon of wooden Art Nouveau villas along the Baltic coast, a legendary Soviet-era resort that is now a quiet, slightly faded place with a very good bakery, a few restored spa hotels, and the best people-watching in the country if you go on a Sunday morning. We walk Jomas Street for an hour or so, get coffee, and I have you back at your Riga hotel by 10:30 AM in time for hotel breakfast.</p>
<h2>The day trips I don't run, and why</h2>
<p>People ask about these, so let me save you the research.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Hill of Crosses (Lithuania).</strong> Photogenic, meaningful, 2.5 hours south. I don't run it because it's really a Lithuanian site and it's a long day in the van for one stop. Do it from Vilnius.</li>
<li><strong>Kuldīga.</strong> Widest waterfall in Europe, beautiful UNESCO-listed old centre. Three hours each way. Twelve-hour day. Nobody's happy at the end of it. Worth a full weekend, not a day trip.</li>
<li><strong>Cape Kolka.</strong> The point where the Baltic Sea meets the Gulf of Riga. Wild, windswept, deeply atmospheric. 3.5 hours each way. Same problem.</li>
<li><strong>The Soviet secret bunker at Līgatne.</strong> Fascinating if you're into that era, but only a 90-minute visit and the logistics don't hold up for a full-day price. I fold it into private-hire days.</li>
<li><strong>Tallinn.</strong> Yes, people ask. It's 4 hours north in another country. A day trip there is a bus trip, not a tour. If you want to see Tallinn, spend two nights.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Can I do any of these without a guide?</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Rundāle:</strong> Yes, by bus via Bauska. Takes effort and timing, but it's doable. Allow a full day.</li>
<li><strong>Sigulda:</strong> Yes, by direct train from Riga. Straightforward. The cable car and Turaida are both walkable from the station.</li>
<li><strong>Ķemeri at sunrise:</strong> Realistically, no. There's no public transport at 4 AM, and the Ķemeri train station is 3.5 km from the boardwalk. You'd need a taxi pre-booked the night before, and you'd miss the point of sunrise by the time you found coffee.</li>
</ul>
<p>If you want to do these without me, I'll tell you exactly how in an email. I would rather you see Latvia than not.</p>
<h2>The practical bits</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Price:</strong> Rundāle and Sigulda, €85 per adult; Ķemeri, €45. All include hotel pickup, air-conditioned minibus, licensed guide, entrance fees where applicable, and bottled water. Rundāle includes a sit-down lunch at a countryside restaurant.</li>
<li><strong>Child price:</strong> €60 on Rundāle and Sigulda, €35 on Ķemeri.</li>
<li><strong>Group size:</strong> Maximum eight. Often fewer. Never more.</li>
<li><strong>Languages:</strong> English and Latvian by default; Russian, German, or French on request, subject to guide availability.</li>
<li><strong>Pickup:</strong> Central Riga hotels only. Tell me your hotel when you book.</li>
<li><strong>Booking:</strong> Reserve today with nothing upfront. 20% deposit taken 48 hours before departure. Balance paid on the day.</li>
<li><strong>Cancellation:</strong> Free up to 24 hours before. Within 24 hours, non-refundable.</li>
<li><strong>Two days in a row?</strong> Yes. Rundāle then Sigulda is the classic Latvia-in-48-hours pairing.</li>
<li><strong>Accessibility:</strong> Ķemeri boardwalk is fully flat and suitable for pushchairs and limited mobility. Sigulda involves some uphill sections and steps at Turaida. Rundāle is mostly flat inside the palace but includes cobblestones at Bauska. Ask me before booking if you have specific needs.</li>
</ul>
<h2>A final thing</h2>
<p>The version of Latvia most travellers get — two days in Riga, a photo of the Freedom Monument, a plate of something pickled — is a perfectly fine holiday, and I don't want to talk anyone out of it. But the version that starts to matter to you, the one you come home and talk about at dinner parties six months later, almost always involves a morning somewhere outside the city. The bog at sunrise. The cable car across the valley. The countryside lunch table with the dog asleep beneath it.</p>
<p>That's the whole argument for day trips from Riga, and it's the reason I started doing this.</p>
<p>If any of the three above sound like your kind of day, the excursion pages have more detail, proper photos, and the booking links. If you're not sure which to pick, write to me at info@barefootbaltic.com — tell me what kind of traveller you are and I'll tell you which. I'd rather you book the right one than any one.</p>

            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-daytripsfr-which-day-trip-from-riga-should-i-pick-i" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Four questions. Is it May through August with a good weather forecast? If yes, you can do Ķemeri at sunrise and still be back at your hotel by 10:30 AM. History person or nature person? History goes to Rundāle; nature goes to Sigulda or Ķemeri. Can you handle a 4:30 AM pickup? Yes puts Ķemeri in play; no means it&#x27;s between Rundāle and Sigulda. Have you seen a baroque palace in the last year? If yes, pick Sigulda. If no, pick Rundāle — it&#x27;s one of the best-restored baroque palaces in this part of Europe and you won&#x27;t get another chance easily.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-daytripsfr-can-you-combine-emeri-and-rund-le-on-the">
            Can you combine Ķemeri and Rundāle on the same day?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-daytripsfr-can-you-combine-emeri-and-rund-le-on-the" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, only in May through August. The Ķemeri sunrise tour starts at 4:30 AM pickup and has you back at your Riga hotel by 10:30 AM. That leaves the afternoon free for the Rundāle excursion, which runs as a full day with lunch at a countryside restaurant. You&#x27;ll be a zombie by 10 PM, but you&#x27;ll have seen the best of Latvia in one day. The pairing only works in the Ķemeri-season window because that&#x27;s the only excursion short enough to leave the afternoon free.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-daytripsfr-can-i-do-day-trips-from-riga-without-a-g">
            Can I do day trips from Riga without a guide?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-daytripsfr-can-i-do-day-trips-from-riga-without-a-g" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Rundāle: yes, by public bus via Bauska. Takes effort and timing, but it&#x27;s doable — allow a full day. Sigulda: yes, by direct train from Riga. Straightforward, and the cable car and Turaida Castle are both walkable from the station. Ķemeri at sunrise: realistically, no. There&#x27;s no public transport at 4 AM, and Ķemeri train station is 3.5 km from the boardwalk. You&#x27;d need a pre-booked taxi the night before, and you&#x27;d miss the point of sunrise by the time you found coffee. If you want to do these without me, write to me and I&#x27;ll tell you exactly how. I&#x27;d rather you see Latvia than not.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-daytripsfr-which-day-trips-from-riga-should-i-skip">
            Which day trips from Riga should I skip?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-daytripsfr-which-day-trips-from-riga-should-i-skip" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>The ones that are technically possible but don&#x27;t make sense as a day trip. Hill of Crosses is really a Lithuanian site and a long day in the van for one stop — do it from Vilnius. Kuldīga has the widest waterfall in Europe and a UNESCO-listed old centre, but it&#x27;s three hours each way, which makes for a twelve-hour day nobody enjoys. Worth a full weekend instead. Cape Kolka is wild and atmospheric, same problem. The Soviet bunker at Līgatne is only a 90-minute visit and doesn&#x27;t hold up for a full-day price. Tallinn is four hours north in another country — that&#x27;s a bus trip, not a tour. Spend two nights if you want to see it.</p>

## The Freedom Monument (Brīvības piemineklis), Riga: Milda, the Three Stars, and What It Means to Latvians

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/freedom-monument-riga-milda.html
**Published:** 2026-05-04
**Summary:** What the Freedom Monument actually is, who Milda is, the three gold stars, and why this 1935 column survived the Soviet occupation. From Daiga, a licensed Latvian guide.
