<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, what the Freedom Monument is</h2>
<p>The Freedom Monument (in Latvian, <em>Brīvības piemineklis</em>) is the 42-metre limestone-and-granite column at the eastern edge of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town, where Brīvības iela crosses the canal that used to be the medieval city moat. On top of it stands a copper figure of a woman with three gold-plated stars raised above her head. Latvians call her <strong>Milda</strong>. The three stars are the three historic regions of Latvia &mdash; Vidzeme, Latgale, and Kurzeme. The inscription on the base, in Latvian, reads <em>Tēvzemei un Brīvībai</em>: &lsquo;For Fatherland and Freedom&rsquo;.</p>
<p>It was built between 1931 and 1935 by the Latvian sculptor Kārlis Zāle, paid for entirely by public donations during Latvia&rsquo;s first period of independence (1918&ndash;1940), survived fifty years of Soviet occupation, and is today the centre of Latvian civic and political life. Every state ceremony, every protest, every quiet flower-laying on a grandparent&rsquo;s name day happens here. It is, simply, the most loaded sculpture in the country.</p>
<p>For visitors: free, open 24/7, two minutes&rsquo; walk from the eastern edge of the Old Town. Honour Guard ceremonies during the day in summer. Five minutes is enough to look; longer if you want to read what&rsquo;s on the base.</p>

<h2 id="history">A short history, because it matters</h2>
<p>Latvia became independent for the first time on 18 November 1918, in the chaos at the end of the First World War. The young republic spent its first decade rebuilding a country (agrarian, broke, just out of the Russian Empire and the German occupations), and by the late 1920s was ready to think about how it wanted to commemorate its existence.</p>
<p>A national competition was held. The winning design came from Kārlis Zāle, then in his thirties, working in a stripped-classical style influenced by his time studying in Berlin. Construction began in 1931. Funded entirely by public donations from a country with a population of under two million, building took four years. The monument was unveiled on 18 November 1935, the seventeenth anniversary of independence.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-freedom-monument/freedom-monument-side-view-bastejkalns-park-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="freedom-monument" data-caption="The Freedom Monument from the side, with Bastejkalns park behind &mdash; the spot the city moat once ran.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-freedom-monument/freedom-monument-side-view-bastejkalns-park-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-freedom-monument/freedom-monument-side-view-bastejkalns-park-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Freedom Monument seen from the side, with Bastejkalns park behind, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Side view, with the canal and Bastejkalns park behind. The hill is the old defensive bastion; the canal is the medieval moat.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>It cost about 3.6 million lats (serious money for a small country), and the donor list included people who gave a single lat from a pension. That detail matters. By the time it went up, the monument was already understood as something belonging to ordinary Latvians, not to a regime.</p>

<h2 id="milda">Milda, and what the three stars mean</h2>
<p>The woman at the top is universally called <strong>Milda</strong> in Latvia, though the name doesn&rsquo;t come from any official inscription. She&rsquo;s &lsquo;Milda&rsquo; the way the Statue of Liberty is &lsquo;Lady Liberty&rsquo;. The figure represents Latvia itself; the three stars she holds are the three historic regions:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Vidzeme</strong>, the central region around Riga. Historically Livonia, formerly under Swedish then Russian rule.</li>
<li><strong>Latgale</strong>, the eastern region. Historically Catholic, longest under Polish-Lithuanian rule, and the only Latvian region with a distinct dialect still in everyday use.</li>
<li><strong>Kurzeme</strong>, the western region, the old Duchy of Courland. The part of Latvia that briefly had its own colony in Tobago in the 17th century.</li>
</ul>
<p>The inclusion of all three regions in one figure is part of what makes the monument do its political work. Latvia in 1935 was still a young federation of pieces that had only recently been on different sides of different empires. Showing them as one figure with three stars was a quiet argument that the country was now whole.</p>
<p>The base of the column, below Milda, has 56 sculptural reliefs covering the history of the Latvian people: scenes from medieval resistance, from the 19th-century national awakening, from the 1905 revolution, from the 1918 independence struggle. The ones at the back, on the side facing the Old Town, are worth a slow look. The ones at the front are the ones photographs catch.</p>

<h2 id="soviet">How it survived the Soviet occupation</h2>
<p>This is the part of the story that almost every Latvian will eventually mention, so I&rsquo;ll tell it the way I tell it on tours.</p>
<p>In June 1940, Latvia was occupied by the Soviet Union. Within months, the new regime was holding parades on this square. The first Soviet plan was to demolish the Freedom Monument and replace it with a statue of Stalin facing the other way. The famous Russian sculptor Vera Mukhina (who had Latvian roots) intervened, arguing that the monument was an artistic masterpiece and should be preserved. The plan was shelved.</p>
<p>Throughout fifty years of Soviet occupation, leaving flowers at the monument was forbidden. The KGB watched the square. Ordinary Latvians did it anyway, especially on 18 November (the suppressed independence day), often disguising the visit as a stop on a longer walk. People were arrested. Many people. The monument stood the entire time, weathered and uncleaned but never demolished. Its survival became part of the meaning.</p>

<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Mēs nelikām ziedus pie pieminekļa. Mēs vienkārši izgājām pastaigā, un ziedi nokrita.</em></p><cite>&mdash; The way an older Latvian friend describes the Soviet years: "we didn&rsquo;t lay flowers at the monument. We just went for a walk, and the flowers fell."</cite></div>

<p>On 23 August 1989, two million people across Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia held hands in a human chain from Tallinn to Vilnius (the Baltic Way), protesting the 50th anniversary of the Molotov&ndash;Ribbentrop Pact that had handed all three countries to the Soviet Union. The chain ran through Riga, past this monument. Independence followed in 1991. On the morning the Soviet flag came down, the monument was where the city gathered. It hasn&rsquo;t stopped being that.</p>

<h2 id="today">The monument today</h2>
<p>If you&rsquo;re here in summer, you&rsquo;ll catch the Honour Guard. Two soldiers from the Latvian National Armed Forces stand watch at the monument, ceremonially relieved every hour by a small marching detail. The ceremony runs through the warm months, daily, from morning to early evening. It&rsquo;s small, quiet, and serious. Latvians around you will go quiet for the minute or so the changeover takes.</p>
<p>If you&rsquo;re here on 18 November (Independence Day) you&rsquo;ll see the city&rsquo;s major civic ceremony, with flowers laid by the President and by ordinary families. On 4 May (Restoration of Independence Day, 1990) you&rsquo;ll see the same. On 14 June (the day Latvians remember the 1941 Soviet deportations) and 25 March (the 1949 deportations) you&rsquo;ll see flowers and candles.</p>
<p>Day-to-day, it&rsquo;s the place couples meet before dinner and the place tourists pause to read what the inscription says. Bastejkalns park behind it is a working park (the canal, the willows, the small bridge with the love-locks), and one of the prettiest five-minute walks in central Riga.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-freedom-monument/laima-clock-meeting-spot-near-freedom-monument-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="freedom-monument" data-caption="The Laima clock on Brīvības iela &mdash; the city&rsquo;s meeting spot since 1924, two minutes south of the Freedom Monument.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-freedom-monument/laima-clock-meeting-spot-near-freedom-monument-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-freedom-monument/laima-clock-meeting-spot-near-freedom-monument-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Laima clock on Brīvības iela near the Freedom Monument, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The Laima clock, two minutes south of the monument. &lsquo;Meet at the Laima&rsquo; has been Riga shorthand for a century. The clock started life in 1924 as a discreet workplace timepiece for Laima&rsquo;s chocolate-factory staff; the rest of the city co-opted it.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="practical">Practical answers</h2>

<h3>Where it is and getting there</h3>
<p>At the junction of Brīvības iela and the Pilsētas Kanāls (the city canal), at the eastern edge of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. From <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, ten minutes&rsquo; walk east. From Riga Central Station, twelve minutes north. The closest tram stop is Brīvības Piemineklis, served by trams 3, 7, 9, 11. Bus 22 from the airport drops you a five-minute walk away.</p>

<h3>Times to visit</h3>
<p>Anytime. It&rsquo;s a public square, free, never closed. The Honour Guard runs roughly 09:00&ndash;18:00 in summer, with the changeover ceremony on the hour. For atmosphere, early morning before the city wakes up gives you the best photographs (low sun on the limestone). For meaning, 18 November (Independence Day) and 4 May (Restoration of Independence) are the days the square fills with Latvians. On those evenings the monument is lit; on others, it isn&rsquo;t especially.</p>

<h3>Combining with the rest of the Old Town</h3>
<p>The Freedom Monument is the eastern bookend of any Old Town walk. From here, you can drop south through the <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">Old Town pillar</a> route &mdash; the <a href="powder-tower-war-museum-riga.html">Powder Tower</a>, the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a>, the <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">cathedral</a> &mdash; or walk five minutes north into the Quiet Centre for the Art Nouveau district. Bastejkalns park immediately behind the monument is a soft place to sit for ten minutes between things.</p>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>
<p>For visitors who don&rsquo;t carry the history, the Freedom Monument can read as &lsquo;a column with a statue on top&rsquo;, and that&rsquo;s the version that ends up on the postcard. That&rsquo;s fine. But it&rsquo;s also the most loaded place in Latvia. If you have ten minutes here, give a couple to reading the inscription, a couple to looking at the back side of the base where the Latvian-history reliefs are carved, and the rest to watching whatever Latvians around you happen to be doing &mdash; laying a single flower, standing for the Honour Guard changeover, walking past on a Tuesday.</p>

<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions about the Freedom Monument</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-1">
      Who is Milda?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-1" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The female figure on top of the Freedom Monument, holding three gold stars above her head. Latvians universally call her Milda. There&rsquo;s no official inscription with that name. It&rsquo;s simply how the country has referred to her since 1935. The figure is meant to represent Latvia itself; Milda is the affectionate, given name.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-2">
      What do the three gold stars mean?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The three historic regions of Latvia &mdash; Vidzeme (centre, around Riga), Latgale (east), and Kurzeme (west). At the time of the monument&rsquo;s unveiling in 1935, these three regions had only recently been brought under one Latvian state; the three stars assert that they are now one country. (Latvia today has four cultural regions if you count Zemgale, in the south; the monument predates that division.)</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-3">
      How tall is the Freedom Monument?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-3" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>42 metres total. The travertine column itself is 19 metres; the base sculptures and pedestal add the rest. The Milda figure on top is nine metres of copper. From across the square, the monument feels taller than it is because it sits on a low rise without competing tall buildings nearby.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-4">
      What does &lsquo;Tēvzemei un Brīvībai&rsquo; mean?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-4" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Latvian: &lsquo;For Fatherland and Freedom&rsquo;. It&rsquo;s the inscription carved on the base of the monument, on the side facing the Old Town. The phrase has become a Latvian national motto in everything but legal status.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-5">
      How did the monument survive the Soviet occupation?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-5" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The Soviet authorities planned to demolish it after the 1940 occupation and replace it with a statue of Stalin. The Russian sculptor Vera Mukhina &mdash; herself born in what is now Latvia &mdash; argued for its preservation as an artistic masterpiece, and the demolition plan was shelved. Throughout the occupation, leaving flowers at the monument was forbidden, and many Latvians were arrested for doing so. The monument stood through fifty years of Soviet rule, weathered but intact, and became one of the most powerful symbols of national continuity through the occupation period.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-6">
      Who designed and built the Freedom Monument?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-6" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The Latvian sculptor Kārlis Zāle (1888&ndash;1942), in collaboration with the architect Ernests Štālbergs. Construction ran from 1931 to 1935 and was funded entirely by public donations from across Latvia. Zāle is also the sculptor of the Brothers&rsquo; Cemetery (Brāļu kapi) on the northern edge of Riga, a different but equally significant Latvian memorial site.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-7">
      Is there an Honour Guard at the Freedom Monument?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-7" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes. Soldiers from the Latvian National Armed Forces stand a ceremonial guard at the monument, with a hourly changeover ceremony, daily during the warmer months (roughly April through October) from about 09:00 to 18:00. In winter the schedule is reduced. The changeover is small, dignified, takes about a minute, and is one of the moments when Latvians around you will go quiet.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-8">
      What&rsquo;s the Laima clock?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>A small ornamental clock pillar on Brīvības iela, two minutes south of the Freedom Monument, installed in 1924 by Laima &mdash; the Latvian chocolate company &mdash; originally as a workplace timepiece for the factory staff nearby. The rest of Riga adopted it as a meeting point. &lsquo;Meet you at the Laima&rsquo; has been a city shorthand for a century. It is still a working meeting spot &mdash; on a Friday evening you&rsquo;ll see twenty people stood around it waiting for friends.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-9">
      What&rsquo;s Bastejkalns park?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Bastejkalns is the small park that wraps around the canal directly behind the Freedom Monument. The hill (kalns) is a former medieval defensive bastion; the canal (Pilsētas Kanāls) is the old city moat, still curving around what used to be the Old Town walls. It&rsquo;s a working city park &mdash; a five-minute walk along the canal, willows, a bridge with love-locks, occasional buskers, and a memorial to the five Latvians killed by Soviet OMON forces here in January 1991. A soft place to sit between heavier sights.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-10">
      When are the Latvian national days I&rsquo;ll see things happening here?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The big four. <strong>18 November</strong> &mdash; Independence Day (anniversary of the 1918 declaration of statehood); state ceremony, flowers from the President, large evening procession. <strong>4 May</strong> &mdash; Restoration of Independence Day (1990); similar ceremony. <strong>14 June</strong> &mdash; commemoration of the 1941 Soviet mass deportations; flowers and candles, no parade. <strong>25 March</strong> &mdash; commemoration of the 1949 deportations; same. On any of those days the square fills with Latvians and the meaning of the monument is impossible to miss.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-11">
      Can I take photographs?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-11" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes, freely. Two practical notes. First, don&rsquo;t pose for cheesy photographs during the Honour Guard changeover. Wait the minute it takes. Second, the climbing or sitting on the base of the monument is treated as a serious offence by the Latvian authorities, and rightly so. Stand on the cobbles around it, not on the monument itself.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-fm-12">
      Can wheelchairs and pushchairs reach the monument?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-fm-12" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes. The monument sits on a flat stone-paved square with smooth approaches from Brīvības iela on both sides. The cobbles immediately around the base are tighter; the wider square has level paving. Bastejkalns park behind has paved paths and is wheelchair-accessible at most points; one bridge over the canal has a small step.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>

## The Hill of Crosses: A Day Trip from Riga to Šiauliai

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/hill-of-crosses-lithuania-from-riga.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** The Hill of Crosses near Šiauliai, Lithuania — a Catholic pilgrimage site the Soviets bulldozed three times and never destroyed. How to visit, when, and what it means.

<p class="article-lede">There is a small hill in northern Lithuania, about twelve kilometres from the city of &#352;iauliai, that does not look like much from the road. A mound, maybe ten metres high, in the middle of flat farmland. Then you get out of the car and you see what is on it, and you stop talking for a while.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: hill-of-crosses-photo-injection -->

<figure class="hoc-hero-figure">
  <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-hill-of-crosses/hill-of-crosses-boardwalk-pilgrim-statue-lithuania.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="hill-of-crosses-hero" data-caption="Boardwalk over the summit of the Hill of Crosses, near Šiauliai, Lithuania — the standing Jesus statue, hand-carved memorials, and the Lithuanian plain stretching out beyond." aria-label="Open photo 1 of 1: Boardwalk over the summit of the Hill of Crosses, near Šiauliai, Lithuania — the standing Jesus statue, hand-carved memorials, and the Lithuanian plain stretching out beyond.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-hill-of-crosses/hill-of-crosses-tile-1200x800.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-hill-of-crosses/hill-of-crosses-tile-1200x800.jpg" alt="The Hill of Crosses (Kryžių kalnas) near Šiauliai, Lithuania — boardwalk path with the standing Jesus statue and crosses in every direction." loading="eager" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1200" height="800">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Boardwalk over the summit of the Hill of Crosses, near Šiauliai, Lithuania — the standing Jesus statue, hand-carved memorials, and the Lithuanian plain stretching out beyond.</figcaption>
</figure>
<p class="hoc-photo-notice"><strong>Photos:</strong> the gallery below opens as a clickable lightbox — tap any thumbnail or hero image to enlarge. Photographed across visits we have made with our guests.</p>
<!-- END: hill-of-crosses-photo-injection -->


<p>Somewhere between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand crosses. Wooden ones the size of a child&rsquo;s hand, hung on rosaries; metal ones taller than a man; carved Lithuanian folk crucifixes; rough pieces of wood lashed together with twine; statues of the Virgin Mary; photographs of people who are not coming back. The wind moves through them and the smaller ones chime softly against each other, and the whole hill breathes.</p>

<p>This is <em>Kryžių kalnas</em>. It is not a museum, it is not a cemetery, and it is not officially anything. The Catholic Church does not own it. The Lithuanian state does not really own it. It belongs, if it belongs to anyone, to the people who keep coming and putting things on it, and have been doing so for almost two hundred years.</p>

<p>It is one of the most quietly extraordinary places in the Baltic states, and from Riga you can be standing on it in less than two hours.</p>

<h2 id="origin">How it began</h2>

<p>Nobody knows exactly when the first cross went up. The most widely accepted account is that it began after the November Uprising of 1831 &mdash; a Polish-Lithuanian rebellion against Russian imperial rule that was crushed brutally. The bodies of the fallen rebels were not returned to their families. Many were buried in unmarked graves, deliberately, so that there would be nowhere to mourn them.</p>

<p>So the families came to this small hill &mdash; the remains of an old hill fort, on common ground, in the middle of nowhere in particular &mdash; and they put up crosses for the dead they could not bury. Not gravestones. Just crosses. Somewhere to grieve.</p>

<p>The 1863 Uprising failed too. More crosses went up. By the time Lithuania declared independence in 1918, the hill was already a place where people came when they did not know what else to do.</p>

<p>This is the part of the story I find most affecting: the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_of_Crosses" rel="noopener external">Hill of Crosses</a> was not built by the Church, or by the state, or by anyone with a plan. It was built by ordinary people who needed somewhere to put their grief, and who made a place out of nothing because no one else would make one for them.</p>

<h2 id="soviets">What the Soviets tried to do</h2>

<p>The Soviets understood, immediately, that this hill was a problem.</p>

<p>It was Catholic, in a regime that was officially atheist. It was Lithuanian, in a regime that wanted Lithuanians to forget they were Lithuanian. It was a place where ordinary people gathered, in a regime that did not want ordinary people gathering anywhere it could not see them. After the deportations of 1941 and 1949, families began coming to the hill to put up crosses for relatives who had been taken to Siberia and never came home. The crosses, increasingly, carried inscriptions that the regime found intolerable.</p>

<p>In April 1961, the Soviets bulldozed the entire hill. Burned the wooden crosses. Sent the metal ones to scrap. Buried the stone ones. The site was guarded.</p>

<p>The crosses came back.</p>

<p>People walked up at night. They brought new crosses hidden under coats. Some of them, when guards were posted on the hill itself, made tiny crosses out of stones and grass and laid them flat in the meadow, where you could not see them from the road but you could find them if you knew where to look. This was the entire point.</p>

<p>The Soviets bulldozed the hill again in 1973, and again in 1975. Each time, the crosses came back within weeks. There were serious proposals to flood the entire area and turn the hill into an unreachable island in an artificial lake. The KGB stationed itself there. Between 1973 and 1975 alone, an estimated five hundred crosses were destroyed every year.</p>

<p>It did not work. The hill outlasted the Soviet Union.</p>

<p>In September 1993, two years after independence, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II" rel="noopener external">Pope John Paul II</a> &mdash; himself a Pole, who had grown up in a country that knew exactly what this hill meant &mdash; came to Lithuania and held Mass at the foot of it. He called it a place of &ldquo;hope, peace, love, and sacrifice.&rdquo; He sent a large crucifix from the Vatican afterwards, and it stands on the hill today, as one of many.</p>

<p>You could fairly say that this is what the Soviet Union actually lost &mdash; not the arms race, not the economic competition, not the diplomatic chess game, but a contest of attrition with people who would not stop bringing pieces of wood to a hill in the middle of nowhere.</p>

<h2 id="why-it-matters">Why it is more than a religious site</h2>

<p>You do not have to be Catholic to feel what is happening here. I am not particularly religious, and the first time I went I did not expect to be moved the way I was moved.</p>

<p>What is on this hill is not really about Catholicism, although Catholicism is its language. It is about what people do when official history will not let them grieve, when their dead have no graves, when their language is forbidden, when their nation has been told it does not exist. They make their own sites of memory. They create a place where the rules of the regime above them simply do not apply. They walk up a hill and put a piece of wood on it and walk back down again, and that small private act, multiplied across decades and tens of thousands of people, becomes a thing no government in the world has been able to destroy.</p>

<p>That is a story about faith, but it is also a story about what humans need. Something to hold on to when nothing else can be held. A small ritual that says <em>I was here, this person was here, this happened, do not let it be forgotten</em>.</p>

<p>When you walk among the crosses you are not really walking among religious objects. You are walking among grief and stubbornness and love and remembrance, which is what religion was always actually doing, underneath the doctrine. The hill makes that visible.</p>

<p>If you have lost someone, this is a place where you can put something for them, and it will stay there with everything else, and the wind will move through it.</p>

<h2 id="the-drive">The drive</h2>

<p>From Riga, the most beautiful way to do this is to combine it with Rund&#257;le Palace, which we already include on one of our day excursions. The route runs south through the Zemgale plain &mdash; flat, fertile, ancient farming country that has been growing wheat and rye for a thousand years &mdash; and then crosses into Lithuania.</p>

<p>You will pass small villages with wooden churches, fields of yellow rapeseed in May, lakes you could swim in if you stopped, roadside stalls selling smoked fish and honey. The countryside slowly slows you down. By the time you arrive at the hill you are already in the right state of mind for it.</p>

<p>The total drive from R&#299;ga to the Hill of Crosses is about two hours each way, depending on traffic and how often you stop for the storks. From Rund&#257;le, it&rsquo;s roughly an hour and a half further south. Combining the two into a single long day works well: Rund&#257;le in the morning, late lunch at one of the village caf&eacute;s near the border, Hill of Crosses in the afternoon when the light is at its best for the crosses&rsquo; long shadows.</p>

<h2 id="storks">A word on the storks</h2>

<p>If you come between <strong>late March and August</strong>, you will see them everywhere.</p>

<p>The white stork &mdash; <em>baltais st&#257;r&#311;is</em> in Latvian, <em>baltasis gandras</em> in Lithuanian, and the official national bird of Lithuania &mdash; is one of the great pleasures of summer driving in this part of Europe. Latvia alone has roughly 10,500 breeding pairs, one of the densest populations anywhere in the world. Drive any rural road between April and August and you will see their enormous stick nests, three or four feet across, perched on every other electricity pylon, every chimney, every disused water tower, every wagon-wheel-on-a-pole that a thoughtful farmer has put up to invite them.</p>

<p>These are magnificent creatures. Adults stand over a metre tall, with a wingspan of nearly two metres, jet-black flight feathers against a brilliant white body, and long red legs and beaks that look as though they have been dipped in paint. They are also genuinely high up the food chain &mdash; they eat frogs, small mammals, snakes, fish, large insects, even the occasional young bird &mdash; and they know it. There is a particular confidence to the way a stork strolls across a freshly ploughed field, head held high, picking off worms and beetles with the unbothered air of a creature that has nothing to fear from anything in the vicinity. Watch one work a furrow for a few minutes and you understand exactly why every culture in their range has woven them into folklore. They look as though they have opinions about the weather.</p>

<p>The migration itself is one of the great avian journeys. Our storks fly to <strong>sub-Saharan Africa</strong> every autumn &mdash; Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, sometimes as far south as the Cape &mdash; and back again every spring. They cannot fly across large bodies of water, because they soar on rising thermals which only form over land, so they take the long way around: south through the Bosphorus, down the Levant, along the Nile valley, into East Africa. The round trip is several thousand kilometres each way. They mate for life, return to the same nest every year, and the older male of a pair will arrive a few days before his mate to make repairs. When she joins him there is an audible greeting &mdash; a rapid clattering of beaks called <em>klabata</em> in Latvian, after a wooden percussion instrument it sounds exactly like.</p>

<p>If you are here between <strong>September and March</strong>, you will see the nests but not their occupants. Empty wooden saucers on poles, waiting. There are worse things to be reminded of, in this country, than that the things one loves do come back.</p>

<p>In Latvian and Lithuanian folklore, a stork pair nesting on your property brings harmony, fertility, and good fortune to the household. People are genuinely pleased when storks choose them. A new pair settling on your chimney is the sort of news you tell your neighbours.</p>

<p>So: if you are doing this drive in the warm months, build in time for stops. The storks will be waiting in the fields.</p>

<h2 id="border">A note on the border</h2>

<p>Latvia and Lithuania have both been in the European Union since 2004 and the Schengen Area since 2007, which means that in normal times you can drive across the border without stopping at all. There is a sign in the forest, in two languages, and that is it.</p>

<p>That said, <strong>bring your passport or national ID card anyway</strong>. Schengen rules technically still permit identity checks at internal borders, particularly during periods of heightened security &mdash; and given everything happening on the eastern frontier in recent years, occasional spot checks do happen. It is also a good idea to have your insurance documents handy if you are driving a hire car. Nine times out of ten you will sail through without seeing a single border officer. The tenth time, you&rsquo;ll be glad you brought the documents.</p>

<h2 id="practical">Practical information</h2>

<p><strong>Hill of Crosses (Kryžių kalnas)</strong></p>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Detail</th><th>Information</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><strong>Location</strong></td><td>About 12 km north of &#352;iauliai, Lithuania. Coordinates: 56.0153&deg;N, 23.4167&deg;E.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Hours</strong></td><td>Open 24 hours a day, every day of the year. There is no gate.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Entry</strong></td><td>Free. There is a small donation box at the visitor centre.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Parking</strong></td><td>Free parking lot at the entrance, with a small souvenir shop and a caf&eacute;. Spaces for cars and motorhomes.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Crosses for sale</strong></td><td>Yes &mdash; small wooden and metal crosses can be purchased at the visitor centre if you want to leave one. Prices range from a couple of euros to twenty or more for hand-carved Lithuanian folk crosses.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>From Riga</strong></td><td>Roughly 123 km, about 1 hour 45 minutes by car via the A7 / E67 (Via Baltica) and the A12. From Rund&#257;le Palace: about 90 minutes further south.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>From Vilnius</strong></td><td>About 220 km, around 2.5 hours.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Plan for</strong></td><td>45 minutes to an hour on the hill itself; longer if you want to walk slowly. Most of the experience is the silence and the time, so don&rsquo;t rush it.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Bring</strong></td><td>Comfortable shoes (the path up is uneven), a layer if it is windy (it is almost always windy on the hill), and your passport for the border crossing.</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>What to leave behind</strong></td><td>If you are bringing your own cross, no permit is needed for anything under three metres tall. If you have something smaller &mdash; a written note, a rosary, a photograph &mdash; those go up too. Many of the most moving things on the hill are not crosses at all.</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h2 id="excursions">On our excursions</h2>

<p>We do not currently include the Hill of Crosses on our standard day trips, because it makes for a long day when combined with Rund&#257;le and we want our guests to enjoy each stop without rushing. But if you are visiting Latvia and you have a day to spend properly, this is one of the most affecting day-and-a-half itineraries we can put together for you: Rund&#257;le Palace and the formal gardens in the morning, lunch somewhere along the route, the Hill of Crosses in the late afternoon, dinner back in Riga.</p>

<p>If you are interested, get in touch. We can arrange a private driver, a flexible itinerary, and proper time at both sites.</p>

<p>But even if you go on your own, go. Take a small cross, or a piece of paper, or nothing at all. Stand on the hill for a while. Listen to the wind moving through the smaller crosses. Read a few of the names you can read.</p>

<p>There are a lot of places in this part of Europe where people have been told their lives did not matter. The Hill of Crosses is the answer that ordinary people, over two centuries, have been quietly building to that.</p>

<p>It is worth the drive.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: cross-sell-cta -->
<p class="article-cta"><em>The Hill of Crosses isn't on our standard excursion list — it's a longer day each way — but we run it as a custom small-group day trip from Riga on request, often combined with the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%A0iauliai" rel="noopener external">Šiauliai</a> sun clock. <a href="/#contact">Get in touch</a> with your dates and we'll quote it.</em></p>

## The House of the Blackheads (Melngalvju nams), Riga: The Most Photographed Building in the City

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html
**Published:** 2026-05-04
**Summary:** What the House of the Blackheads actually is, who the Brotherhood of Blackheads were, why it was rebuilt from 1948 ruins, and what's inside the museum. From Daiga, a licensed Latvian guide.

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, what the House of the Blackheads is</h2>
<p>The House of the Blackheads (in Latvian, <em>Melngalvju nams</em>) is the elaborately decorated red-and-white Dutch Renaissance building on Town Hall Square (Rātslaukums) in the southern half of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. It is the building that ends up on every Riga postcard, every Christmas-market photograph, and every airline ad for the Baltic. It is also &mdash; honestly &mdash; not the original. The original building was built in 1334, badly damaged by Soviet shelling in 1941, the ruins demolished by Soviet authorities in 1948, and the building reconstructed from 1995 to 1999 using historical drawings, photographs, and salvaged stonework.</p>
<p>The reconstruction is meticulously faithful and at the same time honestly modern. Inside is a small museum (silver, history of the Brotherhood, period rooms), the ceremonial Great Hall (used for state events and concerts), and the medieval cellar &mdash; the part that <em>is</em> original. Adjacent to it stands the also-reconstructed <strong>Schwabe House</strong> (now usually included in the same museum visit). Adult ticket around &euro;7&ndash;8. Allow 60&ndash;90 minutes.</p>
<p>Two minutes&rsquo; walk south of <a href="st-peters-church-tower-riga.html">St Peter&rsquo;s Church</a>, three minutes south of <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, on the central square of the Old Town.</p>

<h2 id="brotherhood">The Brotherhood of Blackheads</h2>
<p>The building&rsquo;s name comes from the Brotherhood of Blackheads (in Latvian, <em>Melngalvju br&#257;l&#299;ba</em>), a guild of unmarried German merchants in Riga, founded around 1400. The Brotherhood&rsquo;s patron saint was St Maurice, a Roman-era Christian martyr who was, in the iconography that came down to medieval Europe, depicted as Black; the &lsquo;Blackheads&rsquo; in the guild&rsquo;s name comes from his head, in heraldry. The Brotherhood&rsquo;s coat of arms shows St Maurice&rsquo;s head in profile.</p>
<p>The Blackheads were the younger merchants&rsquo; guild &mdash; you joined as a single man entering the trade, and once you married you graduated to the senior <a href="cat-house-riga-meistaru.html">Great Guild</a>. The Brotherhood functioned as both a professional association and a social club: trade events, banquets, dancing, occasional militia-style civic defence. They occupied this building from the late 15th century onward, gradually rebuilding it in the architectural fashion of each successive period, and using it for some of Riga&rsquo;s most lavish events. The Russian Tsars Peter the Great and Catherine the Great are both supposed to have danced in the Great Hall here. The Brotherhood was dissolved by the Soviet occupation in 1940, restored in independent Latvia in 1995, and exists today as a small ceremonial society.</p>

<h2 id="destroyed-rebuilt">Destroyed in 1941, rebuilt 1995&ndash;1999</h2>
<p>This is the part of the story the postcard never tells. In June 1941, in the opening weeks of Operation Barbarossa, the centre of Riga came under heavy German artillery and Luftwaffe bombing. The House of the Blackheads, the medieval Riga Town Hall opposite it, and most of Town Hall Square were destroyed. The fa&ccedil;ade of the Blackheads survived as a damaged shell into 1948, when the Soviet authorities ordered the ruin demolished. The Latvian SSR built a wide open square here for parades; the bombed building site became a flat plaza for fifty years.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-medieval-cellar-museum-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="blackheads" data-caption="Inside the medieval cellar &mdash; surviving stonework from the original 1334 building, the part that is not a 1990s reconstruction.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-medieval-cellar-museum-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-medieval-cellar-museum-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The medieval cellar inside the House of the Blackheads museum, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The medieval cellar. The part of the building that <em>is</em> original &mdash; brick stonework from 1334, surviving the bombing and the post-war demolition because it was below ground.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>The reconstruction was approved as a project for the 800th anniversary of Riga in 2001, and built between 1995 and 1999. Architects worked from a remarkably full set of historical sources: detailed drawings from the 19th-century restorations, photographs from the 1930s, and salvaged stonework that had been catalogued by Soviet-era museum staff before the 1948 demolition. Some of the salvaged elements (decorative stones, sandstone reliefs, parts of the staircases) were re-incorporated into the new building. The cellars are the original 1334 stonework. Most of what you see above ground is new fabric in old form.</p>
<p>The result is one of the most successful late-20th-century reconstructions in Europe. Some Riga locals object on principle to a reconstructed historic building &mdash; the &lsquo;is it real?&rsquo; question that haunts every Eastern European post-war restoration project. My honest answer: the original is gone; the reconstruction stands faithfully on its place; the fact of the destruction is part of the building&rsquo;s biography now. Visit it as both at once.</p>

<h2 id="facade">What you&rsquo;re looking at on the facade</h2>
<p>The front of the building is one of the densest decorative facades in northern Europe. From bottom to top, the things to look for.</p>
<p><strong>The arcade at street level</strong> has arched openings, statues of biblical figures and mythological allegories, painted reliefs of saints, and the Brotherhood&rsquo;s coat of arms in gold leaf. The smaller doorway in the centre is the original ceremonial entrance.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-front-facade-statues-detail-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="blackheads" data-caption="The Dutch Renaissance front facade with statues, sundial, and bell &mdash; the densest decorative wall in northern Europe.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-front-facade-statues-detail-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-front-facade-statues-detail-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The front facade of the House of the Blackheads with statues, sundial, and inscription, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The front facade. Statues of Neptune, Mercury, Peace, Justice, and Unity flank the second-storey windows; the central sundial works.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>One floor up, large arched windows are flanked by allegorical statues: Neptune, Mercury, Peace, Justice, Unity. These are reconstructions of the originals.</p>
<p>The third storey has smaller windows, more statues, and the central decorative sundial. The sundial works. The gnomon is real bronze and the hour-marks are accurate Riga time. (You can check it against your watch on a sunny day; allow for daylight saving.)</p>
<p>The gable on top is the elaborate stepped pediment with putti, banners, niches, and finials. A small bronze ship-weather-vane sits at the peak &mdash; the Brotherhood&rsquo;s sign, recalling its merchant origins. <em>ANNO 1334</em> is carved into the gable in gilded letters, the year of the building&rsquo;s first construction.</p>
<p>The neighbouring building to the left, the slightly less ornamented but still elaborate <strong>Schwabe House</strong> (<em>Š&v;v&#257;ba nams</em>), is a similar reconstruction of a separate 17th-century merchant house, now usually visited together with the Blackheads as one museum.</p>

<!-- TODO: native Latvian speaker review of pull-quote -->
<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Vecās ēkas vairs nav. Mēs uzcēlām to no jauna, jo veidols mums bija svarīgs, pat ja oriģinālās sienas vairs nav.</em></p><cite>&mdash; A Latvian way of putting it: &ldquo;the old building is gone. We rebuilt it from scratch because the shape mattered to us, even if the original walls aren&rsquo;t there.&rdquo;</cite></div>

<h2 id="inside">Inside &mdash; the museum, the period rooms, the Great Hall</h2>
<p>The visit inside has three parts.</p>
<p><strong>The medieval cellar.</strong> Original 1334 stonework, low ceilings, brick walls. The cellar holds permanent exhibits about the Brotherhood&rsquo;s history, with artefacts (silver, banners, medals) on display. This is the part of the building you cannot get anywhere else &mdash; original medieval Riga, beneath your feet.</p>
<p><strong>The period rooms on the upper floors.</strong> Reconstructed 17th-, 18th-, and 19th-century interiors with appropriate furniture, wallpaper, paintings, and ornament. These reflect the way the Brotherhood actually used the building over centuries: small council chambers, dining rooms, robing rooms, withdrawing rooms.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-great-hall-painted-ceiling-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="blackheads" data-caption="The Great Hall, with its baroque painted ceiling, crystal chandeliers, and parquet floor &mdash; the room Peter the Great is supposed to have danced in.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-great-hall-painted-ceiling-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-house-of-blackheads/house-of-blackheads-great-hall-painted-ceiling-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Great Hall of the House of the Blackheads with painted ceiling and crystal chandeliers, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The Great Hall. Baroque painted ceiling, crystal chandeliers, polished parquet, full-length portraits along the walls. Used today for state ceremonies and chamber concerts.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p><strong>The Great Hall.</strong> The largest room in the building, on the second floor, with a baroque painted ceiling, crystal chandeliers, and a parquet floor. This is the room used for the Brotherhood&rsquo;s lavish banquets and balls in the 17th and 18th centuries; today it&rsquo;s used for Latvian state ceremonies, chamber music concerts, and (occasionally) presidential receptions. If you can time your visit for a concert evening, do; the acoustics are good and the room takes the music well.</p>
<p>The silver collection is worth a slow look. Some pieces are 17th-century originals that survived the bombing because they had been moved to provincial museums before 1941; others are 1990s reproductions; the labelling is honest about which is which.</p>

<h2 id="square">Town Hall Square (Rātslaukums)</h2>
<p>The square in front of the Blackheads is Rātslaukums &mdash; Town Hall Square &mdash; bordered on the south side by the also-reconstructed Riga Town Hall, on the west side by Kaļķu iela leading to the river, and on the east side by the modern Latvian Riflemen monument and the modern Museum of the Occupation. In summer the square has cafés on every side; in late November to early January it is the main Riga Christmas market, voted third best in Europe in 2025&ndash;2026.</p>
<p>The bronze statue in front of the Blackheads is <strong>Roland</strong> &mdash; a copy. Rolands were standard town-hall sculptures across the Hanseatic and free-imperial cities of northern Europe, symbolising civic justice and the autonomy of the merchant town from the local bishop or prince. The original Roland here (early 20th-century, replacing an 18th-century one) is now in the Blackheads&rsquo; museum; what stands on the square is a copy from the 1990s reconstruction. Riga&rsquo;s Roland is the only one in the eastern Baltic.</p>

<h2 id="practical">Practical answers</h2>

<h3>Where it is and getting there</h3>
<p>Rātslaukums 7, in the southern half of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. Two minutes&rsquo; walk south of <a href="st-peters-church-tower-riga.html">St Peter&rsquo;s Church</a>, three minutes south of <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, three minutes from the Daugava embankment. The Old Town is pedestrianised; you arrive on foot. Closest tram stop is N&#257;cionālais te&#257;tris, eight minutes&rsquo; walk away.</p>

<h3>Hours, costs, what to expect</h3>
<p>The exterior of the building is on a public square and is free, accessible 24/7. The museum inside is open Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 11:00&ndash;18:00 (closed Mondays; longer hours in summer). Adult ticket around &euro;7&ndash;8; concessions for students, seniors, children. The visit takes 60&ndash;90 minutes and includes both the Blackheads and the adjoining Schwabe House. Concert tickets for the Great Hall are sold separately and run from around &euro;15.</p>

<h3>Combining with the rest of the Old Town</h3>
<p>The Blackheads is the southern bookend of the central Old Town walk, and pairs naturally with <a href="st-peters-church-tower-riga.html">St Peter&rsquo;s tower</a> two minutes north. The full Old Town circuit &mdash; Freedom Monument, Powder Tower, Three Brothers, Castle, Cathedral, Cat House, Blackheads, St Peter&rsquo;s &mdash; is in the <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">pillar guide</a>. End the day on the platform of St Peter&rsquo;s tower for the panorama at golden hour.</p>

<h3>Christmas market</h3>
<p>The main Riga Christmas market runs on Town Hall Square from late November to early January, with a smaller secondary market on Doma laukums by the cathedral. The Blackheads&rsquo; gilded fa&ccedil;ade lit at night above the market stalls is the photograph you see on every Riga winter advert. Hot mulled wine, smoked meats, hand-knitted mittens.</p>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>
<p>The House of the Blackheads is the building on every Riga postcard, and it deserves the front-page treatment. The faithful reconstruction is impressive on its own terms. The building&rsquo;s actual biography is more interesting than the postcard suggests: medieval origin, 19th-century photographs, 1941 destruction, 1948 demolition by Soviet authorities, 1995&ndash;1999 reconstruction by independent Latvia. Allow an hour for the museum, ten minutes for the facade and the square.</p>

<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions about the House of the Blackheads</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-1">
      Who were the Blackheads?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-1" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The Brotherhood of Blackheads (<em>Melngalvju br&#257;l&#299;ba</em>) was a guild of unmarried German merchants in Riga, founded around 1400. Their patron saint was St Maurice, a Roman-era Christian martyr depicted in medieval European heraldry as Black &mdash; the &lsquo;Blackheads&rsquo; in the guild&rsquo;s name comes from his head, which appears on the Brotherhood&rsquo;s coat of arms. They were the &lsquo;junior&rsquo; merchants&rsquo; guild; once members married they graduated to the senior <a href="cat-house-riga-meistaru.html">Great Guild</a>.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-2">
      Is the building really 14th century?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Originally, yes &mdash; the first building on this site was completed in 1334. But the building you see today is a 1995&ndash;1999 reconstruction. The original was severely damaged by German bombing in 1941, the ruins were demolished by Soviet authorities in 1948, and the present building was rebuilt from historical drawings, photographs, and salvaged stonework for the 800th anniversary of Riga in 2001. The medieval cellar inside <em>is</em> original 14th-century stonework that survived below ground; everything above ground is new fabric in faithful old form.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-3">
      Why was it destroyed?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-3" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>By German artillery and bombing in late June 1941, in the opening weeks of Operation Barbarossa, the German invasion of the Soviet Union (Latvia was at the time a Soviet republic). Most of central Riga&rsquo;s historic buildings were damaged or destroyed in those weeks. The fa&ccedil;ade of the Blackheads survived as a ruin until 1948, when the Soviet occupying authorities ordered the demolition of the remaining shell to clear space for parade-ground use.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-4">
      Can I go inside?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-4" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes &mdash; the building is open to visitors as a museum and concert venue. Adult ticket around &euro;7&ndash;8 includes the medieval cellar (original 1334 stonework with artefacts of the Brotherhood), period rooms on the upper floors, and the ceremonial Great Hall. The neighbouring Schwabe House is included in the same ticket. Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 11:00&ndash;18:00, closed Mondays. Allow 60&ndash;90 minutes.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-5">
      Is the museum worth the ticket?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-5" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes, especially for the medieval cellar (which is the original part of the building) and the Great Hall (one of the most decorative interiors in Latvia). The silver collection is excellent. The period rooms on the upper floors are pleasant, not spectacular. If you have only one paid Old Town interior to visit and you&rsquo;ve already done the <a href="st-peters-church-tower-riga.html">St Peter&rsquo;s tower</a>, this is a strong second choice.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-6">
      What&rsquo;s the Roland statue in front?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-6" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>A medieval statue of Roland (the legendary Frankish knight, nephew of Charlemagne), serving as a civic-justice symbol in front of the town hall. Rolands were standard sculptures in Hanseatic and free-imperial cities across northern Europe; Riga&rsquo;s is the only one in the eastern Baltic. The original (early 20th-century, replacing an 18th-century one) is in the Blackheads museum; what stands on the square is a 1990s copy made for the reconstruction.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-7">

      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-7" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>From the centre of Town Hall Square, ten metres or so south of the building, late afternoon. The fa&ccedil;ade faces north, so it spends most of the day in shadow; in the hour before sunset the gilding catches direct low sun and the building lights up. For the wider postcard shot with St Peter&rsquo;s spire above the gable, stand on the south side of the square. In summer there&rsquo;s usually a small crowd at this exact spot; in winter, particularly during the Christmas market, the square is densely lit and the photograph works at any hour.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-8">

      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The main Riga Christmas market runs on Town Hall Square (Rātslaukums) from late November to early January each year. A smaller secondary market runs at the same time on Doma laukums by <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">the cathedral</a>. The Blackheads&rsquo; gilded fa&ccedil;ade lit at night is the photograph that ends up on every Riga winter advert. December is the cheapest month for Riga hotels.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-bh-9">

    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes, regularly. The Great Hall is used for chamber music concerts, choral performances, occasional jazz nights, and Latvian state ceremonies. Tickets are sold separately from museum admission and run from around &euro;15. The acoustics are good and the room is intimate (around 200 seats). Check the museum&rsquo;s noticeboard at the entrance or ask at the ticket office for the current schedule.</p>

  </div>

    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-bh-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Ten minutes for the exterior alone, including a slow walk around to read the facade. Sixty to ninety minutes if you also do the museum (cellar, period rooms, Great Hall, plus the adjoining Schwabe House). Add another twenty minutes if you sit in one of the cafés on the square afterwards.</p>

## Inside Rundāle Palace: A Room-by-Room Visual Guide

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/inside-rundale-palace-rooms-guide.html
**Published:** 2026-04-28
**Last updated:** 2026-04-29
**Summary:** Every room of Latvia's grandest baroque palace, illustrated with 286 original photos: Gold Hall, White Hall, Duke's enfilade, Duchess's wing.

<p>If you've already decided that Rundāle Palace is on your Latvia itinerary, this article is for you. We're skipping the construction history (we cover that elsewhere) and walking you straight through the doors, room by room, so you know what's waiting for you inside before you ever set foot on the gravel of the front courtyard. Think of this as a written preview of the route you'll take — almost forty rooms across two wings — written in the voice we'd use if we were guiding you ourselves.</p>
<p>A small note before we begin. Rundāle is not a palace where you breeze through three "highlight" rooms and leave. The whole point is the cumulative effect — the way one ceiling speaks to the next, the way the colour of one set of wallcoverings makes the next set feel deliberate, the way the Duke's wing and the Duchess's wing tell two slightly different stories about how an eighteenth-century ruling couple actually lived. This guide is structured the way the visitor route is structured, so you can read it on the bus on the way down from Riga and arrive already oriented.</p>
<p class="rundale-photo-notice"><strong>Photos:</strong> Each section below now opens into a clickable gallery of photographs taken on a real visitor day (286 photographs across 44 rooms). Tap the hero image to enlarge, or pick a thumbnail.</p>

<aside class="rundale-quickfacts" aria-label="Rundāle Palace at a glance">
  <h2 class="rundale-quickfacts__heading">Rundāle Palace at a glance</h2>
  <p class="rundale-quickfacts__intro">The fastest way to know what you&#x27;re walking into.</p>
  <table class="rundale-quickfacts__table">
    <tbody>
  <tr><th scope="row">Built</th><td>1736–1768 (in two phases, interrupted by Duke Biron's exile 1740–1762)</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Architect</th><td>Francesco Bartolomeo Rastrelli — the same architect as the Winter Palace in St Petersburg</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Style</th><td>Baroque exterior, Rococo interiors (1760s phase)</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Commissioned by</th><td>Ernst Johann von Biron, Duke of Courland and Semigallia (1690–1772)</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Rooms on visitor route</th><td>40 rooms restored to 18th-century condition (open to visitors)</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Total rooms</th><td>138 rooms in total</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Modern restoration</th><td>1972–2014, led by Imants Lancmanis</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Gardens</th><td>10-hectare formal French garden, 32-hectare forest park, 2,300+ rose varieties</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Location</th><td>Pilsrundāle, Bauska Municipality, Zemgale region, Latvia</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Coordinates</th><td>56.4147° N, 24.0222° E</td></tr>
  <tr><th scope="row">Distance from Riga</th><td>≈ 80 km / ≈ 75-minute drive south of Riga</td></tr>

    </tbody>
  </table>
</aside>


<h2 id="entrance-vestibule-galleries">Where you arrive: The Entrance Vestibule and Galleries</h2>
<p>You walk in from the great state courtyard and the first room you find yourself in is the central vestibule. The mood here is intentionally restrained — restrained Baroque, to be precise. The architecture of the vestibule mirrors the façades, and the ground floor's interior decoration has actually survived from the very first construction period, which is rare in this building.</p>
<p>Look at the entrance door: it faces the garden, not the courtyard. To either side of you, vaulted galleries with colonnades divide the space and lead toward the two state staircases. Francesco Rastrelli, the architect, originally envisioned something more luxurious for this entry — black and white marble flooring, the sort of finish you'd expect in St Petersburg. But because he was juggling the parallel construction of the Duke's residence in Jelgava, he simplified the plan and laid clay tiles instead. They're still there.</p>
<p>Turn left along the columns toward the east-side staircase. At the bottom of the stairs, before you go up, take the corridor running off to the side — it leads to the palace kitchen.</p>
<figure class="rundale-gallery rundale-gallery--entrance-vestibule-galleries" data-section-id="1" data-section-slug="entrance-vestibule-galleries" aria-label="Photo gallery: Where you arrive: The Entrance Vestibule and Galleries">
  <a class="rundale-gallery__hero" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rundale-rooms/rundale-palace-entrance-vestibule-galleries-1-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="entrance-vestibule-galleries" data-caption="Where you arrive: The Entrance Vestibule and Galleries — Rundāle Palace, Latvia" aria-label="Open photo 1 of 2: Where you arrive: The Entrance Vestibule and Galleries — Rundāle Palace, Latvia">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rundale-rooms/rundale-palace-entrance-vestibule-galleries-1-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">

<h2>The Palace Kitchen</h2>
<p>This is one of only two rooms in the wing where the original clay floor tiles were able to be restored in their original positions. Everywhere else, they're modern reconstructions.</p>
<p>There are four hearths built into the kitchen, and food was prepared on open fire. Full-length flues run the entire height of the palace to create the draft needed to cook for a court. You'll see cauldrons with adjustable hanging devices, spit holders, tripods, and cooking grates. <strong>Pay close attention to the spit rotation device on the second hearth</strong> — it works with a clock-like mechanism. Inside the third hearth there's a masonry platform finished in Dutch tiles, used for preparing smaller dishes.</p>
<p>The collection of utensils includes pots, pans, colanders, cups, cans, and a separate display case showing faience and tinware. Clay bowls — the kind widely used in eighteenth-century European kitchens — were also discovered in archaeological excavations near the palace. The walls are hung with eighteenth-century paintings and engravings of kitchen scenes: two paintings by the eighteenth-century German painter Justus Juncker show activity around a hearth, and two by the Austrian painter Lautter depict shelves with polished dishes. There are ceiling chains and meat hooks for hanging carcasses. A painting by the seventeenth-century Dutch artist Isaac van Ostade above the second hearth shows game ripening on so-called "bacon hooks" — two of which are actually displayed in the third hearth.</p>
<p>In the corners opposite the hearths sit two large brass water containers with lids. Worth knowing: a water pipe was already installed in this kitchen during the Duke's reign, and fragments of it have been preserved in the original location in the basement under the kitchen.</p>
<p>Now we walk back through the hallway and head up.</p>
<h2>Exhibition: "The Green Glass"</h2>
<p>Tucked next to the old kitchen is a small but elegant exhibition called The Green Glass. Four vitrines display a collection of green glass household objects donated to the Museum by Karin von Borbély of Germany. It takes about three minutes if you're moving, ten if you really look — the colour catches differently in each piece.</p>
<h2>The State Staircase</h2>
<p>There are two state staircases at Rundāle, almost identical to each other. We follow the east-side one because that's the one used during festivities. The west-side staircase serves the Duke's family wing, and we'll come to it later.</p>
<p>By 1740, the walls and ceilings of the stairwells had been adorned with stucco decorations — gypsum and lime mass used as decorative sculpture — featuring stylised human faces (mascarons), flowers, palm branches, acanthus leaves, and volutes. Carved pedestals and balusters were finished too, although the railing vases were originally meant to be more luxurious; the ones with sculptures on pedestals never happened.</p>
<p>What makes this staircase remarkable: <strong>it's the only interior from Rastrelli's early period that was actually implemented according to his design and has survived to today.</strong> The stucco work was done by Russian masters called quadrators, working under Pyotr Yefremov, using models created by a German master.</p>
<p>During the restoration, the mirror windows that Rastrelli originally planned were finally installed. Throughout the Duke's era they'd only been faux glazing bars painted on the wall — common Baroque practice, since mirrors create the illusion of a larger space. The stair railings and steps survive from the first construction period; the railing vases were made and installed in the second construction period, then reconstructed during restoration. The ceiling lantern was made after a sample from Kuskovo Palace near Moscow. Lanterns went into rooms where ordinary candles would otherwise be blown out by the draft.</p>
<p>From the top of the staircase, guests could enter either the state rooms (right) or the Duke's state apartments (left). The Duke had a third option — a private door in the middle of the staircase, usually closed because it led to his private rooms.</p>
<p>We turn right, toward the Gold Hall.</p>

<h2 id="antechamber-gold-hall">The Antechamber of the Gold Hall</h2>
<p>We're in the east wing of the palace now — the side where court celebrations took place, which is why the artistic décor here is genuinely opulent. This was made during the second construction period and is considered an outstanding example of decorative art in the then-popular Rococo style. The ground floor reflects the first construction period's Baroque era, but up here on the first floor the visual language has shifted.</p>
<p>Because these rooms had representational functions, they aren't crammed with furniture. Instead, they showcase monumental sculpture and painting — works of art from the Museum's collection.</p>
<p>The Duke's guests would have waited here in the antechamber until the doors of the throne hall opened and they were solemnly announced. <strong>On the left of the door leading to the Gold Hall is a portrait of Duke Ernst Johann himself</strong>, painted in Courland around 1740. The probable author is Christian Sidow.</p>
<p>In the second construction period, the decorative sculptor Johann Michael Graff produced remarkable work here. He was at Rundāle from 1765 to 1768. The ceiling rosette he created has been well preserved. A lot of pieces in this room — parquet, wall panels, doors, doorway decoration — survive from the first construction period because after returning from exile, Duke Ernst Johann wanted to restore his property as quickly as possible. The stove in the corner is one of seventeen copies made in Leningrad in the 1970s, based on preserved samples of painted tiles from the eight original stoves. The walls are upholstered with period-appropriate fabric.</p>
<p>For the convenience of waiting guests, there's seating, a console table, and a clock. Large-format seventeenth-century paintings depict scenes from the antique world and the Bible. Next to the door to the Gold Hall is a painting called <em>Artemisia</em> by the Dutch artist Jan de Bray, depicting the faithful love of Artemisia, widow of King Mausolus. On the opposite side, an unknown Italian painter shows the Roman goddess Juno at the corpse of the many-eyed giant Argus Panoptes. The far end wall holds <em>The Finding of Moses</em> by an unknown Flemish artist.</p>
<p>Through the next door is the Gold Hall itself.</p>

<h2>The Gold Hall</h2>
<p>This is the most luxurious room in the palace. The Duke's throne stood directly opposite the entrance door at the far end of the hall — and it was the only piece of furniture in here, because guests stood. Walk forward and stand where the throne once stood. From there, look up.</p>
<p>The ceiling painting — the <em>plafond</em> — is dedicated to him. The theme is the glorification of the ruler's virtues, an apotheosis. As elsewhere in the palace, the source of inspiration was ancient Roman mythology. The Duke is personified by Mars (god of war), with a ruddy flag and a tilted Saturn's death scythe next to him. The central group of figures depicts the virtues of the ruler: a woman sitting at the obelisk with a trumpet symbolises Fame; a woman with the sun over her head and a green branch in her hand is the Truth. Peace is symbolised by a woman holding a wand with snakes or caduceus in one hand and a flame in the other. A cornucopia held by Generosity, and a design of the building held by Magnificence. In the strip between the walls and the ceiling — the ceiling cove — you can view eighteen allegorical and emblematical paintings executed in grisaille technique, using lighter and darker shades of the same colour.</p>
<p>Children figures depicted in the paintings are <em>putti</em> (singular: <em>putto</em>). Here, the <em>putti</em> represent various art forms and activities. On the left, just above the window by the entrance to the Grand Gallery, a <em>putto</em> supports a plate with the year 1767 — the year the ceiling painting was completed. <strong>The plafond was a collaboration between two Italian artists — Francesco Antonio Martini and Carlo Zucchi.</strong> They came to Rundāle from St Petersburg, where they'd been working on the interiors of the Winter Palace. Martini was born in Ticino in the Italian-speaking part of Switzerland and worked in northern Germany and Denmark; Zucchi was a member of a large family of Venetian artists who'd worked in Dresden and Krakow.</p>
<p>Now the walls. The stucco marble was done by the same master as in many other rooms — Johann Michael Graff — together with his brother Joseph and two assistants, Virgilius Baumann and Andreas Lanz. The colours were originally brighter and the gilded stucco decoration stood out perfectly against the vivid background, but more than 250 years later the green pigment has faded. Stucco decorations are partially covered in the original gilding — it's been preserved and restored.</p>
<p>Sculptural garlands on the walls were also done by Graff's team. They're emblematic — that is, they depict objects that symbolically represent arts and activities supported by the Duke. The wall next to where the Duke's throne used to stand is decorated with garlands glorifying music, science, and architecture. The opposite wall — between the hall and the porcelain cabinet — celebrates fine arts, music, dance, sculpture, painting. The garlands on the side walls are dedicated to fishing, hunting, cattle-breeding, and horticulture. The central square of the far end wall features the initials of Duke Ernst Johann: "EJ", on a silver background.</p>
<p>There were very few chandeliers at Rundāle in the eighteenth century — mostly portable candleholders were used. The Gold Hall is one of the few rooms originally designed with five chandeliers for a particularly festive atmosphere. The current chandeliers are copies of French type with bronze frames and cut crystal glass pendants, made after a sample at Kuskovo Palace. Their lustre is multiplied by trumeau mirrors, which makes the room read as larger and brighter than it actually is. At the time, mirror glass of the required size couldn't be cast in one piece, so each mirror is composed of several pieces.</p>
<p>An open door stands out among the gold. Behind it: light blue and white. That's the Porcelain Cabinet. Let's go.</p>

<h2>The Porcelain Cabinet of the Gold Hall</h2>
<p>This was one of two rooms where the Duke displayed his porcelain collection. Collecting Oriental porcelain was a passion of many European rulers in the eighteenth century — it was a marker of taste and status, the way collecting contemporary art might be today.</p>
<p>The cabinet is deliberately designed to contrast the Gold Hall. Where the larger room is opulent, this one is luxurious in a stylistically opposite key. Light blue and white dominate. The light blue wall planes are divided by white stucco panels, two of which have built-in mirrors that optically expand the space. To display porcelain items, there are 34 shelves or consoles made in rocaille ornamentation. <strong>The vases here are Chinese, of the so-called <em>famille rose</em> range</strong> (French for "pink family"), in which rosy tones stand out.</p>
<p>Directly opposite the Porcelain Cabinet is the Grand Gallery.</p>
<figure class="rundale-gallery rundale-gallery--porcelain-cabinet-gold-hall" data-section-id="7" data-section-slug="porcelain-cabinet-gold-hall" aria-label="Photo gallery: The Porcelain Cabinet of the Gold Hall">
