<h2>Exhibition: "18th-Century Portraits of Courlanders"</h2>
<p>The eighteenth-century portrait gallery of Courlanders represents the Duke's supporters and his opponents among the nobility, as well as professors of the Academia Petrina founded by Duke Peter, and other representatives of the intelligentsia and officials. <strong>Most of these works were created by artists who lived and worked in the territory of Latvia for a longer or shorter period.</strong></p>
<p>The room is dominated by a portrait of Johann Friedrich von Nolde, proprietor of Gramzda Manor, depicted on the background of a palace surrounded by a French garden. It was painted in 1778 by Copenhagen artist Peter Jessen.</p>
<p>To the right of the large painting are five portraits of local nobility, painted in the 1750s and 1760s by Königsberg-born artist Leonhard Schorer. He represents the Baroque era portraiture that flourished in Latvia during the reign of Duke Ernst Johann and Duke Peter when not only Schorer but also Friedrich Hartmann Barisien, Johann Gottlieb Becker and others worked in the capital of the Duchy of Courland. On the same wall between the door and the window, we see a portrait painted by Becker of lawyer Sigismund Georg Schwander, adviser in the court of the Duchy of Courland.</p>
<p>Higher up to the right of the windows is another work by Schorer — it depicts Prince Charles of Saxony who was the Duke of Courland during Ernst Johann Biron's exile. A portrait of Otto Hermann von der Howen, member of the Courland Landtag, is displayed further atop between the windows — he remained a zealous supporter of Duke Charles even after the return of Duke Ernst Johann from exile. The author of this portrait is the virtuoso painter Gottlieb Schiffner who usually worked in Dresden and travelled to Courland only for a short period. <strong>Below is a portrait of the Governor of Courland, Count Peter Ludwig von der Pahlen</strong>, painted by the court painter of the Duchy of Courland Friedrich Hartmann Barisien. To the left of the stove, in the bottom row, are three more works by Barisien painted in the 1780s when he was no longer the Duke's court painter and focused on portraying the local intelligentsia.</p>
<p>Two portraits are exhibited above the work of Barisien: Anna Maria Frederike von Taube, a lady-in-waiting in the court of Duchess Dorothea, and her husband Major of the Russian Army, Baron Friedrich Karl von Taube. They were painted in Dresden in the 1780s by the prominent Swiss portraitist Anton Graff.</p>
<p>The layout of the room is complemented by eighteenth-century furniture and a black glazed tile stove with a relief star motif. <strong>It was made in Vidzeme and was originally located in Bērzaune Rectory.</strong></p>
<p>Pay attention to the display case behind the portrait of Johann Friedrich von Nolde! It features a group of objects that characterize eighteenth-century men's fashion.</p>
<p>The next room invites you to explore the family history of Counts Medem and the life of Duchess Dorothea of Courland.</p>

<h2>Exhibition: "Duchess Dorothea of Courland and the Family of Counts Medem"</h2>
<p>The display in this room was made possible with support from Count Théodor de Medem, the descendant of Count Jeannot von Medem. He presented the Rundāle Palace Museum with family relics which his grandfather Count Theodor von Medem had transported from his estates in Stukmaņi and Vecauce at the end of World War I. <strong>The centrepiece is a cosmetic set that belonged to Duchess Dorothea of Courland.</strong> It consists of 22 porcelain items and was made at the Royal Porcelain Manufactory in Berlin around 1784.</p>
<p>The last Duchess of Courland Dorothea, the full name Anna Charlotte Dorothea, is the most famous representative of the Medem family, born and raised in Mežotne Manor. The life of the whole Medem family changed significantly when at the age of eighteen she accepted a marriage offer from Duke of Courland Peter. To make this marriage possible, Dorothea's father was awarded the title of Count; later her brothers and half-sister often joined the Duchess on trips abroad gaining significant impressions and meeting outstanding personalities. The beauty, charm and wisdom of Duchess Dorothea opened her many doors to the highest society in Europe and allowed her to influence politics informally.</p>
<p>Several portraits of Duchess Dorothea are on display in this room. In the group of paintings to the right of the display case, Duchess Dorothea is depicted by artist Friedrich Hartmann Barisien. Next to the Duchess, there are two portraits of her brother Jeannot and, below, two portraits of the Duchess's half-sister Elisa. To the left of the display case are portraits of the Duchess's father Johann Friedrich von Medem and her brother Karl.</p>
<p><strong>Both Dorothea's brothers were interesting personalities:</strong> the eldest — Karl Johann Friedrich, owner of Vecauce and Remte Manors, was a diplomat and held important political positions in Courland, whereas the younger brother Christoph Johann Friedrich, called Jeannot, inherited Eleja Manor from his father and tried to introduce the latest European art and architectural trends in Courland.</p>
<p>Dorothea's half-sister Elisa von der Recke, born Charlotte Constanzia von Medem, was a writer and became known throughout Europe for her unveiling book about the adventurous Cagliostro who stayed in Jelgava in 1779 and abused the trust of the Medem family. <strong>For this book, the Russian Empress Catherine II granted a life pension to the author.</strong> Elisa's friends and acquaintances included famous European writers, scientists and cultural figures. The two half-sisters remained very close throughout their lives; Elisa was Dorothea's confidant and often accompanied her on various travels.</p>
<p>The exhibition also includes portraits of other members of the Medem family.</p>
<p>Crossing the hallway of the Duchess's apartment one more time, we arrive again at the western state staircase.</p>

    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rundale-rooms/rundale-palace-exhibition-duchess-dorothea-medem-1-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rundale-rooms/rundale-palace-exhibition-duchess-dorothea-medem-1-latvia.jpg" alt="Exhibition: &quot;Duchess Dorothea of Courland and the Family of Counts Medem&quot; at Rundāle Palace, Latvia (photograph 1 of 1)" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="800">
    </picture>
    <figcaption>Exhibition: &quot;Duchess Dorothea of Courland and the Family of Counts Medem&quot; — Rundāle Palace, Latvia</figcaption>
  </a>

</figure>
<aside class="rundale-cta">
  <p class="rundale-cta__kicker">Want a guide on the day?</p>
  <h3 class="rundale-cta__headline">Visit Rundāle with us</h3>
  <p class="rundale-cta__body">We run a small-group day excursion from Riga that anchors a relaxed visit to Rundāle around Bauska Castle and a gentle Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit. Picked-up door-to-door, three things in one day, with a licensed Latvian guide.</p>
  <a class="rundale-cta__button" href="/excursions/rundale-palace-bauska-castle-brewery.html">See the Rundāle excursion — €85</a>
</aside>
<h2>Other Exhibitions Worth Your Time</h2>
<p>If you've made it this far, you've completed the main first-floor route. But Rundāle has more to offer if your day allows for it.</p>
<p><strong>On the ground floor</strong>, you can visit the decorative art exhibition "From the Gothic Style to Art Nouveau", where historical styles ranging from the fifteenth century to World War I are represented in 15 rooms outlining the development of each style in Western Europe and its manifestations in Latvia.</p>
<p><strong>In the palace basement</strong>, several exhibitions await:
- <strong>"The History of Rundāle Palace Construction"</strong> introduces the palace's story based on discoveries in its surrounding area and on the palace premises, archive documents and historical photo documentation.
- <strong>"Stone Carvings and Ironwork in Latvia"</strong> features stone carvings of façades and various ironwork from Latvian manors, as well as tombstones and plaques.
- <strong>"Door and window fittings in Latvia in the 18th and 19th centuries"</strong> continues the same theme.
- <strong>"Pompa funebris"</strong> invites visitors to get acquainted with funerary art — the sarcophagi and decorative coffin plaques in the collection of Rundāle Palace Museum have been acquired from various Latvian churches and the Great Cemetery in Riga. Another Rundāle Palace Museum exhibition dedicated to funerary art is available in the Vault of the Dukes of Courland in Jelgava Palace.</p>
<h2>Planning Your Visit: Practical Notes</h2>
<p>If you've read this far, you know roughly what's coming. A few honest things to factor in before you book:</p>
<p>The full visitor route covers nearly forty rooms across the central building and both wings, plus exhibitions on the ground floor and basement. <strong>Plan a minimum of 90 minutes</strong> for a focused walkthrough, and two and a half hours if you want to actually look at the paintings and read the labels. The gardens — over 32 hectares including a one-hectare formal rose garden with more than 2,000 rose varieties — deserve their own additional hour, especially in summer.</p>
<p>Rundāle is a one-hour drive south of Riga. We include it on our Rundāle Palace, Bauska Castle &amp; Ķemeri Bog Boardwalk day tour from Riga, where the palace is the centrepiece of a longer day in the Zemgale region.</p>
<p>If you'd rather do it independently, the Museum is open year-round (with reduced winter hours), and the gardens reach peak bloom in late June and early July when the historical roses begin to flower.</p>
<h2>A Final Word</h2>
<p>Rundāle Palace works on you slowly. The Gold Hall is the Instagram moment, but the rooms that tend to stay with visitors are the smaller ones — the Duchess's Boudoir with its huge shell-shaped sofa niche, the Hunting Room with its wall of antlers, the unrestored Room for the Palace History Studies that quietly explains, with photographs and stripped-back walls, how much human effort went into bringing all of the rest back from ruin.</p>
<p>Bring comfortable shoes. The east wing alone takes you through nearly a kilometre of walking once you account for doubling back. Bring a friend who likes to stop and look. And if you're doing it as part of a guided tour, ask your guide about the parquet in the Duke's State Bedroom — 170 star-pattern shields in oak, mahogany, black oak, palm and maple, made by Johann Baptist Eger between 1738 and 1739, and the most important example of Baroque parquet in Latvia. Most visitors look up at the ceiling. The floor in that room deserves an equal moment of attention.</p>
<p>We'll see you at the gate.</p>
<p><em>This article is part of an ongoing series on Rundāle Palace published by Barefoot Baltic. Future entries will go deeper on individual rooms, the Rastrelli design lineage, the parallel construction of Jelgava Palace, the gardens through the seasons, and the people who lived here. If you'd like us to take you through Rundāle Palace in person, our small-group day tours from Riga include the palace as the anchor of a longer day in the Zemgale region — including Bauska Castle and a gentle Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit.</em></p>

<section class="faq-section" id="faq" aria-labelledby="faq-heading">
  <h2 id="faq-heading">Frequently asked questions about Rundāle Palace</h2>
  <div class="faq-list" role="list">
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-1">
        Did Duke Biron actually live in Rundāle Palace?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-1" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>Rundāle was designed as the duke's <strong>summer residence</strong>. The main administrative and winter residence of the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia was Jelgava Palace (Mitau), about 40&nbsp;km north. Construction began in 1736, but Duke Ernst Johann von Biron was arrested and exiled to Siberia in 1740 — within weeks of his patron Empress Anna's death — and work stopped. He returned only in the 1760s, in his seventies, and finished the interiors before he died in 1772.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-2">
        Who designed Rundāle Palace?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeo_Rastrelli" rel="noopener">Francesco Bartolomeo Rastrelli</a> — the Italian Imperial-Baroque architect best known for the Winter Palace, the Catherine Palace at Tsarskoye Selo, and Smolny Cathedral in St Petersburg. Rundāle is one of only a handful of intact surviving Rastrelli interiors anywhere. The palace and the gardens were both from his original 1736 plan.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-3">
        How long does the visitor route take?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-3" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>Plan a <strong>minimum of 90 minutes</strong> for a focused walkthrough of the 40 rooms, and two and a half hours if you want to actually look at the paintings and read the labels. The gardens — over 32 hectares including a one-hectare formal rose garden — deserve their own additional hour, especially in summer.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-4">
        How many rooms can you visit inside?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-4" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p><strong>About 40 rooms</strong> across the central building and both wings have been restored to their 18th-century condition. The full 138-room palace is much larger; the rest is museum offices, reserve collections, and rooms kept in their weathered mid-20th-century state as a counterpoint to the restored parts.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-5">
        How does Rundāle Palace compare to Versailles?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-5" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>Every guidebook calls Rundāle &ldquo;the Versailles of the Baltics&rdquo; — and the comparison is misleading. Rundāle was a <strong>private summer residence</strong> for a duke, not a working court for a king of France. Versailles has more than 2,300 rooms; Rundāle has 138, of which you visit 40. The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles is 73&nbsp;m long; the Gold Hall at Rundāle is roughly 20&nbsp;m. The right comparison is to a country palace by the same architect — like Tsarskoye Selo — not the seat of a kingdom.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-6">
        What is the Gold Hall at Rundāle Palace?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-6" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>The throne room — the most luxurious room in the palace, where the duke's throne stood directly opposite the entrance and guests stood. Its <em>plafond</em> ceiling painting (1767) was a collaboration between two Italian artists who came to Rundāle from St Petersburg, <strong>Francesco Antonio Martini</strong> and <strong>Carlo Zucchi</strong>, and depicts the duke as Mars surrounded by the allegorical virtues of a ruler. The walls are gilded stucco marble by Johann Michael Graff and his team.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-7">
        What is the White Hall?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-7" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>The palace's grand ballroom and Rundāle's most intricate room: 22 thematic stucco reliefs above the windows and doors, 76 figures, and roughly 2,050 individually-cast flowers. Each stork's nest is made of real twigs covered in gypsum. The décor reads as a symbolic story: the seasons, the four elements, music, gardening, and hunting all encoded into the walls. Worked by Johann Michael Graff in the 1760s phase.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-8">
        Why did construction stop in 1740 and resume only in the 1760s?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>Because <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Johann_von_Biron" rel="noopener">Duke Biron</a> was arrested. His patron, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_of_Russia" rel="noopener">Empress Anna of Russia</a>, died in October 1740, and within weeks Biron was overthrown by court rivals and exiled to Siberia. He spent <strong>22 years in exile</strong>. In 1762 <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_the_Great" rel="noopener">Catherine the Great</a> released him, restored him as Duke of Courland, and sent him home — already in his seventies. The palace's lavish Rococo interiors were finished by an old man who had spent most of his sixties in Siberia.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-9">
        Who restored Rundāle Palace and when?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>The restoration ran from <strong>1972 to 2014</strong> — longer than the original construction — and was led almost single-handedly by the Latvian painter and art historian <strong>Imants Lancmanis</strong>, whose life's work it became. Decades of patient work brought the palace back from a state of long neglect. The wallcoverings alone took 19 years to weave at the scientific restoration workshops in Moscow — 13 different silk and semi-silk fabrics, almost 4.5&nbsp;km in total.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-10">
        Did Napoleon&#x27;s army damage Rundāle Palace?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>Yes. During the 1812 French campaign the palace was plundered: fabric wallcoverings were torn off and mirrors were shattered. The paintings and stucco decorations survived relatively well. A second wave of damage came in 1919 when the Bermondt-Avalov Army destroyed wood panels and demolished three stoves, and in 1934 a school demolished the Duchess's wing's wood-carved staircase to create an assembly hall. Most of what you see is the result of the 1972–2014 restoration.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-11">
        How do I get to Rundāle Palace from Riga?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-11" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p>Rundāle is <strong>about 80&nbsp;km south of Riga, roughly 75 minutes by car</strong>, or about 90 minutes by public bus via Bauska. There is no direct train. We include Rundāle as the centrepiece of our small-group <a href="/excursions/rundale-palace-bauska-castle-brewery.html">Rundāle Palace, Bauska Castle &amp; Ķemeri Bog Boardwalk day excursion</a> — door-to-door from your central Riga hotel, ten hours, €85 per adult.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
      <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rundale-rooms-12">
        When is the best time to visit Rundāle Palace?<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
      </button>
      <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rundale-rooms-12" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
        <p><strong>Late May to mid-July</strong> for the rose garden — about 2,300 varieties bloom, peaking around mid-June. <strong>September</strong> is the quietest month with the best low light on the south façade and far fewer coach parties; if you're after the empty Gold Hall experience, this is the window. <strong>July and August</strong> are busiest with international tour groups; weekday mornings are still calmer than weekend afternoons. <strong>Winter visits</strong> (December–March) are warm inside, the low light makes the 18th-century colours glow, and the gardens are dormant or snow-covered.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Yes, for most visitors to Latvia, Ķemeri bog is worth it.</strong> It's the single most photogenic natural place near Riga, and most people who walk it call it the highlight of their entire trip.</li>
<li><strong>It's a 10,000-year-old <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raised_bog" rel="noopener external">raised bog</a></strong> — a specific, rare landscape that looks like nowhere else in Europe. Dark mirror pools, dwarf pines knee-high, soft sphagnum moss. A Natura 2000 site, a Ramsar wetland, and home to over 190 bird species.</li>
<li><strong>The boardwalk is 3.4 km as a full loop</strong>, or 1.4 km as a shorter inner loop. Wooden, flat, and accessible to pushchairs. 75–90 minutes at a relaxed pace, including the observation tower.</li>
<li><strong>Two hard rules for DIY visits.</strong> Bring strong mosquito repellent and a head net — Ķemeri has a serious mosquito reputation year-round, worst at dawn and dusk, and repellent alone is often not enough. And never step off the boardwalk without bog shoes and a local guide: a raised bog hides deep pools under the moss carpet, and people sink.</li>
<li><strong>It's free.</strong> No entrance fee, no tickets, no gate. Open 24 hours, year-round. There's a free car park and basic toilets at the trailhead.</li>
<li><strong>Come at sunrise.</strong> The bog is ordinary in flat midday light and extraordinary in the golden hour just after dawn. This is the one detail that makes or breaks a visit.</li>
<li><strong>It's 50 km west of Riga</strong>, about 45 minutes by car, 65 minutes by suburban train (plus a 3.5 km walk from the station, which is the main catch for a DIY visit).</li>
<li><strong>You should skip it if:</strong> you only have 48 hours in Riga and you've never been to Old Town, you can't do a very early start, or you don't want to stay on a boardwalk (more on this below — it matters).</li>
</ul>
<h2>What Ķemeri bog actually is</h2>
<p>I should start with this, because half the people who ask me "is it worth it?" are imagining something wrong.</p>
<p>Ķemeri isn't a swamp. It's a <em>raised bog</em>, which is a specific geological thing: a wetland fed only by rainwater (no streams, no rivers, no groundwater), slowly growing upward over thousands of years as sphagnum moss dies, compresses, and turns into peat. The Great Ķemeri Bog (Lielais Ķemeru tīrelis) has been doing this for about ten thousand years, since the last ice age retreated. The surface you stand on today is roughly eight metres higher than the ground beneath it. Everything you see — the dark pools, the tiny pines, the carpets of moss — is sitting on top of a peat layer as thick as a two-storey house.</p>
<p>The visual effect is hard to describe until you've seen it. A flat, treeless expanse stretches to the horizon. There are no full-sized trees because the bog is too acidic and too waterlogged for their roots. The pines that do grow are dwarfs, knee-high or waist-high, surviving on almost nothing. Between them, dozens of small dark pools reflect the sky like polished mirrors — these are called "bog eyes" in Latvian, and they form where the peat has subsided unevenly. The whole place has a silence you won't find anywhere near a city. No insects buzzing in midday heat, because the open bog is too exposed; no birds calling from nearby forest, because the forest is two kilometres away. Just the wind across moss, and occasionally the distant cry of a crane.</p>
<p>The carnivorous plants are the detail most people miss. Growing right beside the boardwalk, small enough to walk past a hundred times, is the sundew (<em>Drosera rotundifolia</em>). Bright red tentacles tipped with what look like dewdrops, but the drops are a sticky glue that traps insects, which the plant then digests. A tiny meat-eater in a landscape that hasn't changed much since the mammoths left. Once you've seen one, you start seeing them everywhere.</p>
<p>One more thing about the bog surface, which matters if you're visiting on your own. A raised bog is not firm ground. The sphagnum carpet you see from the boardwalk is floating on top of a peat layer up to eight metres deep, with open pools hidden between the vegetation. Step off the boardwalk without traditional bog shoes (<em>purva kurpes</em>) and a guide who knows the terrain, and you can sink — there are anecdotal Baltic stories about heavy vehicles and even soldiers disappearing into bogs that are exaggerated in the telling but built on a real physical fact. <strong>Stay on the boardwalk every time.</strong> If you want to actually walk on the moss, book a guided bog-shoe hike with <a href="https://balticnaturetourism.com/en/tours/bogshoe-hiking" rel="noopener">Baltic Nature Tourism</a> or one of the other Latvian specialist operators — they provide the equipment and the local knowledge. Our Barefoot Baltic sunrise tour is a boardwalk tour and doesn't include off-boardwalk hiking.</p>
<h2>Is it actually worth your day? The honest answer</h2>
<p>Depends on three things: how much time you have in Latvia, what kind of traveller you are, and whether you can come at the right hour.</p>
<p><strong>If you have three or more days in Latvia, yes, almost certainly.</strong> Ķemeri is the thing you'll talk about when you get home. The bog is genuinely unusual, the boardwalk is beautifully built, and the whole trip out and back is half a day at most. For anyone with a normal Latvia itinerary, a morning at the bog slots naturally between your Old Town days and your coastal or countryside days.</p>
<p><strong>If you only have 48 hours in Riga and it's your first visit, maybe not.</strong> Old Town, Central Market, and a half-day for Art Nouveau architecture will give you a more complete picture of Latvia than a morning at a bog will, because the city itself is UNESCO-listed and has eight hundred years of stories stacked on top of each other. Ķemeri is a complement to Riga, not a substitute. If you have to choose, choose Riga.</p>
<p><strong>If you want a big nature hit, absolutely yes.</strong> There are very few places in Europe where you can walk on moss that's 10,000 years old, next to carnivorous plants, in a landscape that looks like Finland crossed with Patagonia, forty-five minutes from a capital city. Nature travellers, photographers, birdwatchers, and anyone who likes quiet places will leave Ķemeri happier than they arrived.</p>
<p><strong>If you hate early starts, you should probably skip it.</strong> I'll explain why in the next section.</p>

<p>Here is the single most important thing about visiting Ķemeri: the bog is two completely different places at sunrise and at lunchtime, and most of the "is it worth it?" complaints I've seen online come from people who visited at the wrong hour.</p>
<p>At sunrise — roughly 4:30 AM in June, 5:30 AM in August, 7:00 AM in October — the bog is at its most beautiful. Mist rises from the dark pools. The low sun turns the sphagnum moss soft amber. The pines throw long shadows. The boardwalk is empty. The air is cool, still, and completely silent except for the occasional distant crane. The photographs that have made Ķemeri viral on Instagram in the last five years were all taken in this window.</p>
<p>At lunchtime in July, the same boardwalk is a different experience. Flat, high sun washes out the colour. The mirror pools look black and lifeless. The mosquitoes are at their peak (and in peak summer, they are serious). Several Baltic-circuit tour buses will have arrived and left. The boardwalk is crowded. The silence is gone. Most importantly, the light that makes the photographs is gone — the bog stops looking like that dreamy Nordic place you saw on Instagram and starts looking like, well, a bog.</p>
<p>This is why our own Ķemeri excursion runs from Riga at 4:30 AM and is back in town by 10:30. We won't pretend the early start is fun — it isn't, it's brutal — but the bog at first light is the whole point. If you can't face a 4 AM wake-up, the next best window is late afternoon in September or October, when the sun is lower and the crowds have gone home.</p>
<h2>How to get there — your four options</h2>
<p>Ķemeri National Park is about 50 kilometres west of Riga, just inland from the Baltic coast and a few kilometres south of Jūrmala. There are four sensible ways to get there, each with trade-offs.</p>

<p>The single most common DIY approach — taking the train — is the one that leads to the most "was Ķemeri really worth it?" feedback I see on TripAdvisor and Reddit, because the train day and the sunrise day are essentially incompatible. If you take the train, you'll see the bog in flat midday light with other day-trippers. If you self-drive, hire a car or join a tour, you can actually get there at the hour when the bog looks like it does in the photographs.</p>
<h2>When to go, month by month</h2>
<p><strong>May</strong> — Spring. Migrating birds arriving, forest floor waking up, long days (sunrise around 5 AM by mid-May), cool temperatures, very few mosquitoes. An excellent month for a first visit.</p>
<p><strong>June</strong> — Peak light. The longest days of the year, sunrise around 4:30 AM, a soft northern dawn that lasts almost an hour. This is the month the best photographs come from. Mosquitoes are serious from June onward — bring strong repellent and a head net, and accept that the first hour of the morning is when they're worst.</p>
<p><strong>July</strong> — Warmest and driest. Everything is green, the sky is often dramatic, and the whole park is at its most vivid. Also peak mosquito season, particularly in the first hour after sunrise. Long sleeves, strong repellent, and a head net are all non-negotiable.</p>
<p><strong>August</strong> — Easiest early start (sunrise around 5:30–6:00 AM) and still warm. A good choice for people who want the sunrise experience without the full June 4 AM ordeal. Our own tour season runs through the end of August because of this.</p>
<p><strong>September</strong> — The quiet window. The light is lower, the mosquitoes are reduced (though not gone until the first hard frost in mid to late October — still bring repellent and a head net), and the bog starts to take on its autumn colours (copper pines, rust-red sphagnum) by mid-month. Sunrise is a civilised 6:30 AM. Fewer visitors, and the trains are emptier. If I had to pick one month for a relaxed DIY visit, September would be it. There's a whole separate post on the autumn version of the bog — see <a href="/blog/kemeri-bog-in-autumn.html">Ķemeri Bog in Autumn</a> for the full treatment.</p>
<p><strong>October</strong> — Full autumn. The bog turns properly copper-coloured for about two weeks in mid-October, and the morning mist is at its most dramatic as the temperature drops overnight. The risk is the first frost and the first rain, which can make the boardwalk slippery.</p>
<p><strong>November through March</strong> — Winter. The boardwalk is open but trails can be icy, the days are very short (sunrise around 8:45 AM in December), and there are no facilities open. For anyone who wants a winter visit, pick a clear bright day after fresh snow and bring proper boots. It's beautiful but less forgiving than the summer version. We don't run our tour in winter, and I wouldn't recommend the train option.</p>
<h2>What to bring</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Layers.</strong> Even in July, a 4:30 AM start on the open bog feels cold. Bring a warm layer you can take off once the sun is up.</li>
<li><strong>Long sleeves and long trousers.</strong> Not for the cold — for the mosquitoes, which are serious from June through August and still active until the first hard frost in mid to late October. The open boardwalk is slightly better than the forest approach because there's more wind, but you will still need cover.</li>
<li><strong>Strong mosquito repellent AND a head net.</strong> DEET-based or picaridin-based spray, not herbal. A head net that covers your face is cheap, light, and standard kit for Latvian bog visits — Ķemeri's mosquito reputation is real and repellent alone is often not enough, particularly in the first hour after dawn. If you're coming on a guided tour with us, repellent and a head net are included.</li>
<li><strong>Stay on the boardwalk.</strong> The one hard rule. See the safety paragraph above — a raised bog is not firm ground and DIY visitors should never leave the wooden planks without bog shoes and a local guide.</li>
<li><strong>Comfortable walking shoes.</strong> The boardwalk is flat but you'll be on your feet for 75–90 minutes. Trainers are fine; heels and sandals are not.</li>
<li><strong>Water.</strong> There's nowhere to buy anything at the trailhead, and the boardwalk has no facilities beyond the starting car park.</li>
<li><strong>A camera with a wide-angle lens</strong>, if you care about the photographs. Phone cameras work, but the dynamic range of a raised bog at sunrise — bright sky, dark pools, shadow pines — is a challenge for phone sensors.</li>
<li><strong>Nothing left on the boardwalk.</strong> No food wrappers, no plastic, no cigarettes. The bog is a Natura 2000 site and the ecosystem is fragile. Rangers do check.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Who Ķemeri bog isn't for</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>People who only have 48 hours in Riga.</strong> Prioritise Old Town, Central Market, and Art Nouveau. Come back for Ķemeri on your second trip.</li>
<li><strong>People who genuinely cannot do a very early start.</strong> The midday version of the bog is much less interesting, and you'll leave thinking you don't understand what the fuss is about. If 4 AM is impossible, consider a September or October afternoon visit instead, or skip it entirely.</li>
<li><strong>People who are claustrophobic about landscape.</strong> The bog is flat and featureless by design. If you need mountains, cliffs, or dramatic topography, go to Sigulda and the Gauja Valley instead.</li>
<li><strong>People who hate mosquitoes and won't wear a head net.</strong> I'm not being dramatic. Ķemeri mosquitoes are serious year-round and ferocious from June through August. Early May or mid-October onward (after the first hard frost) are the only low-mosquito windows. A head net solves most of the problem if you're willing to wear one.</li>
<li><strong>People who want a classic "tourist attraction" with gift shops, audio guides, and a café.</strong> Ķemeri is a national park, not a visitor attraction. There's nothing to buy. There are no plaques explaining things in English. That's the point, but it's not for everyone.</li>
</ul>
<h2>A final thing</h2>
<p>The reason the Ķemeri boardwalk has become the most-photographed wetland in the Baltics in the last five years isn't marketing, and it isn't social media accident. It's that the combination is genuinely rare: a 10,000-year-old landscape that looks like the edge of the world, on a wooden walkway built carefully enough that almost anyone can experience it, forty-five minutes from a working European capital, for free, at an hour when almost no one else is awake.</p>
<p>If you can organise yourself to be there at sunrise, it will be one of the things you remember from Latvia. If you can't, come in September when the light is gentler and the crowds are gone. If neither works, it's fine to skip it. Not every place is for every traveller, and a morning in Old Town Riga with a cup of coffee and the Dome Square bells is also worth remembering.</p>
<p>If you want the sunrise version without having to drive, navigate, or worry about the logistics, our <a href="/excursions/kemeri-bog-jurmala.html">Ķemeri Bog &amp; Jūrmala excursion</a> runs from May to August for €45 per adult, €35 per child. Hotel pickup at 4:30 AM, bog shoes included, back at your hotel by 10:30 AM with the rest of the day still ahead of you. You pay nothing today to reserve, and you get free cancellation up to 24 hours before departure. If you'd rather do it yourself, everything I've said above is what I'd tell my own friends if they asked me how to plan a Ķemeri morning from Riga.</p>
<p>Either way, bring a warm layer. Even in July.</p>
<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-is-emeri-bog-worth-visiting">
            Is Ķemeri bog worth visiting?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-is-emeri-bog-worth-visiting" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, for most visitors to Latvia it&#x27;s one of the most memorable half-days of the trip. The Great Ķemeri Bog is a 10,000-year-old raised bog, a Natura 2000 site and Ramsar wetland, with a 3.4 km wooden boardwalk winding through dwarf pines and dark mirror pools. It&#x27;s a landscape that looks like nowhere else in Europe, it&#x27;s free to walk, and it&#x27;s 50 km from Riga. Most people who come for the first time call it the highlight of their entire Latvia trip. The caveats: the boardwalk itself is short, you need to come at sunrise or late afternoon for the light that makes it photogenic, and the public transport logistics for a DIY visit are awkward.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-how-long-is-the-emeri-bog-boardwalk">
            How long is the Ķemeri bog boardwalk?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-how-long-is-the-emeri-bog-boardwalk" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>The main wooden boardwalk is 3.4 kilometres long as a loop. It starts and ends at the main car park near the village of Ķemeri, and a shorter inner loop of 1.4 km is also available. The full 3.4 km loop takes about 75–90 minutes at a relaxed pace, including the climb up the observation tower at the midpoint. The boardwalk is flat, wooden, and accessible to pushchairs and gentle walkers.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-when-is-the-best-time-to-visit-emeri-bog">
            When is the best time to visit Ķemeri bog?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-when-is-the-best-time-to-visit-emeri-bog" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Early morning in May, June, July, or August. The bog is at its best in the soft golden light just after sunrise, when the mist is still lifting from the dark pools and the boardwalk is empty. Sunrise in Latvia in midsummer is roughly 4:30–5:00 AM, which is the main reason the best organised tours (ours included) start before 5 AM. Late afternoon from September also works for a different, quieter kind of beauty, with copper pines and rust-red sphagnum. Midday in July is the worst time to visit: flat light, tour groups on the boardwalk, and mosquitoes hunting tourists.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-how-do-i-get-to-emeri-national-park-from">
            How do I get to Ķemeri National Park from Riga without a car?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-how-do-i-get-to-emeri-national-park-from" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Three options. One, the suburban train from Riga Central Station to Ķemeri station, which takes about 65 minutes and costs around €3 each way; from the station you walk 3.5 km along a forest road to the main boardwalk car park. Two, a guided tour from Riga (ours runs sunrise May–August, €45 per adult, with hotel pickup). Three, a taxi or Bolt from Riga (around €50–60 each way). Self-driving is also straightforward if you have a hire car — it&#x27;s a 45-minute drive from central Riga on the A10 motorway. The main obstacle for the train option is that the first train arrives at Ķemeri around 7:30 AM in summer, which is already 2–3 hours after sunrise, so you miss the best light.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-is-emeri-bog-free-to-visit">
            Is Ķemeri bog free to visit?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-is-emeri-bog-free-to-visit" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes. The Great Ķemeri Bog boardwalk, the observation tower, and the surrounding trails in Ķemeri National Park are all free to enter, with no entrance fee and no tickets required. There is a small free car park at the trailhead. The bog is open 24 hours a day, year-round. Basic composting toilets are available at the main car park.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-is-emeri-bog-accessible-for-wheelchairs-">
            Is Ķemeri bog accessible for wheelchairs and pushchairs?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-is-emeri-bog-accessible-for-wheelchairs-" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Mostly yes. The main boardwalk is wooden, flat, and wide enough for pushchairs and most wheelchair users. The observation tower has stairs and is not accessible. The 3.5 km walk from Ķemeri train station to the main car park involves forest roads and is not suitable for wheelchairs. For accessible visits, arriving by car or guided tour is essential.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-are-there-mosquitoes-at-emeri-bog">
            Are there mosquitoes at Ķemeri bog?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-are-there-mosquitoes-at-emeri-bog" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, and more than most visitors expect. Ķemeri has a serious mosquito reputation year-round, worst at dawn and dusk, and the problem is at its peak from June through August. Early September can still be heavy, and even October mornings can have active mosquitoes until the first hard frost in mid to late October. Bring strong DEET-based or picaridin-based repellent, long sleeves, and ideally a head net that covers your face — repellent alone is often not enough in peak season. The blanket claim that September is mosquito-free at Ķemeri is simply wrong.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-iskemeribo-is-it-safe-to-step-off-the-boardwalk-at-">
            Is it safe to step off the boardwalk at Ķemeri bog?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-iskemeribo-is-it-safe-to-step-off-the-boardwalk-at-" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>No, not without proper bog shoes and a local guide who knows the terrain. A raised bog is not firm ground — the sphagnum moss carpet floats on top of a peat layer up to eight metres deep, and open pools hide between the vegetation under what looks like solid moss. Without traditional Latvian bog shoes (purva kurpes, wide frames that strap over boots and spread your weight) and a guide who knows which sections are safe, you can sink to your waist or deeper. DIY visitors should stay on the wooden boardwalk at all times. If you want to actually walk on the bog surface, book a guided bogshoe hike with a Latvian specialist operator such as Baltic Nature Tourism — they provide the bog shoes and the local knowledge.</p>

## Is Rundāle Palace Worth Visiting? An Honest Answer

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/is-rundale-palace-worth-visiting.html
**Published:** 2026-04-14
**Summary:** Yes, on a weekday and if you understand it's a country palace, not Versailles. A licensed Latvian guide on what Rundāle is, when to visit, and who should skip it.

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Yes, Rundāle Palace is worth visiting</strong> for anyone who enjoys baroque architecture, 18th-century history, or the idea of having a 138-room palace almost to yourself on a Tuesday morning.</li>
<li><strong>It's designed by Francesco Rastrelli</strong>, the same architect who built the Winter Palace in St Petersburg. Forty rooms of state apartments have been restored to their 18th-century condition, and the 2,300-rose French garden is the finest formal garden in the Baltic states.</li>
<li><strong>It's 70 km south of Riga</strong>, about 75 minutes by car, or roughly 90 minutes by public bus via Bauska. No direct train.</li>
<li><strong>The entry fee is modest</strong> (around €12 for the full-route ticket at the time of writing) and the palace is open year-round, seven days a week.</li>
<li><strong>Come on a weekday or out of peak summer.</strong> The Gold Hall on a Tuesday morning in September is what this place is for; the same room at 1pm on a Saturday in July with four coach parties is not.</li>
<li><strong>Late May to mid-July</strong> is when the rose garden is at its peak, which for garden travellers is the only window that really matters. Outside that window, the palace interiors are the draw.</li>
<li><strong>You should skip it if</strong> you only have 48 hours in Riga and haven't seen Old Town; you don't much care about baroque interiors; or you want a fast city-break day with lots of variety, in which case the Gauja Valley is a better use of the same budget.</li>
</ul>
<h2>What Rundāle Palace actually is</h2>
<p>The short version is that Rundāle is a jewel-box country palace, not a royal court. That distinction matters, because it's the thing that catches most first-time visitors off-guard, and I'll come back to it in the "Versailles" section below.</p>
<p>The history is good enough to be a Netflix series. Rundāle was commissioned in 1735 by <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Johann_von_Biron" rel="noopener external">Ernst Johann von Biron</a>, the ambitious Duke of Courland — a small semi-independent duchy on the Baltic coast that no longer exists as a political entity, but which at its height controlled most of what is now southern Latvia. Biron was the favourite (and, depending on who you believe, the lover) of Empress Anna of Russia. When Anna died in 1740, Biron was briefly made Regent of Russia and then, within three weeks, arrested by his rivals and sentenced to death. The sentence was commuted to exile, and he was sent to Siberia. He stayed there for twenty-two years.</p>
<p>In 1762, Catherine the Great came to the throne, released him, restored him as Duke of Courland, and sent him home. He was in his seventies. The first thing he did on his return to Rundāle was bring Rastrelli back and finish the palace. Construction had been frozen in place for two decades — doors half-mounted, floors half-laid, panels in storage. The second construction period ran from 1764 to 1768, and the man signing off on every decision was the seventy-two-year-old duke who had spent most of his sixties in Siberia. You can see that stubbornness in the building if you know the story. It's in the 1760s herringbone parquet in the Duke's apartments, laid during the final push. It's in the portraits of Biron as an old man in his own palace, not a young favourite at a foreign court.</p>
<p>The palace has 138 rooms in total. Forty of them — the state apartments, the ceremonial halls, the Duke's private quarters, the Duchess's rooms — have been painstakingly restored to their 18th-century appearance. The restoration took from 1972 until 2014, longer than the original construction, and was led almost single-handedly by the Latvian painter and art historian Imants Lancmanis, whose life's work it became. The rest of the building is in various states of use: museum offices, reserve collections, and rooms kept in their weathered mid-20th-century state as a counterpoint to the restored parts.</p>
<p>The formal French gardens were reconstructed from Rastrelli's original 1736 plans and cover ten hectares. They hold about 2,300 roses across 600 varieties, most of them historical cultivars from the 18th and 19th centuries, which flower from late May through July. The rest of the year the gardens are still worth walking, but the roses are what most garden visitors come for.</p>
<h2>Is it actually worth your day? The honest answer</h2>
<p>Depends on how much time you have in Latvia, what kind of traveller you are, and whether you can organise to come on a quiet day.</p>
<p><strong>If you have three or more days in Latvia and you like historic buildings, yes.</strong> Rundāle is the single best baroque interior in the Baltic states, and it's an easy half-day out of Riga. For anyone with a normal Latvia itinerary, a Rundāle day is the obvious companion to your Old Town days and a coast or nature day.</p>
<p><strong>If you only have 48 hours in Riga, probably not.</strong> Riga Old Town is a UNESCO-listed medieval town centre with 800 years of its own history; the Art Nouveau district has one of the densest concentrations of Jugendstil architecture in Europe. Rundāle is a ten-hour day out and back, with five of those hours on a motorway. If you have to choose between Old Town Riga and Rundāle, choose Old Town. Rundāle is a reward for coming back to Latvia a second time.</p>
<p><strong>If you're specifically a baroque, garden, or 18th-century history person, absolutely.</strong> There are a handful of surviving intact Rastrelli interiors in the world. Rundāle is one of them. The Gold Hall is not the biggest or most famous of its siblings in St Petersburg, but it's almost certainly the one you'll be closest to on the day you visit, because there are no 30-deep tour groups filing through it. That's a genuinely rare thing in European palace travel in 2026.</p>
<p><strong>If you want a varied day with history, nature, and landscape, the Gauja Valley is probably a better fit.</strong> Sigulda + Cēsis + Turaida gives you three castles, a forest national park, and two small towns in ten hours. Rundāle gives you one palace, one medieval fortress (Bauska), and a gentle boardwalk into the Great Ķemeri Bog. Both are good days; they're just different kinds of day.</p>
<h2>The "Versailles of the Baltics" thing, and why it's misleading</h2>
<p>Here is the single thing that catches most first-time visitors off-guard, and it's worth getting right before you go.</p>
<p>Every guidebook and travel article I've ever read about Rundāle calls it "the Versailles of the Baltics." It's a useful shorthand and it gets across one true thing, which is that Rundāle is the grandest baroque palace in this part of the world. The problem is that "Versailles" comes with a set of expectations — enormous scale, royal court, endless rooms of gold, thousands of visitors, forty-minute queues, velvet ropes everywhere — and Rundāle is almost none of those things.</p>
<p>Rundāle is much smaller than Versailles. The restored route covers forty rooms; Versailles has more than 2,300 rooms total and you visit hundreds of them. Rundāle was a summer residence for a duke, not a working court for a king of France; the scale of ambition is different by a factor of about ten. The Gold Hall at Rundāle is roughly twenty metres long. The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles is seventy-three.</p>
<p>So if you arrive expecting a small Versailles, you will be disappointed. The scale is wrong, the crowds are wrong, and the politics are wrong. But if you arrive understanding that Rundāle is a country palace — the private summer residence of a duke with excellent architectural taste and a dramatic life — then the whole experience reframes. You're not looking at the court of the Sun King. You're looking at one man's seventy-year project to build himself a beautiful place to retire, interrupted for twenty-two years by Siberia, and finished in his old age by the same architect who had started it when he was young. It's a much more personal building than Versailles, which is part of why it's more moving.</p>
<p>The other thing the "Versailles" comparison gets wrong is the crowds. On a Tuesday morning in September at Rundāle, I have repeatedly walked into the Gold Hall and found no one else in it. Actually no one. Just the parquet and the stucco and the weight of the quiet. That's an experience Versailles stopped being able to offer about a hundred years ago. If you like historic palaces because of how they feel when they're empty, Rundāle is the best option in this half of Europe.</p>
<h2>The rooms that matter, if your time is short</h2>
<p>The full restored route takes around 90 minutes to two hours at a normal pace. If you're shorter on time, or if you want to know what to look for, these are the rooms to slow down in:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The Gold Hall.</strong> The ceremonial main hall, used for state receptions. Gilded stucco, portraits of the Birons, and a ceiling painted with the founding of the palace. The most recognisable room in Rundāle and the one that appears on most postcards. Slow down and look up.</li>
<li><strong>The White Hall.</strong> Directly next door. Used for balls and dances. Rastrelli designed it as a deliberate visual contrast to the Gold Hall — cool plaster-white stucco, a Delft-like blue ceiling, and extraordinary acoustics. If there's classical music playing during your visit (there often is), this is where it sounds best.</li>
<li><strong>The Great Gallery.</strong> The long room that connects the ceremonial halls to the Duchess's apartments. Family portraits, landscapes, and a view onto the French gardens through floor-to-ceiling windows on one side.</li>
<li><strong>The Duke's private apartments.</strong> Where the personal story is strongest. Biron's bedroom, his study, his dressing room. The 1760s parquet here is original, laid when he was in his seventies. Look at the floor as carefully as you look at the walls.</li>
<li><strong>The Duchess's apartments.</strong> Smaller rooms than the Duke's, but often more beautifully preserved. The Chinese Cabinet (the 18th-century European idea of what a Chinese room looked like, which is not the same thing as a Chinese room) is a quiet highlight most visitors rush past.</li>
<li><strong>The Rose Garden</strong> (late May to mid-July only). Ten hectares of formal French parterre, 2,300 roses in 600 varieties, most of them heirloom cultivars. Outside the rose window, the garden is still beautifully maintained but less of a reason to linger.</li>
</ul>
<h2>How to get there — your options</h2>
<p>Rundāle is about 70 km south of Riga, in the village of Pilsrundāle in the Bauska district. There's no train station anywhere near it. There are four practical ways to visit.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table>
<thead>

<p>The bundled guided day is the one most of our guests pick because it solves the two biggest problems with a Rundāle DIY trip: the long driving day in both directions, and the fact that a palace visit by itself is only about two hours of content, which leaves you awkwardly short on the way home. Bundling Bauska Castle and a Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit into the day gives it a proper arc — palace in the morning, medieval fortress after lunch, a 10,000-year-old peatland before the drive home. If you only want the palace and nothing else, self-drive or bus is cheaper.</p>
<h2>When to go, month by month</h2>
<p><strong>Late May to mid-July</strong> is rose-garden season and the only window that matters for garden travellers. The roses bloom in waves, with the peak usually around mid-June depending on the weather. If you want the rose garden version of Rundāle, this is your only window.</p>
<p><strong>July and August</strong> are the busiest months inside the palace, with international coach parties and Baltic-circuit tours at their peak. Weekday mornings are still quieter than weekend afternoons. Avoid Saturdays and Sundays in high summer if you want the calm version of the Gold Hall.</p>
<p><strong>September</strong> is my favourite month to visit. The roses are gone but the gardens are still beautiful, the light on the south façade is extraordinary, the tourist numbers drop sharply after the first week, and the palace feels like it belongs to you on a Tuesday or Wednesday morning. If I had to pick one week, it would be the second week of September.</p>
<p><strong>October and November</strong> are quiet, cool, and often damp. The gardens are going into dormancy. The interiors are warm and atmospheric. Expect short daylight and grey weather, but very few other visitors.</p>
<p><strong>December to March</strong> — winter visits. The palace is open seven days a week year-round, the interiors are heated, and the low winter light coming through the windows makes the 18th-century colours glow in a way you don't get in summer. The gardens are dormant or snow-covered, which can be beautiful in its own right. Worth doing if you're already in Latvia in the quiet season.</p>
<p><strong>April and early May</strong> are a shoulder window. The gardens are waking up but the roses haven't started. Interior is the same quality year-round. Fewer visitors than summer, warmer than winter.</p>
<h2>What to bring, and what to know before you go</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Comfortable shoes.</strong> The restored route is about 90 minutes on your feet, on parquet and stone floors. Comfortable trainers or flat leather shoes are ideal. Heels are a bad idea on 260-year-old parquet.</li>
<li><strong>A light jacket</strong>, even in summer. The palace interiors are kept cool to protect the textiles and gilding.</li>
<li><strong>Cash or card for the ticket office.</strong> Both work. The full-route ticket (palace + gardens) is the one to buy; the garden-only ticket is cheaper but misses the point.</li>
<li><strong>Photography is allowed inside</strong> without flash. Tripods are not. Most rooms are bright enough for phone cameras; a few of the darker rooms need a wider aperture.</li>
<li><strong>Allow two hours inside the palace</strong>, minimum. Another hour for the gardens if it's rose season, half an hour otherwise. Plus travel time each way.</li>
<li><strong>There's a small café on site</strong> for coffee and pastries, but nothing more substantial. Bring a snack if you're coming by bus and have a long afternoon wait.</li>
<li><strong>Rundāle is open seven days a week, year-round.</strong> The restored-route visit sometimes requires an audio guide rental (a few euros extra).</li>
</ul>
<h2>Who Rundāle Palace isn't for</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>People who only have 48 hours in Riga and haven't seen Old Town.</strong> Come back to Rundāle on your second trip. Old Town is the priority.</li>
<li><strong>People who don't much care about historic interiors.</strong> The whole point of the day is baroque rooms, parquet, stucco, portraits, and the story. If those things leave you cold, you will find Rundāle slow. A Sigulda + Cēsis day with castles and forests is a better fit.</li>
<li><strong>People who want a lot of variety in their day.</strong> Rundāle is a single deep experience, not a mix of stops. Our guided day adds Bauska Castle and a Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit to solve this, but the self-drive version is just palace + drive + drive + palace.</li>
<li><strong>People expecting Versailles-scale grandeur.</strong> See the section above. If you arrive with Versailles in your head, you will feel Rundāle is small. If you arrive understanding it's a private ducal residence, you'll see it clearly.</li>
<li><strong>Families with very young children who need to move.</strong> Under-fives in particular find the hush and the velvet ropes and the "don't touch" atmosphere hard. Primary-school-aged children tend to love it, especially the Duke's private rooms and the Chinese Cabinet. Mileage varies.</li>
</ul>
<h2>A final thing</h2>
<p>The reason I keep coming back to Rundāle is not the grandeur. It's the quiet. There are very few places left in Europe where you can stand in an original 18th-century baroque hall, on original 18th-century parquet, in front of portraits of the man who built the room, with no one else within earshot. The Gold Hall on a Tuesday morning in September is that kind of place. So is the Duke's bedroom. So is the garden in the first week of October when the last roses are turning.</p>
<p>If Rundāle is going to be worth it for you, it will be because you give it the time and the silence it needs. A rushed lunchtime visit in a coach party is not the same experience. Come on a weekday, come out of peak summer, and give yourself the hour to slow down in the rooms that matter.</p>
<p>If you'd rather not drive, navigate, or worry about the Bauska bus connection, our <a href="/excursions/rundale-palace-bauska-castle-brewery.html">Rundāle Palace, Bauska Castle &amp; Ķemeri Bog Boardwalk excursion</a> runs year-round for €85 per adult, €70 per child. Central Riga pickup, air-conditioned minibus, palace entrance included, bundled with Bauska Castle and a gentle Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit to turn the day into a proper arc rather than a single stop. You pay nothing today to reserve, and you get free cancellation up to 24 hours before departure. If you'd rather do it yourself, everything in this post is what I'd tell my own friends if they asked me how to plan a Rundāle morning from Riga.</p>
<p>Either way, come in September if you can. And walk slowly in the Duke's apartments. The floor is the story.</p>
<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-palace-worth-visiting">
            Is Rundāle Palace worth visiting?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-palace-worth-visiting" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, for anyone who enjoys baroque architecture, 18th-century history, or the idea of having a 138-room palace almost to yourself on a Tuesday morning. Rundāle is the single best baroque interior in the Baltic states, designed by Francesco Rastrelli (the architect of the Winter Palace in St Petersburg), and 40 rooms have been painstakingly restored to their 18th-century appearance. The 2,300-rose French formal garden is the finest in the Baltics. The caveats: it&#x27;s a long day out and back from Riga, the Versailles comparison misleads visitors, and peak-summer afternoons can be busy. Come on a weekday and out of July-August for the best experience.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-how-much-time-do-you-need-at-rund-le-pal">
            How much time do you need at Rundāle Palace?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-how-much-time-do-you-need-at-rund-le-pal" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Budget two hours for the restored interior route, plus another hour for the French formal gardens (longer if the roses are blooming in late May to mid-July), plus travel time each way. A typical day from Riga is around six hours door-to-door if you self-drive, or ten hours if you join a guided day that adds Bauska Castle and a Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit on the way back. The palace restoration route alone is about 90 minutes at a normal pace, longer if you want to slow down in the Gold Hall and the Duke&#x27;s apartments.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-really-the-versailles-of-the-">
            Is Rundāle really the &#x27;Versailles of the Baltics&#x27;?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-really-the-versailles-of-the-" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>The nickname is a useful shorthand but it sets wrong expectations. Rundāle is much smaller than Versailles — 40 restored rooms on the public route versus hundreds at Versailles, and the Gold Hall is roughly 20 metres long versus the 73-metre Hall of Mirrors. Rundāle was a private summer residence for a duke, not a working royal court for a king of France. What the nickname does capture is that Rundāle is the grandest baroque interior in this part of Europe and one of the few surviving intact Rastrelli buildings. If you arrive understanding it as a jewel-box country palace rather than a smaller Versailles, you&#x27;ll see it more clearly.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-when-is-the-best-time-to-visit-rund-le-p">
            When is the best time to visit Rundāle Palace?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-when-is-the-best-time-to-visit-rund-le-p" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Late September for the quiet interior experience — the roses are gone but the tourist numbers drop sharply after the first week, the light on the south façade is at its best, and a Tuesday or Wednesday morning in September can give you the Gold Hall almost to yourself. For the rose garden, late May to mid-July is the only window that matters, with peak bloom usually around mid-June. Summer months (July and August) are busiest inside the palace; avoid Saturday and Sunday afternoons. Winter visits work well too — the interiors are heated and atmospheric in low light.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-how-do-i-get-to-rund-le-palace-from-riga">
            How do I get to Rundāle Palace from Riga without a car?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-how-do-i-get-to-rund-le-palace-from-riga" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>The cheapest option is a regional bus from Riga to Bauska (around 90 minutes, around €5), then a local connecting bus from Bauska to Pilsrundāle (20 minutes). The Bauska-Rundāle connection runs only a few times a day so you must plan return timings carefully. Alternative options: a taxi or Bolt from Riga (around €80-100 each way, and you need to arrange the return), self-drive hire car (easiest flexibility, 75 minutes each way on the A7 motorway), or a guided day excursion that handles pickup, the entrance, and typically bundles Bauska Castle and a Ķemeri Bog boardwalk visit into the same day. There is no direct train.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-palace-suitable-for-children">
            Is Rundāle Palace suitable for children?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-palace-suitable-for-children" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Primary-school-aged children usually enjoy Rundāle — they like the Duke&#x27;s private apartments, the Chinese Cabinet, and the story of Biron being exiled to Siberia for twenty-two years. Under-fives can find the hush and the velvet ropes hard. The Gold Hall and the ceiling paintings are a good attention hook. The gardens give young kids somewhere to run around after the quiet of the interior. Strollers are permitted on the palace route but the 18th-century parquet means slow and careful. Child entry is discounted.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-palace-wheelchair-accessible">
            Is Rundāle Palace wheelchair accessible?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-isrundalep-is-rund-le-palace-wheelchair-accessible" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Partially. The ground-floor state apartments are accessible via a lift and level entry, which covers the Gold Hall, the White Hall, and the main ceremonial route. The upper floors and the more personal rooms (the Duke&#x27;s private apartments) involve stairs and are harder for wheelchair users. The formal gardens are accessible on gravel paths. Contact the palace museum in advance about specific needs — they are responsive and can sometimes arrange additional access.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
</div>

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Yes, Sigulda and the Gauja Valley are worth visiting</strong> for almost anyone spending more than two days in Latvia. It's the best all-round day out of Riga — history, forest, river valley, and two serious medieval castles in an area you can cover in half a day.</li>
<li><strong>It's 50 km northeast of Riga</strong>, about 50 minutes by car or just over an hour by direct train from Riga Central Station. The easiest day trip in Latvia by public transport, by a long way.</li>
<li><strong>The two main castles are Sigulda Medieval Castle and Turaida Castle.</strong> Both 13th-century originals, both worth the time. Turaida is the red-brick one on the hillside and it's the highlight of the day for most visitors.</li>
<li><strong>Add Cēsis if you have a full day.</strong> Cēsis is 40 minutes further on, has another 13th-century Livonian Order castle (explored by candlelight with a lantern), and is one of Latvia's oldest towns. Three castles in one day is achievable.</li>
<li><strong>Ignore "Switzerland of Latvia."</strong> The nickname sets wrong expectations. It's a gentle river valley with forested slopes, not an alpine landscape. See the honest-insight section below.</li>
<li><strong>Late September to mid-October</strong> is the secret season. Autumn colour in the Gauja Valley is the reason the nickname exists at all, and most visitors come in summer and miss it.</li>
<li><strong>You should skip it if</strong> you only have 48 hours in Riga and you're set on seeing Old Town, if you came for city-break food and nightlife, or if "gentle river valley and medieval castles" genuinely does not sound like your kind of day.</li>
</ul>
<h2>What Sigulda and the Gauja Valley actually are</h2>
<p>Sigulda is a small town on the western edge of <strong>Gauja National Park</strong>, which is Latvia's largest and oldest protected area. The park follows the Gauja river for about 100 kilometres as it cuts through a broad, shallow valley of Devonian sandstone and mixed forest. That valley is the thing you're really coming to see — the town of Sigulda is the entry point.</p>

<figure class="rundale-gallery rundale-gallery--sigulda-what-it-is" data-sigulda-what-gallery="injected" aria-label="Sigulda — what the place actually looks like">
  <a class="rundale-gallery__hero" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/krimulda-gauja-valley-25-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="sigulda-what-it-is" data-caption="Wooden walking path through the Gauja Valley forest, Krimulda, Latvia" aria-label="Sigulda — what the place actually looks like">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/krimulda-gauja-valley-25-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/krimulda-gauja-valley-25-latvia.jpg" alt="Wooden walking path through the Gauja Valley forest, Krimulda, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1920" height="1280">
    </picture>
    <figcaption>Wooden walking path through the Gauja Valley forest, Krimulda, Latvia</figcaption>
  </a>
  <div class="rundale-gallery__thumbs">
    <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/gauja-valley-walking-trails-sigulda-2-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="sigulda-what-it-is" data-caption="Gauja Valley walking trails near Velnu klints, Sigulda, Latvia" aria-label="Gauja Valley walking trails near Velnu klints, Sigulda, Latvia">
      <picture>
        <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/gauja-valley-walking-trails-sigulda-2-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
        <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/gauja-valley-walking-trails-sigulda-2-latvia.jpg" alt="Gauja Valley walking trails near Velnu klints, Sigulda, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="600" height="600">
      </picture>
    </a>
    <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/krimulda-gauja-valley-10-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="sigulda-what-it-is" data-caption="Krimulda walking trails in spring, Latvia" aria-label="Krimulda walking trails in spring, Latvia">

      </picture>
