<h2 id="the-flowers">The flowers, and why daffodils</h2>

<p>The flower part of the day is the youngest tradition on the list. It started in 2014, the 24th anniversary of the 1990 vote, when a small social-media campaign asked Latvians to bring a yellow flower &mdash; specifically a <em>narcise</em>, a daffodil &mdash; to the Freedom Monument that day. The reasoning was practical and a little sentimental: yellow because it is the colour of spring in Latvia after a long winter, and daffodils because they are what is reliably out in the gardens by the first week of May. The idea took. Within three years it was the dominant flower at the monument, and by the late 2010s the lady florists in central Riga had started selling pre-tied bunches of three or five daffodils with a maroon-and-white ribbon for the occasion.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/boys-with-daffodils-folk-costume-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="restoration-day" data-caption="Two boys in folk dress carrying daffodils, walking with the adults of their ensemble.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/boys-with-daffodils-folk-costume-may-4-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/boys-with-daffodils-folk-costume-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="Two small boys in white folk shirts and dark trousers carrying small bunches of daffodils between adults in costume, Riga, 4 May" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>One of the small things you cannot really fake. The flowers are the right size for the children carrying them, the children are the right size for the parents holding their other hand, and the whole arrangement was assembled at home this morning.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>Today there are also tulips, hyacinths, and the small bouquets of any bright spring flower the florist had in stock. There are roses, especially among the older generation. The yellow daffodil is still the symbolic stem &mdash; if I had to choose only one, I would choose that &mdash; but the rule is loose. The point is that you bring something living, you bring it to the monument, and you do it on foot.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/mother-and-child-folk-costume-daffodils-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="restoration-day" data-caption="A mother and her small daughter, both in folk dress, walking the daffodils up Brīvības iela.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/mother-and-child-folk-costume-daffodils-may-4-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/mother-and-child-folk-costume-daffodils-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="A woman in a long folk skirt holds a small girl&rsquo;s hand as both walk toward the Freedom Monument carrying daffodils, Riga, 4 May" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The flowers travel mostly with women and with children. They are bought at the florists at the corners of the avenue, or cut from the gardens at home, or both. The walking is part of the offering &mdash; nobody drives them in.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="the-monument">At the monument itself</h2>

<p>The Freedom Monument &mdash; <em>Br&#299;v&#299;bas piemineklis</em> &mdash; sits at the centre of the avenue named for it, between Old Town and the Esplan&#257;de. It is 42 metres tall, finished in 1935, and the figure on top is a young woman holding three gold stars representing the three historical regions of inter-war Latvia. Latvians call her <em>Milda</em>. She is, as much as any single object can be, the country&rsquo;s family doorway.</p>

<p>The plinth carries an inscription on the western face: <em>T&#275;vzemei un Br&#299;v&#299;bai</em>. <em>For Fatherland and Freedom</em>. In Soviet times the monument was officially nothing &mdash; it was tolerated rather than celebrated, and laying flowers here during the Soviet regime could and did get people in serious trouble. The fact that the country can now stack thousands of flowers at its base, in the open, with no one watching to see who brought them, is the whole point.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/latgale-flag-raised-procession-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="restoration-day" data-caption="A regional contingent passing the monument with the state flag held high.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/latgale-flag-raised-procession-may-4-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/latgale-flag-raised-procession-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="A folk-costume procession passes the Freedom Monument with the maroon-and-white Latvian state flag held high above the heads of the contingent, Riga, 4 May" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>One of the regional contingents passing the front of the monument with the state flag held high. The maroon stripe at the top and bottom and the narrower white band in the middle is the original 13th-century city banner of C&#275;sis &mdash; older than most European national flags by several centuries.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>Two soldiers in dress uniform stand the change-of-guard at the foot of the monument every hour on the hour, on every day of the year. On 4 May the change-of-guard is more crowded than usual, but the crowd is not really there for the ceremony &mdash; it is the slow, patient queue of people waiting their turn to lay a flower at the plinth, with photographers gathered respectfully off to the side. The relief unit is brought in discreetly by car to the back of the monument; the new pair takes the position, the old pair marches off. Nobody salutes the spectators and the spectators do not need them to.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/procession-walking-down-avenue-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="restoration-day" data-caption="The procession funneling toward the monument from Brīvības iela.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/procession-walking-down-avenue-may-4-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/procession-walking-down-avenue-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="A long procession of folk-dressed groups carrying daffodils walks down Brīvības iela toward the Freedom Monument, Riga, 4 May" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The middle of the day, the procession funnelling down toward the front of the monument. The crowd along the pavement here is mostly families &mdash; small children on shoulders, older Latvians in sensible coats &mdash; and a thinner ring of tourists who happened to be on Old Town&rsquo;s edge and walked up to see what the noise was about.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="tablecloth">The white tablecloth, indoors</h2>

<p>The other tradition that runs alongside the procession is quieter and you will not see it on the avenue. It is called <em>Balt&#257; galdauta sv&#275;tki</em>, the White Tablecloth Festival. The instruction, broadcast each year by Latvian state radio and a long list of cultural institutions, is the same: on 4 May, eat your evening meal on a white tablecloth. At home, in a community hall, in a school courtyard, in a park &mdash; wherever you are, the cloth is white, the meal is shared, and the conversation is allowed to slow down.</p>

<p>The cloth is the symbol because, in the older Latvian household, the white tablecloth was reserved for the occasions when the family had something to celebrate together. It was put away the rest of the year. The civic version asks every Latvian to bring it out on the day the country brought itself back. The food does not have to be elaborate &mdash; bread, cheese, smoked fish, roasted potatoes &mdash; and many families try to put one or two dishes on the table in red and white to echo the flag: a beetroot salad, a pink berry-and-whipped-cream dessert. The cloth has to be white.</p>

<p>This part of the day is largely invisible to a visitor unless you happen to be invited into a Latvian house, and most aren&rsquo;t on first acquaintance. But when you walk past V&#275;rmane Garden in the evening and see the trestle tables covered in white linen with families eating on them in folk dress, this is what is happening.</p>

<h2 id="trams">The free trams (and the rest of the practicalities)</h2>

<p>If you are a visitor in Riga today and you want to do this properly, the practical notes are short.</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>All Riga public transport is free</strong> on 4 May. Trams, trolleybuses, buses, and the city minibuses. You do not need to validate; the e-talons are not required. This started as a gesture in 2010 and has become standard practice. It applies city-wide and runs from first service to last.</li>
<li><strong>The procession runs from roughly midday to about 4pm</strong>, with the heaviest density on the central section of Br&#299;v&#299;bas iela between the Esplan&#257;de and the Freedom Monument. Stand on the pavement; do not step into the lane. There is no fixed start; the contingents arrive in their own order.</li>
<li><strong>The change-of-guard at the monument</strong> happens every hour on the hour from 9am to 6pm year-round. On 4 May the noon, 3pm, and 4pm changes have the biggest crowds. The 5pm change is usually quieter and a better time to be close.</li>
<li><strong>Most museums are open as normal,</strong> and several &mdash; the Museum of the Occupation, the Latvian National Museum of Art, the Riga History and Navigation Museum &mdash; have free admission for the day. Check the door.</li>
<li><strong>The flower-laying continues all day,</strong> but the most photographically rich window is roughly 1pm to 3pm, when the contingents are still arriving. Late afternoon is quieter and (in my opinion) the better time to stand at the monument if you want to feel the day rather than capture it.</li>
<li><strong>Bring a flower if you want to.</strong> Visitors are welcome to. The lady at the corner of Br&#299;v&#299;bas and Krišj&#257;ņa Barona has small daffodil bunches with the maroon-and-white ribbon for €3.</li>
</ul>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/solitary-woman-folk-costume-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="restoration-day" data-caption="A lone woman in folk dress walking back along Brīvības iela in the late afternoon.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/solitary-woman-folk-costume-may-4-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-restoration-day-may-4-2026/solitary-woman-folk-costume-may-4-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="A woman in a long brown-striped folk skirt and white blouse walks alone along the wide empty pavement of Brīvības iela in late afternoon, Riga, 4 May" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Late afternoon, the contingents starting to break up. One of the costume women on her way back to wherever she came from. The street is quieter at this point than it has been all day, which is the part I came back for.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="honest">Honest take</h2>

<p>The 4th of May is not the loudest day in the Latvian calendar. November 18 is louder, and the Song and Dance Festival every five years is louder by orders of magnitude. May 4 is the day the country thanks itself for noticing the door was open in 1990 and walking through it. The mood is grateful rather than triumphant. The flowers are spring flowers because the country is, on some level, still a young country and is celebrating a recent thing.</p>

<p>If you are travelling to Riga and the calendar happens to put you here on 4 May, walk Br&#299;v&#299;bas iela in the early afternoon and stand at the monument by 4pm. Take the free tram back to your hotel. If you can find a Latvian friend with a tablecloth in the evening, accept the invitation. If you cannot, eat outside somewhere with a white napkin and watch the city ease down. The day asks nothing more than your attention, and it gives back the rare experience of watching a country on its quiet anniversary, doing the small civic things that keep an independence in working order.</p>

<p class="article-signoff"><em>Daiga</em></p>

---


## Latvian Food: An Honest Guide from a Riga Local

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/latvian-food-honest-guide.html
**Published:** 2026-04-14
**Summary:** A licensed Latvian guide's honest guide to the food: rye bread, smoked everything, the pink summer soup, pickle juice, and where to eat in Riga.

<h2>Short answer, eat these first</h2>
<p>If you only have a few days in Latvia and want to taste the country properly, here&rsquo;s the shortlist I&rsquo;d send any traveller on. The longer post explains each one in detail, but if you&rsquo;re scanning, this is the bite-sized version.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Rupjmaize</strong>, our dense dark <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rye_bread" rel="noopener external">rye bread</a>. Try it plain, then come back for the layered dessert version (Rupjmaizes Kārtojums) and the cold rye-bread soup (Maizes Zupa).</li>
<li><strong>Anything with biezpiens</strong>, the Latvian curd cheese. Savoury with dill and sour cream over potatoes, or sweet as a chocolate-covered childhood snack (Kārums).</li>
<li><strong>A bottle of kefir</strong>. We&rsquo;ve been drinking it for generations; the West has only just discovered it.</li>
<li><strong>Pelēkie zirņi ar speķi</strong>, our national dish: grey peas with smoked bacon, served with a glass of kefir on the side.</li>
<li><strong>Aukstā zupa</strong> in summer (June&ndash;August): the pink kefir-based cold soup with beetroot, cucumber, dill and hard-boiled egg. Properly weird-looking, properly delicious.</li>
<li><strong>Anything smoked at the Central Market</strong>: sprats, eel if you can find it, cheese, pork ribs. The smokehouse tradition here is genuinely world-class.</li>
<li><strong>Karbonāde with chanterelle sauce</strong>, the comfort plate that grandmothers made on Sundays.</li>
<li><strong>Sklandrausis</strong>, the rye-and-root-vegetable pie from the western coast. Strange, sweet, and very Latvian.</li>
<li><strong>A shot of Riga Black Balsam</strong> at the end of the meal, mixed into hot blackcurrant juice if you&rsquo;re a beginner.</li>
</ul>

<figure class="food-image food-image-hero">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/rupjmaize-and-biezpiens.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/rupjmaize-and-biezpiens.jpg" alt="Sliced rupjmaize dark rye bread with a bowl of biezpiens cottage cheese sprinkled with dill" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Anastasia Belousova on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2>The bread shelf, where everything begins</h2>
<p>Latvian food makes no sense without bread. We grew up with it on the table at every meal. We bring it to housewarmings (the salt-and-bread tradition is still alive in 2026). And we have far more types than the visitor expects.</p>

<h3>Rupjmaize, the cornerstone</h3>
<p><strong>Rupjmaize</strong> (literally &ldquo;coarse bread&rdquo;) is our dense, slightly sweet, slightly sour dark rye bread, baked from sourdough rye flour, often with caraway seeds, sometimes with malt syrup. The good stuff is heavy in the hand, dark all the way through, and keeps for a week without going stale. A proper loaf is a serious commitment, you eat it slowly, in thin slices, with butter and cottage cheese and smoked fish, or with honey and quark for breakfast.</p>
<p>Rupjmaize is everywhere because it&rsquo;s genuinely the engine of the cuisine. It is the backbone of the layered dessert <strong>Rupjmaizes K&#257;rtojums</strong> (rye bread crumbs, whipped cream, lingonberry jam in a glass), it&rsquo;s the base of the cold rye-bread soup <strong>Maizes Zupa</strong> (sieved bread, dried fruits, cinnamon, whipped cream on top), and it&rsquo;s the silent partner of essentially every smoked-fish or cottage-cheese plate. If you only buy one food souvenir from Latvia, buy a vacuum-packed loaf of rupjmaize from a proper bakery (try Lāči or Liepkalni) and take it home.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/rupjmaize-with-butter.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/rupjmaize-with-butter.jpg" alt="Slices of rupjmaize Latvian rye bread with butter and a knife on burlap" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Image by congerdesign from Pixabay</figcaption>
</figure>

<h3>Saldsk&#257;bmaize, the sweet-sour cousin</h3>
<p><strong>Sald&shy;sk&#257;b&shy;maize</strong> means &ldquo;sweet-sour bread&rdquo; and that&rsquo;s exactly what it is: a softer, lighter rye, more honeyed than rupjmaize, with a complex sourdough tang. It&rsquo;s easier on the international palate and the version most travellers fall for first. Goes brilliantly with smoked salmon, sliced cheese, or just butter. The Lāči bakery sells it everywhere in Riga.</p>

<h3>Sklandrausis, the strange one from Kurzeme</h3>
<p>This is the dish I most enjoy putting in front of visitors who think they know rustic European baking. <strong>Sklandrausis</strong> is a small, open-faced rye-pastry tart from the western Kurzeme region, filled with a layer of mashed potato topped with mashed carrot, sweetened gently, dusted with caraway, baked until the carrot caramelises slightly on top. It is sweet, it is savoury, it is unmistakably ancient (the recipe is documented from at least the 17th century), and it has EU protected status as a traditional Latvian product. It tastes like nothing else you&rsquo;ve had. Look for it at the Central Market or at autumn farmers&rsquo; markets.</p>



<h3>Kli&#326;&#291;eris, the namesday pretzel</h3>
<p>If you&rsquo;re ever invited to a Latvian birthday or namesday celebration, expect to see one of these in the middle of the table: an enormous saffron-coloured sweet pretzel, easily two feet across, glossy and golden, studded with raisins and almonds. <strong>Kli&#326;&#291;eris</strong> is celebratory bread, you bring it as a guest, and the host slices it ceremonially. It&rsquo;s sweet, soft, slightly cardamom-scented, and impossible to find as a tourist unless you go to a proper bakery and ask. Worth seeking out.</p>

<h3>P&#299;r&#257;gi, the small pleasure</h3>
<p><strong>P&#299;r&#257;gi</strong> are small, crescent-shaped, golden-baked buns filled most traditionally with finely diced smoked bacon and onion. They are the snack of every long bus journey, the buffet table at every gathering, and the thing you&rsquo;ll see piled high in every bakery window. There are also versions with cabbage, with smoked salmon, with carrot, but the bacon version is the canonical one. Three of these and a glass of kefir is a perfectly good lunch.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/piragi-basket.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/piragi-basket.jpg" alt="A basket of golden Latvian pīrāgi sprinkled with seeds, traditional small filled buns" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Karina Kungla on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>The cottage cheese cult</h2>
<p>If I had to pick the single ingredient that best explains Latvian eating, it would not be rye bread, it would be <strong>biezpiens</strong>, our cottage cheese. We eat it more days than not. We eat it sweet and we eat it savoury. We eat it for breakfast, lunch, dinner, and dessert, frequently in the same day. There are entire shelves of biezpiens products in every Latvian supermarket that simply do not exist in the UK or US, and once you understand the texture difference, you start seeing it everywhere.</p>

<h3>What biezpiens actually is</h3>
<p>Biezpiens (pronounced BEE-yez-pee-yens) is a fresh, soft, slightly tangy curd cheese, somewhere between Greek yoghurt and ricotta in texture, but lighter and drier than either. It comes in different fat contents (0%, 5%, 9%, 18%) and gets used differently at each level. The best stuff is made the traditional way from cultured raw milk, slowly drained, and tastes mildly of grass and pasture.</p>

<h3>The savoury versions</h3>
<p>The classic Latvian summer plate: hot boiled new potatoes, a generous spoonful of biezpiens mixed with sour cream and finely chopped dill, a few radishes on the side, a piece of pickled herring, a slice of rye bread. That&rsquo;s lunch. Add fresh chives, spring onion, garlic, salt, pepper. The biezpiens is the unifying element, savoury, cooling, slightly tangy, and it makes everything around it sing.</p>
<p>You&rsquo;ll also see biezpiens stirred into baked dishes (potato gratins, savoury pancakes), used as a filling for stuffed pancakes (<strong>biezpiena pank&#363;kas</strong>), and dolloped onto soups in place of sour cream.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/biezpiens-savoury.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/biezpiens-savoury.jpg" alt="Two slices of dark rye bread topped with biezpiens cottage cheese, fresh chives and sliced radishes on a wooden board" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Image by Barbara from Pixabay</figcaption>
</figure>

<h3>The sweet versions, where it gets interesting</h3>
<p>Here&rsquo;s where Latvia diverges from anywhere I&rsquo;ve eaten in Western Europe. We make sweet biezpiens products that don&rsquo;t really exist elsewhere, and that every Latvian grew up on:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>K&#257;rums</strong> (and its rivals): the chocolate-coated curd cheese bar. Picture a small, palm-sized rectangle of slightly sweetened biezpiens, sometimes with vanilla or rum flavouring or a fruit-jelly centre, completely enrobed in milk or dark chocolate. Every Latvian child grew up eating these. They sit in the dairy aisle, not the chocolate aisle. They cost about a euro. Try one and tell me why this isn&rsquo;t global.</li>
<li><strong>Biezpiena sieri&#326;š</strong>: the more traditional, less sweet version, often without the chocolate, just a small block of sweetened biezpiens with vanilla or fruit. Often eaten for breakfast.</li>
<li><strong>Biezpienmaize</strong>: a soft sweet bread filled with sweetened biezpiens, eaten warm, often with a coffee mid-morning.</li>
<li><strong>Biezpiena pank&#363;kas</strong> with jam: thin pancakes folded around sweetened biezpiens, served with sour cream and lingonberry or raspberry jam. The Sunday breakfast of countless Latvian childhoods.</li>
<li><strong>Rupjmaizes K&#257;rtojums</strong>, the layered dessert: rye bread crumbs, whipped cream, lingonberry jam, sometimes sweetened biezpiens, layered in a glass. Think Eton Mess, but Latvian and rye-based. You&rsquo;ll see this on every modern Latvian restaurant&rsquo;s dessert menu.</li>
</ul>



<hr />

<h2>The kefir paragraph</h2>
<p>Kefir has had a moment in the Western wellness world over the last decade. Whole Foods sells it in glass bottles for &pound;5, &ldquo;gut health&rdquo; influencers post about it like it&rsquo;s an exotic discovery, and Brooklyn cafés put it in smoothies. I find this funny, and so does every Latvian I know, because we have been drinking the stuff every day for generations.</p>
<p>Kefir is fermented milk, slightly fizzy, slightly sour, somewhere between drinking yoghurt and a probiotic buttermilk. The good Latvian stuff is properly tangy, properly thick, and costs about ninety cents for half a litre at any supermarket. It&rsquo;s eaten cold, drunk straight from the glass, poured over hot grey peas (see below), used as a base for cold summer soup, and recommended by every grandmother as the cure for a hangover. There is no Latvian kitchen that doesn&rsquo;t have a bottle in the fridge.</p>
<p>What makes Latvian kefir taste of Latvia rather than Sainsbury&rsquo;s is the milk. We have a huge dairy industry, the cows are mostly pasture-fed, and the cultures used here have been bred locally for generations. Try a small bottle from <strong>Smiltenes Piens</strong> or <strong>T&#363;ja</strong> or <strong>Latvijas Piens</strong>, and you&rsquo;ll taste a depth and tang the supermarket version back home doesn&rsquo;t have. If you like it, buy a few bottles, it travels well in checked luggage if you&rsquo;re mad enough.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/kefir-pour.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/kefir-pour.jpg" alt="Latvian kefir being poured from a bottle into a glass on a wooden table" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Charlotte May on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>Pel&#275;kie zir&#326;i ar spe&#311;i, the national dish</h2>
<p>The Latvian national dish is genuinely strange the first time you see it. <strong>Pel&#275;kie zir&#326;i ar spe&#311;i</strong> means &ldquo;grey peas with smoked bacon&rdquo;, and it is exactly that: large, round, beige-grey peas (a variety almost unique to Latvia and Lithuania), boiled until creamy, mixed with diced smoked bacon and onion fried until golden, served hot, with a glass of cold kefir alongside.</p>
<p>The combination is the point. The peas are starchy and earthy, the bacon is rich and smoky, the kefir cuts everything with a cold, sour edge. It&rsquo;s peasant food, traditionally a winter dish, the kind of meal that kept farming families going through dark months. You&rsquo;ll see it on every traditional restaurant menu and at every winter solstice celebration in December (eating grey peas at solstice is a folk tradition, the legend says you must eat at least nine peas to ensure good fortune).</p>
<p>If you eat it once and decide it&rsquo;s not for you, fair enough, it&rsquo;s an acquired taste. But try it the way a Latvian eats it: with the kefir glass beside it, alternating mouthfuls of hot peas with cold sour kefir. That partnership is the recipe.</p>



<hr />

<h2>Aukst&#257; zupa, the bright pink summer soup</h2>
<p>If you visit Latvia between June and August and don&rsquo;t eat <strong>aukst&#257; zupa</strong> at least once, you&rsquo;ve missed the most photogenic and most refreshing thing in the cuisine. It looks like a Wes Anderson film prop. It tastes brilliant on a hot day. It is somehow both ancient peasant food and the most Instagrammable plate on every modern Latvian restaurant&rsquo;s summer menu.</p>
<p>Aukst&#257; zupa (literally &ldquo;cold soup&rdquo;) is built on a base of <strong>kefir</strong>, often with a little water or buttermilk to thin it. Into the kefir goes finely grated raw beetroot or pickled beetroot juice (which gives it the electric pink colour), diced cucumber, plenty of fresh dill, sliced spring onion or chives, and on top, a hard-boiled egg cut in half. Sometimes with cubes of boiled potato on the side rather than in the soup. Always served properly cold.</p>
<p>What makes a good aukst&#257; zupa is the dill, lots of it, fresh and chopped just before serving, and the kefir, which has to be properly tangy. The bad versions use sour cream and water and taste flat. The good versions taste like a cold beetroot Bloody Mary made by a grandmother who has been making this every summer since 1955. Look for it on summer menus at restaurants like Bibliotēka Nº1 or Vincents in Riga; the Central Market food court does excellent versions for &euro;5.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/auksta-zupa.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/auksta-zupa.jpg" alt="A bowl of bright pink aukstā zupa, the Latvian cold kefir-and-beetroot summer soup, garnished with hard-boiled egg, cucumber and dill" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Valerie de Limoges on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>The smoked everything</h2>
<p>Latvia is a coastal country with a long tradition of smoking absolutely anything that holds still long enough. Walk into the fish hall at the Riga Central Market and the smell hits you before you see anything: hot-smoked sprats, cold-smoked salmon, smoked eel, smoked mackerel, smoked herring, smoked perch. Then walk into the meat hall: smoked ribs, smoked pork shoulder, smoked sausage of every kind, smoked chicken. Then into the dairy hall, where they smoke the cheese.</p>

<h3>Why smoke matters here</h3>
<p>Latvian smoking traditions go back centuries and predate refrigeration by about a thousand years. The Baltic coast has produced smoked fish for the Hanseatic League since the 1200s, and many small fishing villages on the Kurzeme coast (Roja, P&#257;vilosta, Ventspils) still operate traditional smokehouses where the wood is alder or juniper and the fish is laid out in racks above a slow, cool fire. The result tastes nothing like supermarket smoked salmon. It tastes of woodsmoke and fish and time.</p>

<h3>The ones to actually try</h3>
<p><strong>Smoked sprats</strong>: small Baltic herring, hot-smoked whole, eaten on rye bread with a little butter and a slice of hard-boiled egg. The classic Latvian appetiser. The tinned version (Riga Sprats) is iconic and well-loved internationally; the fresh, just-smoked version from the market is a different, far better thing.</p>
<p><strong>Smoked eel from P&#257;vilosta</strong>: this is my honest secret luxury recommendation, the one most travellers miss because they don&rsquo;t know to look for it. P&#257;vilosta is a small fishing town on the western coast, and its smoked eel is the most delicious smoked fish I have ever eaten in my life. It&rsquo;s rich, fatty, woodsmoky, slightly sweet, and it costs around &euro;30&ndash;50 per kilogram, which sounds dear but is half what you&rsquo;d pay for inferior eel anywhere in Europe. Look for it at the Central Market fish hall, or buy direct in P&#257;vilosta if you&rsquo;re on the coast. Eat it cold, on rye bread, with horseradish.</p>
<p><strong>Smoked cheese</strong>: golden-brown rounds of mild cheese smoked over alder. Slice thin, eat with rye bread, a slice of pickled cucumber on the side.</p>
<p><strong>Smoked pork ribs</strong>: served whole, eaten with sauerkraut and boiled potatoes. The kind of thing every Latvian grandmother has an opinion about.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/smoked-sprats-on-rye.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/smoked-sprats-on-rye.jpg" alt="Three smoked sprats on rye bread with sour cream and dill, on a black background" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Vilnis Husko on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/smoked-fish-appetiser.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/smoked-fish-appetiser.jpg" alt="Smoked fish appetiser on toasted rye with cream, dill and radish, served on a black plate" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Sylwester Ficek on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>Pelme&#326;i and the dumpling family</h2>
<p>Honest framing, because I think it matters: <strong>pelme&#326;i</strong> are not uniquely Latvian. They&rsquo;re the small meat-filled dumplings eaten across the entire former Soviet space, originally Russian or Siberian (depending on which folk history you believe), and you&rsquo;ll find them in Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, and Latvia. But they&rsquo;ve been part of the daily Latvian diet for generations, every supermarket sells them frozen in 1kg bags, every Riga restaurant has them on the menu, and every Latvian household has a pelme&#326;i dinner once a month at minimum.</p>
<p>The Latvian version is small, thin-skinned, filled with seasoned minced pork or pork-and-beef, boiled in salted water for a few minutes, and served the way every former-Soviet country serves them: with a generous knob of butter, a spoonful of sour cream, a sprinkle of dill, salt and black pepper. Some people add vinegar. Some people eat them swimming in a clear broth. Both are correct.</p>
<p>If you want a true Latvian dumpling that isn&rsquo;t shared with the rest of the region, look for <strong>karbon&#257;des p&#299;r&#257;gi</strong> (savoury pasties) or <strong>kartupe&#316;u pank&#363;kas</strong> (potato pancakes, also called <em>kartupe&#316;u rieksti</em> in some parts of the country). The potato pancakes are crisp, golden, served with sour cream, and they sit on every traditional restaurant menu.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/pelmeni.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/pelmeni.jpg" alt="Pelmeņi dumplings on a white plate with a sprig of dill, a hand lifting one with a fork" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Polina Tankilevitch on Pexels</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>The pickle question</h2>
<p>Every Latvian fridge has a jar of pickled cucumbers in it. The jar is always there. When the cucumbers are gone, you do not throw away the brine; you drink it.</p>
<p>The pickle-juice tradition has two purposes. First, the morning after a heavy night of celebrating, a small glass of pickle brine is the universally agreed Latvian hangover cure (the science actually backs this up, the salt and vinegar help with electrolyte balance and the lactic acid soothes the stomach). Second, it&rsquo;s a chaser for vodka, a small glass of vodka, a small bite of pickled cucumber, a small sip of brine. Some bars in the Old Town will serve you this combination as a &ldquo;Russian flight&rdquo; without explaining it.</p>
<p>Beyond the brine, pickled cucumbers themselves are the silent partner of every Latvian meal. Sliced thin alongside boiled potatoes. Diced into the cold salad <strong>rasols</strong> (the Latvian potato salad with diced ham, peas, hard-boiled egg, mayonnaise, and pickles, which appears at every birthday and every funeral). Whole and crunchy alongside smoked fish. The good stuff is dill-pickled, lacto-fermented in the traditional way, and tastes nothing like the malt-vinegar British version.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/pickled-cucumbers.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/pickled-cucumbers.jpg" alt="Four glass jars of dill-pickled cucumbers with fresh dill and garlic" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Photo by Townsend Walton on Unsplash</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>The dill question</h2>
<p>Yes, dill is on everything. Yes, this is by design. Yes, we know.</p>
<p>Dill (Latvian: <em>dilles</em>) is the default herb of Northern European cooking and Latvians use it on potatoes, on cottage cheese, on smoked fish, on pelme&#326;i, on salads, in soups (cold and hot), as a garnish for almost any savoury plate. Fresh dill is sold in enormous bunches at every market for around &euro;1, and the average Latvian household goes through a bunch every few days in summer.</p>
<p>What I&rsquo;d say to visitors who find this excessive: try it on a few dishes before deciding. Dill on cold pink soup is the right answer. Dill on hot boiled new potatoes with butter is the right answer. Dill stirred into biezpiens with sour cream is the right answer. Dill is occasionally overdone (when it&rsquo;s used as a desperate garnish on a dish that doesn&rsquo;t need it), and yes, the joke about &ldquo;Latvian fine dining is just adding more dill&rdquo; has some truth to it. But the real food has it for a reason: it cuts richness, it brightens cold dishes, and it pairs with kefir and biezpiens in a way no other herb does.</p>

<hr />

<h2>Karbon&#257;de and the comfort plate</h2>
<p><strong>Karbon&#257;de</strong> is the Latvian take on schnitzel: pork loin, pounded thin, breaded with rye breadcrumbs, fried golden in butter, served with a generous ladle of <strong>creamy chanterelle mushroom sauce</strong>, alongside boiled potatoes and pickled vegetables. It is the Sunday lunch of countless Latvian childhoods, the kind of plate every grandmother has a slightly different recipe for, and the dish I&rsquo;d order at any traditional restaurant where the menu doesn&rsquo;t make me curious.</p>
<p>The chanterelle sauce matters. Latvian forests are full of wild chanterelles in late summer and autumn (foraging is part of the national psyche, more on this in a moment), and a proper karbon&#257;de uses real chanterelles, gently fried in butter with shallot, finished with cream and dill. The cheaper restaurants use button mushrooms; you can taste the difference.</p>

<figure class="food-image">
  <picture>
    <source srcset="/images/food/karbonade.webp" type="image/webp">
    <img src="/images/food/karbonade.jpg" alt="A plate of karbonāde — Latvian breaded pork cutlet — with creamy mushroom sauce, herbed potatoes and roasted vegetables" loading="lazy" decoding="async">
  </picture>
  <figcaption>Image by Matthias Lipinski from Pixabay</figcaption>
</figure>

<hr />

<h2>The drinks shelf</h2>

<h3>Riga Black Balsam</h3>
<p>The Latvian national liqueur, dark as motor oil, 45% alcohol, made from a closely guarded recipe of 24 herbs, roots, and spices, in production since 1752. The honest take: it&rsquo;s an acquired taste, and the way most travellers first encounter it (a shot at room temperature) is the worst possible introduction. <strong>The Latvian way</strong> is to drink it mixed: a tablespoon stirred into a glass of hot blackcurrant juice in winter, or into hot tea with honey, or over ice with a splash of bitter lemon. The blackcurrant version (called Black Balsam Currant, and yes, the company makes a sweeter ready-to-drink version too) is genuinely delicious and is what I&rsquo;d serve a first-time visitor. There&rsquo;s a Black Balsam museum and tasting bar at Riga&rsquo;s Old Town if you want to dive properly in.</p>

<h3>Kvass</h3>
<p>Slightly alcoholic (around 1%), slightly fizzy, slightly sweet fermented rye bread drink. Sold in bottles in every supermarket in summer, served on tap from yellow tanker-trucks parked in city squares in July (this is not a joke, look for them, they&rsquo;re bright yellow and you can&rsquo;t miss them). Kvass tastes a bit like flat dark beer mixed with lemonade and is genuinely refreshing on a hot day. The brand to look for is <strong>Ilg&#257;rzemes Kvass</strong> from the local brewery, but supermarket Cido is fine.</p>

<h3>Beer</h3>
<p>Latvia has a serious beer culture, much older than the craft-beer wave (we&rsquo;ve been brewing for centuries) but reinvigorated by it. The big mass-market brands are Aldaris, Cēsu, and Užavas; all decent, all light lagers. The interesting beers come from small breweries: <strong>Mal&shy;duguns</strong> from Cēsis, <strong>Brū&shy;veris</strong> in Riga, <strong>Vala&shy;tas</strong> in Liepāja. Most Riga restaurants have a small craft-beer list. A pint costs &euro;4&ndash;6.</p>

<h3>Latvian wine</h3>
<p>Yes, this exists, and it&rsquo;s having a moment. We don&rsquo;t grow grapes (too cold), but we make wine from rhubarb, currants, gooseberries, sea buckthorn, and apples, often beautifully. Look for <strong>Abav&shy;nieki</strong> rhubarb wine or any of the small farmhouse wineries in the Vidzeme region. Strange, often sweet, sometimes excellent. Worth at least one bottle as an experiment.</p>

<hr />

<h2>Where to actually eat in Riga</h2>
<p>Three or four genuine recommendations, not a menu of every restaurant in town. These are the places I&rsquo;d send a friend.</p>

<h3>For grazing: the Riga Central Market</h3>
<p>I keep mentioning this market and that&rsquo;s deliberate, it&rsquo;s the single best food experience in Riga and the cheapest. Five enormous Zeppelin-hangar buildings just south of the Old Town, each dedicated to a category: meat, fish, dairy, vegetables, gastronomy. Go for lunch, walk every hangar, taste freely (most stalls will offer samples), and assemble your own meal: smoked fish, rye bread, biezpiens, pickled cucumbers, a piece of smoked cheese, a slice of sklandrausis. Lunch for two for &euro;15. The fish hall is the most photogenic.</p>

<h3>For modern Latvian: Bibliot&#275;ka N&#186;1, Vincents, or 3 Pavāru Restorāns</h3>
<p>If you want to eat the modern, refined version of Latvian food (still local ingredients, still seasonal, still recognisable, but elevated and beautifully plated), these are the three I&rsquo;d send you to. <strong>Bibliot&#275;ka N&#186;1</strong> is the most relaxed of the three and has the best wine list. <strong>Vincents</strong> is the most ambitious and the only one that approaches the Michelin-star end. <strong>3 Pavāru Restorāns</strong> (&ldquo;3 Cooks Restaurant&rdquo;) is the open-kitchen, chef-led, tasting-menu option that locals know about and tourists mostly don&rsquo;t. Reservation needed at all three; expect &euro;40&ndash;80 per person with wine.</p>

<h3>For traditional Latvian without the tourist tax: Lido</h3>
<p>Lido is a Latvian chain of self-service restaurants serving classic Latvian dishes at honest prices. It&rsquo;s not fancy and it&rsquo;s not trying to be, but the food is genuinely good versions of pel&#275;kie zir&#326;i, karbon&#257;de, biezpiens dishes, and rasols, at &euro;8&ndash;15 a plate. The Lido Atp&#363;tas Centrs in the suburbs is the famous big one (huge, with a kids&rsquo; play area, often full of Latvian families on Sundays), but there are smaller branches throughout the city centre. This is where to go if you want to taste twelve traditional dishes in one sitting without a tasting menu price tag.</p>

<hr />

<h2>The seasonal calendar</h2>
<p>Latvian food is properly seasonal. What&rsquo;s on the table genuinely changes month by month. Quick guide:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Spring (March&ndash;May):</strong> first wild garlic in April, fresh dill returning, new potatoes by May, the first asparagus from local farms, fresh kefir tasting different because the cows are back on grass.</li>
<li><strong>Summer (June&ndash;August):</strong> aukst&#257; zupa season, fresh berries (strawberries first, then bilberries, then raspberries, then blackcurrants), foraged chanterelles starting late July, cold smoked fish on the beach, kvass from the yellow trucks.</li>
<li><strong>Autumn (September&ndash;October):</strong> peak mushroom-foraging madness (chanterelles still going, then porcini, then a dozen others), apple and pear season, sklandrausis at the autumn markets, plums for slivovitz.</li>
<li><strong>Winter (November&ndash;February):</strong> pel&#275;kie zir&#326;i for the solstice, hot smoked fish from the market, hearty bread soups, kli&#326;&#291;eris on namesdays, Black Balsam in hot blackcurrant juice on dark afternoons.</li>
</ul>

<hr />

<h2>What to skip, what&rsquo;s overrated</h2>
<p>An honest section, because I owe you that.</p>
<p><strong>Skip the &ldquo;medieval-themed&rdquo; tourist restaurants in the Old Town</strong>, the ones with serving staff in costume and roast wild boar on the menu. The food is mediocre at best, the prices are double the Lido equivalent, and the &ldquo;authentic medieval Latvian recipe&rdquo; on the menu is invented for tourists.</p>
<p><strong>Be honest about Riga Black Balsam at room temperature.</strong> Almost no Latvian drinks it that way. If a bartender pours you a shot at room temperature with no chaser, they&rsquo;re hazing you. Order it mixed with hot blackcurrant juice and you&rsquo;ll see why we love it.</p>
<p><strong>The pel&#275;kie zir&#326;i thing.</strong> I love this dish. But not every visitor will, and that&rsquo;s fine. If you try one bite and decide it&rsquo;s not for you, eat a bit of biezpiens and rye bread instead and we&rsquo;ll call it a draw.</p>
<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions about Latvian food</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-the-most-famous-latvian-dish-1">
            What is the most famous Latvian dish?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-the-most-famous-latvian-dish-1" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Pelēkie zirņi ar speķi &mdash; grey peas with smoked bacon &mdash; is the official national dish, traditionally eaten with a glass of cold kefir on the side. The combination is the point: starchy earthy peas, rich smoky bacon, sharp sour kefir cutting through it all. Honestly though, the most-eaten dish in Latvian homes is probably some combination of biezpiens (cottage cheese) with boiled potatoes and dill &mdash; that&rsquo;s what you&rsquo;ll find on Latvian dinner tables several nights a week.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-rupjmaize-and-why-is-it-so-impor-2">
            What is rupjmaize and why is it so important to Latvian food?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-rupjmaize-and-why-is-it-so-impor-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Rupjmaize is the dense, dark, slightly sweet-and-sour Latvian rye bread, made from sourdough rye flour and often caraway seeds. It&rsquo;s the cornerstone of the cuisine &mdash; eaten with smoked fish, with cottage cheese, with butter and honey, used to make a layered dessert (Rupjmaizes Kārtojums) and a cold sweet bread soup (Maizes Zupa). A proper loaf is heavy, dark all the way through, and keeps for a week. Lāči and Liepkalni are the two most-recommended bakery brands; vacuum-packed loaves travel well as souvenirs.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-biezpiens-and-what-do-latvians-d-3">
            What is biezpiens and what do Latvians do with it?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-biezpiens-and-what-do-latvians-d-3" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Biezpiens is fresh Latvian curd cheese &mdash; somewhere between Greek yoghurt and ricotta in texture but lighter and slightly tangy. Latvians eat it more days than not, both savoury (mixed with sour cream and dill, served over hot boiled potatoes) and sweet (as the chocolate-coated bar called Kārums, in stuffed pancakes, or in the layered dessert Rupjmaizes Kārtojums). If you understand biezpiens, you understand half of Latvian food. Every supermarket has a whole shelf of biezpiens products that simply don&rsquo;t exist outside the Baltics.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-have-latvians-always-drunk-kefir-or-is-i-4">
            Have Latvians always drunk kefir, or is it a recent thing like in the West?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-have-latvians-always-drunk-kefir-or-is-i-4" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>We&rsquo;ve been drinking it for generations &mdash; kefir has been part of daily Latvian life long before it became a Western wellness trend. It&rsquo;s fermented milk, slightly sour and slightly fizzy, and every Latvian fridge has a bottle in it. We drink it cold from the glass, pour it over hot grey peas, use it as the base for cold pink summer soup, and recommend it as the universal hangover cure. A half-litre bottle costs around 90 cents at any supermarket. Try the brands Smiltenes Piens, Tūja, or Latvijas Piens for properly tangy, properly local versions.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-the-pink-latvian-soup-called-and-5">
            What is the pink Latvian soup called and when can I try it?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-the-pink-latvian-soup-called-and-5" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Aukstā zupa (literally &rsquo;cold soup&rsquo;) &mdash; the bright pink Latvian summer soup, available June through August. It&rsquo;s built on a kefir base with grated raw beetroot or pickled beetroot juice (which gives the electric pink colour), diced cucumber, plenty of fresh dill, sliced spring onion, and a hard-boiled egg cut in half on top. Always served properly cold. The Central Market food court does excellent versions for €5; Bibliotēka Nº1 and Vincents serve refined versions in summer.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-why-is-everything-in-latvian-food-garnis-6">
            Why is everything in Latvian food garnished with dill?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-why-is-everything-in-latvian-food-garnis-6" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Dill is the default herb of Northern European cooking and Latvians use it on essentially every savoury dish &mdash; boiled potatoes, cottage cheese, smoked fish, pelmeņi, salads, soups. Fresh dill is sold in big bunches at every market for around €1 and the average Latvian goes through a bunch every few days in summer. We&rsquo;re aware it can seem excessive, but try it on the right dishes &mdash; cold pink soup, hot new potatoes with butter, biezpiens with sour cream &mdash; and you&rsquo;ll see why. Dill cuts richness, brightens cold dishes, and pairs with kefir in a way no other herb does.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-is-latvian-smoked-fish-actually-special--7">
            Is Latvian smoked fish actually special, or is it the same as Scandinavian?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-is-latvian-smoked-fish-actually-special--7" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Latvian smoked fish is its own tradition, distinct from Scandinavian. The Baltic coast has been producing smoked fish since the Hanseatic League era (1200s), and small fishing villages on the western Kurzeme coast &mdash; Roja, Pāvilosta, Ventspils &mdash; still operate traditional alder-wood and juniper smokehouses. Try smoked sprats (the classic, served on rye bread with a slice of hard-boiled egg) and smoked eel from Pāvilosta &mdash; the latter is the secret luxury most travellers miss, properly rich and woodsmoky, around €30&ndash;50/kg at the Riga Central Market fish hall.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-sklandrausis-and-where-do-i-try--8">
            What is sklandrausis and where do I try it?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-sklandrausis-and-where-do-i-try--8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Sklandrausis is a small open-faced rye-pastry tart from the western Kurzeme region, filled with mashed potato topped with sweetened mashed carrot, dusted with caraway, baked until the carrot caramelises slightly. It&rsquo;s sweet, savoury, and unlike anything else &mdash; the recipe is documented from the 17th century and it has EU Protected Designation of Origin status. Look for it at the Riga Central Market or at autumn farmers&rsquo; markets. Most travellers have never heard of it; it&rsquo;s one of the more rewarding things you can try.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-are-pelme-i-a-latvian-dish-9">
            Are pelmeņi a Latvian dish?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-are-pelme-i-a-latvian-dish-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Honest answer: not exclusively. Pelmeņi are the small meat-filled dumplings eaten across the entire former Soviet space &mdash; Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Latvia. They&rsquo;ve been part of daily Latvian eating for generations and every supermarket sells them frozen, but they&rsquo;re not uniquely Latvian. The Latvian way to serve them is boiled, with a generous knob of butter, sour cream, dill, salt, and pepper. For something genuinely Latvian, look for kartupeļu pankūkas (potato pancakes) or sklandrausis instead.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-the-latvian-pickle-juice-traditi-10">
            What is the Latvian pickle juice tradition?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-the-latvian-pickle-juice-traditi-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Every Latvian fridge has a jar of dill-pickled cucumbers, and when the cucumbers are gone, you don&rsquo;t throw away the brine &mdash; you drink it. Two purposes: as a hangover cure (the science actually backs this up &mdash; salt, vinegar and lactic acid all help), and as a chaser for vodka in the traditional vodka-pickle-brine sequence. The pickled cucumbers themselves are also the silent partner of every Latvian meal &mdash; diced into rasols (the Latvian potato salad), sliced alongside boiled potatoes, eaten whole with smoked fish.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-karbon-de-11">
            What is karbonāde?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-karbon-de-11" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Karbonāde is the Latvian take on schnitzel: pork loin pounded thin, breaded with rye breadcrumbs, fried in butter, served with a creamy chanterelle mushroom sauce, boiled potatoes, and pickled vegetables. The chanterelle sauce matters &mdash; proper karbonāde uses real wild chanterelles from Latvian forests (foraged in late summer and autumn), gently fried in butter with shallot and finished with cream and dill. It&rsquo;s the Sunday lunch of countless Latvian childhoods and the dish to order if a traditional restaurant menu doesn&rsquo;t make you curious.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-is-riga-black-balsam-and-how-do-i-d-12">
            What is Riga Black Balsam and how do I drink it?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-is-riga-black-balsam-and-how-do-i-d-12" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Riga Black Balsam is the dark, bitter, 45% Latvian herbal liqueur made from a closely-guarded recipe of 24 herbs, roots and spices, in production since 1752. Almost no Latvian drinks it as a room-temperature shot &mdash; that&rsquo;s how tourists get hazed. The proper way: a tablespoon stirred into a glass of hot blackcurrant juice in winter, into hot tea with honey, or over ice with bitter lemon. The blackcurrant version (Black Balsam Currant) is genuinely delicious and what I&rsquo;d serve any first-time visitor. There&rsquo;s a Black Balsam museum and tasting bar in Riga&rsquo;s Old Town.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-where-should-i-eat-traditional-latvian-f-13">
            Where should I eat traditional Latvian food in Riga?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-where-should-i-eat-traditional-latvian-f-13" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Four honest recommendations: the Riga Central Market for grazing (assemble your own lunch from the smoked fish, cheese, bread, and biezpiens stalls &mdash; €15 for two); Lido for traditional Latvian self-service at honest prices (€8&ndash;15 per plate, all the classics); Bibliotēka Nº1, Vincents, or 3 Pavāru Restorāns for the modern refined versions of Latvian food (€40&ndash;80 per person with wine). Skip the medieval-themed tourist restaurants in the Old Town with costumed staff &mdash; the food is mediocre and twice the price.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-is-riga-central-market-worth-visiting-ju-14">
            Is Riga Central Market worth visiting just for the food?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-is-riga-central-market-worth-visiting-ju-14" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, and it&rsquo;s the single best food experience in Riga. Five enormous Zeppelin-hangar buildings just south of the Old Town, each dedicated to a category: meat, fish, dairy, vegetables, gastronomy. Go for lunch, walk every hangar, taste freely (most stalls offer samples), and build your own meal. Smoked sprats on rye bread, biezpiens with dill, a piece of smoked cheese, sklandrausis, pickled cucumbers &mdash; €15 for two people, the most authentic lunch in Riga. The fish hall is the most photogenic.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-s-the-best-latvian-dish-for-a-veget-15">
            What&rsquo;s the best Latvian dish for a vegetarian?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-s-the-best-latvian-dish-for-a-veget-15" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Plenty of options. Boiled new potatoes with biezpiens, sour cream, and dill is the everyday Latvian summer plate and is naturally vegetarian. Sklandrausis (the rye-and-carrot tart from Kurzeme) is vegetarian. Aukstā zupa (the pink summer soup) is vegetarian. Biezpiena pankūkas (sweet stuffed pancakes) are vegetarian. Most modern Riga restaurants have at least one or two excellent vegetarian Latvian options. The harder challenge is vegan &mdash; Latvian food is dairy-heavy, and biezpiens, kefir, and sour cream are everywhere &mdash; but it&rsquo;s doable with planning.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-is-latvian-food-good-for-fussy-eaters-an-16">
            Is Latvian food good for fussy eaters and children?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-is-latvian-food-good-for-fussy-eaters-an-16" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, mostly. The bread is excellent and unfussy. Boiled potatoes with butter and dill are a safe bet. Karbonāde is essentially a high-quality breaded pork cutlet that any child who likes schnitzel will eat. Sweet biezpiens products (Kārums bars, biezpiena pankūkas with jam) are a hit with kids. The trickier ones are the strongly-flavoured smoked fish, the cold pink kefir soup, and pelēkie zirņi &mdash; these are acquired tastes. The Lido self-service restaurants are great with children: they can see and point at what they want, prices are fair, and there are familiar options alongside the traditional ones.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-food-souvenirs-should-i-take-home-f-17">
            What food souvenirs should I take home from Latvia?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-food-souvenirs-should-i-take-home-f-17" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Vacuum-packed rupjmaize from a proper bakery (Lāči or Liepkalni &mdash; keeps a week, travels in checked luggage). A bottle of Riga Black Balsam from the duty-free shop. A jar of lingonberry or sea buckthorn jam. Smoked cheese, vacuum-packed. Tinned smoked sprats (the classic Riga Sprats are an iconic gift). If you have a cool bag and you&rsquo;re flying short-haul, a chunk of Pāvilosta smoked eel is the secret luxury souvenir. Avoid liquid kefir for travel; if you love it, buy a starter culture instead.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-are-kvass-and-beer-commonly-drunk-in-lat-18">
            Are kvass and beer commonly drunk in Latvia?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-are-kvass-and-beer-commonly-drunk-in-lat-18" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes to both. Kvass is a slightly alcoholic (around 1%), slightly fizzy, slightly sweet fermented rye-bread drink, sold in bottles in every supermarket and served from bright yellow tanker-trucks parked in city squares throughout July (this is not a joke &mdash; look for them). Beer culture is serious here, both mass-market (Aldaris, Cēsu, Užavas &mdash; all decent light lagers) and craft (Malduguns from Cēsis, Brūveris in Riga, Valatas in Liepāja). A pint costs €4&ndash;6 in most Riga restaurants.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-what-s-the-typical-price-of-a-meal-in-a--19">
            What&rsquo;s the typical price of a meal in a good Latvian restaurant?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-what-s-the-typical-price-of-a-meal-in-a--19" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Riga is genuinely good value. A self-service plate at Lido is €8&ndash;15. A solid mid-range traditional restaurant dinner is €25&ndash;40 with a glass of wine. The modern, refined Latvian restaurants (Bibliotēka Nº1, Vincents, 3 Pavāru) sit at €40&ndash;80 per person with wine. A proper tasting menu at the most ambitious end might reach €100+. Compared to Tallinn or Stockholm, you&rsquo;re paying roughly half. The Riga Central Market is the cheapest option of all &mdash; €15 for two people grazing across the food halls.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-food-which-season-is-best-for-trying-latvian--20">
            Which season is best for trying Latvian food?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-food-which-season-is-best-for-trying-latvian--20" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Honestly, all of them, but for different reasons. Summer (June&ndash;August) gives you aukstā zupa, fresh berries, the start of mushroom season, kvass from the yellow trucks, and the freshest dill. Autumn (September&ndash;October) is peak foraging &mdash; chanterelles, porcini, a dozen others &mdash; and you&rsquo;ll see sklandrausis at the autumn markets. Winter has pelēkie zirņi at the solstice, hot smoked fish from the market, hearty bread soups, and Black Balsam in hot blackcurrant juice. Spring brings new potatoes and the first wild garlic. If forced to pick one, I&rsquo;d say September: the weather is still warm, the foraging is at its peak, and the Central Market is at its most abundant.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
</div>
</section>

## The Rose of Turaida: A Real 1620 Latvian Murder Case

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/legend-of-rose-of-turaida.html
**Published:** 2026-05-01
**Summary:** Maija — the Rose of Turaida — was murdered on 6 August 1620. The 1620 court protocol, a sandstone cave, a linden tree planted by the bridegroom that's still alive."medieval" legends in Latvia that turns out to be a real lawsuit. A 1620 court protocol, a sandstone cave, a linden tree planted by the bridegroom, and a grave that newlyweds still visit on their wedding day.

<p class="article-lede">There is a small grave at Turaida, on the left side of the wooden church, that newly-married couples in Latvia still visit on their wedding day. They lay the bridal bouquet on the stone, take one photograph, and sometimes leave the flowers behind. The grave is for a girl named <strong>Maija</strong>, known to four centuries of Latvian children as the <strong><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_of_Turaida" rel="noopener external">Rose of Turaida</a></strong>, who died in a sandstone cave on the Gauja river on <strong>6 August 1620</strong>. The story is one of the few medieval-feeling legends in this country that turns out to be true. There is a court protocol. There are dates. There is a name carved on a stone, and the linden tree her bridegroom planted in 1620 is still alive.</p>

<figure class="rose-hero">
  <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rose-of-turaida/gutmanis-cave-turaida-sigulda-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="rose-of-turaida-hero" data-caption="Gutmaņa ala — Gutmanis Cave on the Gauja, where Maija was killed on 6 August 1620. The smaller cave Viktor Heil cut for her flowers is on the left." aria-label="Open photo 1 of 1: Gutmaņa ala — Gutmanis Cave on the Gauja, where Maija was killed on 6 August 1620. The smaller cave Viktor Heil cut for her flowers is on the left.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rose-of-turaida/gutmanis-cave-turaida-sigulda-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-rose-of-turaida/gutmanis-cave-turaida-sigulda-latvia.jpg" alt="Gutmanis Cave (Gutmaņa ala), Sigulda, Latvia — sandstone cave on the Gauja river where the Rose of Turaida (Maija) was killed in 1620." loading="eager" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1205">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Gutmaņa ala — Gutmanis Cave on the Gauja, where Maija was killed on 6 August 1620. The smaller cave Viktor Heil cut for her flowers is on the left.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>This is why we send our guests there.</p>

<h2 id="legend">A foundling named Maija</h2>

<p>In the spring of <strong>1601</strong>, in one of the smaller skirmishes of the long Polish-Swedish war over Livonia, Swedish troops took the castle of Turaida. After the battle, a clerk in the Swedish administration named <strong>Greif</strong> walked through the burned-out village and found, among the murdered bodies, a small girl who was still alive. Weeks old. Hungry but uninjured. He took her home, fed her, and decided to bring her up.</p>

<p>He named her <strong>Maija</strong>, after the month she was found.</p>

<p>Twenty years pass. The clerk's foster daughter has grown up to be such a beauty that the people of Turaida have stopped calling her by her name and call her, simply, <em>the Rose</em> &mdash; <strong>Turaidas Roze</strong>. Her bridegroom is <strong>Viktor Heil</strong> (<em>Vikturs Heils</em> in Latvian), a young gardener employed at the new castle of <strong>Sigulda</strong>, on the other side of the Gauja river. In the evenings, he and Maija meet at the cave called <strong>Gutmaņa ala</strong> &mdash; Gutmanis Cave &mdash; a sandstone hollow scooped out of the river bank, where a freshwater spring still runs. To make her happier, Viktor cuts a smaller cave on the left side of the main one, where he leaves flowers for her to find. She is, after all, the Rose.</p>

<h3>The two soldiers</h3>

<p>Garrisoned at Turaida castle are two Polish mercenaries left over from the wars: <strong>Adam Jakubovsky</strong> and <strong>Peter Skudritz</strong>. Skudritz is the more dangerous of the two &mdash; older, harder, fascinated with Maija to the point of obsession. He asks Jakubovsky, who has a softer way with women, to act as a go-between and help him win her. Maija refuses both of them. Several times.</p>

<p>Skudritz decides to take her by force. Jakubovsky agrees to help.</p>

<h3>6 August 1620</h3>

<p>On the morning of 6 August 1620, a messenger arrives at the new castle of Sigulda for Maija, with a note he says is from Viktor: <em>come to the cave urgently</em>. Maija leaves immediately, walks the path to Gutmaņa ala, and finds the two Poles waiting for her. She understands at once.</p>

<p>She fights. Jakubovsky grips her by the shoulders; she pulls free; she shouts at him to leave her alone. Then, according to the court testimony recorded later, she does something strange. She tells Adam she will give him the most precious gift in the world, <em>one that not even a king can give:</em> her magic scarf, which makes the wearer invulnerable to any weapon. To prove it, she ties the scarf around her own neck and tells Adam to strike her with his sword. He does. The scarf does not protect her. He kills her with the first blow.</p>

<p>What had happened was that Maija had decided to die rather than be defiled. Skudritz had been expecting Adam to murmur some incantation; Adam, trusting that the magic was real, had swung with full force. He stood over her body for a long time, not believing it. Then he ran.</p>

<p>Skudritz disappeared. Adam was found later in the woods near the cave, having killed himself with his own sword &mdash; driven into the trunk of a tree, falling forward onto the blade. The freshwater spring beside which he died is still there.</p>

<p>The next afternoon, Viktor came to the cave to wait for Maija and found her instead.</p>

<h2 id="survivors">What the court did</h2>

<p>The case was heard by the <strong>Royal Land Court of Livland</strong> in the weeks that followed. Viktor, accused first &mdash; the bridegroom is always the first suspect &mdash; denied it; the physical evidence pointed elsewhere. Skudritz held out under questioning. The thing that finally cracked the case was that <strong>Skudritz's eight-year-old daughter</strong> told the judges what she had heard her father say at home. He was convicted.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Peter Skudritz</strong> was sentenced to be exiled to Lithuania, his motherland &mdash; a fate the court considered a mercy, because the alternative was execution. His body, when he died years later, was buried with all his weapons in a deep bog near the <strong>Nurmizu estate</strong>, so that he could not return.</li>
  <li><strong>Adam Jakubovsky's</strong> body, since suicide ruled out a Christian burial, was sentenced to four months of public exposure as an old Livonian punishment. He was then buried in a marsh.</li>
  <li><strong>Viktor Heil</strong> was acquitted. He buried Maija on the left side of the new wooden church at Turaida, planted a linden tree on her grave, said a prayer, and left Latvia. He went home to <strong>Württemberg</strong>, in the south-west of what is now Germany. He never married. The booklet sold at Turaida puts it: <em>his broken heart could not find peace here.</em></li>
</ul>

<p>The wooden Church of Turaida he buried her next to &mdash; built in 1750, one of the oldest wooden churches still standing in Latvia &mdash; is still there. The linden tree is still there. The stone over her grave reads, in Latvian, the words the legend has always put in her mouth: <em>Labāk man dvēselīte cieta, nekā mans gods un mīlestība.</em> &mdash; "Better my soul should suffer than my honour and my love."</p>

<h2 id="real">How we know any of this</h2>

<p>This is the part of the story that we, as Latvian guides, find most interesting. The Rose of Turaida is not a folktale that grew up over centuries. It is a <strong>lawsuit</strong>.</p>

<p>In <strong>1848</strong>, a German-Baltic jurist named <strong>Magnus von Wolffeldt</strong> &mdash; a member of the Supreme Court of Livland &mdash; published a forbidding two-volume book in Riga and Leipzig with the title <em>Mittheilungen aus dem Strafrecht und dem Strafprocess in Liv-, Estland und Kurland</em> &mdash; <em>Notes on Criminal Law and Criminal Procedure in Livland, Estland and Kurland</em>. Inside it, in the second volume, was the <strong>original 1620 court protocol</strong> of the Royal Land Court of Livland: signed by the steward of Turaida, <strong>Pavel Schildhelm</strong>, and the presiding judge. Names. Dates. Charges. The disposition of the bodies.</p>

<p>For most of the 19th and 20th centuries, scholars assumed Wolffeldt had invented the underlying case to teach a moral lesson about Livonian criminal procedure. They thought he was a glib lawyer with a romantic streak. They were wrong. In the <strong>middle of the 19th century</strong>, when Riga Castle was being reconstructed, archive documents of the old Livland Supreme Court were uncovered in the underground cellars. Among them was the <strong>original murder report from the cave of Gutmanis</strong>, signed by Pavel Schildhelm, steward of Turaida castle. Two independent documents, recovered from two different places, describing the same case in the same words.</p>

<p>The legend is real. Maija is real. We don't know exactly what she said before she died &mdash; that part is the legend doing what legends do &mdash; but we know that on 6 August 1620, in a sandstone cave on the Gauja, a young woman from Turaida castle was murdered by two Polish soldiers, and a young gardener from Württemberg buried her on his own.</p>

<h2 id="afterlife">The afterlife of the story</h2>

<p>After 1848, the case escapes the lawyers and enters Latvian and German literature.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>1848</strong> — the German-Baltic poet <strong>Adalbert Kammerer</strong> publishes <em>Die Jungfrau von Treyden</em> &mdash; <em>The Maiden of Turaida</em> &mdash; in Riga. (A modest poem; later commentators called him "a glib composer of verses, full of romantic flourishes and antique deities.")</li>
  <li><strong>1857</strong> — the Latvian writer <strong>Juris Dauge</strong> publishes a Latvian-language version, <em>Turaidas Roze</em>, in Dorpat (now Tartu). For Dauge, Maija is not a Romantic German heroine in a tower. She is "an ordinary, honest, loving girl who chose to die rather than lose her dignity." This is the version that becomes the Latvian national one.</li>
  <li><strong>1865</strong> &mdash; an Estonian translation appears.</li>
  <li><strong>1887</strong> &mdash; first Latvian reprint. By 1987 there have been four editions.</li>
  <li><strong>1926</strong> &mdash; Latvia's national poet <strong><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainis_(poet)" rel="noopener external">Rainis</a></strong> writes <em>Mīla stiprāka par nāvi</em> (<em>Love Stronger Than Death</em>), staged the same year by the great director <strong>Eduards Smilģis</strong> at the Daile Theatre in Riga. The play is a hit. People start travelling to Turaida specifically to see Maija's grave; Rainis himself never doubted the truth of the legend.</li>
  <li><strong>1966</strong> &mdash; the composer <strong>Jānis Kepitis</strong> writes a ballet, <em>The Rose of Turaida</em>, staged in Riga.</li>
  <li><strong>1976</strong> &mdash; a film, <em>In the Shadow of the Sword</em>, is shot.</li>
  <li><strong>1997</strong> &mdash; the Latvian Post issues a <strong>EUROPA stamp</strong>, <em>Legenda par Turaidas Rozi</em>, designed by <strong>Juris Utāns</strong> and printed in the Netherlands. (It's the stamp at the top of this page.)</li>
  <li><strong>2000</strong> &mdash; the Latvian National Opera premieres <em>Rozes un Asinis</em> &mdash; <em>Rose and Blood</em> &mdash; composed by <strong>Zigmārs Liepiņš</strong> to a libretto by <strong>Kaspars Dimiters</strong>.</li>
  <li><strong>2001</strong> &mdash; the Latvian painter <strong>Jānis Anmanis</strong> publishes a set of aquarelles, <em>The Rose of Turaida</em>, that are now considered the definitive visual treatment.</li>
</ul>
