<h2 id="visit">Visiting Maija today</h2>

<p>Maija's grave is at the <strong>Turaida Museum Reserve</strong>, on the hill of Turaida just outside Sigulda, about 50 km north-east of Riga.</p>

<p>You walk up from the parking lot toward the wooden church, which is the <strong>second-oldest wooden church still standing in Latvia</strong> (1750). Maija's grave is on the left side of it, marked by a low stone with a Latvian inscription. The original linden tree planted by Viktor in 1620 is still alive; another linden has grown up next to it. People leave flowers on the stone year-round.</p>

<p>It is a Latvian wedding tradition to come to this grave on the day of one's wedding &mdash; usually right after the registry-office ceremony, in a small group. The newly-married couple lays the bridal bouquet on Maija's stone, takes one photograph, and leaves. Some couples leave the bouquet behind. (The booklet at the Turaida Museum, <em>The Legend about the Rose of Turaida</em>, sells well partly because foreign tourists ask, slightly bewildered: <em>what are these brides doing here? are we allowed to watch?</em>)</p>

<p>From the grave, walk down the hill toward the river. <strong>Gutmaņa ala</strong> &mdash; Gutmanis Cave &mdash; is a fifteen-minute walk on a marked path. It's a real working sandstone cave, ten metres deep, with a freshwater spring at the back that has always been considered curative. The smaller hollow Viktor cut for Maija's flowers is still there. So is the carved graffiti &mdash; visitor names from the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries scratched into the soft sandstone, including initials supposedly belonging to soldiers who passed through during the Northern War.</p>

<p>It is, if you pause for a minute, an unsettling place to stand.</p>

<h2 id="why">Why we send guests</h2>

<p>Latvians don't have many medieval saints. The Lutheran Reformation of the 16th century scrubbed most of them out, and the few that survived &mdash; like the Madonna of Aglona &mdash; are Catholic, in a country that is statistically one of the most secular in Europe. What we do have, instead, is a <strong>young woman from a frontier castle in 1620 who chose to die rather than be raped, and a court that believed her.</strong></p>

<p>Maija isn't a saint. She is not in any liturgy. But she occupies, in Latvian culture, the same emotional space a saint occupies. Couples ask for her blessing on their marriage. People plant flowers at her grave. She gets onto the postage stamps.</p>

<p>If you have a day in Sigulda &mdash; and you should &mdash; give it half an hour. Walk up to the wooden church. Stand at the grave on the left side. Walk down to the cave. Read the names cut into the sandstone walls. Decide for yourself whether there is anything to the story.</p>

<p>We think there is.</p>

<p><em>Want to see Turaida &mdash; the cave, the wooden church, Maija's grave &mdash; as part of a wider trip through the Gauja valley? <a href="/#contact">Get in touch.</a> Our small-group walking tours through Sigulda are designed around exactly this kind of detail.</em></p>

## Orthodox Churches in Latvia: A Visitor's Guide to Riga's Four

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/orthodox-churches-latvia.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** Riga's four Orthodox churches — Nativity Cathedral, Holy Trinity Pārdaugava, St Alexander Nevsky, Grebenshchikov — what to see, etiquette, and the history behind the gold domes.

<p class="article-lede">There&rsquo;s a moment, walking down Br&#299;v&#299;bas bulv&#257;ris on a low autumn afternoon, when the sun catches the five gilded domes of Riga&rsquo;s Nativity of Christ Cathedral and the whole sky seems to tilt. Locals barely look up &mdash; they pass it every day. But for a visitor, it stops you. Latvia is a country most people associate with Lutheran spires and Catholic basilicas, so the sudden Byzantine drama of an Orthodox cathedral, all gold and ochre and copper, can feel like accidentally walking into the wrong fairytale.</p>

<p>That surprise is the doorway. If you take it, you&rsquo;ll find one of the most layered religious traditions in the Baltics &mdash; older than the Lutheran reformation, deeply tied to Latvia&rsquo;s Russian-speaking communities, and in many ways the most visually generous of all the Christian traditions you&rsquo;ll encounter here.</p>

<p>This guide is for the curious traveller. You don&rsquo;t need to be religious. You don&rsquo;t need to be Christian. Orthodox churches in Latvia are, almost without exception, open to visitors of every faith and none &mdash; and a quiet hour spent inside one is one of the more transformational things you can do in Riga.</p>

<h2 id="why-visit">Why visit an Orthodox church at all?</h2>

<p>If you&rsquo;ve already done St Peter&rsquo;s tower and Riga Cathedral and you&rsquo;re wondering what&rsquo;s left, here&rsquo;s the honest answer: Orthodox churches are <em>experienced</em> differently. There are no pews. You don&rsquo;t sit. You don&rsquo;t process from A to B. You stand, you wander, you light a candle if you want to, you stop in front of an icon that catches you, and you let the place do its work. The senses are deliberately overloaded &mdash; beeswax and incense in the air, deep choral singing if a service is happening, gold leaf catching every flicker of candlelight. It&rsquo;s the most unapologetically beautiful form of Christian worship you&rsquo;ll find in Europe, and you can simply walk in.</p>

<p>For travellers used to the austere whitewashed interiors of Lutheran churches just streets away, the contrast is the whole point.</p>

<h2 id="churches">Orthodox churches to visit in Riga</h2>

<p>All four of the main Orthodox churches in Riga are working parishes, but they receive visitors warmly outside service times. None charges admission. A small donation in the candle box is the polite way to say thank you.</p>

<p>A note on the Grebenshchikov community: they&rsquo;re <em>Old Believers</em>, who broke from the Russian Orthodox Church in 1653 over liturgical reforms imposed by Patriarch Nikon and have practiced an older form of the rite ever since. Not strictly Orthodox in the canonical sense &mdash; but worth seeking out if you want to understand how schisms inside Eastern Christianity played out on Latvian soil.</p>

<h2 id="how-to-visit">How to visit: opening hours and practical info</h2>

<tr><td><strong>Entry</strong></td><td>Free</td><td>Free</td><td>Free</td><td>Free</td></tr>

<p>Hours flex around services and major feast days. For active worship visitors, services typically run early morning (around 8:00) and evening (around 17:00), with the main liturgy on Sunday mornings. If you want quiet contemplation rather than active worship, mid-afternoon on a weekday is the most reliable time.</p>

<h2 id="etiquette">Visitor etiquette: the rules</h2>

<p>Orthodox churches are open and hospitable, but they&rsquo;re also working houses of prayer. The rules are simple, sensible, and the same ones that would apply at any serious religious site anywhere in the world.</p>

<h3>Dress code</h3>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Everyone:</strong> cover shoulders and knees. Vests and shorts will get you turned away.</li>
  <li><strong>Women:</strong> head coverings are traditional &mdash; most cathedrals keep a basket of scarves at the entrance for visitors who haven&rsquo;t brought one. Carry a light scarf in your bag if you&rsquo;re unsure.</li>
  <li><strong>Men:</strong> remove all hats and caps before entering.</li>
  <li><strong>Avoid:</strong> tight clothing, low necklines, mini-skirts, anything with loud logos.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Behaviour inside</h3>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Stand quietly.</strong> There are no pews &mdash; Orthodox worship is conducted standing. Benches along the walls are reserved for the elderly and infirm.</li>
  <li><strong>Don&rsquo;t cross the central aisle</strong> during a service.</li>
  <li><strong>Speak in whispers, or not at all.</strong> Sound carries dramatically under Orthodox domes.</li>
  <li><strong>Move slowly.</strong> No rushing, no calling across the nave.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Photography</h3>
<ul>
  <li><strong>No photos inside.</strong> Even when no signs are posted, this is universal. Especially during services.</li>
  <li><strong>Photograph the exterior</strong> as much as you like.</li>
  <li><strong>No flash, no tripods, no video</strong> under any circumstances.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Lighting a candle (you&rsquo;re welcome to)</h3>
<ul>
  <li>Drop a coin in the box, take a thin beeswax candle, light it from one already burning, place it in the sand or holder.</li>
  <li>You don&rsquo;t need to be Orthodox or Christian. It&rsquo;s a quiet contemplative gesture extended to all visitors.</li>
  <li>If a service is in progress and the candle stand is up front, wait until afterwards.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Icons and relics</h3>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Don&rsquo;t venerate icons</strong> (kissing, touching) unless you&rsquo;re a believer doing so deliberately. It&rsquo;s not offensive to skip &mdash; it&rsquo;s expected of non-Orthodox visitors.</li>
  <li><strong>If you do choose to:</strong> never wear lipstick or balm. It damages the surface.</li>
  <li><strong>Don&rsquo;t lean on icon stands</strong> to take photos of yourself.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="how-many-orthodox">How many Latvians are Orthodox?</h2>

<p>Depending on the survey, somewhere between 13% and 26% of Latvia&rsquo;s population identifies as Orthodox Christian &mdash; making it the third-largest, or on some measures even the largest, Christian denomination in the country.</p>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Source</th><th>Year</th><th>Orthodox %</th><th>Lutheran %</th><th>Catholic %</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Latvian Ministry of Justice</td><td>2022</td><td>13%</td><td>37%</td><td>19%</td></tr>
<tr><td>SKDS sociological survey</td><td>2018</td><td>26%</td><td>17%</td><td>20%</td></tr>
<tr><td>Pew Research Center</td><td>2017</td><td>31%</td><td>19%</td><td>23%</td></tr>
<tr><td>ISSP survey</td><td>2015</td><td>19.7%</td><td>17.8%</td><td>18.5%</td></tr>
<tr><td>CIA World Factbook</td><td>2017</td><td>19.1%</td><td>36.2%</td><td>19.5%</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p>The discrepancy is a familiar one in post-Soviet states &mdash; it depends whether you count active parish membership (lower numbers) or cultural self-identification (higher numbers).</p>

<p>What&rsquo;s unambiguous is that Orthodoxy is concentrated in two places: Riga and the eastern region of Latgale. It&rsquo;s overwhelmingly tied to the Russian-speaking minority, though there has always been a Latvian-speaking Orthodox community too &mdash; services in Latvian were granted as far back as the 1840s.</p>

<h2 id="orthodox-world">Where in the world are Orthodox Christians found?</h2>

<p>Orthodox Christianity is the second-largest branch of Christianity globally, after Catholicism, with somewhere between 220 and 260 million adherents. Unlike Catholicism, it never spread through Western European colonisation, so its geography is concentrated and recognisable: a belt running through Eastern Europe, the Balkans, the Caucasus, and into the Levant.</p>

</table>

<p>A note on Ethiopia: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has around 36 million members, making it one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world. But it&rsquo;s part of the <em>Oriental</em> Orthodox communion (along with the Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, and Eritrean churches), not Eastern Orthodox &mdash; the two have been separate since the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451.</p>

<p>A quirk worth noting: Romania is the country in Europe where this catches travellers out most often. Romanian is a Romance language (Latin-derived, like Italian and Spanish) &mdash; which makes Romania linguistically Western. But the country sat on the historical dividing line between Rome and Constantinople, and after the Great Schism of 1054 its church aligned with Constantinople. Romanian Orthodox today number about 16 million, second only to the Russian Orthodox Church in Eastern Orthodoxy.</p>

<h2 id="history">A brief history of Orthodoxy in Latvia</h2>

<p>Orthodoxy came to Latvian soil very early &mdash; in the 11th century, as a mission outpost of the Russian Orthodox diocese of Polotsk, predating the Catholic crusades that converted the region in the 12th and 13th centuries. Some Latgalian noblemen converted voluntarily in this period; archaeological evidence shows Eastern Orthodox churches operating in the principality of Jersika before the Teutonic conquest.</p>

<p>The big change came after Latvia was absorbed into the Russian Empire in the 18th century, following the Great Northern War. Russian settlers, soldiers, and officials brought their faith with them, and the imperial state funded churches as a matter of policy.</p>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Period</th><th>What happened</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><strong>11th century</strong></td><td>Orthodoxy first arrives via missions from Polotsk</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>13th century</strong></td><td>Catholic Teutonic Order conquers Latvia; Orthodoxy reduced to merchant communities</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>18th century</strong></td><td>Latvia annexed to Russian Empire; Orthodox population grows</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>1840s</strong></td><td>40,000 Latvian peasants convert from Lutheranism to Orthodoxy; Latvian-language services permitted</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>1876&ndash;1884</strong></td><td>Nativity of Christ Cathedral built in Riga</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>1917&ndash;1918</strong></td><td>German occupation turns the Cathedral into a Lutheran church</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>1921</strong></td><td>Archbishop J&#257;nis Pommers defends the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvian_Orthodox_Church" rel="noopener external">Latvian Orthodox Church</a> under independence</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>1934</strong></td><td>Pommers murdered; canonised in 2001</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>1940&ndash;1991</strong></td><td>Soviet occupation: churches closed, the Nativity Cathedral becomes a planetarium</td></tr>

</tbody>
</table>

<h2 id="differences">What makes Orthodoxy different from other forms of Christianity?</h2>

<p>The split that created Eastern Orthodoxy &mdash; the Great Schism of 1054 &mdash; divided Christianity along roughly geographical lines: Latin-speaking West (which became Roman Catholic, and later spawned the various Protestant traditions) and Greek-speaking East (which became Orthodox).</p>

<p>Orthodoxy never had a Reformation, so it never stripped its churches of imagery or simplified its liturgies. It never had a Counter-Reformation either, so it never rationalised or systematised its theology in the way Catholicism did at Trent. What you see in an Orthodox church today is, in its essential form, what a Christian in Constantinople would have seen in the 9th century.</p>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Feature</th><th>Orthodox</th><th>Catholic</th><th>Protestant</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><strong>Central head</strong></td><td>None &mdash; communion of national churches</td><td>Pope in Rome</td><td>Varies / none</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Calendar</strong></td><td>Often Julian (Christmas Jan 7)</td><td>Gregorian</td><td>Gregorian</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Clergy marriage</strong></td><td>Parish priests can marry</td><td>Celibate (Latin rite)</td><td>Most allow</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Icons</strong></td><td>Venerated &mdash; &ldquo;windows into heaven&rdquo;</td><td>Used but not central</td><td>Generally avoided</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Liturgy</strong></td><td>Sung throughout, no instruments</td><td>Spoken or sung, often with organ</td><td>Varies widely</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Iconostasis</strong></td><td>Yes &mdash; central architectural feature</td><td>No</td><td>No</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Pews</strong></td><td>None traditionally</td><td>Yes</td><td>Yes</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Service language</strong></td><td>Local language or Church Slavonic/Greek</td><td>Local language (was Latin until 1960s)</td><td>Local language</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Number of sacraments</strong></td><td>7 (&ldquo;mysteries&rdquo;)</td><td>7</td><td>Usually 2</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h2 id="architecture">Why all the gold? Why blue? Why so much ornamentation?</h2>

<p>This is the question every visitor asks, and there&rsquo;s a real theology behind it.</p>

<p><strong>The gold is light.</strong> Gold leaf in Orthodox iconography and architecture isn&rsquo;t decorative wealth &mdash; it&rsquo;s a representation of uncreated divine light, the same light that surrounded Christ at the Transfiguration. When candles flicker against gilded surfaces in a darkened church, the entire space becomes a moving icon of divine presence. The effect is the message.</p>

<p><strong>The blue is heaven.</strong> Blue in Orthodox interiors, particularly inside domes, represents the heavens. Combined with gold stars and the figure of Christ Pantocrator (Ruler of All) at the apex, the dome becomes a visual cosmology: when you stand under it, you stand at the meeting point of heaven and earth. This is why Orthodox churches are typically built around a central dome rather than a long nave &mdash; the building itself is meant to <em>be</em> a microcosm of creation.</p>

<p><strong>The ornamentation is theological.</strong> Orthodoxy resolved an internal crisis about religious imagery &mdash; the iconoclast controversy of the 8th and 9th centuries &mdash; by declaring that because God became human in Christ, matter itself can be holy. Wood, paint, gold, stone, incense, beeswax, song: all of these can carry sacred meaning. So the maximalism isn&rsquo;t decorative excess. It&rsquo;s a deliberate theological argument that the physical world matters and can be transfigured by grace.</p>

<p><strong>The iconostasis</strong> &mdash; that wall of icons separating the nave from the altar &mdash; is the most distinctive feature. It evolved over centuries from a low screen into a full wall, organised in tiers (Christ, Mary, John the Baptist, Apostles, Prophets, Feast Days). It functions both as a barrier (the altar is the &ldquo;Holy of Holies&rdquo;, entered only by clergy) and as a window (when the central Royal Doors open during the liturgy, heaven is symbolically opened to earth).</p>

<h2 id="comparisons">How does this compare to Greek, Armenian, and Anglican churches?</h2>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Tradition</th><th>Family</th><th>In communion with Eastern Orthodox?</th><th>Visual style</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><strong>Russian Orthodox</strong></td><td>Eastern Orthodox</td><td>Yes</td><td>Onion domes, gold-and-blue, tall iconostases</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Greek Orthodox</strong></td><td>Eastern Orthodox</td><td>Yes</td><td>White marble, lower iconostases, Mediterranean light</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Serbian Orthodox</strong></td><td>Eastern Orthodox</td><td>Yes</td><td>Frescoes, Byzantine geometry</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Romanian Orthodox</strong></td><td>Eastern Orthodox</td><td>Yes</td><td>Some Latin influences, painted exteriors in Bucovina</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Armenian Apostolic</strong></td><td>Oriental Orthodox</td><td>No (separated 451 AD)</td><td>Conical domes, simpler stone interiors</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Coptic Orthodox</strong></td><td>Oriental Orthodox</td><td>No (separated 451 AD)</td><td>Egyptian-influenced, distinctive iconography</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Ethiopian Tewahedo</strong></td><td>Oriental Orthodox</td><td>No (separated 451 AD)</td><td>Round churches, drum-led liturgy</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Roman Catholic</strong></td><td>Western Christianity</td><td>No (separated 1054)</td><td>Long nave, statues, organ music</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Anglican</strong></td><td>Western Protestant</td><td>No</td><td>Stained glass, pews, hymns</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Lutheran</strong></td><td>Western Protestant</td><td>No</td><td>Austere whitewashed interiors</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p>Greek and Russian Orthodox are the closest cousins to what you&rsquo;ll see in Riga &mdash; same theology, same sacraments, different aesthetic accents. Armenian churches share the icon-rich sensibility but belong to a different communion. Anglican and Lutheran churches sit in a fundamentally different theological world, with no iconostasis, no veneration of icons, and a different sacramental theology.</p>

<h2 id="outside-riga">Notable Orthodox churches outside Riga</h2>

<p>Latvia is small, and a day&rsquo;s drive can take you to several remarkable Orthodox sites that most tourists never see.</p>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Church</th><th>Location</th><th>Notable for</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td><strong>Sts Boris &amp; Gleb Cathedral</strong></td><td>Daugavpils (Church Hill)</td><td>Largest Orthodox church in Latvia (capacity 5,000); ten gilded cupolas; built 1900&ndash;1905</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>St Nicholas Naval Cathedral</strong></td><td>Karosta, Liep&#257;ja</td><td>Tsarist naval cathedral 1900&ndash;1903; gilded domes against Soviet-era submarine base; foundation laid by Tsar Nicholas II</td></tr>

</tbody>
</table>

<p>The <strong>Latgale region</strong> in eastern Latvia has the highest density of small wooden Orthodox and Old Believer churches in the country. <strong>Daugavpils Church Hill</strong> is a particularly remarkable stop: four churches of four different denominations (Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Old Believer) standing within a few hundred metres of each other &mdash; a unique demonstration of religious coexistence.</p>

<h2 id="final-thought">A final thought</h2>

<p>If you&rsquo;re in Riga for two or three days, walk into one Orthodox church. Just one. Don&rsquo;t research it beforehand. Don&rsquo;t read the Wikipedia entry. Cover your shoulders, slip on a scarf if you have one, push open the heavy door, and stand still for ten minutes.</p>

<p>You&rsquo;ll notice the quality of the silence first &mdash; different from a Lutheran or Catholic silence, somehow heavier with incense and beeswax. Then the gold will start to register, then the eyes of the icons, then the deep choral hum if a service is happening somewhere in the distance. You won&rsquo;t understand the language. That&rsquo;s fine. The architecture is doing most of the talking.</p>

<p>This is one of those encounters travel makes possible &mdash; not because Latvia &ldquo;owns&rdquo; Orthodox Christianity (it doesn&rsquo;t), but because Latvia is one of the few places in Europe where the full richness of the Eastern Christian tradition sits, alive and accessible, alongside the Lutheran and Catholic traditions that more visitors expect. To skip past the Orthodox churches because they look unfamiliar is to miss half the story of this country.</p>

<p>Walk in. They&rsquo;re waiting for you.</p>

## Your First 48 Hours in Riga: An Honest Itinerary

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/planning-first-48-hours-in-riga.html
**Published:** 2026-04-14
**Summary:** A licensed Latvian guide's honest 48-hour Riga itinerary: what to actually see, what to skip, where to eat, and the practical answers most travellers want.

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<p>If you only have 48 hours in Riga, here&rsquo;s the version I&rsquo;d build for friends. I live here and I run tours here, so I have opinions, but this is the version that wastes the least time and makes you want to come back.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Day one (arrival day):</strong> Walk <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">the Old Town</a> slowly, climb St Peter&rsquo;s for the panorama, lunch at the Central Market, then a long afternoon in the Art Nouveau district around Alberta iela. Dinner in the quiet streets behind the Cathedral.</li>
<li><strong>Day two (the real day):</strong> Get out of the city. Either Ķemeri bog at sunrise (May to August only), or Rundāle Palace and Bauska Castle (year-round), or Sigulda and Cēsis in the Gauja Valley (year-round, best in autumn). Back in Riga by evening for one last dinner.</li>
</ul>
<p>That&rsquo;s the whole answer. The rest of this post is the longer version, with the practical things travellers actually ask me about: how safe is it, how do I get from the airport, how much should I tip, and what&rsquo;s the deal with the language.</p>

<h2>Why 48 hours is the right length (and why most people get it wrong)</h2>
<p>Riga is not a 24-hour city. The Old Town is the largest of the three Baltic capitals at 438 hectares, and the Art Nouveau district is a separate world to the north of it. Trying to do both in one day means you do neither properly. But Riga is also not a five-day city for most travellers, the city itself runs out at about three days unless you have specific museum interests, and the real magic of Latvia is what&rsquo;s outside the city.</p>
<p>So 48 hours splits cleanly: one day in the city, one day out of it. This is what I&rsquo;d send anyone on if they asked.</p>

<h2>Day one: the city, slowly</h2>
<h3>Morning, Old Town and St Peter&rsquo;s tower</h3>
<p>Start in the Old Town (Vecrīga) early, by 9 AM if you can. The cobblestones are quieter, the light is good, and the cruise day-trippers haven&rsquo;t arrived yet (they tend to flood in around 11 AM in summer). Walk a slow loop: Cathedral Square, the House of the Blackheads, the Three Brothers (the oldest stone houses in Riga), Riga Castle from the outside, the Swedish Gate. Don&rsquo;t worry about a fixed route, the Old Town is small enough to wander without getting lost.</p>
<p>The one thing I&rsquo;d book a ticket for is the <strong>St Peter&rsquo;s Church tower</strong>. It&rsquo;s the best panorama of the city, you can see the red rooftops of the Old Town, the Daugava river, the Art Nouveau district to the north, and on a clear day all the way to Jūrmala on the coast. The lift takes you most of the way up. Tickets are around &euro;9, you can buy on the door, and it&rsquo;s most beautiful in late afternoon when the light goes golden, but morning works too.</p>

<h3>Lunch at the Central Market</h3>
<p>The Riga Central Market (Centrāltirgus) is one of the largest markets in Europe and is housed in five enormous buildings that started life as Zeppelin hangars in the First World War. It&rsquo;s a 10-minute walk from the Old Town. Go for lunch and graze: smoked sprats, fresh rye bread, pickled cucumbers, smoked cheese, hot pīrāgi (small filled buns), and whatever&rsquo;s in season. The fish hall is the most photogenic. The dairy hall has the best cheese.</p>
<p>This is also a much better lunch than most of the Old Town restaurants, where you&rsquo;ll pay tourist prices for average versions of dishes that are excellent ten metres outside the cobblestones. If you want a sit-down lunch instead, the cafés on Miera iela in the Quiet Centre (15 minutes&rsquo; walk north of the Old Town) are where actual locals eat.</p>

<h3>Afternoon: the Art Nouveau district</h3>
<p>This is the part of Riga most travellers don&rsquo;t realise exists, and it&rsquo;s genuinely the city&rsquo;s strongest cultural asset. Riga has the densest concentration of Art Nouveau (Jugendstil) buildings of any city in Europe, more than 800 of them, most built between 1900 and 1914 in a frenzy of confidence before the First World War broke everything. About a third of the city centre is Art Nouveau.</p>
<p>The street most people photograph is <strong>Alberta iela</strong>, designed almost in one go by the architect Mikhail Eisenstein (yes, the father of Sergei). Walk its full length and look up: peacocks, screaming faces, women with their hair on fire, weeping sphinxes. Then walk the parallel streets, Strēlnieku and Elizabetes, which are quieter and just as good. The Art Nouveau Museum at Alberta iela 12 is small but worth an hour if you want context, you walk through a perfectly preserved 1903 apartment of the architect Konstantīns Pēkšēns.</p>

<h3>Evening: dinner in the quiet streets</h3>
<p>Skip the restaurants on Kaļķu iela in the Old Town, this is the busy main pedestrian street and the food is correlated with how loudly the menu is shouted at you. Walk one street back, the lanes around the Cathedral and the Convent Yard have small, properly-run restaurants where you&rsquo;ll get a good plate of modern Latvian food for &euro;15 to &euro;25, with wine. <strong>Bibliotēka Nº1</strong> on Tērbatas, <strong>Vincents</strong> if you want something fancier, <strong>Kanepe Cultural Centre</strong> for casual.</p>
<p>If you&rsquo;ve still got energy, end the night with a drink at one of the bars on Miera iela, the nearest thing Riga has to a hipster quarter. Or, if you&rsquo;re tired (you arrived this morning, this is reasonable), an early night and a good breakfast for tomorrow, because day two starts properly.</p>

<hr />

<h2>Day two: out of the city</h2>
<p>This is where 48-hour itineraries usually go wrong. People stay in Riga both days because they think that&rsquo;s what you do with a city break. But Riga is a small capital surrounded by three of the most underrated day-trip destinations in Northern Europe, and one of them is almost always within a day&rsquo;s reach. Pick one. They&rsquo;re all guided as small-group day excursions from Riga, including by us, and a guided day saves you the logistics of public transport on a tight schedule.</p>

<h3>Option A: Ķemeri bog at sunrise (May–August only)</h3>
<p>If your dates fall in May, June, July, or August, this is the one I&rsquo;d pick first. The Great Ķemeri Bog is a 10,000-year-old raised bog about 50 km west of Riga, a flat treeless landscape of dark mirror pools and dwarf pines, and at sunrise it&rsquo;s the most photographed wetland in Latvia for good reason. The wooden boardwalk is empty, the mist lifts off the pools as the sun rises, and most visitors say it&rsquo;s the highlight of their trip.</p>
<p>Pickup is around 4:30 AM (the early start is the price of admission), and you&rsquo;re back in Riga by 10:30 AM. Most people then have a long breakfast, a slow afternoon in the Art Nouveau district if they didn&rsquo;t do it on day one, and dinner in town. It&rsquo;s the easiest two-in-one day Riga offers. <a href="{{path.home}}excursions/kemeri-bog-jurmala.html">Our Ķemeri tour is here</a> at &euro;45 per adult.</p>

<h3>Option B: Rundāle Palace and Bauska Castle (year-round)</h3>
<p>If your dates are outside the bog season, or you&rsquo;re an architecture and history person rather than a nature one, Rundāle is the day to do. It&rsquo;s a 138-room baroque palace 75 km south of Riga, designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli (the same architect who did the Winter Palace in St Petersburg) for a Russian aristocrat in the 1730s. The Gold Hall, the White Hall, and the formal French gardens are the highlights, and the rose garden has 2,300 varieties at peak in late June and July.</p>
<p>The day usually combines the palace with medieval Bauska Castle (a different period, a different mood, properly atmospheric), lunch at a local restaurant, and a small Latvian family brewery on the way back. It&rsquo;s a 10-hour day, &euro;85 per adult, and runs year-round. <a href="{{path.home}}excursions/rundale-palace-bauska-castle-brewery.html">Our Rundāle tour is here</a>.</p>

<h3>Option C: Sigulda, Cēsis, and the Gauja Valley (year-round)</h3>
<p>The Gauja River valley is the closest national park to Riga, about an hour northeast, and is the best of the three options for autumn (September and October are spectacular for foliage). You visit three medieval castles in one day: Sigulda, Turaida (the red-brick one in every postcard), and Cēsis (which you explore by candle lantern, properly atmospheric). The valley itself, with the Gauja cliffs and the cable car ride if it&rsquo;s running, has earned the nickname &ldquo;the Switzerland of Latvia,&rdquo; which is generous but not entirely wrong.</p>
<p>Same price as Rundāle, &euro;85, also a 10-hour day, also year-round. Best in autumn, brilliant in winter when the snow on Turaida is properly beautiful, lovely in spring and summer for the forests. <a href="{{path.home}}excursions/sigulda-cesis-gauja-valley.html">Our Sigulda &amp; Cēsis tour is here</a>.</p>

<h3>Which to pick if you genuinely can&rsquo;t decide</h3>
<p>I get this question almost every week. Three quick filters:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Are you here in May, June, July, or August?</strong> Do Ķemeri at sunrise. The other two run year-round; this one only runs now.</li>
<li><strong>Are you a palaces-and-baroque person, or a forests-and-castles person?</strong> Rundāle for the first, Sigulda for the second.</li>
<li><strong>Is it autumn?</strong> Sigulda. The Gauja Valley in September and October is one of the best autumn landscapes in Europe and most travellers haven&rsquo;t heard of it.</li>
</ul>
<p>If you&rsquo;re still stuck after that, message me at <a href="mailto:info@barefootbaltic.com">info@barefootbaltic.com</a>, tell me what kind of traveller you are, and I&rsquo;ll tell you which.</p>

<hr />

<h2>Practical things travellers ask me before they arrive</h2>
<p>Before I get to the FAQs at the bottom, four things I want to address up front because they come up in every booking conversation.</p>

<h3>Is Riga safe?</h3>
<p>Yes, properly. Riga is safer than most Western European capitals on most metrics, and Latvia as a whole has been a member of NATO and the European Union since 2004. The often-asked question of whether Latvia is at risk because of Russia, the honest answer is that Latvia takes its national defence seriously, NATO has reinforced its presence here significantly since 2022, and daily life is entirely normal. Tourism numbers are up, not down.</p>
<p>For ordinary city safety, Riga is calm and well-lit. The one thing I&rsquo;d flag is that Old Town nightlife on weekend evenings can attract loud stag-party groups (mostly British), and a small number of bars on Kaļķu iela have a long-standing reputation for overcharging tourists who walk in off the street. Avoid bars where someone in the street is trying to pull you in, drink in places that look like residents are also there, and you&rsquo;ll have a fine time. Solo female travellers regularly tell me they feel safer in Riga than in London or Paris, and they&rsquo;re right.</p>

<h3>Money, tipping, and prices</h3>
<p>Latvia is in the eurozone. ATMs are everywhere and contactless payment is accepted in essentially every café, restaurant, supermarket, and taxi, often even in markets. You can have a perfectly normal week in Riga without ever drawing cash, though I&rsquo;d carry &euro;20 to &euro;30 for tips and the occasional cash-only place.</p>
<p><strong>Tipping is not the American 20%.</strong> Restaurant service is properly paid here and tipping is not socially expected. If service is good, 5 to 10% is generous and very much appreciated. Round up the taxi fare, leave a euro or two for housekeeping. Tour guides (including ours): tipping is appreciated but not expected, &euro;5 to &euro;10 per guest in cash if you had a great day. If you don&rsquo;t tip, please don&rsquo;t feel awkward, an honest review is worth more to us.</p>
<p>Riga is genuinely good value compared to Western European capitals. A solid mid-range restaurant dinner is &euro;25 to &euro;40 with wine. A 4-star hotel in the Old Town in shoulder season is &euro;90 to &euro;150 a night. A coffee is &euro;3. A pint of local beer is &euro;4 to &euro;6.</p>

<h3>Getting from the airport to the city</h3>
<p>Riga International Airport (RIX) is 13 km from the city centre, about 25 minutes by car. Three options:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Bus 22:</strong> &euro;2 if you buy from the kiosk, &euro;3 from the driver, runs every 10 to 30 minutes from outside the terminal, takes 30 to 40 minutes, terminates at the central market and Old Town. This is what locals use. It&rsquo;s easy.</li>
<li><strong>Bolt or Yandex (taxi apps):</strong> typically &euro;10 to &euro;15 to anywhere central, app-based, reliable, drivers speak basic English. This is what I&rsquo;d use with luggage or kids.</li>
<li><strong>Airport taxi rank:</strong> the official taxis are fine but cost two to three times the app price. Don&rsquo;t use unmarked &ldquo;helpers&rdquo; in the arrivals hall who offer rides, this is the one consistent airport scam.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Language</h3>
<p>The official language is Latvian, which is one of only two living Baltic languages (the other is Lithuanian). It&rsquo;s ancient and properly difficult, you don&rsquo;t need to attempt it. <strong>Almost everyone in tourism, hospitality, and the under-50 generation speaks English fluently.</strong> Russian is also widely spoken, mostly by the older generation.</p>
<p>Two phrases will earn you smiles: <strong>Paldies</strong> (PAL-dee-yes) means thank you. <strong>Lūdzu</strong> (LOO-dzoo) means please, you&rsquo;re welcome, and here you go, all at once. That&rsquo;s genuinely all you need.</p>

Daily life in Riga is entirely normal &mdash; restaurants are full, tourism numbers are up year-on-year, the city is calm and well-lit. The Latvian government takes national defence seriously and the practical effect on visitors is essentially zero. ## The Powder Tower (Pulvertornis) and Latvian War Museum, Riga: The Free Museum That Explains Latvia

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/powder-tower-war-museum-riga.html
**Published:** 2026-05-04
**Summary:** What the Powder Tower actually is, the cannonballs still in the wall, and why the free Latvian War Museum inside is one of Riga&rsquo;s best-curated stops. Honest local's guide.

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, what this stop is</h2>
<p>The Powder Tower (in Latvian, <em>Pulvertornis</em>) is the only surviving tower of Riga&rsquo;s medieval city walls. It stands on Smilšu iela at the northern edge of the Old Town, and it has been there in some form since the 14th century. It is a thick squat round tower of dark brick, three storeys, with a conical wooden roof and nine cannonballs still embedded in its north face from a 1656 siege.</p>
<p>Inside the tower, and the long yellow building extending east from it, is the <strong>Latvian War Museum</strong> (<em>Latvijas Kara muzejs</em>) &mdash; the second-largest history museum in Latvia, free to enter. Covers Latvian military history from the medieval Livonian wars through both World Wars, the Soviet and Nazi occupations, the road to independence, and the present. Allow 90 minutes for a moderate visit, two hours if you read every label.</p>
<p>Three minutes&rsquo; walk south of the <a href="freedom-monument-riga-milda.html">Freedom Monument</a>, three north of the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a>, on the way between the eastern and western halves of the Old Town. If you only have one museum stop in Riga, this is one of the two contenders (the other being the <a href="why-visit-occupation-museum-riga.html">Museum of the Occupation</a>).</p>

<h2 id="history">A short history</h2>
<p>The Powder Tower was first mentioned in 1330, originally called the Sand Tower (<em>Smilšu tornis</em>) for the sandy approach beneath it. It was part of a ring of defensive towers along Riga&rsquo;s medieval city walls; at the height of the system there were around 25 towers and eight gates. The Sand Tower was rebuilt several times after sieges &mdash; the 1656 siege by Russian forces under Tsar Alexei is the most consequential, and the cannonballs still in the north wall date from then. By the 17th century the tower had been adapted as a gunpowder store, which is where the modern name comes from.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-powder-tower/latvian-war-museum-coats-of-arms-gable-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="powder-tower" data-caption="The Latvian War Museum extension, with the coats of arms of Latvian towns and regions painted in checker pattern on the gable.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-powder-tower/latvian-war-museum-coats-of-arms-gable-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-powder-tower/latvian-war-museum-coats-of-arms-gable-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The yellow gable of the Latvian War Museum extension, with coats of arms of Latvian towns, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The yellow gabled extension of the Latvian War Museum, with the coats of arms of every Latvian town and region painted in checker pattern.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>The medieval city walls were largely demolished in the mid-19th century by the Russian Imperial authorities to make way for boulevards, parks, and the Bastejkalns canal. The seven other surviving gates went with them. The Powder Tower stayed because it had become useful &mdash; a working gunpowder store, then briefly a prison, then a corporate clubhouse for the Riga student fraternity Rubonia in the late 19th century. In the 1930s, in independent Latvia, the building was converted to its present role as the Latvian War Museum, with a long extension built east along the line of the old wall. The museum was preserved through the Soviet occupation as the &lsquo;Museum of the Latvian SSR Revolution&rsquo;, then re-curated as a Latvian state museum after independence in 1991.</p>

<h2 id="outside">What you&rsquo;re looking at outside</h2>
<p>From Smilšu iela the tower reads as squat and round &mdash; thick walls (three metres at the base), small windows, conical wooden roof. Walk around to the north side and look at the wall: nine cannonballs are visibly embedded in the brick face, mostly at first-floor height. They&rsquo;re from the 1656 siege; the practice of leaving siege damage in place instead of repairing it &lsquo;invisibly&rsquo; was a Riga tradition that locals quite liked, as a public memorial to defended urban autonomy. The tradition has been kept on subsequent restorations.</p>
<p>The yellow gabled building extending east from the tower is the early-20th-century museum extension. Look at the gable: the coats of arms of every Latvian town and historic region are painted on it in a checker pattern, with bigger arms (Riga, Daugavpils, Liep&#257;ja) more central and smaller ones along the edges. It&rsquo;s a quiet civic detail and was painted in the 1930s as the museum was being expanded. Worth a minute&rsquo;s reading.</p>

<!-- TODO: native Latvian speaker review of pull-quote -->
<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Deviņas lodes joprojām sienā. Mēs tās neizņemam, jo tās ir atgādinājums.</em></p><cite>&mdash; What an old Latvian guide used to say: &ldquo;nine cannonballs still in the wall. We don&rsquo;t take them out, because they are a reminder.&rdquo;</cite></div>

<h2 id="museum">The Latvian War Museum &mdash; what&rsquo;s inside</h2>
<p>The museum is the largest single reason to plan more than five minutes here. It is the second-largest history museum in Latvia, after the National History Museum in <a href="riga-castle-rigas-pils.html">Riga Castle</a>, and entry is free. The chronology runs across multiple floors, roughly:</p>
<ul>
  <li>medieval Livonian conflicts</li>
  <li>the 17th-century siege wars</li>
  <li>the 1812 Napoleonic period (Riga held against the French)</li>
  <li>the 1905 revolution</li>
  <li>the Latvian Riflemen of the First World War</li>
  <li>the wars of independence, 1918&ndash;1920</li>
  <li>the armed forces of the first independent Latvia</li>
  <li>the Second World War, with serious attention to Latvian conscription into both Soviet and German forces, and what that meant for ordinary families</li>
  <li>the Soviet occupation, the resistance, and the road to restored independence in 1991</li>
  <li>the contemporary Latvian armed forces and NATO membership</li>
</ul>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-powder-tower/latvian-war-museum-wwii-riga-diorama-display-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="powder-tower" data-caption="A diorama of Riga in the Second World War, in the Latvian War Museum.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-powder-tower/latvian-war-museum-wwii-riga-diorama-display-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-powder-tower/latvian-war-museum-wwii-riga-diorama-display-latvia.jpg" alt="A diorama of Riga in the Second World War, in the Latvian War Museum, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>One of the museum&rsquo;s most-stopped-at displays: a painted diorama of Riga during the Second World War, with a fortified position in the foreground and the city beyond.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>The 20th-century section is the heart of the museum, and is properly weighty. Latvia&rsquo;s 20th century includes the country being occupied three times in ten years (1940 Soviet, 1941 German, 1944 Soviet again), the deportations of 1941 and 1949, the &lsquo;forest brothers&rsquo; partisan resistance that lasted into the 1950s, the slow Sovietisation that followed, and the 1989 Baltic Way and 1991 restored independence. The museum doesn&rsquo;t ask you to take a side. It documents what was and what happened to families. English-language signage is full and good.</p>
<p>One small note. The museum&rsquo;s coverage of the Latvian Legion and Waffen-SS-conscripted Latvian units in the Second World War is presented honestly &mdash; the museum explains that men were drafted, that refusing meant deportation or execution, and that the Latvian Legion has nothing to do with the modern far-right (a confusion that occasionally surfaces in international press). If you want to understand why the 16 March commemoration is contested, the museum is where to start.</p>

<h2 id="practical">Practical answers</h2>

<h3>Where it is and getting there</h3>
<p>Smilšu iela 20, on the northern edge of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. Three minutes&rsquo; walk south of the <a href="freedom-monument-riga-milda.html">Freedom Monument</a>, three north of the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a>, three west of the <a href="swedish-gate-zviedru-varti.html">Swedish Gate</a>. The Old Town is pedestrianised; you arrive on foot.</p>

<h3>Hours, costs, accessibility</h3>
<p>The exterior of the tower is on a public street, free, accessible 24/7. The Latvian War Museum is open Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 10:00&ndash;17:00 (closed Mondays; longer in summer; check the door for the current schedule). <strong>Entry is free</strong> &mdash; one of the few free major museums in Riga. Photography is allowed, no flash. The ground floor and several upper floors are wheelchair-accessible via lift; the top of the medieval tower is reachable only via narrow stairs. Allow 90 minutes for a moderate visit; two hours for a deeper one. The museum is at its quietest mid-morning Tuesday through Thursday and busiest weekend afternoons.</p>

<h3>Combining with the rest of the Old Town</h3>
<p>The Powder Tower sits naturally on the northern arc of an Old Town walk, between the <a href="freedom-monument-riga-milda.html">Freedom Monument</a> and the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a>, with the <a href="swedish-gate-zviedru-varti.html">Swedish Gate</a> and the medieval wall section three minutes south. A satisfying half-day: Freedom Monument, Bastejkalns park, Powder Tower + War Museum, Swedish Gate, Three Brothers, <a href="riga-castle-rigas-pils.html">Riga Castle</a>, ending with coffee on Pils iela. The full circuit is in the <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">pillar guide</a>.</p>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>
<p>The Powder Tower is a quick exterior stop &mdash; five minutes for the cannonballs and the gable. The War Museum inside is one of the two museums in Riga that I send first-time visitors to (the other is the <a href="why-visit-occupation-museum-riga.html">Museum of the Occupation</a>, which is more focused on the 1940&ndash;1991 period). The War Museum is broader, covers more centuries, and is free. The 20th-century galleries are the heart of it.</p>
<p>And the cannonballs in the wall outside, on your way in or out, are worth two minutes of looking up.</p>

The thick walls (three metres at the base) made it suitable for keeping volatile materials safely. The original medieval name was the Sand Tower (<em>Smilšu tornis</em>) for the sandy approach below it; that name now belongs to the street, Smilšu iela.</p>

  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">

    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-pt-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes. Nine cannonballs are still embedded in the north face of the tower, mostly at first-floor height. They date from the 1656 siege of Riga by Russian forces under Tsar Alexei. The tradition in Riga has been to leave siege damage in place instead of repairing it invisibly &mdash; partly as a public reminder of the city&rsquo;s defended autonomy, partly because removing them would have been more destructive than leaving them in. They have been preserved through subsequent restorations.</p>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">

Audio guides and special temporary exhibitions occasionally have a small fee, but the main collection is always free.</p>

## Religion in the Baltics: How Three Countries Believe Differently

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/religion-estonia-latvia-lithuania-compared.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** Estonia is the world's most secular country, Latvia is split between Lutheran and Catholic, Lithuania is overwhelmingly Catholic. One border, three religions, three histories.

<p class="article-lede">To a visitor flying in from anywhere west of Berlin, the three Baltic states look interchangeable. Three small countries lined up along the eastern Baltic coast, each occupied by the Soviet Union, each independent again since 1991, each in the EU since 2004, all three speaking languages outsiders cannot tell apart, all three with snow in winter and wooden houses and pine forests and storks on the chimney.</p>

<p>This is a wonderful and forgivable mistake, but it is a mistake. Once you scratch any deep aspect of culture &mdash; language, food, music, architecture &mdash; the three countries diverge sharply. Religion is the most striking case of all. By any measure you can think of, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia are religiously about as different from each other as three small neighbouring countries can be.</p>

<p><strong>Lithuania is one of the most Catholic countries in Europe.</strong> Roughly three-quarters of its population identifies as Roman Catholic &mdash; a higher share than Italy, France, or Spain. The Pope is a major cultural figure. The country is dotted with crosses and shrines.</p>

<p><strong>Latvia is split three ways.</strong> It is the only country in the European Union with no clear religious majority &mdash; Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox in roughly that order, with a substantial non-religious population added on top. The Lutherans are clustered in the west and centre; the Catholics in the east; the Orthodox among the Russian-speaking minority everywhere.</p>

<p><strong>Estonia is, by some measures, the least religious country in the world.</strong> Around 45% of Estonians identify with no religion at all. Of those who do, the largest groups are roughly equal: Russian Orthodox (mostly ethnic Russians) and Lutheran (mostly ethnic Estonians). Only 14% of Estonians say religion is important in their daily lives &mdash; the lowest figure recorded in the European Social Survey.</p>

<p>How did this happen? Three neighbouring small countries, sharing centuries of common Soviet experience and similar pre-Christian Baltic-Finnic pagan roots, ending up so different? The answer is in the history. Let me walk through it.</p>

<h2 id="pre-christian">Pre-Christian Baltic religion: what was here before</h2>

<p>For roughly a thousand years, while most of Europe was being Christianised, the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea was the great holdout. The Latvians and Lithuanians (Baltic peoples, speaking Indo-European languages of the Baltic branch) and the Estonians (a Finnic people, related linguistically to Finns and Hungarians) all practised forms of nature-based polytheism well into the medieval period.</p>

<p>Latvian and Lithuanian paganism shared a Baltic pantheon &mdash; sky god <em>Dievs</em> (Lithuanian <em>Dievas</em>), the goddess of fate <em>Laima</em>, the earth-mother <em>M&#257;ra</em> / <em>Žemyna</em>, the thunder god <em>P&#275;rkons</em> / <em>Perk&#363;nas</em>, and many more. The forests had spirits, the rivers had spirits, the household had spirits. There were sacred groves where animals were not hunted and trees were not cut. Folk songs (the Latvian <em>dainas</em>, of which over a million were eventually transcribed) preserved these beliefs in coded form, even after centuries of Christianity.</p>

<p>Estonian pagan belief was structurally different &mdash; Finnic rather than Baltic &mdash; with its own pantheon, its own sky-god <em>Taara</em>, its own veneration of sacred places (<em>hiis</em>), and its own cosmology centred on natural sites rather than abstract deities. Like the Baltic peoples, the Estonians embedded their religion in their daily relationship with the forest, the field, and the sauna.</p>

<p>What happened next is determined entirely by who arrived to convert them, when, and how violently.</p>

<h2 id="crusades">The Northern Crusades: how Latvia and Estonia became Christian</h2>

<p>In the late 12th century, the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church" rel="noopener external">Catholic Church</a> and the kingdoms of northern Europe &mdash; German, Danish, Swedish &mdash; turned their attention to the last pagans in Europe. Pope Celestine III formally authorised what became known as the <strong>Northern Crusades</strong> in 1195, and the long, brutal process of Christianising the eastern Baltic by force began.</p>

<p>Latvia and Estonia were the easier targets. The land was flatter, the population smaller and more dispersed, no centralised state to coordinate resistance. A German monk named <strong>Meinhard</strong> arrived at the mouth of the Daugava River in 1184 and built a small church at Ikš&#311;ile. Peaceful conversion did not work. By 1202 the Bishop of Riga had founded a militant order &mdash; the <strong>Brothers of the Sword</strong> &mdash; to convert the locals at sword-point. Riga itself was founded as a crusader colony in 1201.</p>

<p>What followed was nearly a century of grinding warfare. The Livonian Crusade against the Latvians and Estonians ran roughly from 1198 to 1290. Whole tribes were exterminated, villages burned, sacred groves cut down, pagan priests killed. The Estonians revolted repeatedly &mdash; the famous <strong>St. George&rsquo;s Night Uprising of 1343</strong> was a last desperate attempt to overthrow German rule and return to the old gods, and it was crushed with characteristic violence. By the late 13th century the indigenous populations had been forcibly baptised and a German military aristocracy had installed itself permanently as the ruling class of Livonia (modern Latvia and Estonia).</p>

<p>This is the <strong>first key point</strong> for understanding modern Baltic religion: in Latvia and Estonia, Christianity arrived as a foreign occupation. The native peoples were converted by violence, ruled by a German Catholic nobility for centuries afterwards, and remained tenant peasants on land owned by Baltic Germans. Christianity in Latvia and Estonia was the religion of the conquerors. This matters enormously when we get to the modern period.</p>

<h2 id="lithuania">Lithuania: the holdout</h2>

<p>Lithuania was a different story entirely.</p>

<p>While the Latvians and Estonians were being Christianised by force, the Lithuanians did something extraordinary: <strong>they built a state, expanded it, and stayed pagan for another 200 years.</strong></p>

<p>In the 13th century, while the Teutonic Knights were grinding their way through Latvia, the Lithuanian dukes &mdash; Mindaugas, Gediminas, Algirdas, K&#281;stutis &mdash; consolidated a state that eventually grew into the largest country in Europe, the <strong>Grand Duchy of Lithuania</strong>, stretching from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. This pagan state held off the Teutonic Order in repeated wars, conducted complex diplomacy with the Catholic West and the Orthodox East, and used its religious ambiguity as a political tool. Mindaugas accepted baptism in 1251 to gain a royal crown from the Pope, then quietly abandoned Christianity again. Gediminas wrote letters promising baptism in exchange for political concessions and never delivered. The Lithuanian dukes kept their options open for over a century.</p>

<p>The conversion finally came in 1387, and even then it was a political deal. Grand Duke <strong>Jogaila</strong> married Queen Jadwiga of Poland, became King of Poland (as W&#322;adys&#322;aw II Jagie&#322;&#322;o), and accepted Catholicism for himself and his people as part of the bargain. Vilnius Cathedral was built on the site of a demolished pagan temple. Sacred groves were felled. The eternal fire of Perk&#363;nas in the temple at Vilnius was extinguished.</p>

<p>But &mdash; and this is critical &mdash; even Jogaila&rsquo;s official Christianisation of Lithuania left <strong>Samogitia</strong> (the western region, <em>Žemaitija</em> in Lithuanian) unconverted until 1413. Lithuanian villages in remote regions continued to practise the old religion well into the 16th century. The Christianisation of Lithuania was the slowest and gentlest in Europe.</p>

<p>This is the <strong>second key point</strong>: Lithuania was Christianised on its own terms, by its own ruler, as part of a strategic alliance with Poland that gave it Western legitimacy without erasing its political independence. Catholicism in Lithuania became, almost from the start, a marker of <strong>national identity</strong> rather than foreign occupation. To be Lithuanian was to be Catholic, in a way that being Latvian or Estonian was never quite to be Lutheran.</p>

<h2 id="reformation">The Reformation: Estonia and most of Latvia turn Lutheran</h2>

<p>The third great religious rupture came in the 16th century with <strong>Martin Luther&rsquo;s Reformation</strong>. This is where the religious paths of the three countries finally split definitively.</p>

<p>In Latvia and Estonia, the Baltic German nobility &mdash; the actual landowning, governing class &mdash; converted to <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism" rel="noopener external">Lutheranism</a> in the 1520s and 1530s, and dragged their peasant populations along with them. The first Lutheran sermon in Riga was preached in 1521. By 1561, when the old Livonian Order finally collapsed, most of Latvia and Estonia was officially Lutheran. The first book ever printed in Estonian was a Lutheran catechism, in 1535. By the early 20th century, around <strong>80% of Estonia and 55% of Latvia were Lutheran</strong>.</p>

<p>Lithuania, meanwhile, was Catholic and stayed Catholic. The Reformation made some inroads among the Lithuanian-Polish nobility, but the Counter-Reformation &mdash; driven hard by the Jesuits, who arrived in Vilnius in 1569 and built one of the great universities of Eastern Europe there &mdash; pushed it back almost entirely. Catholicism became further entrenched as a marker of Lithuanian and Polish identity against the Lutheran Germans to the north and the Orthodox Russians to the east.</p>

<p>The exception within Latvia was <strong>Latgale</strong>, the eastern region. Latgale spent the late 16th and 17th centuries inside the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth rather than under Swedish or German rule, and so it stayed Catholic when the rest of Latvia turned Lutheran. To this day, Latgale is the Catholic heartland of Latvia. If you visit the <strong>Aglona Basilica</strong> in eastern Latvia, you are in essentially a Polish-Lithuanian Catholic landscape, transposed onto Latvian soil. Driving from Riga to Daugavpils, you pass an invisible religious border somewhere east of Kr&#257;slava, beyond which the Lutheran churches give way to Catholic ones.</p>

<h2 id="orthodoxy">Russian Orthodoxy arrives</h2>

<p>The fourth layer arrived with the <strong>Russian Empire</strong>. Latvia and Estonia were absorbed into Russia after the Great Northern War (1721); Lithuania was absorbed in the partitions of Poland (1772&ndash;1795). For the next two centuries, all three countries lived under Russian Orthodox tsars who actively encouraged Orthodox missionary work, settlement of Russian Orthodox populations, and (sometimes) outright pressure for Latvian and Estonian peasants to convert to Orthodoxy as a path out of German feudal control.</p>

<p>Some did. In the 1840s there was a wave of Latvian and Estonian peasant conversions to Russian Orthodoxy, partly driven by hopes of better treatment under a tsar than under their German lords. These converts and their descendants make up part of the Latvian Orthodox population today, though most modern Latvian Orthodox are descendants of Russian-speaking settlers from the Tsarist and Soviet periods.</p>

<p>Russian Orthodoxy in Lithuania remained marginal &mdash; a religion of the Russian minority and some borderland communities &mdash; because Lithuanian Catholic identity was simply too strong to displace.</p>

<h2 id="20th-century">The 20th century: independence, occupation, atheism</h2>

<p>Each country emerged briefly independent between the world wars (1918&ndash;1940), with religious life roughly as the long history had left it: Lithuania heavily Catholic, Latvia majority Lutheran with a Catholic east and an Orthodox minority, Estonia overwhelmingly Lutheran. Each had its own national church.</p>

<p>Then came <strong>Soviet occupation</strong> (1940&ndash;1941, 1944&ndash;1991, with German occupation in between). Soviet policy was state atheism: church property confiscated, clergy arrested or murdered, religious education banned, theological seminaries closed, public religious practice driven underground.</p>

<p>But the three countries&rsquo; religious traditions handled the pressure differently, and this is what produced the modern picture.</p>

<p>In <strong>Lithuania</strong>, the Catholic Church became &mdash; quietly, then loudly &mdash; the central institution of national resistance. Catholic identity and Lithuanian identity were so fused that suppressing one meant suppressing the other, and the Soviet regime never fully managed it. The famous <strong>Hill of Crosses</strong> north of &#352;iauliai, where Lithuanians erected crosses by the tens of thousands as acts of defiance against the Soviet authorities (which bulldozed the hill at least three times &mdash; 1961, 1973, 1975 &mdash; and each time the crosses came back), is the most visible monument to this resistance. When Pope John Paul II visited the site in 1993, he treated it as a kind of sacred ground of Catholic survival. Lithuanian Catholicism came out of the Soviet period weakened but still central to Lithuanian identity.</p>

<p>In <strong>Latvia</strong>, the same pressure came down on a much more divided religious landscape. The Latvian Lutheran Church, already historically associated with the German nobility, lacked the deep popular legitimacy that Lithuanian Catholicism had. Many Latvians had complicated feelings about &ldquo;their&rdquo; church even before the Soviets arrived. Soviet suppression hit Lutheranism harder than it hit Catholicism (the Catholic Latgale region, with strong Polish-Lithuanian connections, held out better), and the result was a postwar Latvia where the gap between Lutheran and Catholic narrowed dramatically, and a large fraction of the population &mdash; having lost the habit of religion &mdash; never picked it back up.</p>

<p>In <strong>Estonia</strong>, the suppression effectively destroyed organised religion as a mass phenomenon. Estonian Lutheranism, like Latvian Lutheranism, had always carried the historical baggage of German foreign rule. When the Soviets came down on it, very little popular resistance defended it. The chain of religious tradition broke in most Estonian families, and in the 50 years that followed, secularism became the cultural default. This is why Estonia today is one of the most secular countries on Earth &mdash; not because Estonians made some sudden Enlightenment decision, but because the existing religious institutions were already weakly tied to popular identity and the Soviet period broke what remained.</p>

<h2 id="today">Where things stand today</h2>

<p>The most recent reliable surveys (Pew Research, Latvian Ministry of Justice, Estonian Council of Churches, Lithuanian census) give roughly the following picture, as of 2022&ndash;2024:</p>

<p><strong>Lithuania</strong> is around <strong>74% Catholic</strong>, with about 4% Russian Orthodox (mostly the small ethnic-Russian minority), small Lutheran and Old Believer populations, and around 10&ndash;15% non-religious. It is the only majority-Catholic country among the three Baltic states, and the world&rsquo;s northernmost Latin Catholic-majority nation. Pope Pius XII called it &ldquo;the northernmost outpost of Catholicism in Europe&rdquo; in 1939, and that hasn&rsquo;t changed.</p>

<p><strong>Latvia</strong> is, by Ministry of Justice 2022 data, roughly <strong>37% Lutheran, 19% Catholic, 13% Latvian Orthodox</strong>, with the remaining 30%+ non-religious or other. The geographic split is clear: Lutheran in Riga, Vidzeme, and Kurzeme; Catholic in Latgale; Orthodox among the Russian-speaking minority everywhere. Surveys differ on the exact percentages, but every survey shows Latvia as a three-way religious country with no majority. About 7% of the population attends services regularly &mdash; quite low.</p>

<p><strong>Estonia</strong> is approximately <strong>14% Lutheran, 13% Russian Orthodox, less than 3% Catholic, around 45% no religion</strong>, with the remainder split among other Christian denominations, neopagans, and various smaller groups. Estonia is regularly identified by the Gallup International &ldquo;Religion Index&rdquo; as one of the world&rsquo;s least religious countries by self-reported importance of religion, alongside the Czech Republic, Sweden, and a handful of others.</p>

<p>If you want a single sentence: <strong>Lithuania kept its religion through everything; Estonia lost it; Latvia ended up split.</strong></p>

<h2 id="orthodox-split">A recent turn: the Orthodox split from Moscow</h2>

<p>One of the most striking recent stories &mdash; barely noticed outside the region &mdash; is what happened to Baltic Orthodoxy after the <strong>Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022</strong>.</p>

<p>Russian Orthodoxy in the Baltic states had always been institutionally subordinate to the Moscow Patriarchate. In 2022, when Patriarch Kirill of Moscow publicly endorsed the war and described Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine as making &ldquo;sacrifices in the name of the fatherland&rdquo; that &ldquo;redeemed their sins,&rdquo; the political position of his subordinate churches in NATO countries became immediately untenable.</p>

<p>Latvia acted first. On 8 September 2022, the Latvian parliament passed a law making the <strong>Latvian Orthodox Church autocephalous</strong> &mdash; fully independent of the Moscow Patriarchate. It was, in effect, a state-imposed schism, justified on national security grounds. Moscow rejected the move; the Latvian Orthodox Church reluctantly complied. The split is unrecognised by most of the global Orthodox communion, but in legal and practical terms, the Latvian Orthodox Church is no longer Russian.</p>

<p>Estonia and Lithuania have been moving in similar directions, with their respective Orthodox churches navigating jurisdictional changes more slowly and through different mechanisms. The Estonian government has been pressuring the Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate to break its ties; in Lithuania, a small group of priests transferred to the jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople in 2022.</p>

<p>For visitors interested in the religious texture of the region, this is a live story. The Orthodox cathedrals you walk past in Riga, Tallinn, and Vilnius are at the centre of an ongoing geopolitical and theological reordering that is genuinely making history.</p>

<h2 id="pagan-revival">The pagan revival</h2>

<p>The other genuinely interesting modern story is the <strong>slow revival of pre-Christian Baltic religion</strong> &mdash; not as serious mass religion, but as a culturally significant minority movement.</p>

<p>In Latvia, the movement is called <strong>Dievtur&#299;ba</strong> (literally &ldquo;those who hold to <em>Dievs</em>&rdquo;), founded in 1925 by Ernests Brasti&#326;š and based on the <em>dainas</em> &mdash; the corpus of Latvian folk songs that preserve the pre-Christian cosmology. Repressed under the Soviets, exiled to communities in North America, and revived in Latvia after 1990, Dievtur&#299;ba received unprecedented legal recognition in <strong>2024</strong> through a new Latvian law that endorses its claim of continuity with Latvia&rsquo;s ancient past.</p>

<p>In Lithuania, the movement is called <strong>Romuva</strong>, founded by the philosopher Vyd&#363;nas in the early 20th century and carried forward after Soviet repression by the high priest Jonas Trink&#363;nas, consecrated as the country&rsquo;s first <em>krivis</em> (pagan priest) in 600 years in 2002. Lithuania&rsquo;s Catholic establishment resisted official recognition of Romuva for decades, but in <strong>2024</strong>, under pressure from the European Court of Human Rights, the state finally granted it legal status as a recognised religion.</p>

<p>In Estonia, the indigenous religion is called <strong>Maausk</strong> (literally &ldquo;earth faith&rdquo;) and <strong>Taaraism</strong> (named for the sky-god Taara). It has fewer adherents than the Latvian and Lithuanian movements but has grown significantly since the 1990s. A 2014 University of Tartu study found that <strong>61% of Estonians believed neopaganism was the &ldquo;true&rdquo; religion of Estonia</strong> &mdash; a striking number, even if most of those Estonians don&rsquo;t actually practice it.</p>

<p>The numbers of formal adherents in all three movements remain small (a few thousand each), but the cultural footprint is wider than the membership: many Latvians and Lithuanians who attend Catholic or Lutheran services for weddings and funerals will quietly observe pagan-rooted seasonal festivals &mdash; the <strong>summer solstice (<em>J&#257;&#326;i</em> in Latvian, <em>Jonin&#279;s</em> in Lithuanian, <em>Jaanip&auml;ev</em> in Estonian)</strong> is celebrated more enthusiastically than Christmas in many households, and is openly understood to be a survival of the pre-Christian solar year.</p>

<h2 id="visitor">What you&rsquo;ll see as a visitor</h2>

<p>If you spend time in all three countries, the religious differences become physically visible.</p>

<p>In <strong>Lithuania</strong>, you see crosses everywhere. Cemeteries are full of them, hilltops are crowned with them, the Hill of Crosses near &#352;iauliai has hundreds of thousands. Vilnius Old Town is a textbook of Catholic Counter-Reformation architecture: Baroque churches on every block, the Gate of Dawn with its miraculous icon of the Virgin, the white cathedral on Cathedral Square where every Lithuanian president still takes the oath. On Sundays, churches are full. People cross themselves passing a roadside shrine.</p>

<p>In <strong>Latvia</strong>, you see religious diversity laid out geographically. Lutheran spires in Riga and the western towns. The great Baroque Catholic basilica at Aglona in the Latgale countryside. Russian Orthodox onion domes &mdash; the magnificent <strong>Nativity of Christ Cathedral</strong> in Riga, gold and white in the centre of the city &mdash; serving the Russian-speaking minority. Wooden Old Believer prayer houses in the suburbs of Riga and Daugavpils. And, equally striking, plenty of beautiful old churches with empty Sunday congregations.</p>

<p>In <strong>Estonia</strong>, you see the historical Lutheran heritage &mdash; the great medieval <strong>St. Olaf&rsquo;s Church</strong> in Tallinn, the <strong>Dome Church</strong> on Toompea Hill &mdash; but the churches are largely museum pieces. Sunday services are sparsely attended. Most Estonians visit a church for weddings, funerals, and the occasional Christmas Eve service, but the relationship is cultural rather than devotional. Russian Orthodox cathedrals (the <strong>Alexander Nevsky Cathedral</strong> in Tallinn) are active mostly among the Russian-speaking population. The dominant religious mood is friendly secularism.</p>

<h2 id="deeper-pattern">The deeper pattern</h2>

<p>What I find genuinely interesting about all this is what it tells you about how religion actually works in the long run.</p>

<p>Lithuania kept its religion because Catholicism arrived <strong>late and on Lithuanian terms</strong> &mdash; it was associated from the start with national sovereignty and political independence, never with foreign occupation. Even after centuries of Russian rule and a brutal Soviet occupation that targeted the Church specifically, Lithuanian Catholicism survived because Lithuanians experienced Soviet attacks on the Church as attacks on Lithuania itself.</p>

<p>Estonia lost its religion because Lutheranism arrived <strong>as part of a foreign aristocratic occupation</strong> that lasted seven centuries. When the Soviets attacked the Lutheran Church in the 1940s, very few Estonians experienced the attack as personal. The Church was the Germans&rsquo; church, then the Russians&rsquo; church to suppress, and most Estonians shrugged.</p>

<p>Latvia ended up in between because Latvia is, in some sense, two countries religiously &mdash; a Lutheran west whose story is closer to Estonia&rsquo;s, and a Catholic east whose story is closer to Lithuania&rsquo;s. Plus an Orthodox minority that doesn&rsquo;t quite belong to either narrative. The split was already there before the Soviets arrived; it&rsquo;s still there today.</p>

<p>And underneath all three, the pagan substrate persists &mdash; in folk songs, in solstice fires, in the protected sacred groves that Lithuanian and Latvian forestry law still recognises, in the names of the days of the week (the Latvian Thursday, <em>ceturtdiena</em>, was historically <em>P&#275;rkona diena</em> &mdash; Thunder God&rsquo;s day &mdash; long after Christianisation).</p>

<h2 id="excursions">On our excursions</h2>

<p>Religion is a thread that runs through almost every excursion we run, whether we&rsquo;re explicitly talking about it or not. The Hill of Crosses excursion is, fundamentally, about Lithuanian Catholic resistance to Soviet rule &mdash; though we also try to explain the deeper pagan continuity that puts the crosses in such a particular emotional context. Rund&#257;le Palace and the Bauska region take you through Baltic German Lutheran territory, with the great old churches that were the centres of the German manorial estates. &#280;emeri Bog and J&#363;rmala are rich in pre-Christian sacred-landscape associations &mdash; the Latvian relationship to the bog and the sea is deeply pre-Christian and never really got displaced. And Sigulda and C&#275;sis put you in the heartland of medieval crusader territory, where you can still walk the walls of the castles built specifically to enforce the Christianisation of the Latvian peoples by force.</p>

<p>If you have specific religious-history interests &mdash; Catholic, Lutheran, Orthodox, pagan, or just the curiosity of seeing three closely linked countries that took completely different religious paths &mdash; let us know. Daiga can adjust any of our standard excursions to spend more time on the religious dimension, and there are several specialised stops (Aglona Basilica in Latgale; the wooden Old Believer churches of the Daugavpils region; the pagan sacred groves preserved within &#280;emeri National Park) that we can build into a custom day if there&rsquo;s interest.</p>

<p>The story is, in the end, more interesting than the simple fact of three small countries practising three different religions. It&rsquo;s the story of how religious geography is built up over a thousand years, how it survives or doesn&rsquo;t survive political pressure, and how the past keeps showing up in the present in ways that the people living it sometimes don&rsquo;t even notice. The three Baltic countries are, in this respect, a small but unusually clear laboratory.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: cross-sell-cta -->

If you want this story told inside the actual churches and cathedrals across all three Baltic capitals, <a href="/#contact">get in touch</a> with your dates and we'll design the route.</em></p>
