<p>Note that these are averages from the last ten years. Actual winters vary wildly. We've had a green Christmas and we've had −20 °C in January within the same week. Pack for the cold version.</p>
<h2>Is Riga worth visiting in winter?</h2>
<p>Yes, with one condition: it depends on <em>which winter</em>.</p>
<p>December in Riga is one of the most underrated city breaks in Europe right now. The reason the numbers have shifted — December 2024 was Riga's best December since before the pandemic — is mostly that word has got out that the Christmas market here is as good as the ones everyone already knows about and costs half as much. Riga's Old Town is already a UNESCO-listed medieval survivor. Add pine trees, mulled wine in clay cups, a Christmas tree on Dome Square where (locals will tell you) the world's first decorated Christmas tree stood in 1510, and a December hotel bill that doesn't ruin January, and you have a reason to come.</p>
<p>January and February are a different question. The market closes in early January. The weather tightens. The days are short, wet, and grey when they aren't beautiful and white. The city's cultural programme is quieter. It's still a valid trip — the restaurants are open, the museums are excellent, and you'll be the only tourist in Rundāle Palace — but it's a trip for people who are genuinely into northern winter, not people hoping to recreate a December weekend in milder weather.</p>
<p>The sweet spot, if I had to pick one week, is <strong>the first full week of December</strong> — the market is open, the pre-Christmas concerts have started, the restaurants are busy enough to feel alive but not full enough to book two weeks ahead, and the UK/Scandinavian weekend flights are still reasonably priced before the mid-December rush.</p>
<h2>Riga's Christmas market: the honest version</h2>
<p>Riga's main Christmas market runs on <strong>Dome Square</strong> (Doma laukums) in the Old Town. It opens in <strong>late November</strong> each year — the 2026 opening is expected around <strong>28 November</strong> based on the last three years' pattern — and closes in <strong>early January</strong>, typically around <strong>4–7 January</strong>, after the Orthodox Christmas.</p>
<p>A smaller satellite market runs at the <strong>Esplanāde</strong> park in the newer city, which is more family-focused with an ice rink nearby.</p>
<p>What you actually get:</p>
<ul>
<li>Wooden stalls selling Latvian handicrafts: linen, amber jewellery, woven belts and mittens (the Latvian mitten is a proper thing — each region has its own pattern), wooden toys, honey products, beeswax candles.</li>
<li>Food stalls with <strong>pīrāgi</strong> (bacon and onion pies), grilled sausages, smoked fish, fresh-baked black bread, sauerkraut, and the inevitable candied almonds.</li>
<li><strong>Mulled wine</strong> in a clay cup (~€5) and <strong>mulled beer</strong> in the same cup (~€5). Yes, mulled beer. Try it once.</li>
<li>A live music programme on most evenings — choir, folk ensembles, sometimes a brass band.</li>
<li><strong>The Christmas tree on Dome Square</strong>, which Rigans will tell you commemorates the 1510 original, with the small brass plate in the square itself reading "The first New Year Tree in 1510" to make the point. Historians quibble over whether it was a Christmas tree or a New Year's tree and whether it happened in Riga or Tallinn. I am telling you what the plate says.</li>
<li><strong>Path of Light</strong> — a free self-guided night walk through the Old Town with light installations on the facades. Runs for roughly a week in mid-December. Check the latviatravel website for the current year's dates.</li>
</ul>
<h3>What the market is not</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>It is not Nuremberg.</strong> It is smaller, less polished, and less deep into the Germanic tradition. If you came expecting the biggest Christmas market in Europe, you'll feel Riga is modest. If you came expecting a real working market in a real Old Town square at a real Northern European latitude, you'll love it.</li>
<li><strong>It is not crowded.</strong> Weekends in the week before Christmas are busy, but nothing like Strasbourg or Cologne. Most evenings you can get a mulled wine without queuing.</li>
<li><strong>It does not solve a whole trip.</strong> Plan on spending an hour, maybe two, at the market itself. Use the rest of the day for the actual city — which is the point.</li>
</ul>
<h2>What to wear in Riga in winter</h2>
<p>This is the question I get most from first-time winter visitors, and the honest answer is that most people from the UK, Western Europe, or the southern US underestimate it.</p>
<p><strong>Your baseline kit:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>A proper winter coat. Not a waxed jacket, not a puffer gilet, not a fashion wool coat. An actual coat rated for −10 °C. A down-fill parka below the knees is ideal.</li>
<li><strong>Thermal base layer</strong> — merino or synthetic, long sleeves, leggings. Not cotton.</li>
<li><strong>A warm hat that actually covers your ears.</strong> Beanies are fine if they're wool and they reach the tops of your ears. Berets and fashion hats are decorative.</li>
<li><strong>Proper gloves.</strong> Not driving gloves. Insulated ones. A pair of cheap warm gloves from H&amp;M in Riga costs €10 if you get here and realise yours aren't enough.</li>
<li><strong>Winter boots with grip.</strong> This is the single most important item. Latvian pavements are gritted but they ice up between gritting passes. Trainers and smooth-soled boots are a twisted-ankle waiting to happen.</li>
<li><strong>A scarf.</strong> Wrapped, not dangling.</li>
<li><strong>Two pairs of socks</strong> — a thin wicking pair underneath, a thick wool pair on top. Not one chunky pair; the sweat will freeze.</li>
<li><strong>Hand warmers</strong> if you're doing outdoor activities. €3 in any Rimi supermarket.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>What you don't need:</strong> snow trousers, ski goggles, gaiters, ice grips (unless you're planning to walk on a frozen lake, in which case ask me first).</p>
<p><strong>What you should bring even in December:</strong> sunglasses. The winter sun at this latitude is low, slanting, and bright — especially if there's snow on the ground.</p>
<h2>Day trips from Riga in winter</h2>
<p>Two of my three excursions run year-round. One doesn't.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th><strong>Excursion</strong></th>
<th><strong>Runs in winter?</strong></th>
<th><strong>What changes</strong></th>
<th><strong>Winter verdict</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>Rundāle Palace + Bauska + Brewery</strong></td>
<td><strong>Yes</strong></td>
<td>Gardens are dormant (no roses); interior is fully heated and at its most atmospheric in low winter light. Brewery lunch is unchanged and the dark beer hits differently at −5 °C.</td>

<p>If you're here specifically for a winter day out of Riga and you want something quieter than Rundāle or Sigulda, I can build a private-hire day around Jūrmala's winter beach (which is wilder and emptier than its summer self), a short walk at the Lake Lielais Baltezers ice if it's safely frozen, or the Ethnographic Open-Air Museum at Brīvdabas, which is quiet and gorgeous under snow. Write to me.</p>
<h2>Getting to Riga in winter</h2>
<p><strong>From the UK:</strong> Ryanair and Wizz Air both fly direct from several UK airports to Riga year-round. Fares in December are typically £80–150 return from London if you book four to six weeks ahead; January/February can drop to £40–80.</p>
<p><strong>From Germany, Finland, Sweden, Norway:</strong> airBaltic, Finnair, and the budget carriers all run winter routes. Helsinki–Riga is 50 minutes. Stockholm–Riga is 70 minutes. Frankfurt–Riga is 2 hours. Oslo has direct seasonal flights.</p>
<p><strong>From Estonia and Lithuania:</strong> Lux Express and Ecolines run comfortable coaches — Tallinn to Riga in 4–4.5 hours, Vilnius to Riga in 4 hours, both for around €15–25 one-way. These run year-round and the winter landscape through the forests is part of the experience.</p>
<p><strong>From further afield:</strong> no direct flights from North America. Most US travellers connect through London, Frankfurt, Helsinki, or Warsaw. Allow extra layover time in December for weather delays.</p>
<p><strong>Getting from Riga airport into town:</strong> the number 22 bus is €2 cash (€1.15 with an e-ticket) and runs every 10–15 minutes; it gets you to the central station in 25 minutes. A Bolt from the airport to most Old Town hotels is €10–15 depending on the time of day. Uber does not operate in Latvia.</p>
<h2>How much does a December weekend in Riga actually cost?</h2>
<p>For two people, three nights, arriving Friday afternoon and leaving Monday morning:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Flights (London return, booked 6 weeks ahead):</strong> £180 per person = €420</li>
<li><strong>Hotel</strong> (central Old Town, 4-star, 3 nights): €280–450 total</li>
<li><strong>Food and drink</strong> (restaurants, cafés, mulled wine, one nicer dinner): €200–300 total</li>
<li><strong>One day excursion</strong> (Rundāle, €85 per adult × 2): €170</li>
<li><strong>Transit, museums, miscellaneous:</strong> €60–100</li>
<li><strong>Total for two people, three nights, all-in:</strong> roughly <strong>€1,150–1,450</strong></li>
</ul>
<p>The same weekend in Tallinn or Prague is typically 40–80% more. That's the zeitgeist explanation in one paragraph: Riga in December is genuinely good and genuinely cheap, and word is getting out.</p>
<h2>Who this trip isn't for</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>People who hate the cold.</strong> Not "people who prefer warm weather" — people who are genuinely miserable below freezing. You will be miserable. Come in May.</li>
<li><strong>People who need 10 hours of daylight.</strong> Mid-December gives you about 6.5 hours of usable daylight. If you're here for outdoor photography, plan around that.</li>
<li><strong>People expecting a Southern European Christmas market vibe.</strong> This isn't Barcelona in December. It's the Baltic in December.</li>
<li><strong>People relying on Uber.</strong> Bolt works, but Uber doesn't operate here. If that matters to you, know it before you land.</li>
<li><strong>Last-minute bookers hoping to dodge the crowds.</strong> The week before Christmas is the one time of year Riga hotels sell out. Book four to six weeks ahead.</li>
</ul>
<h2>A final thing</h2>
<p>The case for Riga in winter isn't that it's the warmest Christmas market in Europe, or the biggest, or the most famous. It's that it's genuinely good, it's genuinely cheap, and it's quiet enough that you can still hear the wooden stalls creaking and the choir practising at the cathedral when you walk past. It's a trip you come home and tell people about because they haven't heard of it, and because you had the mulled wine without queuing, and because the palace was empty when you got there.</p>
<p>If December sounds like your kind of city break, the Rundāle excursion runs year-round and is even better in the cold. If you're unsure, write to me at info@barefootbaltic.com and tell me what you're hoping for. I'll tell you honestly whether December is right for you or whether you should wait for spring.</p>

<h2>Frequently asked questions</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-is-riga-worth-visiting-in-winter">
            Is Riga worth visiting in winter?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-is-riga-worth-visiting-in-winter" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, with a condition: it depends on which winter. December in Riga is one of the most underrated city breaks in Europe right now. The Christmas market on Dome Square is the sweet spot — ranked third in Europe for 2025–2026, with a central 4-star hotel running €60–120 a night, a fraction of Western European prices. January and February are a different question. The market closes in early January, the weather tightens, and the days are short. Still a valid trip for people who are into northern winter, but not for people hoping to recreate a December weekend in milder weather. The sweet spot, if I had to pick one week, is the first full week of December.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-when-does-the-riga-christmas-market-open">
            When does the Riga Christmas market open and close?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-when-does-the-riga-christmas-market-open" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Riga&#x27;s main Christmas market runs on Dome Square (Doma laukums) in the Old Town. It opens in late November — the 2026 opening is expected around 28 November — and closes in early January, typically around 4–7 January, after Orthodox Christmas. A smaller satellite market runs at Esplanāde park, more family-focused with an ice rink nearby. The full holiday programme, including evening concerts and the Path of Light night walk through the Old Town, is concentrated in December. Check the latviatravel website for the current year&#x27;s exact dates.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-is-the-riga-christmas-market-worth-visit">
            Is the Riga Christmas market worth visiting?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-is-the-riga-christmas-market-worth-visit" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, if you know what it is and isn&#x27;t. It isn&#x27;t Nuremberg — it&#x27;s smaller, less polished, less deep into the Germanic tradition. If you came expecting the biggest Christmas market in Europe, you&#x27;ll feel Riga is modest. If you came expecting a real working market in a real Old Town square at a real Northern European latitude, you&#x27;ll love it. It isn&#x27;t crowded — weekends in the week before Christmas are busy, but nothing like Strasbourg or Cologne. Most evenings you can get mulled wine without queuing. It doesn&#x27;t solve a whole trip — plan on spending an hour or two at the market itself and use the rest of the day for the actual city, which is the point.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-how-cold-does-riga-get-in-december">
            How cold does Riga get in December?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-how-cold-does-riga-get-in-december" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>December in Riga averages 0 °C in the daytime and −4 °C at night, with about 6–7 hours of usable daylight. January is colder at −3 °C daytime and −7 °C overnight. February is typically the coldest month at −3 °C daytime and −8 °C overnight. These are ten-year averages — actual winters vary wildly. We&#x27;ve had a green Christmas and we&#x27;ve had −20 °C in January in the same week. Pack for the cold version. This is not &#x27;wear an extra jumper&#x27; cold; it&#x27;s gloves-and-a-real-coat cold, and most UK, Western European, or Southern US visitors underestimate it.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-what-should-i-wear-in-riga-in-winter">
            What should I wear in Riga in winter?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-what-should-i-wear-in-riga-in-winter" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>A proper winter coat rated for −10 °C, not a waxed jacket or a fashion wool coat. A down parka below the knees is ideal. Merino or synthetic thermal base layer, long sleeves and leggings — not cotton. A wool hat that covers your ears. Insulated gloves, not driving gloves. Winter boots with grip — this is the single most important item, because Latvian pavements are gritted but they ice up between gritting passes. A scarf, two pairs of socks (thin wicking underneath, thick wool on top). Hand warmers if you&#x27;re doing outdoor activities — €3 in any Rimi supermarket. Bring sunglasses even in December; the low winter sun is bright, especially on snow.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-how-much-does-a-december-weekend-in-riga">
            How much does a December weekend in Riga cost?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-how-much-does-a-december-weekend-in-riga" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>For two people, three nights, arriving Friday afternoon and leaving Monday morning: flights from London, booked six weeks ahead, around £180 per person (€420 total); a central Old Town 4-star hotel, three nights, €280–450 total; food and drink including one nicer dinner, €200–300; one full-day excursion such as Rundāle Palace at €85 per adult, €170 for two; transit, museums, and miscellaneous, €60–100. That comes to roughly €1,150–1,450 all-in for two people, three nights. The same weekend in Tallinn or Prague is typically 40–80% more.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-do-day-trips-from-riga-still-run-in-wint">
            Do day trips from Riga still run in winter?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-do-day-trips-from-riga-still-run-in-wint" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Two of my three excursions run year-round. The Rundāle Palace excursion is highly recommended in winter — the gardens are dormant, but the interior is at its most atmospheric in low winter light, and the brewery lunch hits differently at −5 °C. Often you&#x27;ll be the only small group inside the palace. Sigulda and the Gauja Valley also runs in winter, though the cable car closes if the wind is too high and some trails can be icy. Walking-grip boots are non-negotiable for this one. The Ķemeri bog and Jūrmala sunrise tour only runs May–August; the whole point of that tour is golden-hour light, which you don&#x27;t get in winter.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigainwint-who-should-not-visit-riga-in-winter">
            Who should not visit Riga in winter?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigainwint-who-should-not-visit-riga-in-winter" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>People who hate the cold — not &#x27;people who prefer warm weather,&#x27; but people who are miserable below freezing. You will be miserable. Come in May. People who need 10 hours of daylight; mid-December gives you about 6.5 hours of usable daylight. People expecting a Southern European Christmas market vibe — this isn&#x27;t Barcelona in December, it&#x27;s the Baltic in December. People relying on Uber; Bolt works, but Uber doesn&#x27;t operate in Latvia. Last-minute bookers hoping to dodge the crowds; the week before Christmas is the one time of year Riga hotels sell out, so book four to six weeks ahead.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
</div>
</section>

## Riga Old Town: A Local's Guide to Vecrīga

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/riga-old-town-guide.html
**Published:** 2026-04-14
**Summary:** A licensed Latvian guide's deep guide to Riga Old Town (Vecrīga): what to see, what to skip, three walking routes, where to eat, safety, and seasons.

<h2>Short answer, what Riga Old Town actually is</h2>
<p>Riga Old Town (Vecrīga in Latvian) is the medieval and Hanseatic core of the Latvian capital, founded in 1201 by the German Bishop Albert. It is UNESCO-listed, 438 hectares in size (the biggest Old Town of the three Baltic capitals), and it sits on the right bank of the Daugava river. You can walk the whole thing slowly in one day, see the headline sights in half a day, and lose a satisfying weekend in the side streets if you want to.</p>
<p>If you only have a few hours, this is what to do, in order:</p>
<ul>
<li>Start at the Freedom Monument, walk south into the Old Town past the Powder Tower.</li>
<li>Cathedral Square, House of the Blackheads, the Three Brothers, Riga Castle from the outside.</li>
<li>Climb the St Peter&rsquo;s Church tower for the best panorama of the city.</li>
<li>Lunch at the Central Market (technically just outside the Old Town walls but a 5-minute walk south).</li>
<li>Walk back through the Old Town in the late afternoon when the light is golden and the day-trippers are leaving.</li>
</ul>
<p>The rest of this guide is the longer version, with the practical things travellers ask me about: the best walking routes, where to actually eat, what to skip, how to avoid the bar scams, and what changes in winter. If you want broader Riga planning, see the <a href="planning-first-48-hours-in-riga.html">48-hour Riga planning piece</a>; for food specifically, the <a href="latvian-food-honest-guide.html">Latvian food guide</a> is the deeper read.</p>

<h2>How big is the Old Town, and how to think about its layout</h2>
<p>Vecrīga is roughly L-shaped, bounded by the Daugava river to the west and the Pilsētas Kanāls (a curving canal that was once the city moat) to the east. From the Freedom Monument at the northern edge to St Peter&rsquo;s Church at the southern edge is a 15-minute slow walk. From the river edge to the canal is a 10-minute walk. You cannot get truly lost; if in doubt, walk towards the spires (St Peter&rsquo;s, the Cathedral, St Jacob&rsquo;s) or towards the river.</p>
<p>The Old Town breaks down into four loose neighbourhoods that locals don&rsquo;t name but which the visitor will feel:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The Cathedral quarter</strong> in the north-centre, around Doma laukums (Cathedral Square). This is the most photographed area, the most crowded in summer, and the most architecturally layered. Expect tourist crowds 11 AM to 4 PM in season.</li>
<li><strong>The Town Hall and Blackheads quarter</strong> in the south-west, around Rātslaukums (Town Hall Square). Home to the famous reconstructed House of the Blackheads, the statue of Roland, and Riga&rsquo;s most-photographed building.</li>
<li><strong>The Convent quarter</strong> in the east-centre, behind the Cathedral, full of small lanes and quiet small restaurants. The best evening dining is here.</li>
<li><strong>The Castle quarter</strong> in the north-west, towards the river, where Riga Castle (the President&rsquo;s residence) sits. Quietest area; nice late-afternoon walk along the Daugava.</li>
</ul>

<h2>The headline things to see</h2>

<h3>The Cathedral and Cathedral Square (Doma baznīca)</h3>
<p>Riga Cathedral is the oldest medieval building in the Baltic states still in use, founded in 1211, expanded over six centuries. The interior is more austere than you might expect (the Reformation stripped most of the original Catholic decoration in 1524), but the famous attraction is the organ — built in 1884 by Walcker of Ludwigsburg, with 6,718 pipes, one of the largest in the world. Lunchtime organ recitals run several times a week; check the schedule on the door. Cathedral Square outside is the best place in Riga for a coffee and people-watching. <em><a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Full deep dive on Riga Cathedral →</a></em></p>

<h3>St Peter&rsquo;s Church and the tower (Sv. Pētera baznīca)</h3>
<p>The most distinctive Old Town landmark — a red-brick Gothic church first mentioned in 1209, with a 123-metre tower that is the city&rsquo;s defining silhouette. The tower was destroyed twice (lightning in 1721, German artillery in 1941) and most recently rebuilt in concrete-and-steel in 1973, but the lift to the viewing platform takes you up in two stages and the panorama is the best in the city. You can see the entire Old Town in red rooftops, the curve of the Daugava, the Art Nouveau quarter to the north, and on a clear day all the way to Jūrmala on the coast. Tickets are around &euro;9, no need to book ahead. Best at golden hour (one hour before sunset). <em><a href="st-peters-church-tower-riga.html">Full deep dive on St Peter&rsquo;s tower →</a></em></p>

<h3>The House of the Blackheads (Melngalvju nams)</h3>
<p>The most photographed building in Riga, on Rātslaukums. The original was built in 1334 for the Brotherhood of Blackheads (an unmarried German merchants&rsquo; guild), destroyed by Soviet shelling in 1941, and meticulously reconstructed between 1995 and 1999 using historical drawings. The exterior is an absurdly elaborate Dutch Renaissance facade in red, gold, and white. The interior is a museum and event space; worth a visit if you have time. The square it stands on holds the Christmas market in December and is where most of Riga&rsquo;s public events happen. <em><a href="house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html">Full deep dive on the House of the Blackheads →</a></em></p>

<h3>The Three Brothers (Trīs brāļi)</h3>
<p>Three medieval houses standing side by side at Mazā Pils iela 17, 19, and 21. The oldest (number 17) is the oldest stone dwelling house in Riga, dating to around 1490. The middle (number 19) is from the 17th century. The youngest (number 21) is from the late 17th century. Each has a different facade, and together they form one of the most photographed corners of the Old Town. The middle house contains the small Latvian Museum of Architecture; even if you don&rsquo;t go in, the courtyard behind is open and worth a look. <em><a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Full deep dive on the Three Brothers →</a></em></p>

<h3>Riga Castle (Rīgas pils)</h3>
<p>On the riverfront at the north-western edge of the Old Town. Built in 1330 by the Livonian Order, expanded by successive rulers, and now the official residence of the President of Latvia. You cannot tour the interior (it&rsquo;s a working presidential office), but the exterior is impressive in late-afternoon light and the riverside walk along the Daugava in front of it is one of the prettiest short walks in Riga. <em><a href="riga-castle-rigas-pils.html">Full deep dive on Riga Castle →</a></em></p>

<h3>The Powder Tower (Pulvertornis)</h3>
<p>The only surviving tower of the medieval city walls. Now houses the Latvian War Museum, which is free, well-curated, and a quietly excellent overview of Latvia&rsquo;s 20th-century military history (the World Wars, the Soviet occupations, the road to independence). Allow an hour. Worth it even if military history isn&rsquo;t your usual interest. <em><a href="powder-tower-war-museum-riga.html">Full deep dive on the Powder Tower &amp; War Museum →</a></em></p>

<h3>The Swedish Gate (Zviedru vārti)</h3>
<p>The only surviving city gate, cut through the medieval wall in 1698 during the Swedish period to give one merchant private access to his warehouse outside the walls. Tiny, easy to miss, on Torņa iela. The narrow lane on both sides of the gate (Torņa iela) is one of the best preserved medieval streets in the Old Town. <em><a href="swedish-gate-zviedru-varti.html">Full deep dive on the Swedish Gate →</a></em></p>

<h3>St Jacob&rsquo;s Cathedral (Sv. Jēkaba katedrāle)</h3>
<p>The Catholic cathedral of Riga, smaller and quieter than the Lutheran Doma baznīca. Sits beside the Latvian Parliament building (the Saeima). Worth a stop for the contrast — austere Gothic exterior, gilded Baroque interior, very different from the Lutheran cathedrals around it. <em><a href="st-james-cathedral-riga.html">Full deep dive on St James&rsquo;s Cathedral →</a></em></p>

<h3>The Freedom Monument (Brīvības piemineklis)</h3>
<p>At the eastern edge of the Old Town, where Brīvības iela crosses the canal. A 42-metre limestone column from 1935, designed by Kārlis Zāle, with a copper figure of a woman (Milda) holding three gold-plated stars representing Latvia&rsquo;s three historic regions. Built entirely from public donations during Latvia&rsquo;s first independence; survived the Soviet occupation; still the centre of every state ceremony, protest, and quiet flower-laying. The Honour Guard ceremony runs daily in the warm months. <em><a href="freedom-monument-riga-milda.html">Full deep dive on the Freedom Monument →</a></em></p>

<h3>The Cat House (Kaķu nams)</h3>
<p>A yellow Art Nouveau building on Meistaru iela with two black bronze cats on the roof. The story (depending on which version a guide tells you): the merchant who built the house was refused membership of the Great Guild across the street, so he placed the cats on his roof with their tails turned towards the Guild&rsquo;s windows in protest. The Guild eventually relented, the cats were turned around to face the building properly, and everyone got along. A small thing, but every Old Town walk passes it and every Latvian knows the story. <em><a href="cat-house-riga-meistaru.html">Full deep dive on the Cat House →</a></em></p>

<h3>V&#275;rmanes d&#257;rzs &mdash; Riga&rsquo;s oldest park</h3>
<p>Just east of the Freedom Monument, in the Quiet Centre, is V&#275;rmanes d&#257;rzs &mdash; Riga&rsquo;s oldest public park, founded 1817. Not on the standard Old Town route, but the right place to sit for twenty minutes between sights, especially in May when the Japanese cherries are out and the city decides summer has begun. <em><a href="vermanes-darzs-merkela-park-riga.html">Full deep dive on V&#275;rmanes d&#257;rzs →</a></em></p>

<h2>Three walking routes, depending on how much time you have</h2>

<h3>The 1-hour highlights walk</h3>
<p>Start at the Freedom Monument. Walk south down Brīvības iela into the Old Town. Powder Tower (look at the cannonball still embedded in the wall). Pop into the War Museum if you have 30 minutes; otherwise continue along Torņa iela, through the Swedish Gate, past the Three Brothers, to the Cathedral. Quick walk around Cathedral Square. South down Šķūņu iela to the Cat House on Meistaru. South-west to Town Hall Square and the House of the Blackheads. End at St Peter&rsquo;s tower (the lift up is worth the &euro;9 even if you&rsquo;re short on time). About 2 km of walking in total.</p>

<h3>The half-day slow walk (3-4 hours)</h3>
<p>Same route as above, plus: 30 minutes inside Riga Cathedral (try to time it for an organ recital), 30 minutes in the small Museum of the Occupation of Latvia near Town Hall Square (which covers the Soviet and Nazi occupations and is short, sharp, and important context), and a coffee in one of the cafés on Mazā Pils iela near the Three Brothers. Add a 20-minute walk down to the river along Pils iela, past Riga Castle, for the Daugava view.</p>

<h3>The full-day slow walk (with lunch and detours)</h3>
<p>Morning: the half-day walk above, ending at the Central Market for lunch (graze across the five Zeppelin-hangar food halls, 90 minutes is plenty). Afternoon: walk back into the Old Town and lose yourself in the small lanes behind the Cathedral and around the Convent Yard (Konventa sēta) — the prettiest, quietest part of the Old Town and the area where most travellers don&rsquo;t go. End at St Peter&rsquo;s tower at golden hour (90 minutes before sunset). Dinner in one of the Convent quarter restaurants.</p>

<h2>Where to actually eat in the Old Town</h2>
<p>This is the section where I have the most opinions. The Old Town has roughly 200 restaurants and cafés, most clustered along Kaļķu iela (the main pedestrian street) and around Cathedral and Town Hall Squares. As a rule, the more aggressively a restaurant&rsquo;s menu is shouted at you in five languages from the street, the worse the food and the higher the price. Walk one street back from the busiest tourist arteries and the quality goes up sharply.</p>
<p>Specific recommendations:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Vincents</strong> &mdash; the most ambitious modern Latvian restaurant in Riga, on the edge of the Old Town. Tasting menu around &euro;75&ndash;90 per person, &agrave; la carte from &euro;40. Reservations needed.</li>
<li><strong>Bibliotēka N&deg;1</strong> &mdash; modern Latvian, relaxed, excellent wine list, around &euro;35&ndash;50 per person. On Tērbatas (just outside the Old Town to the north).</li>
<li><strong>3 Pavāru Restorāns</strong> &mdash; the chef-led tasting menu option that locals know about. &euro;60&ndash;80 per person, open kitchen, around 12 seats.</li>
<li><strong>Folkklubs Ala Pagrabs</strong> &mdash; cellar tavern off Peldu iela, traditional Latvian dishes done well, very Latvian crowd, live folk music some evenings. The honest, casual end of the spectrum, around &euro;15&ndash;25 per person with a beer.</li>
<li><strong>Riga Central Market</strong> &mdash; not in the Old Town strictly but a 5-minute walk south. The single best food experience in Riga. Lunch for two for &euro;15&ndash;20 across the food halls.</li>
<li><strong>Lido (Vērmanes Garden branch)</strong> &mdash; the Latvian self-service chain, classic dishes done properly at &euro;8&ndash;15 per plate. A few minutes&rsquo; walk from the Old Town along Elizabetes iela.</li>
</ul>

<h2>What to skip and what to watch out for</h2>
<p>Three honest warnings.</p>
<p><strong>Skip the medieval-themed tourist restaurants</strong> with serving staff in costume and "wild boar" on the menu. The food is mediocre, the prices are double the local equivalent, and the "authentic medieval Latvian recipe" is invented for tourists. You&rsquo;ll spot them on Kaļķu iela and around the Town Hall Square.</p>
<p><strong>The Kaļķu iela bar scam</strong>. This is the long-standing one: an attractive young woman approaches a male tourist (often a solo traveller or a stag party) on the street and invites him to a "great bar" she knows nearby. Once inside the bar, the drinks bill becomes &euro;200&ndash;500 instead of the &euro;20 it should be, and large bouncers explain that yes, this is the bill. The scam still operates. The rule: do not follow strangers from the street into bars you have not chosen yourself. If you want a drink, walk into a place that obviously has locals in it.</p>
<p><strong>Old Town nightlife on weekend evenings can attract loud stag-party groups</strong>, mostly British. Some streets (especially Kaļķu and parts of Tirgoņu) get rowdy after 10 PM on Friday and Saturday. If this isn&rsquo;t your scene, the Convent quarter and the area around Cathedral Square stay calm.</p>

<h2>The Old Town in different seasons</h2>

<h3>Summer (June&ndash;August)</h3>
<p>Long days (sunset around 10:30 PM in late June), warm weather, packed cafés and outdoor seating in every square. Cruise day-trippers flood in mid-morning and leave by mid-afternoon, so early mornings (before 9 AM) and evenings are when the Old Town is at its best. Midsummer (Jāņi, June 23&ndash;24) sees the city largely empty out as Latvians head to the countryside for the festival; restaurants run reduced hours.</p>

<h3>Autumn (September&ndash;October)</h3>
<p>The best season for Old Town walking. Cool weather, golden light on the red brickwork, fewer tourists, restaurants properly themselves again. Pierogi season at the bakeries. The mushroom-foraging cult in full swing in the surrounding forests &mdash; many restaurants put fresh chanterelles on the menu.</p>

<h3>Winter (November&ndash;February)</h3>
<p>Short days (sunrise 9 AM, sunset 4 PM in December), cold (often -5&deg;C to -15&deg;C), and properly atmospheric &mdash; the Old Town in snow with the Christmas lights up is one of Northern Europe&rsquo;s best winter sights. The Christmas market on Cathedral Square runs late November to early January and was voted third best in Europe for 2025&ndash;2026. Hotel prices are at their lowest and restaurants are full of locals rather than tourists. See the <a href="riga-in-winter.html">Riga in Winter post</a> for the deeper take.</p>

<h3>Spring (March&ndash;May)</h3>
<p>The shoulder season. March is still cold and grey; by mid-April the city is properly warm and the cafés put their outdoor seating back. May is excellent &mdash; long days returning, blossom in the parks, summer prices not yet kicked in. The first proper week of Old Town terrace-drinking is usually the second week of May.</p>

<h2>Where to stay in the Old Town</h2>
<p>The Old Town has roughly 30 hotels, ranging from &euro;60-a-night guesthouses to &euro;400 boutique places. Three honest categorisations:</p>
<p><strong>Quiet, central, mid-range:</strong> Neiburgs Hotel (a beautiful Art Nouveau-revival building), Hotel Justus (small, family-run, in a 16th-century merchant&rsquo;s house), Dome Hotel (on Cathedral Square, 5-star, romantic).</p>
<p><strong>Boutique with character:</strong> Pullman Riga Old Town, Wellton Old Riga Palace, Konventa S&#275;ta (in the historic Convent Yard).</p>
<p><strong>What to avoid:</strong> the budget hotels along Kaļķu iela (above the noisiest bars). The room is fine; the noise after 11 PM on a Friday is not.</p>
<p>If you&rsquo;re here for more than three nights and want quiet without sacrificing walkability, the Quiet Centre (Klusais centrs) just north of the Old Town &mdash; around Elizabetes, Antonijas, Strēlnieku &mdash; is the better choice. Equally beautiful Art Nouveau buildings, much less weekend nightlife noise, 10-minute walk into the Old Town.</p>

<h2>Practical things travellers ask about Old Town Riga</h2>

<h3>How to get there from the airport</h3>
<p>Bus 22 from Riga Airport runs to the city centre every 10&ndash;30 minutes, &euro;2 from the kiosk and &euro;3 from the driver, terminating at the central market and the Old Town. Bolt (the local taxi app) costs &euro;10&ndash;15 to anywhere in the Old Town and is the easiest option with luggage. Avoid unmarked "helpers" offering rides in arrivals &mdash; the one consistent airport scam.</p>

<h3>Cobblestones, mobility, and accessibility</h3>
<p>The Old Town is genuinely cobblestoned, almost throughout. This is part of its character but is also a real challenge for wheelchairs, mobility aids, pushchairs, and high heels. Some streets (Kaļķu iela, around Cathedral Square) have smoother paving; others (the lanes around the Three Brothers and Swedish Gate) are aggressively medieval. If you have specific mobility needs, the Quiet Centre and the area around Vērmanes Garden are easier to navigate than the Old Town interior.</p>

<h3>Public transport in and around the Old Town</h3>
<p>The Old Town itself is small enough to walk; you don&rsquo;t need transport inside it. Trams, trolleybuses, and city buses skirt the Old Town perimeter. The most useful stops for visitors: Stacijas Laukums (Central Station, also Central Market) at the south, Brīvības Piemineklis (Freedom Monument) at the north. A single ticket is &euro;1.50 from the Mobilly app or kiosks, &euro;2 from the driver. The Mobilly app is genuinely the best way to pay for any urban transport in Latvia.</p>

<h3>Cash, cards, and tipping in the Old Town</h3>
<p>Contactless payment is accepted essentially everywhere &mdash; restaurants, cafés, supermarkets, taxis. You can have a perfectly normal week in the Old Town without drawing cash. Tipping is not the American 20% &mdash; 5 to 10% for good restaurant service is generous and appreciated; round up taxi fares; small change for a coffee. Service workers are properly paid here.</p>

<h3>Public toilets</h3>
<p>Sparse and often pay-to-enter (&euro;0.50&ndash;&euro;1). The reliable ones: at the Central Market, at the Riga Central Station, in the larger cafés around Cathedral Square (free if you&rsquo;ve bought a coffee), and in any of the larger hotels (their lobby toilets are accessible without a room key). McDonald&rsquo;s on Kaļķu iela has free clean toilets if all else fails.</p>

<h2>What the Old Town is, and isn&rsquo;t</h2>
<p>One last honest thing, because this guide has been long. Riga Old Town is not Tallinn. It is not a perfectly preserved single-era medieval set-piece. It is a layered, lived-in, working European old town &mdash; medieval bones, Hanseatic merchant houses, Tsarist-era boulevards bordering it, Art Nouveau just outside the walls, Soviet-era reconstructions sitting alongside genuine 14th-century stonework. The result is messier and more interesting than Tallinn&rsquo;s, but it doesn&rsquo;t deliver the single Disney-photograph moment some visitors expect.</p>
<p>What it does deliver, if you walk it slowly, is a Northern European capital that is still small, still affordable, still real, with proper food, proper culture, and a working population that lives and works inside the medieval walls. That&rsquo;s the version most travellers come home talking about, and it&rsquo;s why we built this whole business around it.</p>

House of the Blackheads in late afternoon when the gold ornament catches the sun.</p>

            <p>Yes but they&rsquo;re sparse and usually pay-to-enter (€0.50&ndash;€1). Reliable ones: the Central Market (just south of the Old Town), the Central Station, the larger cafés around Cathedral Square (free if you buy a coffee), and the lobby toilets of the larger hotels. The McDonald&rsquo;s on Kaļķu iela has free clean toilets if all else fails.</p>

        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-is-the-latvian-war-museum-worth-visiting-19">
            Is the Latvian War Museum worth visiting?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-is-the-latvian-war-museum-worth-visiting-19" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, especially if you have an hour. Housed in the medieval Powder Tower at the northern edge of the Old Town. Free entry. The exhibition is well-curated and covers Latvia&rsquo;s 20th-century military history &mdash; both World Wars, the Soviet and Nazi occupations, and the road to independence. Even visitors who aren&rsquo;t usually into military history come out saying it gave them important context for understanding modern Latvia.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-what-s-the-difference-between-the-old-to-20">
            What&rsquo;s the difference between the Old Town and the Quiet Centre?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-what-s-the-difference-between-the-old-to-20" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>The Old Town (Vecrīga) is the medieval and Hanseatic core inside the former city walls &mdash; cobblestones, narrow lanes, the famous sights. The Quiet Centre (Klusais centrs) is the elegant Art Nouveau district just north of the Old Town, built between 1900 and 1914. It&rsquo;s the part of Riga with the densest concentration of Jugendstil buildings (over 800), with wider streets, less tourist traffic, and Alberta iela as its photography hotspot. For a 48-hour visit, the Quiet Centre is one of the four headline experiences and a 10-minute walk from the Old Town.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-when-is-riga-old-town-busiest-21">
            When is Riga Old Town busiest?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-when-is-riga-old-town-busiest-21" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>July and August between 11 AM and 4 PM &mdash; peak summer plus peak cruise day-trip hours. The Christmas market period (late November to early January) is also busy at weekends. Quietest times: weekday mornings before 9 AM in any season, late autumn (October&ndash;November), and February. The shoulder weeks of May and September are the sweet spot &mdash; pleasant weather, full restaurant operation, lighter crowds.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-is-riga-old-town-worth-visiting-in-winte-22">
            Is Riga Old Town worth visiting in winter?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-is-riga-old-town-worth-visiting-in-winte-22" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, properly. The Old Town in snow with the Christmas lights up is one of Northern Europe&rsquo;s best winter sights. December has the famous market, lower hotel prices, and a city that&rsquo;s full of locals rather than tourists. The downside is short days (sunrise 9 AM, sunset 4 PM) and cold weather (-5°C to -15°C). January and February are the quietest months &mdash; atmospheric, very cheap, and the Old Town all to yourself. See the Riga in Winter post for the deeper take.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-can-i-see-all-of-riga-old-town-in-one-da-23">
            Can I see all of Riga Old Town in one day?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-can-i-see-all-of-riga-old-town-in-one-da-23" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, comfortably &mdash; Vecrīga is small enough to walk in one day even at a slow pace, with proper time for the headline sights, a long lunch, and an hour or two of just wandering. The full-day walking route (highlights walk plus the Convent quarter and a Central Market lunch) is roughly 4 km of total walking spread over 6&ndash;8 hours, with plenty of café stops. Two days lets you add the Cathedral interior, the Latvian War Museum, the Museum of Occupation, and the Daugava riverfront walk.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-where-should-i-stay-in-or-near-the-old-t-24">
            Where should I stay in or near the Old Town?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-where-should-i-stay-in-or-near-the-old-t-24" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Three honest categories. For mid-range with character in the Old Town itself: Neiburgs Hotel (Art Nouveau revival), Hotel Justus (16th-century merchant house, family-run), Dome Hotel (5-star on Cathedral Square). For boutique with proper history: Konventa Sēta in the Convent Yard. For quiet without sacrificing walkability, the Quiet Centre just north of the Old Town (around Elizabetes, Antonijas, Strēlnieku) is genuinely the better choice for stays of 3+ nights &mdash; equally beautiful buildings, much less weekend nightlife noise, 10-minute walk in. Avoid the budget hotels on Kaļķu iela above the noisiest bars.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-oldtown-is-riga-old-town-like-tallinn-old-town-25">
            Is Riga Old Town like Tallinn Old Town?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-oldtown-is-riga-old-town-like-tallinn-old-town-25" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Different cities, different feels. Tallinn Old Town (113 hectares) is smaller, more perfectly preserved, more single-era medieval &mdash; the Disney-postcard version of a Hanseatic old town. Riga Old Town (438 hectares) is bigger, more layered, more lived-in &mdash; medieval bones, Hanseatic merchant houses, Soviet-era reconstructions, all sitting alongside genuine 14th-century stonework. Tallinn delivers the single perfect photograph; Riga delivers a working European capital that&rsquo;s still affordable and still real. Most travellers who visit both end up preferring Riga for its scale and its food, and Tallinn for its medieval atmosphere. The Riga vs Tallinn vs Vilnius post on this blog covers the comparison in detail.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
</div>

## Riga's TV Tower: The Tallest Free-Standing Building in the EU

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/riga-tv-tower-tallest-eu.html
**Published:** 2026-04-30
**Summary:** At 368.5 m, Riga's TV Tower is the tallest free-standing structure in the European Union — taller than the Eiffel Tower. The history, the design, and how to visit.

<p class="article-lede">If you stand on the Stone Bridge in Riga and look downriver, your eye is pulled, almost involuntarily, to a strange three-legged silver spire rising out of an island in the middle of the Daugava. It does not look quite like anything else in the city. It does not look quite like anything else in the European Union, in fact &mdash; and there is a good reason for that.</p>
<!-- BEGIN: tvtower-hero -->

<figure class="tv-hero">
  <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-tv-tower/riga-tv-tower-368m-tallest-free-standing-eu-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="tvtower-hero" data-caption="Riga&#x27;s TV Tower on Zaķusala island, in the middle of the Daugava river. At 368.5 m it has been the tallest free-standing structure in the EU since the day it opened in 1986 — and remains so today, taller than the Eiffel Tower (330 m)." aria-label="Open full-size: Riga&#x27;s TV Tower on Zaķusala island, in the middle of the Daugava river. At 368.5 m it has been the tallest free-standing structure in the EU since the day it opened in 1986 — and remains so today, taller than the Eiffel Tower (330 m).">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-tv-tower/riga-tv-tower-368m-tallest-free-standing-eu-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-tv-tower/riga-tv-tower-368m-tallest-free-standing-eu-latvia.jpg" alt="Riga TV Tower — red-and-white triangular tower against blue sky." loading="eager" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1067" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Riga&#x27;s TV Tower on Zaķusala island, in the middle of the Daugava river. At 368.5 m it has been the tallest free-standing structure in the EU since the day it opened in 1986 — and remains so today, taller than the Eiffel Tower (330 m).</figcaption>
</figure>
<!-- END: tvtower-hero -->


<p>This is the <strong>Riga Radio and TV Tower</strong> &mdash; <em>R&#299;gas radio un telev&#299;zijas tornis</em> &mdash; and at <strong>368.5 metres</strong>, it is <strong>the tallest free-standing structure in the European Union</strong>. It has held that title for over twenty years, since Latvia joined the EU in 2004, and despite a wave of skyscraper-building in Warsaw, Frankfurt and Madrid in the last decade, nobody has come close to overtaking it.</p>

<p>It is also a building that almost no visitor to Riga knows the real story of. So this is a long-form guide for those who want it.</p>

<h2 id="context">How tall is tall? The numbers in context</h2>

<p>Towers are measured differently from buildings. A <strong>building</strong> has habitable floors with people working in them. A <strong>free-standing tower</strong> is a structure that supports itself without guy wires (so a guyed mast &mdash; the kind held up by cables &mdash; does not count). The Riga TV Tower is a true free-standing structure: three concrete-and-steel legs splay outward at the base and meet again at 88 metres up, then carry the central shaft and antenna mast skyward without any external support. It can withstand winds of 44 metres per second &mdash; about 160 km/h, full hurricane force &mdash; without noticeable vibration at the top.</p>

<p>To give you a sense of scale, here is how Riga&rsquo;s tower compares to other notable European structures.</p>

<table>
<thead>
<tr><th>Structure</th><th>Location</th><th>Height</th><th>Notes</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Ostankino Tower</td><td>Moscow, Russia</td><td>540 m</td><td>Tallest free-standing structure in Europe overall (outside the EU)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Kyiv TV Tower</td><td>Kyiv, Ukraine</td><td>385 m</td><td>Second-tallest in Europe (a guyed lattice tower)</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Riga Radio and TV Tower</strong></td><td><strong>Riga, Latvia</strong></td><td><strong>368.5 m</strong></td><td><strong>Tallest free-standing structure in the EU</strong></td></tr>
<tr><td>Berlin TV Tower (<em>Fernsehturm</em>)</td><td>Berlin, Germany</td><td>368 m</td><td>Half a metre shorter than Riga</td></tr>
<tr><td>Eiffel Tower</td><td>Paris, France</td><td>330 m (with antenna)</td><td>40+ metres shorter than Riga</td></tr>
<tr><td>Varso Tower</td><td>Warsaw, Poland</td><td>310 m</td><td>Tallest <em>habitable building</em> in the EU (since 2022)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Commerzbank Tower</td><td>Frankfurt, Germany</td><td>259 m</td><td>Was the tallest <em>building</em> in the EU before Varso</td></tr>
<tr><td>The Shard</td><td>London, UK</td><td>309 m</td><td>Tallest in the UK; not in the EU</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p>A few things are worth noticing in this table.</p>

<p>First, the Eiffel Tower &mdash; the structure most people instinctively think of as Europe&rsquo;s tall tower &mdash; is <strong>almost forty-five metres shorter than the Riga TV Tower</strong>. It is also much further south, in a much more famous city, and almost nobody outside Latvia realises that the Eiffel Tower has been outclassed in height since 1989 by a tower on a Latvian river island.</p>

<p>Second, the Berlin Fernsehturm &mdash; which has been the icon of East Berlin for sixty years and is featured on a million postcards &mdash; is <strong>half a metre shorter</strong> than Riga&rsquo;s tower. Half a metre. The two are essentially the same height, but Berlin gets the recognition.</p>

<p>Third, the Varso Tower in Warsaw, completed in 2022, is the EU&rsquo;s tallest <em>building</em> &mdash; but a building and a tower are different categories. Even fully built, Varso is <strong>almost sixty metres shorter</strong> than the Riga TV Tower. The Riga tower has held its title for so long because nobody else in the EU is in the business of building radio masts that tall any more &mdash; terrestrial broadcasting is a Soviet-era ambition that the EU&rsquo;s western half largely skipped.</p>

<p>Globally, the tower currently sits at around the <strong>fifteenth-tallest free-standing tower in the world</strong>, and the <strong>third-tallest in Europe</strong> as a whole, behind only Moscow&rsquo;s Ostankino and Kyiv&rsquo;s TV tower.</p>

<h2 id="architecture">The architecture: a tripod from the late Soviet imagination</h2>

<p>The Riga TV Tower was built between <strong>1979 and 1989</strong>, with money from the central Soviet government in Moscow. It was finished just months before the Soviet Union began to come apart. In some sense, it is a Soviet building that was never meant to be a Latvian one &mdash; and yet it has become, against all expectation, one of the things Latvians are quietly proud of.</p>

<p>The architecture is unusual enough that the tower stands out even among Soviet-era radio towers. It belongs to a small family of late-Soviet <strong>tripod towers</strong> &mdash; designed with three load-bearing legs rather than the more common single shaft. There are only two other &ldquo;tall&rdquo; towers like this in the world: the <strong>&#381;i&#382;kov Television Tower</strong> in Prague (1985&ndash;1992) and the <strong>Avala Tower</strong> in Belgrade (originally built 1965, destroyed by NATO bombing in 1999, rebuilt 2010). Riga&rsquo;s is the tallest of the three.</p>

<p>Here is roughly how the tower is put together, from bottom to top:</p>

<p>The <strong>base section</strong> rises the first 88 metres and is the most distinctive part of the structure. It comprises three curved legs &mdash; really, three enormous reinforced-concrete pillars &mdash; splayed out at the bottom and converging higher up. Two of the pillars contain <strong>inclined high-speed lifts</strong> (running on rails, much like a funicular) that climb the slope of the leg in roughly 42 seconds. The third pillar contains the staircase and technical rooms. This sloping-elevator system was unusual for its time and is part of why engineers from across the Soviet bloc came to study the building.</p>

<p>The <strong>middle section</strong>, from 88 to 222 metres, is a cylindrical shaft clad in <strong>COR-TEN steel</strong> &mdash; that distinctive rust-coloured weathering steel that develops a stable patina over time and protects itself from further corrosion. (American architects on the same continent &mdash; Eero Saarinen, who Gun&#257;rs Birkerts of National Library fame worked under, was an early adopter &mdash; were using the same material around the same time. Late-Soviet architecture was much more in dialogue with Western modernism than Cold War mythology suggests.)</p>

<p>The <strong>top section</strong>, from 222 to 368 metres, is the slim antenna spire that gives the tower its broadcasting function. The Soviet engineers used a clever construction trick here: rather than build the spire upwards in the normal way, they assembled it <strong>from the top down</strong>. The very tip was put together first, fixed between three partially completed legs, and then jacked up incrementally as new sections were welded on below it. The antenna effectively grew downwards. This was necessary because the tower cranes available at the time could only reach about 107 metres &mdash; far short of the spire&rsquo;s eventual height.</p>

<p>The foundation goes 27 metres into the bedrock of Za&#311;usala island, with the base itself sitting about 7 metres above mean sea level. A particular detail that engineers love: because of Riga&rsquo;s enormous temperature swings &mdash; over 65 degrees Celsius from the coldest winter day to the hottest summer day, recorded in 2010 &mdash; the very tip of the antenna can move as much as <strong>2.4 metres</strong> sideways through thermal expansion alone. The structure is engineered to sway with it.</p>

<p>The <strong>observation level</strong> &mdash; when it is open to the public &mdash; sits at <strong>97 metres</strong>, just above where the <em>V&#275;ja roze</em> (&ldquo;Wind Rose&rdquo;) restaurant used to operate from 1989 until it closed in 2006. The original observation deck has never been one of those vertigo-inducing glass-floor European viewpoints; it was a Soviet-era technical building first and a tourist destination second. But on a clear day it offers a view that reaches as far as <strong>fifty kilometres</strong> &mdash; across the whole of Riga, the Daugava and its bridges, out to the Gulf of Riga, and on the rare clearest days even as far as Sigulda inland. (See the <strong>practical note</strong> at the end of this article &mdash; the tower is currently closed for renovation.)</p>

<h2 id="1991">January 1991: the night the country could have lost it</h2>

<p>This is the part of the tower&rsquo;s story that does not appear in tourist brochures, but that no Latvian who lived through it has forgotten.</p>

<p>To understand what happened around the TV Tower in January 1991, you have to understand what was happening in the Soviet Union at the time. By late 1990, the Soviet Union was visibly coming apart at the seams. Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia &mdash; which had been forcibly absorbed into the USSR in 1940 &mdash; had already begun the process of declaring restored independence. Latvia had passed its <strong>Declaration on the Restoration of Independence</strong> on 4 May 1990. The Latvian government, the <em>Augst&#257;k&#257; Padome</em> (Supreme Council), was operating in Riga as if the country were already free. Moscow refused to accept this.</p>

<p>In Moscow, hardline elements within the Soviet state began to plan a forceful response. The plan, in essence, was simple: take control of the <strong>strategic infrastructure</strong> of each Baltic capital &mdash; the parliament, the broadcasting facilities, the international telephone exchange, the bridges &mdash; and from those buildings, declare that legitimate Soviet rule had been restored. If you control the radio and television, you control the narrative; if you control the parliament and the telephone exchange, you control the apparatus of government.</p>

<p>The instrument for this in the Baltics was the Soviet <strong>OMON</strong> &mdash; <em>Otrjad militsii osobogo nazna&#269;enija</em>, &ldquo;special-purpose police detachment.&rdquo; Riga had its own OMON unit, originally established as part of the Latvian Soviet militia, which by late 1990 had defected to Moscow&rsquo;s side and refused to take orders from the Latvian government. They were heavily armed, well organised, and willing to use force. They had already seized the Latvian national printing house &mdash; the <em>Preses Nams</em> &mdash; on 2 January 1991.</p>

<p>Then, on the night of <strong>13 January 1991</strong>, the situation in neighbouring Lithuania exploded. Soviet troops &mdash; some of them from the elite Alpha special forces unit &mdash; stormed the <strong>Vilnius TV Tower</strong>. They used tanks. They drove through unarmed civilians who had gathered to defend the building. <strong>Thirteen Lithuanian civilians were killed and over 140 wounded.</strong> A young woman named Loreta Asanavi&#269;i&#363;t&#279;, a 24-year-old seamstress, was crushed under a tank.</p>

<p>In Riga, the news arrived overnight. Nobody slept.</p>

<p>The next morning, <strong>13 January 1991</strong>, the Latvian Popular Front &mdash; the political movement that had led the country towards independence &mdash; called the population to Dome Square in the Old Town. By midday, around <strong>half a million people</strong> had gathered along the Daugava embankment, in a country with a total population of about 2.6 million. (Some accounts put the eventual barricade participants closer to 700,000 once you count people from outside Riga who came in to defend their capital &mdash; roughly <strong>one third of the entire population of Latvia</strong>.)</p>

<p>The instructions went out by radio. Build barricades. Defend the strategic objects. Do not give them what they need to take over.</p>

<p>That evening, in temperatures well below freezing, ordinary people &mdash; farmers from the countryside, fishermen from Liep&#257;ja, miners from Latgale, doctors and university students from Riga &mdash; began stacking concrete blocks, milk trucks, logs, lumber, agricultural machinery, and anything else heavy enough to slow down an armoured vehicle, around the buildings that mattered. The list of defended sites was clear:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The <strong>Supreme Council</strong> building in the Old Town (now the Saeima, the Latvian parliament)</li>
  <li>The <strong>Council of Ministers</strong></li>
  <li><strong>Latvian Radio</strong>, in the Old Town near Riga Cathedral</li>
  <li>The <strong>International Telephone Exchange</strong> on Dzirnavu street</li>
  <li>The <strong>bridges across the Daugava</strong></li>
  <li><strong>And the TV Tower on Za&#311;usala.</strong></li>
</ul>

<p>People came to the TV Tower with whatever they had. One man drove a tractor with a snow plough from his collective farm 300 kilometres away and parked it across the access road to the island. Brass bands set up at the foot of the tower and played to keep people warm. There were bonfires on the ice. People played football on the frozen ground at night to keep moving. Around 50,000 active defenders rotated through the barricades over the next two weeks; many more thousands provided food, transport, accordions, blankets, hot tea.</p>

<p>OMON did try to take the TV Tower. They got into the lower floors of the broadcasting building one evening &mdash; which is how Latvia&rsquo;s most famous live-television moment of the period came about. The presenter Velta Puri&#326;a was reading the evening news bulletin live on the <em>Panor&#257;ma</em> programme when she announced, on air, that the ground floor of the building was at that moment being occupied by armed OMON officers and that the broadcast might have to be cut. The technicians in the control room, confronted by armed men, <strong>switched off only the studio monitors</strong> &mdash; and kept the actual broadcast running. The whole country watched in real time as their own television tower was being raided. It was one of those moments where you feel the line between civilian life and history get very thin.</p>

<p>The deadliest violence of the period, however, did not happen at the TV Tower. It happened a few kilometres away in the Old Town, on the night of <strong>20 January 1991</strong>, when OMON forces stormed the <strong>Latvian Ministry of the Interior</strong> near Bastejkalns Park. <strong>Five people were killed</strong>:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Vladimirs Gomanovi&#269;s</strong>, a militia lieutenant</li>
  <li><strong>Sergejs Kononenko</strong>, an internal-affairs department inspector</li>
  <li><strong>Andris Slapi&#326;&#353;</strong>, a documentary cameraman and director of the Riga Film Studio, shot while filming the attack</li>
  <li><strong>Gvido Zvaigzne</strong>, another cameraman, fatally wounded that night and dying of his injuries on 5 February</li>
  <li><strong>Edijs Riekstin&#353;</strong>, a 17-year-old schoolboy who had simply come to see what was happening</li>
</ul>

<p>Slapi&#326;&#353; and Zvaigzne were among the cinematographers documenting the events for the world-renowned Latvian filmmaker <strong>Juris Podnieks</strong>. Their footage &mdash; including the moment they themselves were shot &mdash; survived. A few days earlier, on <strong>16 January</strong>, a young driver named <strong>Roberts M&#363;rnieks</strong> had already been killed by OMON gunfire while approaching a barricade at Vecm&#299;lgr&#257;vis bridge. In all, <strong>six people died</strong> during the Barricades of January 1991. There are small memorial stones today in the canalside park opposite Bastejkalns at the exact spots where each of them fell. If you walk through that park you will see them. Most tourists pass them without noticing.</p>

<p>The barricades stayed in place until 27 January, when most defenders went home. Some of the actual concrete blocks remained on Riga streets until <strong>autumn 1992</strong>.</p>

<p>And the TV Tower stayed in Latvian hands.</p>

<p>When the Soviet coup attempt of August 1991 finally failed in Moscow, Latvia&rsquo;s full independence was confirmed within weeks. <strong>Iceland was the first country in the world to formally recognise the restored Republic of Latvia</strong>, on 22 August 1991. The Soviet Union itself recognised Latvian independence on 6 September. Three months later the USSR no longer existed.</p>

<p>Every year on <strong>20 January</strong>, Latvia marks the <strong>Commemoration Day of the Defenders of the Barricades</strong>. Bonfires are lit at Dome Square in the Old Town and at the foot of the TV Tower on Za&#311;usala &mdash; often by people who were there in 1991, and increasingly now by their grandchildren. If you are in Riga on 20 January, go.</p>

<h2 id="visit">How to visit (and what is and isn&rsquo;t open right now)</h2>

<p>A direct and honest note for visitors: <strong>the observation deck of the TV Tower has been closed to the public since May 2019</strong> for a major renovation project called <strong>TV Tower 2.0</strong>. The reopening date has slipped several times. As of 2026, work is still ongoing, with the eventual scope including a refurbished restaurant at the 100-metre level, new glass observation cubes that will protrude outward at around 100 and 130 metres, an open-air platform with safety harnesses at 220 metres for the genuinely brave, and even a 500-kilogram <strong>Foucault pendulum</strong> in the lobby. When it does reopen, the renovated tower will be one of the more ambitious viewpoint experiences in the Baltics. We will update this article when there is firm news.</p>

<p>But the tower is still extraordinary to visit, even now, from the outside. Here is how.</p>

<h3>Getting to Za&#311;usala island</h3>

<p>The tower stands on <strong>Za&#311;usala</strong> &mdash; <em>Hare Island</em> &mdash; a long, narrow island in the middle of the Daugava, just south of central Riga. The island is reached by the <strong>Salu Bridge</strong> (<em>Salu tilts</em>), which carries traffic and pedestrians over the river.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>By bus or trolleybus</strong> &mdash; the easiest route is to take <strong>bus 17</strong> from central Riga, which crosses the Salu Bridge with a stop close to the tower. The journey from the centre is about 15 minutes.</li>
  <li><strong>By bicycle</strong> &mdash; Riga has expanded its riverbank cycling infrastructure considerably in the last few years. The ride from the Old Town to Za&#311;usala is flat and pleasant, around 4 km.</li>
  <li><strong>On foot</strong> &mdash; about 40-45 minutes from the Old Town, mostly along the riverbank. Best done on a clear day; the views of the tower as you approach are some of the best you can get.</li>
  <li><strong>Taxi or Bolt</strong> &mdash; five to six euros from the centre of the city.</li>
</ul>

<p>There is a small park around the base of the tower with benches and information panels. You can walk right up to the legs of the structure and stand directly under the antenna. Looking straight up the 368-metre shaft from the base is one of those small, weirdly affecting moments &mdash; a pure feat of engineering hovering above your head. Children love this part.</p>

<h3>How long to spend</h3>

<p>If the observation deck is closed (currently the case), plan for <strong>45 minutes to an hour</strong> at the tower itself. Walk around the base, read the small information panels, photograph the structure from a few angles, and look across the river back at the Old Town skyline.</p>

<p>If you combine the tower with the <strong>memorial stones at Bastejkalns</strong> in the Old Town &mdash; the small commemorative markers for the five people killed on 20 January 1991 &mdash; and with the <strong>Museum of the Barricades of 1991</strong> on Kr&#257;mu street near the cathedral, you can build a half-day around the story. We would strongly recommend doing this. The museum is small and free, and the people who run it lived through what is on the walls.</p>

<h3>When the observation deck is open</h3>

<p>When the renovated tower does reopen, the standard visit length will likely be <strong>one to two hours</strong>, including time on the lift, time on the observation deck itself, and time on the planned interpretive exhibits about the tower&rsquo;s history and the events of 1991. In its previous incarnation the tower drew around 20,000 visitors a year &mdash; a number that the renovation is designed to multiply. Expect crowds when it does reopen; book ahead.</p>

<h3 id="view">The view from the tower (when accessible)</h3>

<p>Even from the comparatively modest 97-metre height of the previous observation deck, the panorama covers:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The whole of central Riga, with the spires of St Peter&rsquo;s, the Dome Cathedral and the Castle of Riga clearly visible</li>
  <li>The Daugava and all five of its bridges through central Riga</li>
  <li>The Castle of Light (Latvian National Library), the other great modern structure on the river</li>
  <li>The ribbon of the P&#257;rdaugava neighbourhoods on the left bank</li>
  <li>The Riga Hydroelectric Power Plant about 30 km upriver in Salaspils</li>
  <li>On clear days, the Gulf of Riga to the north and the inland forests stretching towards Sigulda</li>
</ul>

<p>When the new observation cubes at 130 metres open, the view will be roughly equivalent to standing on top of a forty-storey building &mdash; well above anything else in the city.</p>

<h3>What to do nearby while you are on Za&#311;usala</h3>

<p>The island itself is mostly undeveloped: a broad band of riverside green space, walking paths, fishermen on the banks. Locals come here to walk dogs, picnic in summer, ice-fish in winter. There is no caf&eacute; or restaurant directly at the tower (yet &mdash; the renovation will fix this), so plan for either a packed picnic or a coffee in the centre of Riga before or after.</p>

<p>A particularly nice approach: walk from the <strong>Castle of Light</strong> (the Latvian National Library) down the left bank of the Daugava towards Za&#311;usala. It is about 25 minutes on foot along the riverbank and you have the tower in front of you the whole way, with the Old Town spires across the river to your right. On a clear winter evening, with the tower&rsquo;s permanent xenon-light installation lighting the antenna in slowly shifting colours after dark, the walk is one of the more memorable hours in central Riga.</p>

<h2 id="why">Why we tell this story</h2>

<p>There is a particular kind of building you can visit anywhere in Europe: a tall structure with an observation deck, a gift shop, a coffee, a queue, and a panoramic view that looks roughly like all the other panoramic views. The Riga TV Tower is not that. It is a Soviet broadcasting tower that became, accidentally, one of the most important buildings in the modern history of Latvia &mdash; because it stood at the centre of the night when ordinary people decided their country was worth standing in the snow for.</p>

<p>You can see the Eiffel Tower in Paris. You can see the Berlin Fernsehturm. You can go up the Shard. Riga&rsquo;s tower is taller than all of them, but that is not actually why we send people to see it. We send people because of the story it carries.</p>

<p>The architects who designed it never intended it to mean anything except <em>Soviet broadcasting reach across half of Latvia</em>. By an irony of history, in 1991, those broadcasts &mdash; produced by Latvian staff, defended by Latvian citizens &mdash; became one of the most important instruments through which the country told the world it was free. The same building. A different country.</p>

<p>It is the tallest free-standing structure in the European Union. But that is the least interesting thing about it.</p>

<p><em>If you&rsquo;d like to walk Riga&rsquo;s twentieth-century history with us &mdash; the Barricades sites, the TV Tower, Soviet-era apartments, the human stories of Latvian independence &mdash; <a href="/#contact">get in touch</a>. Our small-group tours are designed for travellers who want to understand a place, not just photograph it.</em></p>

## Riga vs Tallinn vs Vilnius: An Honest Comparison

**URL:** https://barefootbaltic.com/blog/riga-vs-tallinn-vs-vilnius.html
**Published:** 2026-04-14
**Summary:** A licensed Latvian guide's honest comparison of Riga, Tallinn, and Vilnius. Which Baltic capital to pick, which does what best, and who each is wrong for.

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<p>If you only have time to visit one Baltic capital, here's my honest take. I live in Riga and run tours here, so take the Riga verdict with a pinch of salt — but I've spent real time in Tallinn and Vilnius and I'll tell you when they genuinely do something better.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pick Tallinn</strong> if you want the best-preserved medieval old town in Europe, you're coming in for a weekend from Helsinki or Stockholm, and you want the fairytale Instagram version of the Baltics.</li>
<li><strong>Pick Riga</strong> if you want the best-value Baltic capital, the most serious Art Nouveau architecture on the continent, the best food scene of the three, and quieter streets. It also has the biggest old town of the three.</li>
<li><strong>Pick Vilnius</strong> if you want baroque Catholicism, the Northern European old town most people haven't heard of, the warmest atmosphere, and the cheapest beer.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>If you have a week, do two or three of them.</strong> They're all within 4 hours of each other by bus, and the differences between them are large enough that seeing two in one trip isn't repetitive — it's how you actually understand the Baltics.</p>
