<h2>How to pick in 30 seconds</h2>
<p>Four questions.</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Is this your first trip to the Baltics, and you have 2–3 nights?</strong> Pick the one closest to your arrival airport. Don't agonise. They're all good.</li>
<li><strong>Do you care more about medieval or modern?</strong> Medieval → Tallinn. Early-20th-century modern (Art Nouveau, post-Soviet renewal) → Riga. Baroque → Vilnius.</li>
<li><strong>Are you on a tight budget?</strong> Vilnius is the cheapest, Riga is second, Tallinn is the most expensive, especially in summer.</li>
<li><strong>Are you combining with Helsinki, St Petersburg (no longer recommended), or Stockholm?</strong> Tallinn is the natural Baltic partner for Finland/Sweden trips. Riga is the most central if you're doing more than one.</li>
</ol>
<h2>Who this piece isn't for</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>People who want a ranking.</strong> There isn't one. These are three genuinely different cities and the "best" one depends on what you like. Anyone who tells you Tallinn beats Riga beats Vilnius in some absolute sense is either a tourist board or lazy.</li>
<li><strong>People who want to do all three in 48 hours.</strong> It's physically possible but you'll spend more time on buses than in old towns. Minimum time for the three-capital run is 6 days, ideally 8–10.</li>
<li><strong>People who hate cities.</strong> The three capitals are the gateway but they're not the whole story. If what you want is forests, coastline, and villages, read my day-trips post instead.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2>Now the longer version</h2>
<p>I'll tell you what each city does best, what each does worst, and when I'd honestly send a visitor to one of the others.</p>
<h3>What Tallinn does best</h3>
<p>Tallinn has the most perfectly preserved medieval old town in Northern Europe, and probably in Europe full stop. The town walls are still there, intact, for most of their length. The Town Hall is the oldest still-functioning one in Northern Europe. Toompea hill gives you the postcard view that everyone who's been to Tallinn has in their phone.</p>
<p>Tallinn is also the best Baltic capital for a short weekend break from a Nordic country. The ferry from Helsinki takes 2 hours and costs €20–60 return. Stockholm is an overnight ferry away. If you're Finnish or Swedish and you want a foreign weekend, Tallinn is closer than anywhere on your own coastline.</p>
<p>Estonia's tech culture — e-Residency, the mobile-first government, the way you can buy a bus ticket by SMS that has worked since 2003 — gives Tallinn a character the other two don't have. There's a real innovation quarter at Telliskivi and Noblessner with craft breweries, restored industrial buildings, and Michelin-starred restaurants. If you want your Baltic weekend to feel like Copenhagen with a medieval core, Tallinn is the pick.</p>
<p>The Estonian sauna culture is also the most developed of the three. A proper smoke sauna experience in Estonia is a genuinely different thing from the hotel-spa version most people know.</p>
<p><strong>What Tallinn does worst.</strong> It's the most expensive of the three and the gap has widened since the Finns replaced the Russians as the dominant visitor group. Old Town restaurants on Raekoja plats charge Helsinki prices and serve Helsinki-adjacent food. The old town itself is tiny (113 hectares) and you can see it all in one long afternoon, which means the "this is too short" feeling hits harder here than in Riga or Vilnius. And because the old town is so concentrated, it's the most touristy of the three — in July you will queue for things.</p>
<h3>What Riga does best</h3>
<p>Riga has the biggest old town of the three at 438 hectares, and it doesn't feel touristy the way Tallinn's can. You can walk from the Freedom Monument to the Daugava without being photographed by a stag party or a bus tour group, which is increasingly rare in European capitals at our price point.</p>
<p>The real Riga advantage is the Art Nouveau district. I've said this in other posts but it bears repeating: Riga has the densest concentration of Art Nouveau architecture of any city in Europe — over 800 buildings, more than half the city's centre. Alberta iela is the street most people photograph, but there are dozens of others. If you care about architecture at all, this is a reason to come to Riga and not to either of the other two.</p>
<p>Riga also has, in my biased opinion, the best food scene of the three. Not because Latvian cuisine is fancier than its neighbours — it isn't, and Lithuanian food is arguably warmer and more generous — but because the modern restaurant scene here has quietly become very good. The Michelin guide added Latvian restaurants in 2024 and there are places in Riga now serving proper tasting menus at half the price of Tallinn or Stockholm.</p>
<p>And Riga has the best Christmas market of the three. It was voted third in Europe for 2025–2026 and the hotel prices in December are genuinely cheap. I wrote a whole piece on Riga in winter if that's what you're here for.</p>
<p>Finally, Riga is the middle Baltic capital geographically, which makes it the natural base if you want to do two or all three in one trip.</p>
<p><strong>What Riga does worst.</strong> It doesn't have Tallinn's fairytale medieval postcard. The old town is beautiful but it's more of a layered European old town — a bit of medieval, a bit of Hanseatic, a lot of Art Nouveau — than a single-era set piece. If what you want is a pure medieval Disney moment, Riga is not it. And the UK stag-weekend scene is real in Riga, more than in Tallinn or Vilnius, which means one or two of the Old Town bars are actively unpleasant on Saturday nights.</p>
<h3>What Vilnius does best</h3>
<p>Vilnius has the largest old town of any city in Northern Europe — 359 hectares, also UNESCO-listed — and it's the most atmospheric of the three. The baroque and the Catholic history give the city a warmth the Protestant Baltics don't quite match. Over 65 churches in the old town, most of them baroque, most of them in daily use. The Gate of Dawn with its icon is the kind of thing you stumble onto by accident and then can't leave.</p>
<p>Vilnius is the most affordable of the three Baltic capitals. A beer in an old town bar is often under €4. A meal is €12–25 for something genuinely good. Hotels are €60–100 for a proper 4-star in September. If your trip budget is tight, Vilnius gives you more for your money.</p>
<p>And Vilnius has the warmest atmosphere of the three. I mean this literally in summer (slightly further south, slightly warmer), but also socially. Lithuanians are more outgoing than Latvians and Estonians — we're all quiet northerners by British or Spanish standards, but Lithuania is the least quiet of the three. The Užupis neighbourhood, the self-declared "republic" of artists across the Vilnia river, has a playful streak the other two capitals genuinely don't have.</p>
<p>Vilnius also has the best day trip of any Baltic capital — <strong>Trakai Island Castle</strong>, a red-brick 14th-century fortress on an island in a lake 30 km from the city, which is the single most photographed thing in Lithuania and lives up to its pictures. If I ran tours out of Vilnius, I'd run this one every day.</p>
<p><strong>What Vilnius does worst.</strong> It has the weakest international flight access of the three. It's a Ryanair budget hub but airBaltic prioritises Riga, and there are no direct long-haul flights. If you're coming from North America or Asia you'll probably land in Warsaw, Frankfurt, or Helsinki and transfer. The food scene, while warm and generous, is less developed in the Michelin-guide sense than Riga's or Tallinn's. And Vilnius is further from the Baltic Sea than the other two — it's an inland capital, not a coastal one, which matters if a beach day is part of your plan.</p>
<h3>The bigger picture: how the three fit together</h3>
<p>People lump us together and we all find it a little funny. Very roughly:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Estonia</strong> is the northernmost, the smallest, the richest, the most Nordic-feeling, and the one that identifies most with Finland. Estonian is a completely different language family from Latvian and Lithuanian — it's Finno-Ugric, related to Finnish and Hungarian, not Indo-European at all.</li>
<li><strong>Latvia</strong> is the middle one — middle size, middle temperament, middle latitude, and, historically, the most ethnically mixed because of its long position between Russia and the German Hanseatic world. Latvian is Baltic (Indo-European), along with Lithuanian.</li>
<li><strong>Lithuania</strong> is the southernmost, the largest, the most Catholic, and historically the most powerful — the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 14th–16th centuries was one of the biggest states in Europe, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Lithuanian is often cited by linguists as the most archaic living Indo-European language, closer to Sanskrit than any other European tongue.</li>
</ul>
<p>The three countries were incorporated into the Russian Empire at different times, were briefly independent between the wars, were annexed by the Soviet Union during WWII, and regained independence between 1990 and 1991 via the Singing Revolution — the name given to the mass non-violent independence movements across all three countries. The 2-million-person Baltic Way human chain in August 1989 ran from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius, about 600 kilometres, and is still one of the most moving things in recent European history. If you're visiting more than one Baltic capital, learn about the Baltic Way before you come. It's the single most important context for why the three cities feel both separate and deeply linked.</p>
<h3>If you have a week: the multi-city play</h3>
<p>Here's what I'd do with 7 to 10 days if you want all three capitals.</p>
<p><strong>The 7-day version (tight but doable):</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Day 1–3: Tallinn — arrive, see the Old Town, day trip to Lahemaa, evening in Telliskivi.</li>
<li>Day 4: Bus to Riga (Lux Express or Ecolines, 4.5 hours, €20). Afternoon and evening in Riga's Art Nouveau quarter.</li>
<li>Day 5: Day trip from Riga — my pick would be Rundāle Palace if you want big history, Sigulda if you want forests, or Ķemeri bog at sunrise if it's May to August. Evening back in Riga.</li>
<li>Day 6: Bus to Vilnius (4 hours, €18). Afternoon in Old Town, evening in Užupis.</li>
<li>Day 7: Day trip to Trakai, fly out from Vilnius.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>The 10-day version (the one I'd actually recommend):</strong></p>
<p>Same structure but with breathing room: 3 nights in Tallinn, 4 nights in Riga with two day trips, 3 nights in Vilnius with a day trip to Trakai. The extra nights in Riga matter because Riga is where you need the most time to actually understand what the city is doing — the Art Nouveau district, the Central Market, the food scene, and at least one of the proper day trips.</p>
<p><strong>The order.</strong> I'd go Tallinn → Riga → Vilnius, north to south. This is because you typically fly into Tallinn from a Nordic country (natural for UK/Finland/Sweden travellers) and fly out of Vilnius (Ryanair hub, easy onward to Warsaw, Barcelona, Rome, etc.). But the reverse works fine too if your flight logistics are cheaper that way. The bus routes run both directions.</p>
<h3>The practical bits</h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Flights from the UK:</strong> Ryanair and Wizz Air cover all three capitals from various UK airports. Riga has the most airBaltic connections. Tallinn has the most Nordic connections. Vilnius has the most Polish and central European connections.</li>
<li><strong>Flights from the US:</strong> No direct flights to any of the three. Connect through London, Frankfurt, Warsaw, Helsinki, or Amsterdam. Helsinki-Tallinn is the single shortest international hop if you want the fastest path into the Baltics (50 minutes by air, 2 hours by ferry).</li>
<li><strong>Moving between capitals:</strong> Lux Express and Ecolines are the two comfortable coach operators. Tallinn-Riga is 4.5 hours and €15–25 one-way. Riga-Vilnius is 4 hours and €15–22. Both coaches have WiFi, plug sockets, and coffee machines. There is currently no through train network (the long-promised Rail Baltica project is under construction and will open in 2030-ish). For speed, there are direct flights between all three capitals but they cost €80–150 and the airport transfers eat most of the time saving.</li>
<li><strong>Currency:</strong> All three use the euro.</li>
<li><strong>Language:</strong> All three capitals have near-universal English under 40. Russian is a common second language in Riga and Tallinn among older people, less so in Vilnius.</li>
<li><strong>Safety:</strong> All three are EU and NATO members, all three at US State Department Level 1. Riga has a lively stag-weekend scene that can make a couple of Old Town streets unpleasant on Saturday nights; avoid Skyline Bar and the area around Kaļķu iela past midnight and you'll be fine.</li>
<li><strong>When to visit:</strong> Late May through early September for weather, December for Christmas markets. Shoulder months (April, October) are the best-value trips if you don't mind a coat.</li>
</ul>
<h3>A final thing</h3>
<p>The three Baltic capitals are different enough that picking between them is a real decision, and similar enough that most people who visit one will want to come back for the others. That's the thing the guidebooks don't quite capture — they rank the three like they're competing, when actually they're a set.</p>
<p>If you're reading this and you've already decided on Riga, the day trips post is next. If you're deciding on Tallinn or Vilnius instead, I'm genuinely happy for you — they're both excellent, and I'd rather you pick the right one and love it than pick mine and feel let down. If you want to do two or three, write to me at info@barefootbaltic.com and I'll tell you what I'd do in your specific case. I'm the wrong guide for the other two cities but I can point you at the right people in each.</p>

        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-is-cheapest">
            Which Baltic capital is cheapest?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-is-cheapest" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Vilnius is the cheapest of the three, Riga is the middle, Tallinn is the most expensive — and the gap has widened since the Finns replaced the Russians as Tallinn&#x27;s dominant visitor group. Old Town restaurants on Tallinn&#x27;s Raekoja plats charge Helsinki prices. A beer in a Vilnius old town bar is often under €4, a proper meal is €12–25, and a central 4-star hotel in September runs €60–100. The equivalent in Tallinn is €5–8 for a beer, €20–35 for a meal, and €90–150 for the hotel. Riga sits in between, with Christmas market weekends at a fraction of Western European prices.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-has-the-best-food-s">
            Which Baltic capital has the best food scene?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-has-the-best-food-s" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Riga, in my biased opinion. Not because Latvian cuisine is fancier than its neighbours — Lithuanian food is arguably warmer and more generous — but because the modern restaurant scene here has quietly become very good. The Michelin guide added Latvian restaurants in 2024, and there are places in Riga now serving proper tasting menus at half the price of Tallinn or Stockholm. Tallinn&#x27;s food scene is solid and Finnish-inflected, with a Michelin cluster in the Telliskivi innovation quarter, but Helsinki prices follow. Vilnius food is warm, Polish-inflected, and the best value of the three, though less developed in the Michelin sense.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-has-the-best-christ">
            Which Baltic capital has the best Christmas market?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-has-the-best-christ" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Riga. It was voted third in Europe for 2025–2026 by European Best Destinations (72,804 votes from 179 countries) and third best-value by the UK Post Office. The main market runs on Dome Square in the Old Town from late November to early January. A central 4-star hotel in Riga for a December weekend is typically €60–120 a night — roughly half of Tallinn or Vienna. Vilnius has the warmest atmosphere of the three and lights up beautifully, but the market scale is smaller. Tallinn&#x27;s market is charming but suffers from the same Helsinki-adjacent pricing as the rest of the city in season.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-what-is-the-best-order-to-visit-riga-tal">
            What is the best order to visit Riga, Tallinn and Vilnius?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-what-is-the-best-order-to-visit-riga-tal" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>I&#x27;d go Tallinn → Riga → Vilnius, north to south, with 3 nights in Tallinn, 3–4 nights in Riga, 3 nights in Vilnius. You typically fly into Tallinn from a Nordic country and fly out of Vilnius via Ryanair&#x27;s hub, which makes the north-to-south direction cheaper for most travellers. The reverse works fine if your flights are cheaper that way — Lux Express and Ecolines buses run in both directions, 4–4.5 hours between each pair, around €15–25 one-way. The extra night in Riga matters because Riga is where you need the most time to understand what the city is actually doing, especially the Art Nouveau district and at least one of the proper day trips.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-can-i-visit-all-three-baltic-capitals-in">
            Can I visit all three Baltic capitals in one week?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-can-i-visit-all-three-baltic-capitals-in" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, in 7 days, tightly. Day 1–3 in Tallinn for the Old Town and a Lahemaa day trip. Day 4 bus to Riga, afternoon in the Art Nouveau quarter. Day 5 a day trip from Riga — Rundāle Palace if you want big history, Sigulda for the forests, Ķemeri bog at sunrise if it&#x27;s May to August. Day 6 bus to Vilnius. Day 7 Trakai Island Castle and fly out. The 10-day version is the one I&#x27;d actually recommend: same structure with breathing room, 3 nights Tallinn, 4 nights Riga with two day trips, 3 nights Vilnius. Under 6 days, pick two capitals, not three — the bus time eats into the sightseeing.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-what-is-the-difference-between-latvia-li">
            What is the difference between Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-what-is-the-difference-between-latvia-li" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Very roughly: Estonia is the smallest, the richest, the most Nordic-feeling, and the one that identifies most with Finland. Estonian is Finno-Ugric — a different language family entirely, related to Finnish and Hungarian. Latvia is the middle country in size, temperament, and latitude, historically the most ethnically mixed because of its long position between Russia and the German Hanseatic world. Latvian is Baltic, like Lithuanian. Lithuania is the largest, the most Catholic, and historically the most powerful — the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was one of the biggest states in Europe in the 14th–16th centuries. The three countries were annexed by the Soviet Union during WWII and regained independence together in 1990–1991 via the Singing Revolution.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-has-the-biggest-old">
            Which Baltic capital has the biggest old town?
            <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-rigavstall-which-baltic-capital-has-the-biggest-old" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Riga, at 438 hectares, has the biggest UNESCO-listed old town of the three. Vilnius is second at 359 hectares, which is the largest in Northern Europe. Tallinn is the smallest at 113 hectares. Size isn&#x27;t the whole story — Tallinn has the most perfectly preserved medieval character, intact town walls, and the oldest functioning Town Hall in Northern Europe, all packed into a compact area you can walk in one long afternoon. Riga is bigger and more layered — medieval, Hanseatic, and Art Nouveau mixed together. Vilnius is the most atmospheric, with over 65 baroque churches in the old town, most of them still in daily use.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
</div>
</section>

<h2>Short answer, read this first</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Yes, you can do Sigulda and Cēsis in one day from Riga</strong> — but only if you accept trade-offs. You'll see the main castles and the Gauja Valley headline viewpoints, and you'll miss the slower version of either place.</li>
<li><strong>It's a ten-hour day, door to door.</strong> Leave Riga around 8:30 AM, back by early evening. Cēsis is 90 minutes northeast; Sigulda is 50 minutes from Riga; the two towns are about 35 minutes apart.</li>
<li><strong>Do Cēsis first, Sigulda second.</strong> The long drive while you're fresh, the Gauja Valley viewpoints in the late-afternoon light. Reversing it wastes the good hour of the day.</li>
<li><strong>Three castles is achievable.</strong> Cēsis medieval castle (13th-century Livonian Order, explored by candlelight with a lantern), Sigulda Castle ruins and its New Castle museum, and Turaida Castle on the hillside above the Gauja. All three fit in ten hours, tight but not rushed.</li>
<li><strong>Train is viable for two castles but not three.</strong> DIY by train costs about €10–12 return per person and works if you skip Turaida. Adding Turaida is the point at which a guided day or a hire car starts earning its money.</li>
<li><strong>This combo is wrong for you</strong> if you want to do the adventure side of Sigulda (bobsleigh, bungee, cable car, serious hiking). Pick one town and stay.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Why this question is harder than it looks</h2>
<p>I get asked this question more than almost any other, and the reason is that Sigulda and Cēsis are both sold in online guides as "easy day trips from Riga." Which is true, separately. What nobody tells you is that once you decide to do them both on the same day, you have a geography problem, a timing problem, and a decision problem about whether Turaida Castle is part of the deal.</p>
<p>Here's the honest picture. Cēsis is 90 kilometres northeast of Riga, about 90 minutes by car on the A2 motorway. Sigulda is 50 kilometres from Riga on the same road, about 50 minutes. The two towns are roughly 35 kilometres apart, 35–40 minutes of driving between them. So you aren't doubling back on yourself — you're running along one corridor, stopping twice. Good news for the day plan.</p>
<p>The bad news is that each town is worth a full day on its own, and squeezing both into ten hours means deciding what not to do. Below is what I'd cut, what I'd keep, and why.</p>
<h2>What each place actually gives you</h2>
<h3>Cēsis</h3>
<p>Cēsis is one of Latvia's oldest towns. The medieval castle was built by the Livonian Order in the 13th century and it's the thing people come for. The unusual part is how you visit it: instead of walking the towers under museum floodlights, the curators hand you a candle lantern at the gate and you explore the stairwells and upper chambers by candlelight. It's the closest you'll get to actually feeling what a northern European castle was like in 1300, and as far as I know there's nowhere else in the Baltics that runs it this way.</p>

<figure class="rundale-gallery rundale-gallery--what-each-place-gives-you" data-cesis-gallery="injected" aria-label="What each place gives you, in pictures">
  <a class="rundale-gallery__hero" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/turaida-castle-aerial-red-brick-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="what-each-place-gives-you" data-caption="Sigulda half: aerial of red-brick Turaida Castle" aria-label="What each place gives you, in pictures">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/turaida-castle-aerial-red-brick-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/turaida-castle-aerial-red-brick-latvia.jpg" alt="Sigulda half: aerial of red-brick Turaida Castle" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1920" height="1280">
    </picture>
    <figcaption>Sigulda half: aerial of red-brick Turaida Castle</figcaption>
  </a>
  <div class="rundale-gallery__thumbs">
    <a href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/turaida-castle-museum-reserve-05-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="what-each-place-gives-you" data-caption="Sigulda half: inside the Turaida Museum Reserve" aria-label="Sigulda half: inside the Turaida Museum Reserve">
      <picture>
        <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/turaida-castle-museum-reserve-05-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
        <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/exc-sigulda/turaida-castle-museum-reserve-05-latvia.jpg" alt="Sigulda half: inside the Turaida Museum Reserve" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="600" height="600">
      </picture>
    </a>

<p>Beyond the castle, Cēsis Old Town is small, walkable, and has a handful of good cafés. If you've come for a half-day visit you want roughly 2 hours: the castle visit (around 75 minutes with the candlelit tour), a walk through the old town (30 minutes), and a quick lunch.</p>
<h3>The Gauja Valley (Sigulda + Turaida)</h3>
<p>Sigulda is the gateway to Gauja National Park, which is Latvia's largest and oldest. "Switzerland of Latvia" is the nickname it gets in brochures — which sounds like a stretch until you actually see the valley, which is properly deep, properly wooded, and in autumn turns spectacular shades of amber and rust.</p>
<p>The sights fall into two groups. On the Sigulda town side: the ruins of Sigulda Castle (13th-century Livonian Order, partially restored), the 19th-century Sigulda New Castle with a small but genuinely good museum about the region, and the cable car across the valley. On the Turaida side, reached by a short drive or a longer walk across the valley: Turaida Castle, a restored red-brick medieval fortress with a tower you can climb for one of the best views in Latvia, surrounded by a sculpture garden, a historic wooden church, and a reconstructed Liv farmstead.</p>
<p>For a half-day visit you want roughly 3 hours in the Gauja Valley: a brief stop at Sigulda Castle ruins (30 minutes), Turaida (90 minutes, including the tower climb), and a viewpoint on the valley itself (15 minutes). The cable car takes another 30 minutes if you add it, which on a combo day you probably won't.</p>
<h2>The realistic timeline, hour by hour</h2>
<p>Here's what the day looks like if you do it properly. The times below assume you leave central Riga at 8:30 AM and drive yourself or take a guided minibus. If you go by train, see the section below — it's slower.</p>

<p>Ten hours door to door, three castles, one valley, one candlelit medieval tour, one proper Latvian lunch, and the good afternoon light where it matters. That's what a realistic combo day looks like.</p>
<h2>Where most people get this wrong</h2>
<p>The two most common mistakes I see from people who try to plan this day themselves:</p>
<p><strong>Mistake one: doing Sigulda first.</strong> Sigulda is closer to Riga, so it feels natural to start there, get it out of the way, and push on to Cēsis. It's a trap. You arrive at Sigulda at 9:30 in the morning, which is the wrong hour — the Gauja Valley viewpoints are not at their best before the sun is high, and the castle visitor flow is optimised for the lunchtime rush. Then you're driving to Cēsis in the middle of the day, which wastes the good afternoon light on the motorway instead of on Turaida tower. Do Cēsis first.</p>
<p><strong>Mistake two: trying to add the cable car or the bobsleigh track.</strong> Both are fun. Neither belongs in a combo day. The cable car takes 30 minutes when you factor in the wait and the ride both ways. The bobsleigh track is a 90-minute commitment minimum. If you add either, something else has to go — usually Turaida, which is a mistake because Turaida is the single best sight on the day. If you want the adrenaline side of Sigulda, pick a Sigulda-only day and stay the whole afternoon.</p>
<p><strong>Mistake three: not booking the castle tour ahead.</strong> The candlelit Cēsis castle tour is guided and runs on a schedule. In peak season (June through August) it can sell out by mid-morning. Book the day before, or first thing when you arrive.</p>
<h2>Two sensible ways to do this day</h2>
<p>Assuming you've decided the combo makes sense, there are two reasonable ways to actually execute it.</p>
<h3>Option A: The DIY train day (cheaper, two castles, no Turaida)</h3>
<p>Latvia's rail network handles the Cēsis–Sigulda–Riga corridor properly, which is unusual for a Baltic country. Trains from Riga Central Station to Cēsis take about 1 hour 30 minutes and run roughly every 2 hours. Cēsis to Sigulda by train is another 40 minutes. The tickets are cheap (around €5–6 each way) and you can book them day-of at the station or through the Pasažieru Vilciens website.</p>
<p>A realistic train-day plan:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>08:06</strong> — Riga Central Station to Cēsis (direct, 1h 25m).</li>
<li><strong>09:30–13:00</strong> — Cēsis old town, castle, lunch.</li>
<li><strong>13:20</strong> — Cēsis to Sigulda by train (40 minutes).</li>
<li><strong>14:00–17:00</strong> — Sigulda town and castle ruins. <strong>No Turaida</strong> — it's 6 km from Sigulda town and requires a local bus or a €15 taxi each way, which the timing doesn't comfortably allow.</li>
<li><strong>17:19</strong> — Sigulda to Riga (1h 05m).</li>
</ul>
<p>Total cost: around €10–12 per person in train tickets, plus whatever you spend on lunch and castle entrance fees (around €15 combined). <strong>The trade-off: you lose Turaida</strong>, which is arguably the best sight on the day. If you can live without it, this is the most budget-efficient way to do Sigulda and Cēsis in one day from Riga.</p>
<h3>Option B: The guided or self-drive day (all three castles, full value)</h3>
<p>If you want all three castles — Cēsis, Sigulda, Turaida — you need a vehicle. Either hire a car in Riga (around €40–60 per day plus fuel, easy to arrange through Sixt or Europcar at the airport) and drive yourself, or join a guided day that handles all the logistics.</p>
<p>The self-drive version gives you total flexibility — you stop where you want and you set your own pace. The downside is that you're the driver, which means you can't fully relax at Turaida tower with a camera in one hand and a phrase half-formed about why this valley matters in the other. The other thing nobody warns you about is that Latvian road signs in the countryside can be sparse, and the Sigulda-area turnoffs are easy to miss on the first pass.</p>
<p>The guided version (ours is ten hours for €85 per adult, €70 for children) gives you a Latvian guide who actually grew up with these castles in her school history books, all three entrance fees included, an air-conditioned minibus, and the candlelit Cēsis castle tour arranged in advance. You don't drive, you don't navigate, you don't queue, and the day is shaped around the good light rather than the easy logistics. It's more expensive than the DIY train day and costs roughly the same as a hire car once you factor in fuel, parking, and three castle entrance fees.</p>
<p>Which is right for you depends mostly on whether you want to drive and whether Turaida is a dealbreaker. If you want Turaida and you don't want to drive, join a tour. If you're happy to skip Turaida, the train is excellent value. If you want Turaida and you do want to drive, rent a car.</p>
<h2>What about adding Gauja National Park hiking or the cable car?</h2>
<p>Short answer: don't.</p>

<p>Longer answer: the Gauja Valley has properly good hiking — the Līgatne nature trails, the paths between Sigulda and Turaida through the ravines, the longer routes out to Krimulda — and if you're a hiker you'll be frustrated that a combo day gives you none of it. The cable car, the bobsleigh track, the Vienkoču Parks open-air museum, and the Līgatne rehab centre Soviet bunker are all worth doing, and none of them fit in a combo day.</p>
<p>If any of that sounds important, the right move is a Sigulda-only day (or a two-day split where you spend one full day in the Gauja Valley and a separate shorter day in Cēsis). The combo day I've described above is designed to deliver the three headline castles plus the valley views, and that's the most you can honestly fit into ten hours.</p>
<h2>Seasonal notes</h2>
<p>The combo day works year-round, but each season has its character.</p>

<p><strong>Late September to mid-October</strong> is the photographer's window. The Gauja Valley turns spectacular colours, and the late-afternoon light at Turaida tower in autumn is the single reason to do this trip. If you're in Latvia for anything between two days and two weeks and the calendar lets you, aim for this window.</p>
<p><strong>June to August</strong> is the warmest, longest-day version. You can leave Riga at 8:30 and there's still usable daylight at 9 PM. The castles are busier, particularly Cēsis where the candlelit tours need advance booking, but nothing is crowded by Western European standards. July weekends are the busiest.</p>
<p><strong>Spring (April–May)</strong> is quiet, cool, and the forests are full of wildflowers. The valley is still bare of leaves until late April, which makes the viewpoints less photogenic but the castles more stark and atmospheric.</p>
<p><strong>Winter</strong> works for the hardy. The castles are open, the drive is manageable if the roads are clear, and Turaida in snow is beautiful. The risk is that trails ice up and some paths close, and the short daylight window compresses the afternoon. If you're doing this combo in December or January, start earlier (8:00 AM departure) and plan to be out of Turaida before 4 PM when the light goes.</p>
<h2>Who this combo day isn't for</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>People who want the adventure side of Sigulda.</strong> Bungee, bobsleigh, cable car, zipline, serious hiking — none of it fits. Pick a Sigulda-only day instead.</li>
<li><strong>People with limited mobility.</strong> Cēsis castle has stairs and uneven stone floors. Turaida involves a steep path to the castle and a tower climb with narrow spiral stairs. Sigulda Castle ruins have loose ground. If any of that is a problem, a combo day will be a hard day.</li>
<li><strong>People who want to slow down and absorb a place.</strong> This day is about moving efficiently between sights. If you're the kind of traveller who wants to sit in a café for an hour watching a small Latvian town go about its morning, do one town and stay. Cēsis is my recommendation if you have to pick.</li>
<li><strong>People who are tired already.</strong> Ten hours is ten hours. If you've just flown in or you're on day 8 of a Baltic circuit, consider a shorter day out of Riga instead.</li>
</ul>
<h2>A final thing</h2>
<p>The reason I'm writing this post is that half the people who ask me about Sigulda and Cēsis end up frustrated by guides that either tell them both towns are "easy from Riga" (technically true, unhelpfully incomplete) or that dodge the question entirely. The honest answer is: yes, both in one day, but only if you plan it with the geography and the light in mind, and only if you're happy to trade the slow version of either place for the highlight version of both.</p>
<p>If you want all three castles done in one day with the candlelit Cēsis tour pre-booked, a Latvian guide who grew up with these places, and no navigating on your end, our <a href="/excursions/sigulda-cesis-gauja-valley.html">Sigulda, Cēsis &amp; the Gauja Valley excursion</a> runs year-round for €85 per adult and €70 for children. You pay nothing today to book: a 20% deposit goes out 48 hours before departure and the rest settles at the van on the morning. If you'd rather do it yourself, everything in this post is what I'd tell my own friends if they asked me how to plan it.</p>
<p>Either way, come back with pictures from Turaida tower in the late afternoon. That's the one shot you shouldn't leave Latvia without.</p>

<div class="faq-list" role="list">
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">

            Can you realistically do Sigulda and Cēsis in one day from Riga?

          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-siguldaand-can-you-realistically-do-sigulda-and-c-s" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>Yes, but only if you accept trade-offs. Cēsis is 90 minutes from Riga and Sigulda is 50 minutes; the two are about 35 minutes apart. A realistic day gives you roughly 2 hours in Cēsis (old town plus the Livonian Order castle), a quick lunch, and 3 hours in the Gauja Valley covering Sigulda Castle, Turaida Castle, and a viewpoint. You&#x27;ll leave Riga around 8:30 AM and get back around 6:30 PM. It works. What you&#x27;ll sacrifice is the slower version of either place — no cable car ride, no bobsleigh track, no hiking in Gauja National Park beyond the main sights.</p>
          </div>

          </button>
          <div class="faq-a" id="faq-siguldaand-how-far-is-c-sis-from-sigulda" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
            <p>About 35 kilometres, or 35–40 minutes by car on the A2 motorway. Both towns sit on the same corridor heading northeast out of Riga, which is why combining them in one day is geographically sensible — you&#x27;re not doubling back, you&#x27;re continuing along the same route.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-siguldaand-is-it-better-to-visit-sigulda-or-c-sis-f">

Cēsis is further from Riga (about 90 minutes versus 50), so doing the long drive first while you&#x27;re fresh and tackling the closer one on the way back makes the day feel less tiring. It also means you visit the candlelit Cēsis castle tour in daylight and arrive at the Gauja Valley viewpoints in the warm late-afternoon light, which is when they&#x27;re at their best.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
          <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-siguldaand-can-you-do-sigulda-and-c-sis-by-train-fr">

Trains from Cēsis to Sigulda take about 40 minutes. The downside: you lose 15–20 minutes at each end walking from the stations to the sights, you can&#x27;t add Turaida Castle easily (it&#x27;s 6 km from Sigulda town and requires a bus or taxi), and you&#x27;re locked into the train schedule. Realistic plan: 08:06 Riga–Cēsis, 4 hours in Cēsis, 13:00-ish Cēsis–Sigulda, 2 hours in Sigulda town only (no Turaida), 17:00 Sigulda–Riga. Total cost around €10–12 return per person in train tickets.</p>

            <p>The three castles usually referred to are Cēsis Castle (13th-century Livonian Order, famously explored by candlelight with a lantern), Sigulda Medieval Castle (ruins from the same period, next to the 19th-century New Castle museum), and Turaida Castle (a restored red-brick fortress on a hillside above the Gauja river, with a tower, a sculpture park, and an old wooden church). All three are in Gauja National Park. Doing all three in one day is possible but tight — the Barefoot Baltic Sigulda, Cēsis and Gauja Valley excursion covers all three from Riga in ten hours, leaving at 8:30 AM and returning by 6:30 PM.</p>

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, what St James&rsquo;s is</h2>
<p>St James&rsquo;s Cathedral (in Latvian, <em>Sv. J&#275;kaba katedr&#257;le</em>) is the Roman Catholic cathedral of Riga, on Jēkaba iela in the western half of the Old Town, directly next to the Latvian Parliament building (the Saeima). It is older than its more famous neighbour, <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, by some accounts &mdash; first mentioned in 1225, and built mostly between the 1220s and the 1330s. It is smaller, slimmer, and significantly less visited than the Lutheran Doma bazn&#299;ca, but it is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Riga, and one of the prettier interiors in the Old Town once you go through the door.</p>
<p>It&rsquo;s also the most stylistically restless church in Riga &mdash; it&rsquo;s been Catholic, Lutheran, briefly Catholic again under Polish-Swedish dispute, Orthodox-flavoured under Tsarist administration, and Catholic again since 1923. The interior reflects all of that. The famous red-and-white baroque entrance portal is from the 1660s.</p>
<p>Free to enter, open most days. Five minutes&rsquo; walk from <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a> and the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a>.</p>

<h2 id="history">A short history</h2>
<p>St James&rsquo;s was first mentioned in a 1225 document and was the parish church of the part of medieval Riga that lay outside the original bishop&rsquo;s palisade &mdash; the side of town where the artisans, the merchants, and most of the Latvian population lived (German burghers preferred the cathedral side). It was not founded by the bishop and not run by him; it was built and maintained by the lay community of this neighbourhood. That distinction made it the more popular church, the more politically restive, and eventually the focus of Riga&rsquo;s most charged religious switches.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/st-james-cathedral-spire-with-contrail-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="st-james" data-caption="The slim spire of St James's, with a contrail in the sky, Riga, Latvia.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/st-james-cathedral-spire-with-contrail-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/st-james-cathedral-spire-with-contrail-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The slim spire of St James's Cathedral with a contrail above, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The spire from below. Slim, plain, much less ornamented than St Peter&rsquo;s &mdash; a parish-church silhouette, not a cathedral one.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>When the Reformation arrived in Riga in 1522, St James&rsquo;s went Lutheran with the rest of the city, and stayed Lutheran until the 1582 Polish-Swedish dispute returned it briefly to Catholicism. Through the 17th century, under Swedish administration, it was used variously as a Latvian-language Lutheran church, a Polish-Catholic church, and at one point as a Jesuit centre. The red-and-white baroque entrance portal dates from this restless period (1660s). Under the Russian Empire after 1721 it was again Lutheran, with a Latvian-speaking congregation. In 1923, in independent Latvia, the building was returned to the Catholic Church and made the cathedral of the newly created Archdiocese of Riga; it has been Catholic since.</p>
<p>This switching is part of why the building reads visually as a layered hybrid: medieval Gothic bones, baroque furniture and portal, 19th-century glass, and 20th-century Catholic restoration sitting on top of each other.</p>

<h2 id="exterior">What you&rsquo;re looking at from Jēkaba iela</h2>
<p>The body of the church is brick Gothic, mostly 13th to 14th century. The spire stands around 80 metres &mdash; tall by Old Town standards but shorter than St Peter&rsquo;s, and considerably slimmer. It carries a small golden weather-cock at its top, like the cathedral and St Peter&rsquo;s; collectively the three roosters are one of Riga&rsquo;s skyline signatures.</p>
<p>The most-told story about the St James&rsquo;s rooster is the &lsquo;ringing&rsquo; legend. Older Riga guides will tell you that the cock used to ring or crow out loud whenever an unfaithful wife passed underneath it &mdash; the kind of folkloric warning attached to many medieval church towers across northern Europe. The sound, of course, was the wind catching the rooster&rsquo;s metal vanes; the legend pinned a moral story onto a meteorological one. It hasn&rsquo;t rung audibly in the modern reconstruction. People still tell the story. I tell it on tours.</p>
<p>The most striking detail of the exterior is the <strong>red-and-white baroque entrance portal</strong> on the south side of the church, on Jēkaba iela. White stone framing in alternating bands of red &mdash; almost like a candy-stripe &mdash; with broken pediments and a fan-light over the door. From the 1660s, original work, restored in the 1990s. It&rsquo;s the prettiest entrance door in the Old Town and is the photograph people don&rsquo;t expect to take.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/st-james-cathedral-red-white-baroque-portal-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="st-james" data-caption="The red-and-white baroque entrance portal of St James's Cathedral on Jēkaba iela, Riga, Latvia.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/st-james-cathedral-red-white-baroque-portal-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/st-james-cathedral-red-white-baroque-portal-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The red-and-white baroque entrance portal of St James's Cathedral, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The red-and-white baroque portal, 1660s. The candy-striped frame is unique in the Old Town and is the photograph people walk past without noticing.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="interior">Inside</h2>
<p>The interior is significantly more ornate than its Lutheran counterparts a few minutes away. Catholic worship needs an altar you can look at and pictures of saints, and Lutherans tend to clear those away. The result inside St James&rsquo;s is a tall Gothic nave with red-brick walls, white-vaulted ceilings, stained glass in the side aisles, and a high altar with a painted Madonna and child as its centre. The pulpit is dark baroque wood, modestly carved. The pews are dark and modern. The whole thing reads as an honest working parish church. Modest, unfussy, in regular use.</p>

<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Sv. J&#275;kabs ir maz&#257;k&#257; pils&#275;tas baznīca, kura ir liel&#257;ka par to, ko Jūs pirmoreiz redz&#275;sit.</em></p><cite>&mdash; A Latvian way of putting it: "St James&rsquo;s is the smaller city church that&rsquo;s bigger than what you first see."</cite></div>

<p>If you have ten minutes inside, the things to look at: the high altar; the stained-glass windows in the south aisle (mostly 19th- and early-20th-century replacements after fire damage); a small side chapel dedicated to John Paul II, who visited Riga in September 1993 and held a Mass at this cathedral; a few baroque memorial slabs in the floor near the western end. The acoustics are good &mdash; if you happen to walk in during a recital or a Mass with sung liturgy, stay.</p>

<h2 id="saeima">Next door to Parliament</h2>
<p>St James&rsquo;s shares a wall with the <strong>Saeima</strong>, the Latvian parliament, on Jēkaba iela. The Saeima building is the large yellow-stuccoed structure with the Latvian flags hung from its facade; it was built in 1867 in a romantic neo-Renaissance style as the headquarters of the Vidzeme provincial government, became Latvia&rsquo;s parliament in 1922, was used by the Soviet authorities under occupation, and returned to its parliamentary role at independence in 1990.</p>
<p>A few practical things follow from the adjacency. Security is visibly present on Jēkaba iela (police cars, occasional checkpoints, sometimes restrictions on vehicle access), but pedestrians can walk freely and access to the cathedral is unaffected. The small square in front of the Saeima is also one of the venues for civic gatherings &mdash; protests, vigils, the occasional state ceremony &mdash; so on those days the area gets busier. And there is the photograph: medieval cathedral spire, 19th-century parliament, both on one short cobblestone lane, the Latvian flag flying from one and the rooster on the other.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/saeima-parliament-jekaba-iela-with-st-james-spire-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="st-james" data-caption="The Saeima with St James&rsquo;s spire above &mdash; the small civic geography of independent Latvia, on one cobblestone lane.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/saeima-parliament-jekaba-iela-with-st-james-spire-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-james-cathedral/saeima-parliament-jekaba-iela-with-st-james-spire-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Saeima parliament with the St James's spire above, on Jēkaba iela, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>Saeima and St James&rsquo;s, photographed together. The parliament hangs Latvian flags from its facade most days; the cathedral keeps its small golden rooster.</figcaption>
</figure>

<h2 id="practical">Practical answers</h2>

<h3>Where it is and getting there</h3>
<p>Jēkaba iela 9, in the western half of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. Five minutes&rsquo; walk west of <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, three minutes south of the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a>, four minutes north of the <a href="cat-house-riga-meistaru.html">Cat House</a>. The Old Town is pedestrianised. There is occasional traffic on Jēkaba iela because of the Saeima, but visitors walk in.</p>

<h3>Hours, costs, services</h3>
<p>Open daily, free to enter. Sunday Mass in Latvian; some weekday services in Latgalian (the eastern Latvian dialect, closer to Catholic communities); a Polish-language Mass on some Sundays for the Polish Catholic community in Riga. Candles for sale near the entrance, small donation expected. Photography is allowed in non-service hours, no flash; please don&rsquo;t walk around with cameras during a Mass.</p>

<h3>Combining with the rest of the Old Town</h3>
<p>St James&rsquo;s pairs naturally with <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a> as a Catholic-Lutheran contrast (do them in either order; ten-minute walk between). Add the <a href="three-brothers-oldest-houses-riga.html">Three Brothers</a> and the <a href="riga-castle-rigas-pils.html">Castle</a> for the western half of the Old Town walk; the <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">pillar guide</a> stitches the whole circuit together.</p>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>
<p>St James&rsquo;s is the church I most often have to talk visitors into going inside. People come to Riga for <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, hear the organ, and walk back out toward Town Hall Square. It&rsquo;s a small mistake. The interior here is more decorative than the cathedral&rsquo;s, the baroque portal outside is the prettiest in the Old Town, and the cobbled lane in front puts the cathedral on one side and the working parliament on the other. There is not another street in Riga that does the same thing in the same fifty metres.</p>
<p>Allow twenty minutes. Stop at the portal, walk inside, sit in a pew for two minutes, look at the stained glass and the altar, walk out the way you came. Pair with a coffee on Jēkaba iela afterwards. That&rsquo;s the visit.</p>

<section class="faq-section">
<h2>Frequently asked questions about St James&rsquo;s Cathedral</h2>
<div class="faq-list" role="list">

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-1">
      Is St James&rsquo;s the same as Riga Cathedral?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-1" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>No &mdash; they are two different cathedrals. <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral (Doma bazn&#299;ca)</a> is the Lutheran cathedral, the larger of the two, on Doma laukums. St James&rsquo;s Cathedral (Sv. J&#275;kaba katedr&#257;le) is the Roman Catholic cathedral, smaller and slimmer, on Jēkaba iela, next door to the Saeima parliament. Five minutes&rsquo; walk between them. Both are worth visiting, for different reasons.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-2">
      How old is St James&rsquo;s Cathedral?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-2" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>First mentioned in a document of 1225, with construction running mostly through the 1220s to the 1330s. Most of the visible Gothic body is 13th and 14th century. The spire and roof have been rebuilt several times after fires; the red-and-white baroque entrance portal is from the 1660s; the current Catholic interior fittings are mostly 20th-century.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-3">
      Why is it called a cathedral?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-3" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Because it is the seat of a bishop &mdash; specifically, the Archbishop of Riga of the Roman Catholic Church. It became a cathedral in 1923, when independent Latvia&rsquo;s newly created Catholic Archdiocese of Riga chose this church as its seat. Before that, it was a parish church. The other Riga cathedral, Doma bazn&#299;ca, is the Lutheran archbishopric&rsquo;s seat.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-4">
      Has it always been Catholic?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-4" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>No &mdash; far from it. It was Catholic from its founding to 1522 (the Reformation), then Lutheran, with brief Catholic returns under Polish administration, then back to Lutheran under Swedish and Russian rule, and Catholic again since 1923. The interior reflects all of that &mdash; medieval Gothic bones, 17th-century baroque furniture, 19th-century glass, 20th-century Catholic fittings.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-5">
      What&rsquo;s the rooster legend about?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-5" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Older Riga guides will tell you that the small golden rooster on top of the St James&rsquo;s spire used to crow or ring out whenever an unfaithful wife passed beneath it. It&rsquo;s a folkloric story attached to a working weather-vane; the actual sound came from the wind catching the rooster&rsquo;s metal vanes. The legend doesn&rsquo;t apply to the modern reconstructed rooster, but it&rsquo;s still the version told on tours, because it&rsquo;s a story Riga has been telling itself for a few centuries.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-6">
      Is the cathedral open to visitors?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-6" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes &mdash; the cathedral is open daily for visitors, free to enter. Hours vary slightly with the season; usually 10:00&ndash;18:00 with a lunchtime closure. Sunday morning is reserved for Mass; please don&rsquo;t walk the church with cameras during a service. There is no admission charge; donations for candles or church upkeep are appreciated.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-7">
      Can I climb the tower?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-7" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>No &mdash; the St James&rsquo;s tower is closed to the public. The Old Town tower you can climb is at <a href="st-peters-church-tower-riga.html">St Peter&rsquo;s Church</a>, ten minutes&rsquo; walk south, with a lift in two stages and a viewing platform at 72 metres.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-8">
      What&rsquo;s the building next to it?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-8" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>The Saeima &mdash; the Latvian parliament. Built in 1867 in a neo-Renaissance style as the headquarters of the Vidzeme provincial government under the Russian Empire, became Latvia&rsquo;s parliament in 1922, used by Soviet authorities under occupation, and returned to its parliamentary role at independence in 1990. The Latvian flags hung from its facade most days are a small civic detail of the Riga skyline. Pedestrians can walk freely on Jēkaba iela; access to the cathedral is unaffected by the Saeima&rsquo;s security.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-9">
      Did the Pope visit?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-9" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Yes &mdash; Pope John Paul II visited Riga in September 1993, two years after Latvia&rsquo;s restored independence, and held a Mass at this cathedral. There is a small commemorative chapel inside dedicated to that visit. Pope Francis has not visited Latvia in person; he sent a delegation in 2018 for the centenary of Latvian independence.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="faq-item" role="listitem">
    <button class="faq-q" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="faq-sj-10">
      Is St James&rsquo;s wheelchair-accessible?
      <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" aria-hidden="true"><polyline points="6 9 12 15 18 9"/></svg>
    </button>
    <div class="faq-a" id="faq-sj-10" role="region" aria-hidden="true">
      <p>Partly. The main nave is accessible from the south portal entrance; there is a small step at the door. The side aisles and chapels are reachable. Jēkaba iela outside is cobblestoned and uneven, which is the usual challenge for wheelchairs and pushchairs in the Old Town.</p>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>
</section>

    </a>
  </div>
  <p class="rundale-gallery__caption">The church, the tower, the inside, and the panorama from the top &mdash; click any image for the full-size view.</p>
</figure>

<h2 id="short-answer">Short answer, what St Peter&rsquo;s is</h2>
<p>St Peter&rsquo;s Church (in Latvian, <em>Sv. P&#275;tera bazn&#299;ca</em>) is the great red-brick Gothic church on Skārņu iela in Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. It is the building with the tall green spire you see on every postcard of Riga &mdash; the city&rsquo;s defining silhouette since the 13th century. The tower stands 123 metres tall, and the lift takes you in two stages to a viewing platform at 72 metres with a 360-degree view of the Old Town, the Daugava river, the Art Nouveau quarter, and on a clear day all the way out to J&#363;rmala on the coast.</p>
<p>It is, in my honest opinion, the single best paid sight in Riga. Tickets are around &euro;9, the lift is fast, the panorama is the panorama, and the church itself is the most striking medieval interior in the city. Allow an hour. If you only have one tower-climb, this is the one.</p>
<p>First mentioned in 1209. Tower destroyed twice (lightning 1721, German artillery 1941) and rebuilt in steel in 1973. Open daily; check seasonal hours.</p>

<h2 id="history">A short history, because the rebuilding matters</h2>
<p>St Peter&rsquo;s was first mentioned in 1209 in a written record &mdash; two years before the cathedral was founded &mdash; and was a parish and merchant&rsquo;s church, not the bishop&rsquo;s. That distinction matters: while the cathedral was built and run by the German ecclesiastical authorities, St Peter&rsquo;s was built and run by the Riga merchant class, which made it the more independent of the two churches and, eventually, the more architecturally ambitious.</p>
<p>The Gothic body of the church we see today is mostly 14th and 15th century, with the rebuilding of the eastern choir and the heightening of the tower running into the 16th. By the time the Reformation arrived in Riga in 1522, St Peter&rsquo;s was already the largest non-cathedral church in the eastern Baltic. The Reformation, when it came, started here. Andreas Knopken &mdash; the German Lutheran preacher whose sermons in 1522 swung the city &mdash; was based at St Peter&rsquo;s. The small square at the eastern end of the church is now called Reform&#257;cijas laukums, Reformation Square, in his memory.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-church-reformation-square-plaque-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="st-peters" data-caption="The Reformation Square plaque on the church wall: Riga adopted Lutheranism here in 1522, five years after Luther&rsquo;s theses.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-church-reformation-square-plaque-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-church-reformation-square-plaque-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Reformation Square plaque on the wall of St Peter's Church, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The plaque on the east wall, in Latvian. Riga adopted Lutheranism in 1522, five years after Luther&rsquo;s theses &mdash; one of the first cities in the world to do so. Andreas Knopken preached here.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>The tower has had four different versions. The medieval Gothic tower was lost to a great fire in 1666 and rebuilt taller, in baroque, finished in 1690 and topped with a wooden spire that for a period made it one of the tallest wooden structures in Europe. That spire was struck by lightning and destroyed in 1721. Rebuilt in 1746, it stood for almost two centuries. In June 1941, in the first weeks of the German invasion of the Soviet Union, the tower was hit by German artillery shells fired from across the Daugava. It burned down. The walls of the church burned out with it. The Soviet-era reconstruction, finished in 1973, used a steel framework inside the rebuilt brick to keep the silhouette honest while making the structure stable enough to take a lift. That&rsquo;s the version you climb.</p>
<p>The choice to rebuild in steel instead of wood was controversial at the time and is still debated by Riga architecture nerds. The compromise: the silhouette is faithful, the structure is modern, and the tower will probably stand longer than any of its predecessors did.</p>

<h2 id="tower">Climbing the tower</h2>
<p>The lift goes in two stages, with a small intermediate landing at 57 metres and the main viewing platform at 72 metres. The whole trip up takes about three minutes. The viewing platform is wrapped around the outside of the tower with a chest-high railing, and on a clear day the panorama is a full 360 degrees. There are larger windows you can lean against and smaller telescope-mounted spotting scopes if you want to look at the Latvian National Library or the bridges over the Daugava in detail.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-tower-panorama-daugava-national-library-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="st-peters" data-caption="From the top of St Peter's: the Daugava river, the Vanšu bridge, and the Latvian National Library on the far bank, Riga, Latvia.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-tower-panorama-daugava-national-library-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-tower-panorama-daugava-national-library-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Daugava river and Latvian National Library seen from St Peter's tower, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1600" height="1200">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>From the platform: the Daugava, the Vanšu bridge, and the dark glass mountain of the <a href="castle-of-light-latvian-national-library.html">Latvian National Library</a> on the far bank.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>What you can see, in rough order of compass: north toward the Cathedral and the Castle, with the curve of the Daugava heading out to the Gulf of Riga; east over the Old Town rooftops, then the leafy line of the canal, then the dense block of the Art Nouveau quarter; south toward Town Hall Square and the green-domed Latvian Academy of Sciences (the &lsquo;Stalin Cake&rsquo;) further out; west across the Daugava to the National Library, the Spīķeri district, and the railway bridges. On clear days you can see all the way to the smokestacks of the Riga power station and, if you know where to look, the spire of Doles sala.</p>

<!-- TODO: native Latvian speaker review of pull-quote -->
<div class="pull-quote"><p><em>Šis ir vienīgais Vecrīgas tornis ar liftu.</em></p><cite>&mdash; What I tell visitors: &ldquo;this is the only Old Town tower with a lift.&rdquo;</cite></div>

<p>Practical: tickets are around &euro;9 for adults, less for students and children, sold at the entrance inside the church. The lift queue is rarely longer than ten minutes outside peak July. Best light is in the hour before sunset (golden hour over the rooftops); the worst light is mid-morning when you&rsquo;re shooting into the sun on the eastern side. Take a jacket &mdash; it&rsquo;s windier 72 metres up than at street level.</p>

<h2 id="interior">The interior</h2>
<p>People walk past the interior on the way to the lift, and shouldn&rsquo;t. Inside St Peter&rsquo;s is, to my eye, the most striking medieval church interior in Latvia &mdash; a tall Gothic nave with red-brick walls, vaulted ceilings of star-pattern brickwork, and the post-1973 reconstruction sympathetic to the bones of the medieval building. Most of the interior fittings burned in 1941 and were not replaced; the church now serves as a working Lutheran parish but also as an exhibition space.</p>

<figure class="article-figure">
  <a class="article-figure__link" href="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-church-gothic-vaulted-altar-interior-riga-latvia.jpg" data-lightbox-gallery="st-peters" data-caption="Inside St Peter's: Gothic vaulting, red-brick nave, modest altar &mdash; the post-1941 reconstruction left it austere.">
    <picture>
      <source srcset="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-church-gothic-vaulted-altar-interior-riga-latvia.webp" type="image/webp">
      <img src="https://barefootbaltic.com/images/blog-st-peters-church/st-peters-church-gothic-vaulted-altar-interior-riga-latvia.jpg" alt="The Gothic vaulted nave and altar inside St Peter's Church, Riga, Latvia" loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1200" height="1600">
    </picture>
  </a>
  <figcaption>The interior. The red-brick walls and the vaulted ceilings are the bones of the medieval church; what burned in 1941 was the woodwork.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p>One thing that did survive the 1941 fire and is still in place: a handful of baroque memorial tombs and family chapels along the side aisles, behind iron grilles. Look for them on the southern side. They are the families that mattered in 17th- and 18th-century Riga &mdash; merchants, mayors, the men whose names ended up on streets and chapels. Their carved arms and Latin inscriptions are still legible.</p>
<p>There&rsquo;s usually a small temporary art exhibition running in the side aisles &mdash; ceramics, photography, occasionally textiles. Worth a slow walk through.</p>

<h2 id="outside">Around the church</h2>
<p>Two small things outside that are worth pausing for.</p>
<p><strong>The Bremen Town Musicians.</strong> A small bronze sculpture against the east wall of the church, on Sk&#257;rņu iela. A donkey, a dog, a cat, and a cockerel piled on top of one another, all looking through what they imagine is a window. Donated by Riga&rsquo;s twin city of Bremen in 1990, in a year when both cities were emerging from a difficult forty years &mdash; West Germany reunifying with East, Latvia inching toward independence from the Soviet Union. The sculpture is by Christa Baumgartel after a Brothers Grimm fable. People rub the donkey&rsquo;s nose for luck; you&rsquo;ll see it polished bright.</p>
<p><strong>The Roland statue.</strong> A copy of the medieval Roland statue stands on Town Hall Square three minutes south, in front of the <a href="house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html">House of the Blackheads</a>. The original (early 20th-century, an 18th-century replacement of a medieval one) is now in the museum inside the Blackheads. Rolands were standard town-hall sculptures across the Hanseatic world &mdash; symbols of civic justice, market rights, and the autonomy of the merchant town from the local bishop. Riga&rsquo;s is the only one in the eastern Baltic.</p>

<h2 id="practical">Practical answers</h2>

<h3>Where it is and getting there</h3>
<p>Sk&#257;rņu iela 19, in the southern half of Riga&rsquo;s Old Town. Five minutes&rsquo; walk from <a href="riga-cathedral-doma-baznica.html">Riga Cathedral</a>, two minutes from the <a href="house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html">House of the Blackheads</a>. The Old Town is pedestrianised; you arrive on foot.</p>

<h3>Hours, tickets, photography</h3>
<p>Open daily, roughly Tuesday to Saturday 10:00&ndash;18:00 plus Sunday 12:00&ndash;18:00, with shorter winter hours and longer summer hours. Closed Mondays in the off-season. Adult ticket around &euro;9, including the tower lift. Children, students, and seniors get reduced prices. Photography is free inside the church and from the tower platform; tripods are allowed if the church isn&rsquo;t crowded.</p>

<h3>The lift, the queue, accessibility</h3>
<p>The lift goes to the platform at 72 metres in two stages, takes about three minutes, and runs continuously. Queues are usually short outside peak summer. The platform is wheelchair-accessible (the lift takes wheelchairs all the way up); the platform itself has waist-high railings. The church interior is wheelchair-accessible from the south portal; ask staff at the main entrance.</p>

<h3>Combining with the rest of the Old Town</h3>
<p>St Peter&rsquo;s is the southern bookend of an Old Town walk and pairs naturally with the <a href="house-of-blackheads-melngalvju-nams.html">House of the Blackheads</a> two minutes south, with the cathedral five minutes north, and with the Bremen Town Musicians sculpture against the east wall of the church itself. End the day at the panorama in golden hour; that&rsquo;s the photograph you came for. The full circuit is in the <a href="riga-old-town-guide.html">Old Town pillar guide</a>.</p>

<h2 id="honest">My honest take</h2>
<p>Climb it for the view. The ticket pays for itself on that alone. There&rsquo;s a second reason that surprises people once they&rsquo;re up there: from above, the rest of your visit on the cobbles makes more sense. The Old Town is small enough that you can take it in as a single object from the platform, and the half-day you&rsquo;re going to spend walking around it gets a kind of mental map. The third reason is quieter. You can look down on the cathedral spire. There aren&rsquo;t many spots in central Riga where you can do that.</p>
